issues.title: Public Troubleshooting Flags
issues.author: martinduke
issues.body:
Something that came up in Tokyo was the need for service providers (i.e. middleboxes) to troubleshoot performance issues in the network. Packet Number Echo (#269) could partially address this problem., particularly for RTT measurement. But it is imperfect for measuring other problems.

As someone who has spent quite a bit of time debugging TCP packet traces from service providers, there are two other things that would help greatly in answering the question "why is my QUIC slow", without significantly compromising privacy. To do both would take two bits in the public flags, which may be available depending on how some other issues turn out.

(1) QUIC endpoints MAY set the BLOCKED bit if they include a BLOCKED frame in the packet. If you want to get fancy, you could have a different bit for "stream blocked" and "connection blocked", but flow control issues are a common cause of traffic pauses with no other discernable symptoms.
(2) QUIC endpoints MUST (SHOULD?) set the RETRANS flag in any packet that contains retransmitted data. This would help operators identify that a connection is slowing down because it is responding to loss, and would allow for very reliable loss statistics for the downstream network.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
The blocked bit is an interesting idea.

The retrans bit has a problem, which is that a QUIC connection may not retransmit the same thing or may not retransmit anything at all.  However, if we make it a LOSS_DETECTION bit, and say it mean "this bit means I detected a packet loss", I believe it conveys the exact signal you're hoping to achieve, and typically it would end up being the retansmit bit.

<Warning, bad idea ahead> If we were feeling clever, we could abuse the packet echo bit for the loss detection case by specifying half the packet number space as valid for echo and the other half for delta to lost packet number.  The only reason this would be useful is to allow us to create time-sequence diagrams without decrypting the payload.

The worst part about abusing the packet echo bit is that consuming extra bytes to indicate a packet number means we can fit less data into packets, and may cause a retransmission to be split into two packets.  I suspect this may be enough hassle implementations wouldn't bother implementing it.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body:
LOSS_DETECTION sounds good, though we have to set the bit for each lost packet in a burst loss, or we have the same problem of incomplete data. So in effect, this is the same as the "RETRANS" bit except we have to find a packet to put it on for unretransmittable packets.

The "bad idea" sounds complicated, but I'm open to discussing it.

comments.author: mirjak
comments.body:
Yes, I agree, blocked it interesting. I didn't think about blocked bit yet but I'm also not sure if I understand the use case fully (see below). 

All in all, my first reaction, however, in-line with ian's comment about naming of the retrans/loss bit, is that this exposes the wrong semantics. Rather than 'just' exposing anything we do in the transport, we should consider what's the information the network actually wants/needs.

In case of loss/retrans, this is probably inline of what ConEx is/was trying to do. We called this whole-path-congestion and it was only based on ECN/CE (not loss) because loss was already exposed in TCP when monitoring retransmissions. I've been also thinking about exposing the ECN counters and potentially a loss counter, however, I wasn't sure if the overhead is worth the win. So the signal the network actually needs is, I think, 'I saw congestion and that's the reason why I'm slowing down (congestion control)'; I guess this could be accounted by using one bit for both together loss or ECN/CE (if the packet rate is high enough to signal multiple losses in a timely manner).

Regarding the blocked bit, I think this is related. My understanding of the use case is that you (the network) sees that a flow is slowing down/sending less data than previously or than possible and the network wants to distinguish the case where it's limited by the endpoint (flow control) or there is something wrong in the network. 
However, there are actually (at least?) three cases how a connection can be limited:
1) limited by the application itself: there is simply no more data to send
2) limited by the flow control in the endpoint's transport
3) limited by a bottleneck in the network (and respectively congestion window)

I guess what you'd like to expose it the difference between 3 and 1/2, right? Or would it be also helpful to expose the difference between 1 and 2 e.g. for wireshark like debugging at the endpoint? Then I guess we would need two bits...

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
I think the blocked bit is less useful than I originally thought.  I think connections are in two states of the world:
1) Not blocked
2) Blocked, but you'd have to have access to the encrypted context to understand why.
  - ie: A stream is blocked because of a slow server backend?  

TCP flow control is not truly end-to-end, unlike QUIC.  And so I think it means it needs to be debugged end to end.  Also, the path has no control over flow control in QUIC, so I don't think it provides actionable data for a network operator.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body:
> Also, the path has no control over flow control in QUIC, so I don't think it provides actionable data for a network operator.

I agree that there is no direct action that the operator can take, but it is a very clear signal that there is no action to take. It is useful as a "stop worrying" bit.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body:
> We called this whole-path-congestion and it was only based on ECN/CE (not loss) because loss was already exposed in TCP when monitoring retransmissions

I think there is a case that the ECE/CWR bits should be in the public flags, rather than the ACK frame, and this discussion is (sort of) happening in the ECN issue #68.

> However, there are actually (at least?) three cases how a connection can be limited:
> 
> 1. limited by the application itself: there is simply no more data to send
> 2. limited by the flow control in the endpoint's transport
> 3. limited by a bottleneck in the network (and respectively congestion window)

#1 is hard to detect, even in TCP, and tends not to bring customer complaints. So I think it's really down to 2 or 3, and the BLOCKED bit would handle this.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: The flow control one might run afoul of attacks like [HEIST](https://www.blackhat.com/docs/us-16/materials/us-16-VanGoethem-HEIST-HTTP-Encrypted-Information-Can-Be-Stolen-Through-TCP-Windows-wp.pdf) which benefit from being able to observe flow control.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
Re 2, Flow control issues are to easily monitor end-to-end, and in QUIC, flow control  is not modifiable by middleboxes, so QUIC removes responsibility for flow control issues from the network operators entirely.  As a person who's debugged my share of flow control issues, I'm trying to imagine a case where you or a network operator would have to debug flow control issues with QUIC, and I can't come up with one.  

Re 3, That's congestion control's domain, not flow control(which uses BLOCKED), and definitely feels like it's the sender's responsibility.  In most applications, the sender is congestion control limited a large portion of the time, so I wouldn't expect this to be a useful signal, as most connections would see it.

I'm not excited about putting ECE/CWR bits in the unencrypted portion of the packet, as I can't imagine a use case.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body:
I agree that there is no action a middlebox can take on flow control. As I said above, I think this is a "stop worrying" bit when service providers are trying to diagnose performance issues, which is logistically hard to do at endpoints.

ECE/CWR in the public flags would be sort of like the LOSSDETECT bit, if we wanted to separate those signals. But I don't think it would hurt much to encrypt them, as long as LOSSDETECT is there.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
I understand the "stop worrying" bit, but I'm hoping flow control is rarely the limiting factor for QUIC.  TCP has suffered from a variety of flow control problems, but QUIC doesn't inherit any of those issues.

That's not to say all implementers of QUIC will implement flow control correctly, but it's more likely website A's upload performance will be awful than it will be a widespread problem.  As such, it's incentive compatible for both the client and server to implement flow control well, because otherwise performance will suffer.  

For example, I believe Chrome's flow control window is 8MB, which is vastly larger than the TCP defaults.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: To add to what @ianswett says, Firefox uses a different strategy for h2.  While you might see flow control limits being hit on individual streams (push in particular), that doesn't mean that there is a problem.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body:
Obviously if BLOCKED frames are exceedingly rare, then the it's not worth the real estate in the public header. But then, then (different issue) perhaps BLOCKED doesn't make any sense either. 

But if they're not exceedingly rare...
> As such, it's incentive compatible for both the client and server to implement flow control well, because otherwise performance will suffer.

This is true of TCP, too. HOL blocking problems are much diminished in QUIC, but not quite eliminated in the case of large streams.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: @martinduke, Google also proposed BLOCKED for h2.  You can see for yourself the results of that.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
BLOCKED frames are rare, but tend to be isolated to a small number of services, which either are slow at consuming data or serve clients with much higher than average bandwidth.  As such, they serve as an excellent monitoring and debugging tool if you understand the full context.

If this was available in QUIC, what use cases would you expect it to help with?

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body:
> BLOCKED frames are rare, but tend to be isolated to a small number of services, which either are slow at consuming data or serve clients with much higher than average bandwidth. As such, they serve as an excellent monitoring and debugging tool if you understand the full context.
> 
> If this was available in QUIC, what use cases would you expect it to help with?

Are you asking me to defend BLOCKED frames, or the header bit? In the use case where BLOCKED would be helpful, the bit would be helpful for monitoring performance of provider networks. The BLOCKED _frame_ makes window-limitation more obvious, but if you have the decrypted payload, you can also glean this from WINDOW_UPDATE frames.

I can see three possibilites:
- window-limited connections are a common occurrence in QUIC: in this case, the header bit is essential to have any idea what is a real network performance problem and what comes from client configuration. In some cases, it might lead to a mobile software update that fixes the config.
- window-limited connections are extremely rare: it is not worth it to take a bit in the header. In the extreme limit, there is no need for flow control at all because QUIC endpoints have ample memory resources and reduced HOL blocking.
- window-limited connections are "sort of" rare: in which case we ought to have flow control and BLOCKED, but it's not worth a valuable public header bit. I _think_ this is where you believe we are.

Obviously, I have no real-world QUIC deployment experience, so I can't state with authority where we are on this spectrum, and if current experience is relevant to a future with IoT devices, etc. All I can say is that in TCP the flow control information is very valuable to have, and it's not hard to see how certain applications and implementations in QUIC might have the same problems.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
Yes, I believe we're in the third case, at least today.  I may be able to produce some stats on what percentage of connections see blockage with existing settings, but it's very close to 0 today from server to client.  It's low, but not that close to 0 from client to server, where the flow control windows are much smaller.

But yes, it will depend upon the application, and so I can't forsee every possible use case.

I'm also a bit concerned about privacy leakage, as Martin pointed out, even though I wouldn't anticipate that being an information rich channel.

I'm happy to defend BLOCKED frames.  They've been amazingly useful in debugging and monitoring specific services and detecting implementation bugs.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body:
@martinthomson I have now taken a look at HEIST, and I won't pretend to fully understand it. But I'm having trouble seeing if a BLOCKED bit will generally introduce a larger problem.

To defeat the cwnd attack, I believe QUIC has to insert PADDING frames prior to the full delivery of the last STREAM data, to make the delivery of the resource consistent (in terms of RTTs) regardless of echoed requests. This is all orthogonal to BLOCKED, of course. Even this only works if PADDING counts against cwnd, which I don't believe is established.

If we can resolve this issue, there has to be access to the IFCW to have a problem. This is in the clear, but  I'm not sure it's visible to the javascript the attacker has installed on the browser. But if the attacker can overcome these issues, I can see a problem where a blocked bit, specifically tied to connection flow control, can indicate when the actual payload has exceeded the flow control. If we reach this point, I would probably abandon the idea of having a blocked bit specifically related to connection flow control, and instead make it deliberately ambiguous between stream and connection flow control. That probably makes things ambiguous enough to defeat this attack.

Anyway, I'd have to define exactly what the blocked bit is, to have a proposal that security guys could properly shoot at. The intent of this issue was to gauge general interest in a PR that would specify one or both concepts. The signal I'm getting is mixed, to say the least.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body: See the PR in #418 so that there is a coherent proposal to shoot at.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: Tokyo conclusion: v2.

issues.title: Promising more than the client concurrency limit
issues.author: martinthomson
issues.body:
In HTTP/2, streams states were modified at the point that a PUSH_PROMISE was sent, but actually using that stream could be deferred.  The "reserved" state didn't count toward concurrency limit, those streams would count only when packets were first sent.

If the client had a low concurrency limit, that could mean that use of promised streams had to be deferred until active streams could be closed.  QUIC maintains a similar model, but that model is incompatible with QUIC.  In HTTP/2, any promised streams can be opened without creating any ambiguity about the state of other reserved streams.  HTTP/2 also allowed endpoints to skip stream numbers.

In QUIC the lack of ordering between streams (a feature!) forces us to insist on having a strict monotonic sequence of stream numbers.  If a stream number appears to be skipped, that is only because a packet using it has not yet arrived.  This ensures much simpler accounting for streams and avoids adding latency to stream creation.

This creates a problem for promises.  Servers cannot use streams in any order, only those streams within the window of streams permitted by the client concurrency limit are free to be used.

For example, a client could have an MSPC of 2.  That allows just one server push at a time.  A server that wants to push two resources could advertise one push on streams 4+6 and the other on 8+10.  However, unlike in HTTP/2 the server cannot start the second push first.  Opening stream 8 would imply that streams 4 and 6 are also open, violating the concurrency limit.

It's not clear that this problem needs a solution, but it is a functional regression that we should at least consider and make a conscious decision to accept.

comments.author: krasic
comments.body:
Apologies for chiming in late.  

But it appears that this issue is a result of "simplifying" the state diagram to its present form as of the -02 mapping.    The previous reserved remote state exactly allowed the number of promises to be larger than the concurrency limit.    There would of course be a separate limit on the number of outstanding PUSH_PROMISES, and a corresponding ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM error when exceeded.   

I would propose adding back the "reserved" state as in the -01 revision.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: This has nothing to do with the removal of the reserved state, which had no material effect on the protocol.  As you say, there was no limit on reserved streams.  Though the state doesn't appear, the value is still unlimited.  The problem is that you can't *use* a reserved stream.

comments.author: krasic
comments.body: Ok, but the state diagram in the -02 mapping draft indicates that a stream can be opened if a higher stream id was received.   In effect, this means opening one stream can imply the opening of others.  This was not the case in the prior state diagram.   Also, the text of prior revisions may have not called it out, but having a limit associated with the number of reserved streams independent of the number of open streams is the natural way to allow promises beyond the concurrency limit, but within a (higher) bound.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: The change to have a stream open when a higher-numbered stream is used is a bug fix that was made at the same time as removing reservation.  You have to account for streams that you haven't seen, but are open anyway otherwise you have uneven accounting for concurrent streams.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: Closed by #701.

issues.title: Ignore Version Negotiation if it was already done
issues.author: martinthomson
issues.body:
The text currently says:

> Once a client receives a packet from the server with the VERSION flag unset, it MUST ignore the flag in subsequently received packets.

I don't know how to interpret this.  What should a client do if it receives a packet with the VERSION flag set after completing version negotiation?  Maybe should should mandate ignoring the packet not just the flag.

comments.author: marten-seemann
comments.body:
Ignoring the packet is the correct behavior, and is what current implementations do.
Otherwise it would be easy for an attacker to interfere with a connection, since version negotiation packets are not authenticated.

comments.author: RyanTheOptimist
comments.body: That text is definitely unclear. What it's *trying* to say, is that after the client and server have negotiated a version, the client needs to ignore any version negotiation packets its receives. This is because 0-RTT packets sent with the old version may have elicited version negotiation packets which may end up delivered out of order.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: It probably needs to go further and recommend that the client not change its mind more than once.  That is, if it receives a version negotiation packet that would cause it to select a *third* version, that's reason enough to ignore the packet.

issues.title: Policing packet number size
issues.author: martinthomson
issues.body:
From the document:

> DISCUSS: Should the receiver be required to enforce this rule that the sender MUST NOT exceed the inflight limit? Specifically, should the receiver drop packets that are received outside this window?

As a reminder, we require that the packet number size be determined based on the number of outstanding (undefined, but assumed to be packets that are sent but not yet acknowledged).

A requirement like this would be virtually impossible to enforce.  The receiver would have to know what of its acknowledgments had arrived at the sender in order to know what was outstanding when the sender generated the packet.  That's only possible in a narrow set of cases.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: I would lean towards not enforcing it.  And if one was going to enforce it, there should be a connection close error associated with it, because debugging silent failures would be virtually impossible.

issues.title: Outstanding packets and packet number size
issues.author: martinthomson
issues.body:
The text for packet number size calculation says:

> a QUIC sender MUST NOT have more than 2^(packet_number_size - 2) in flight

What it means to be "in flight" is not defined.  It seems like it might mean unacknowledged, not including packets that were marked as "lost" by the recovery algorithm.  The difference between the current packet number and the highest acknowledged packet number might also work.

The more that I think about this, the more that I'm convinced that this is made up of 90% fudge.  Neither of the above definitions for "in flight" is perfect and the constant (4) is pure fudge.

What we might ideally want to ask before determining how big the packet number encoding needs to be is how far out of order a packet could possibly get during transit - and at what point we consider excessive reordering to be considered loss.  If we assume either definition, the current mandate assumes that we want to recover from delay of 4 times the RTT (with the first definition, add four times the reordering threshold).

That seems excessive.  Given that we should be getting at least an ACK per RTT in these cases, that much delay will likely result in retransmission several times over unless all of the ACK packets are similarly delayed.

While we might make some recommendations, "MUST" doesn't seem correct.  I suspect that we need data on reordering (or packet delays) under real-world conditions before we could make a better recommendation.

I think that we need to make the following changes: 
1. define "in flight" (or use a new definition based on RTT and the reordering threshold)
2. make this a recommendation rather than a requirement
3. update the values in the recommendation based on data
4. maybe advise being conservative: spending an extra byte or two occasionally might be wise if it means avoiding packets being lost

This issue should wait for the outcome of the header discussions, it could become moot.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: Alternative definition that might be even better: the difference between this packet and the lowest packet number that has neither been acknowledged nor declared lost.

comments.author: RyanTheOptimist
comments.body:
"Alternative definition that might be even better: the difference between this packet and the lowest packet number that has neither been acknowledged nor declared lost."

That sounds like a good definition to me. It's simple and clear.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
In this case, using in flight would be wrong if packet numbers were skipped.

However, I think we would prefer "the difference between this packet and the largest acknowledged packet."  We may have smaller packets that are unacknowledged, but the algorithm only relies upon the largest received packet.  I don't think there's a need to talk about packets declared lost in this case, since we're abandoning using in flight in this context.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: Also, this doesn't really become moot even if we adopt a fixed packet number length.  That just means we have a fixed maximum on the gap between the packet currently being sent and the largest acked.

issues.title: Skipping packet numbers
issues.author: martinthomson
issues.body: According to @marten-seemann, they occasionally skip a packet number.  This might mess with congestion control if it is done too often, but it seems like a perfectly reasonable thing to do.  The draft currently forbids this.  Maybe it shouldn't.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
The sender is skipping packet numbers and also doing congestion control, so it shouldn't have any adverse side effects, since it knows which numbers were skipped.

Where is it forbidden in the draft?  In 7.2 it says "A sender MAY intentionally skip packet numbers to introduce entropy into the connection, to avoid opportunistic ack attacks."

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: Nope, you are right, I misread.

issues.title: Avoid using Public Reset where possible
issues.author: martinthomson
issues.body:
The draft currently says:

> In this case, an endpoint SHOULD send a Public Reset packet to indicate the failure. 

(This is in the context of discovering that the MTU is too small.)

Given that it doesn't take much to send an authenticated CONNECTION_CLOSE in a packet that won't risk breaking even the minimum IPv4 MTU, I think that this suggestion too much.  I would change this to "treat this as a connection error of SOME_ERROR_CODE" either defining a new MTU_TOO_SMALL error code, or reusing an existing one.

comments.author: RyanTheOptimist
comments.body: Completely agree. I think Public Reset should be used as sparingly as possible. Perhaps only the case when a server receives a packet for a connection ID it has no state for.

comments.author: mcmanus
comments.body:
sorry about the dup - it seems I still have trouble mining the github issue system effectively.

While we're at it the language in 6.4 that allows an endpoint to send a public_reset at any time to abruptly terminate an active connection should be significantly tightened or removed.. we don't want this to become the mechanism to ending things.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
Agreed, I think it's important to clarify when connection closes should be sent and when public resets are sent.  I think there's a lot of agreement around this, but there's not much text clarifying it yet.

The rules on processing them could be clarified as well.  ie: Should public resets before handshake completion be ignored, because there's no reason to ever send them?

issues.title: Don't haphazardly suggest retrying over TCP
issues.author: martinthomson
issues.body:
> The application SHOULD attempt to use TLS over TCP instead.

(This is in the context of finding that the MTU is too small.)

The text includes a very specific recommendation to use TLS over TCP for one particular case.  This is unwise for two reasons:
1. we don't know if all protocols that build on QUIC will have a TCP over TLS option available to them; DNS over QUIC might be an example of where TLS over TCP is an inadvisable fallback option
2. we should rely on a generic error handling section that includes generic advice about things like falling back to a backup protocol

Marked as editorial, I hope that's not controversial.

comments.author: RyanTheOptimist
comments.body: Good point!

comments.author: hardie
comments.body:
I understand why we don't want to recommend a specific fallback, but there's an implication here we may want to keep.  If you want to use QUIC with a fallback, that fallback should have roughly equivalent security properties or blocking QUIC is a downgrade attack.  So the DNS example might be falling back to DNS over DTLS, but it would *not* be falling back to plaintext UDP.  That may be better expressed in a document about which protocols could theoretically adopt QUIC than here, but I don't want to lose it entirely.

Note that I'm assuming here silent fallback, where the user is never told which protocols are in use under the hood.  I'm sure there are other choices for when the user is looped in, but I don't think those are QUIC's business.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: Good points Ted.  I wonder whether DNS over QUIC would be done opportunistically or not.  That changes the calculations too.  No one currently has any real expectation that DNS is confidential (/me makes a sad face).

comments.author: mirjak
comments.body: I think this is input for the applicability statement. It's partly in section 2.1 of draft-kuehlewind-quic-appman but only talking about fallback to TLS/TCP. We didn't consider the DTLS/UDP case; should add that.

issues.title: ACKing ACK
issues.author: martinthomson
issues.body:
The text says:

> However, since it is possible that an endpoint might only send packets containing ACK frames (or other non-retransmittable frames), the receiving peer MAY send an ACK frame after a reasonable number (currently 20) of such packets have been received.

"currently 20" seems pretty arbitrary.  That smells like something from the Google QUIC implementation.  We should be more concrete about this, if that behaviour even makes sense.

If an endpoint is receiving nothing but ACKs but is sending itself, then acknowledging those ACKs is probably fine.

An endpoint with nothing to say can generate a lot of ACKs over time, but if both endpoints are being quiet other than ACKs, it's probably time to shut up entirely.  Maybe we should say that the peer SHOULD generate an ACK frame only if it has other frame types to send.

Limiting the number of PING frames that a peer will respond to is a separate issue, and may motivate a limit with a number attached to it.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
Your nose is correct.  That being said, acking every 20 acks has worked out relatively well, so it may make sense to change this to "the receiving peer SHOULD send an ACK frame after 20 ack only packets."  

If both endpoints are being quiet, the rule that "a receiver MUST NOT generate an ack in response to every packet containing only ACK frames." causes them to stop sending packets quite quickly.  The recommended acking behavior could be specified more explicitly, either here or in the recovery doc, if you think it's warranted.

What's the motivation for limiting PING frames?

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
So the current text recommends throttling back on ACK when you are sending lots of packets.  The 20 packet thing keeps the rate low, but it is too arbitrary.  I can justify sending an ACK when you have other things to send, I can justify slowing the rate of ACK generation when you have nothing of value to acknowledge, but I can't justify the specific number.  Anything above 1 probably has the desired effect.

If you aren't careful, PING can waste time and bandwidth, especially since it demands access to the fast path.  Limiting the number that you will respond to is a DoS mitigation.

comments.author: hardie
comments.body: Forgive the stupidity on my part, but why do PING frames really need access to the fast path? If a peer sends a PING to detect liveness and reachability, any other packet arriving will serve as a demonstration of that, right?  So the ACK of PING could be serviced right after the PING arrives (if things are quiescent) or after other frames bound to the same peer, and still get the same demonstration at the peer.  Or am I missing something?

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body: Presumably because they can also be used to get a transit time measurement, though any other ACK-able frame would also provide the same effect.  That inclines me toward PING not being higher priority than anything else.  PING is the frame you send when you want to get an ACK, but aren't sending anything ACKable.  If you are, why did you send it?  If you aren't, there's no interference.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
Now that I've thought about it more, I think the best rule is to not ack acks, and if the peer wants an RTT measurement, it can use a PING frame.  Acking acks just feels odd.  So I suggest we remove the text about acking every 20 acks.

In regards to limiting PING frames, there are lots of ways to waste time and bandwidth.  In TCP or QUIC, you can send a bunch of packets with single byte payloads, which the peer would also ack.  I'm not sure what you mean about fast path?  A PING frame would be acked at whatever rate other ACK-able packets are.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: @ianswett, in light of #358 and its suggestion to use PING are we still OK to remove permission to occasionally acknowledge an ACK?

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: Definitely, reviewing your PR now.

issues.title: Does any portion of the QUIC framing require 4 byte alignment?
issues.author: ianswett
issues.body:
@martinthomson Wrote up a public header proposal that implies 4 byte alignment is an important goal of the public header.

Is it necessary, as it does constrain the design space substantially?  And if there are environments it's necessary, is it only a requirement for non-endpoint devices(aka middleboxes), so only applies to the non-protected portion of the packet.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: The answer is no.  That was an emergent property only.

comments.author: janaiyengar
comments.body: I don't think we need this. I'd like to close this issue since I didn't / don't see anyone asking for it.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: I misinterpreted Martin's proposal as asking for it, so closing this.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
For the record, since the person who reported this to me didn't follow up as I requested they do...

At the meeting in Chicago, I was approached by someone (and my apologies to this person for forgetting their name), who said that they do hardware implementations of protocols and not having 4 octet alignment would be a huge hassle for them.  I'm not reopening the issue, but I wanted to record this as a data point in case this comes up again.

issues.title: Does the connection id need to be in a consistent location?
issues.author: ianswett

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: I thought that it was nice to have, but not a deal-breaker.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: Agreed.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body: #361 purports to address this; please re-open or file a new issue if that's incorrect.

issues.title: Ignore version negotiation if the client version is present
issues.author: martinthomson
issues.body: That is, if the client picks X and the server returns a version negotiation packet that lists X, then something is badly wrong.  That version negotiation packet needs to be treated like internet-detritus.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: Note that this isn't necessarily badly wrong; it could be a second version negotiation packet sent by the server in response to a retransmission of the initial client packet.  But we don't need to go into that level of detail.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: Closed in #474.

issues.title: Connection ID on a version negotiation packet
issues.author: martinthomson
issues.body: Given that we have opted to go with #119 universally, it might be reasonable to think that the server could make a proposal for the connection ID on a version negotiation packet.  However, it probably isn't a good idea.  Since version negotiation is stateless, there is less need to have stable routing for this packet.  Echoing the connection ID gives the client better assurance that its initial packet was what generated the response.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: Hmm, not sure if this is a duplicate of #244.

comments.author: igorlord
comments.body:
The first part ("should a version negotiation packet from the server -- a proposal to the client to change its version -- contain a Server-generated Connection ID?") is a new issue.  On one hand, I agree with you that this seems a bit like a kludge.  On the other hand, stable routing may actually be required by some systems.

Imagine a pop with a load balancer and a number of backends behind it.  One may want to roll out a new experimental version of QUIC on a subset of backends. To do that, the system should ensure that the same server that send a version negotiation packet proposing a new QUIC protocol version actually receives packets using the new version (if the client accepts that new version).  Our mechanism to make sure this happens is to encode the backend ID in the Server-proposed Connection ID.

The second part (proving that the sender of the version negotiation packet is on-path) is a dup of #244.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body: #361 purports to address this; please re-open or file a new issue if that's incorrect.

issues.title: GREASE and Version Negotiation Hint
issues.author: MikeBishop
issues.body:
In #278, @martinthomson says that clients MAY choose a GREASE value for their initial packet to force version negotiation.  I would argue that no self-interested client will do so if the connection is latency-sensitive, since you incur an RTT, unless the spec has this at a higher level than MAY and with specific timing.

However, for HTTP, bringing up a connection to a new Alternative is not latency-sensitive (because you still have your connection to the original host).  In the case where you're bringing up a connection to an alternative instead of to the origin, you've likely talked to the alternative before.

We could consider dropping the Alt-Svc version hint entirely, and saying that clients SHOULD open with a reserved version unless it has previously connected to the server and remembers a version list.

comments.author: davidben
comments.body:
HelloRetryRequest in TLS 1.3 has a similar problem. My thought there was clients could [with low probability|experimentally after a connection is established|subject to resource limits|insert idea heres] do a key_share-less probe to servers they talk to. If a key_share-less probe fails to connect for any reason, put the server in some "HelloRetryRequest probation" cache. All connections to hosts on probation will be key_share-less until they can satisfactorily connect with HelloRetryRequest [even if there is a socket open?].

But we haven't gotten to playing with this yet. It might not work. Putting hosts on probation or probing too aggressively can degrade performance, while not being aggressive enough will just look like a flaky failure, which probably won't be effective. I'm hoping there's a middle ground that satisfies both constraints.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
Unfortunately, the current state of TLS 1.3 implementations is that HRR isn't consistently implemented, so it's not something you can do right away.  And you are right that flaky doesn't get us what we want.

I am hoping that the development process for QUIC will force early implementations to use version negotiation a lot.  That was what happened in HTTP/2 and I see no reason why that wouldn't happen again here.  That was not the case with TLS 1.3 and HRR, TLS 1.3 implementations without HRR weren't (and aren't) punished.

comments.author: RyanTheOptimist
comments.body:
I love the idea of being able to GREASE things in QUIC! 

Dropping the version hint is definitely possible, but it has a downside. There will be old clients out there which speaks versions of QUIC that a server no longer supports. As a result, it is desirable for the server to be able to advertise QUIC, but in such a way that it doesn't lure old client to waste bandwidth trying to speak QUIC with an old version that the server will never support.

I'm also not sure that adding an additional RTT to the first QUIC connection from Alt-Svc is not really latency sensitive. We'd noticed in our QUIC deployment that the more requests go over the TCP connection before switching the QUIC, the less effective QUIC is. (Among other things QUIC and TCP end up competing for bandwidth).

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: Fair points.  I would say that for a background tab (or an ad, or anything else non-critical), I think that I'd be willing to suck up some latency anyway.  And while it might be suboptimal, the occasional use of greasing won't destroy performance in the same way that it might during a reconnect where QUIC is the only thing that is tried.

comments.author: RyanTheOptimist
comments.body: Having the client *occasionally* sending a GREASED connection attempt seems quite reasonable. One caveat, of course, is that if we're talking about QUIC in the HTTP context, it's quite likely that the client will have built in TCP fallback. If a server does not properly handle GREASED connections, is there an obvious feedback mechanism?

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: No more than what we get when the server advertises a QUIC that is broken in other ways.  That's what Alt-Svc is like.

comments.author: RyanTheOptimist
comments.body: Hm. That's too bad :( If there's no feedback channel (because of Alt-Svc's graceful fallback) will the incentives line up for GREASE to actually help keep the ecosystem working? As I understand it, with TLS, GREASE errors end up user visible, which makes it obvious to server administrators. Maybe we should make GREASE in QUIC actually fatal?

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
The problem here is that any failure in an alternative is buried by design.  You have to expect the alternative to fail.  We could promote certain types of failures so that they tear down all communication to the origin, but that isn't reliable.

If the way that version negotiation failures manifest is a black hole - an unfortunately common failure mode we deal with - how do we tell the difference between that and a server that is off the network?

comments.author: RyanTheOptimist
comments.body:
Yeah, I totally hear you. I'm just saying that (as I understand it) the reason that GREASE works for TLS is that when an endpoint doesn't do the right thing, it's a fatal error which is visible to the user.

If Alt-Svc (by design) hides failures from the user will GREASE work for QUIC?

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
It depends on how visible QUIC usage is to the server.  If they never see requests over QUIC, or the rate is low by some significant proportion, then there is a *chance* that it could work.   But you are right that it's probably not great.

There is an alternative, but it's disruptive.  Flip the version negotiation on its head.  Have the client include a list of versions in its initial packet and have the server pick the version (and reject if necessary).  No risk there of ever having a wasted RTT.  (There are other latency improvements that can be salvaged from such a design, but they are harder to acquire.)

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body: I get the impression that we're content with publishing actual versions to clients.  Implementations can decide whether to offer grease negotiation values themselves.

issues.title: Remove the quic parameter from Alt-Svc
issues.author: martinthomson
issues.body:
Ostensibly, the `quic` parameter is a performance optimization for Alt-Svc.  A client can learn what QUIC version is most likely to succeed and use that version.  That increases the chances that version negotiation succeeds and thereby reduces the chance that the QUIC connection setup costs an extra round trip.

However, alternative services is precisely the point where performance is not critical.  The client already has a perfectly functional HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 connection to the server.  This is a point where they could afford an additional round trip on connection setup.

@MikeBishop suggested that if we are serious about greasing version negotiation, perhaps we could remove the `quic` parameter from the Alt-Svc header field and force clients to always pick a greased version number for their initial packet.

Advantages: grease more often and version negotiation actually gets a real workout, disadvantages: an extra round trip every time you use Alt-Svc.

This came up in #278.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: OK, duplicate of #296.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body: Race!

issues.title: Rename transport parameters
issues.author: martinthomson
issues.body:
The cryptic 4 lettter names for these are a relic of the encoding in Google QUIC.  We can afford to use words since we're identifying them with numbers (assuming #122 ever moves). For example,

* MSPC → maximum concurrent streams (or max_streams)
* CFCW → initial connection flow control offset (conn_fc_offset)
* SFCW → new stream flow control offset (str_fc_offset)
* etc...

comments.author: RyanTheOptimist
comments.body: Great idea. Using the full words sounds clearest to me.

issues.title: Packet number skipping and entropy
issues.author: martinthomson
issues.body:
> skipping packet numbers between 1 and 255 effectively provides up to 8 bits of efficient entropy on  demand, which should be adequate protection against most opportunistic acknowledgement attacks.

Aside from the odd phrasing, I think that this is incorrect.  Aside from the obvious point that 1-255 is only  7.994 bits of entropy, you also have to take into account the probability that a sender chooses to skip (a probability of 2^-8 would give the answer here).  Add to that the fact that any entropy accumulates with every packet sent.  Choosing to send or withhold each packet number could add up to a bit of entropy over time, so the difficulty in guessing could be higher over time.

No matter what strategy it's always safe for an attacker to guess high, so the amount of effective entropy against an attacker is probably less than claimed.  Of course, guessing high has an effect on congestion control, because that is marked by the sender as loss.  That could be as effective in mitigating the optimistic acknowledgment attack as the gap itself.

Then there is real packet loss.  If you randomly decide to skip 255 numbers, then real packet loss on the packet after the gap makes it difficult to acknowledge (you have to send two ACK frames if there is a gap >255).  Burst loss makes that even more likely.

In any case, I'd recommend removing any claim about entropy.  I also recommend removing any mention of specific numbers.  Skipping more packets is fine, but it means that you run the packet number space down faster and you get less efficiency in ACK packets.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body: Is there any good reason to allow large gaps in packet sequences? The optimistic ACK attack could be handled by other means that will not complicate received packet handling. If the maximum packets in flight is limited in range, it is simpler to implement filtering of duplicate packets without DoS concerns, for example using a sliding bitmap. It also simplifies resource allocation for ack management and timestamps. There can be gaps from lost packets, but these count against packets in flight.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: I think that @mikkelfj has it right here, the notion that we might somehow gain some signal from skipping packets is a roundabout way of doing this.  We could be far more direct and add an ARE_YOU_THERE frame.  ARE_YOU_THERE would contain some randomness and could be used to solicit a YES_I_AM frame that echoes that randomness, thereby providing that it was successfully received.  We probably want that for #161 anyhow.  Then we can do away with this slightly dodgy language.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body: Just to be clear - my comment was also a request for a guarantee that sequence numbers do not have large unnatural gaps such that packets with unexpected gaps can be rejected early. Otherwise such gaps can be exploided by maliciously inserting gaps to harm a poorly implemented end-point and consequently end-points must implement logic to protect against this, for example using comparatively slow balanced search trees instead of linear buffers.

comments.author: janaiyengar
comments.body:
You definitely do not want to disallow large gaps in sequence spaces, since large BDPs can have large gaps. 

QUIC packet numbers are different from TCP sequence numbers in that the receiver handles these cases, allowing servers to do interesting things with packet numbers. There are server architectures that can use this to good effect, but splitting sending of different objects over different packet number spaces.

I don't see the DoS here, BTW -- this is the data receiver, meaning that it's getting data from the server. How do you DoS by adding a gap in packet number? Gaps needs to be handled at the receiver and the size of the gap does not help really, since it's not like you're allocating a bitmap for packet numbers (if you are, you really shouldn't be.) Bear in mind that any gaps that are reported or state at the receiver with a large gap in it only lasts for 1 RTT, after which the receiver can discard this state entirely. I would strongly encourage you to write code that does not assume sequential packet numbers. Sequential shoukd be the common case, but the receiver shouldn't collapse on large gaps.

comments.author: janaiyengar
comments.body:
@martinthomson Using a packet number jump isn't a hack -- it's a design principle and we should use it to good effect. The packet number was designed to be separate from everything else. The client associates no particular semantic with gaps -- note that the receiver does not assume *anything* about gaps, except that they need to be reported. Gaps are ultimately for the sender to manage. And once the receiver is certain that the sender has heard about the gap, it stops reporting them. All this allows a sender to freely use packet number space in innovative ways, including this one.

Further, remember that for a DDoS towards a victim, you need a large number of such connections, and the attacked has to guess the jump correctly for *all* these connections. For a large enough jump, that's diminishing probabilities.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body:
> You definitely do not want to disallow large gaps in sequence spaces, since large BDPs can have large gaps.

This is not what I am a saying - you can have gaps associated with the number of expected packets in flight, and it can be large - but you need to allocated state for all these packets one way or another. Sometimes it can be done compactly as run length encoded maps etc., but the point is that it is bounded and controllable, and that violating sequences beyond that can easily be rejected. So I am suggesting that the sender is not permitted to issue unnecessary gaps. (Connection migration might be an exception).

> QUIC packet numbers are different from TCP sequence numbers in that the receiver handles these cases, allowing servers to do interesting things with packet numbers. There are server architectures that can use this to good effect, but splitting sending of different objects over different packet number spaces.

But still limited by the connection flow control window. Again I'm not arguing against gaps as long as all sequences are being used timely - but it is a good point that you should not require packets to be transmitted in sequence.

> I don't see the DoS here, BTW -- this is the data receiver, meaning that it's getting data from the server.

You cannot make any assumptions on who is sending what, and who is hostile. The classic http client/server model is just one use case, and even here massive data volumes can flow both ways.

> How do you DoS by adding a gap in packet number? Gaps needs to be handled at the receiver and the size of the gap does not help really, since it's not like you're allocating a bitmap for packet numbers (if you are, you really shouldn't be.)

The DoS is preventable - the point is that it forces the implementation to take preventative measures. For example some part of the Linux Kernel is using an AVL tree instead of a hash (as I understand) because hash tables are vulnerable to collision attacks. So the possibility of DoS is a burden on quality implementations and a real concern for lesser implementations. As I recall a study showed many vulnerabilities in DNS name lookups.

The attack on a quality implementation still exists because you design data such every packet requires a distance to the next packet. For example an binary search tree node typically requires 3x8 bytes, and more for interval handling so at least 32 bytes. When ranges fall in line, a single node can handle several sequences but if not you use that much space. For 1 million packets in flight that is 32MB which is not enough for a serious DoS attack, especially since the sender must provide data to feed the attack. But the implementatation still needs to take its precautions. If you could allocate a bitmap for 1 million packets, you would only need  125K to track which packets have been seen already. This also impacts cache performance and overall system load. Even if the binary interval tree was lucky to handle more dense ranges, it likely couldn't achieve the same density as a bitmap, especially if the bitmap is clustered - meaning that ranges for all ones can be collapsed. You can get clever and mix binary search trees and bitmaps for arbitrary ranges, but it is much more complex and likely not done in the typical implementation you will see.

So overall, no it is not a DoS attack if handled correctly, but it is an extra burden on the implemtation.

> Bear in mind that any gaps that are reported or state at the receiver with a large gap in it only lasts for 1 RTT, after which the receiver can discard this state entirely.

For 1 RTT you can draft a sequence space spanning 2^31 values, but you are right that it does limit the effectiveness of an attack. And as far as I can see (not 100% sure) you cannot limit this to 1 RTT because an attacker is not required to submit timely ACKs' and the receiver cannot reasonable discard state after 1 RTT if it on average expects lazy ACK's.

EDIT: when I wrote my first post, ranges could be larger than 2^31 but since then sequence numbers cannot be represented by more than 32-bits which places the 2^31 constraint.

> I would strongly encourage you to write code that does not assume sequential packet numbers. Sequential shoukd be the common case, but the receiver shouldn't collapse on large gaps.

Absolutely - I just saying that it would be much simpler to implement effective guards when the spec provides stronger contraints on valid ranges.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body:
What is the status on packet number gaps? The current editorial states:

> There are two possible mitigations to this attack. The simplest one is that a server can unilaterally create a gap in packet-number space. In the non-attack scenario, the client will send an ACK frame with the larger value for largest acknowledged. In the attack scenario, the attacker could acknowledge a packet in the gap. If the server sees an acknowledgment for a packet that was never sent, the connection can be aborted.

But do we still want this, or should there be recommendation to keep packet number gaps as small as possible, or within some limit (someone will argue something about block allocations for concurrent transmission subsystems).

Decision on packet number gaps affects both gaps in ongoing ack framing discussion and also choice of data structure in implementations.

issues.title: Subsequent Delta LA values
issues.author: martinthomson
issues.body:
The definition of "Delta Last Acked" is the same for all of the timestamp entries.  This implies that every packet number in the timestamp block is expressed relative to the "Last Acked".  That would make it impossible to provide timestamps for packets more than 255 packet numbers behind the last acknowledged packet and multiple ACK frames would be needed to do that.

I don't think that's right, but that subsequent deltas apply to the last timestamp.  That is:
```diff
  packet_number[0] = last_acknowledged - delta_last[0]
- packet_number[n] = last_acknowledged - delta_last[n]
+ packet_number[n] = last_acknowledged - sum(1, n, delta_last[i])
```

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
Actually, that's how it works today, and I didn't particularly consider it a problem, since TCP and QUIC by default ack every two packets.  One can imagine schemes that ack less often, and I've implemented two of them, but even then, acking over 200 packets at once would be a bit crazy.

There was a choice between ordering the timestamps by time or by packet number.  I ended up choosing time.

Given timestamps are not retransmitted, they're best effort feedback, and the loss of a small number of timestamps cannot be a critical issue.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: This appears to be fixed by #360.

issues.title: "retransmitting" old timestamps in ACK frames
issues.author: martinthomson
issues.body:
We need to include advice on the creation of ACK frames when an ACK frame was lost.  The advice from @ianswett is that new timing information isn't valuable.  Both endpoints only need to maintain timing information for individual packets for a short period, so retransmission of old timing information isn't valuable.

Thus, we should recommend that endpoints do just that: maintain a short list of packets that they want to provide timing for.  They should then not worry about re-sending any timestamps from lost packets.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: Closed by #360.

issues.title: Missing return statements
issues.author: martinthomson
issues.body: The descriptions for `OnAlarm` and `OnPacketAcked` both claim a return value.  The pseudocode doesn't show any return value.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: This has already been fixed.

issues.title: Use packets or packet numbers in algorithms/pseudocode
issues.author: martinthomson
issues.body: The text for `DetectLostPackets` claims that `acked_packet` is a packet number, but the code shows it as having a `packet_number` field, as well as a `time_sent` field.  Maybe a TimeSent() lookup function would work, but at the level that this code operates, I think that it would be better to talk about packets in the abstract.  A real implementation might not carry around all the information a packet might accumulate, but that's for real implementations to worry about.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: FWIW, I've fixed this in #304, but only for this specific function.  The same problem exists in other functions.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: Fixed by PR #394

issues.title: GREASE the packet type octet
issues.author: ianswett
issues.body:
Google-QUIC had an issue where post-handshake QUIC packets were being dropped, because a bit changed in the public flags, and a middlebox no longer identified it as QUIC.

In order to ensure the entire public flags byte is usable, I suggest we GREASE it by defining the entire space as valid.

Building on Jana's proposal for the public header with a flags byte as a set of codepoints: https://gist.github.com/janaiyengar/b05acb3af17d6e938d25befc69c11eae

The goal is to provide a simple mathematical mapping from any value of the public flags onto a frame type.  

My suggestion is to lookup the frame type, and if it's not defined, mod the flags value by the number of frame types defined in that phase(short or long form) and pick the type with that index when ordering the frame types by value.

If an initial packet number is chosen randomly, and the connection ID is as well, greasing the flags byte and version (#112 and #296) covers everything that is not encrypted.

comments.author: marten-seemann
comments.body:
I like this idea very much. 

If I understand @ianswett's proposal correctly, we might have to be a bit more careful when it comes to the long packets. Different QUIC versions might define a different number of packet types, so we can't grease before version negotiation is finished. If I understand that correctly, excluding the long packets from greasing would solve that problem (we do slightly modified greasing here if we define a fixed modulo value that is guaranteed to stay constant between all QUIC versions). 

Furthermore, in order to simplify the mapping, if we define an ordering of the frame types anyway, wouldn't it be easier to get rid of the explicit values defined in Jana's proposal? I.e. the packet type would just be numbered 1 to n. 

Then the rule for the sender is easy: Just add *random number* x *number of frame types* to the type number (mod 256). Decoding boils down to a simple mod operation as well.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: Consecutive numbers would be easier, but it does present deployment challenges for Google and anyone else who has Google-QUIC deployed, as we transition from one flags approach to another.  This might be solvable other ways, but it'd take some serious thought.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body: It's worth pointing out that this absolutely requires authentication of the public header. Otherwise firewalls could zero out the greased bits to avoid potential information leakage.

comments.author: RyanTheOptimist
comments.body: Agreed. I think we have consensus on that point, but we should confirm on the list. (Google QUIC authenticates the public header.)

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
This requires positive identification of short vs. long form.  I think that it also fixes the size of the space in which long form packets can be sent.  If the next version of the protocol needs an additional long-form packet, then n_long increases and greased packets suddenly fall into different slots.

That's not workable if you ever want to change this protocol.  I believe that long form packets are most in need of this sort of protection - experience with TLS shows that issues are most likely to occur on the very first packet.  That doesn't mean that greasing the short form isn't valuable, it's just that greasing the initial packets is more important.  We need to balance that with having an escape valve - a way to deploy a new version of the protocol.

We could say that version has to be understood before identifying type (else, send a version negotiation packet and don't grease type there).  That requires that only long form packets either be distinct from short form or that only long form packets arrive prior to establishing state. The latter of these doesn't work in light of NAT rebinding, since short form packets will arrive with no context.  That leads me to conclude the distinguishing long and short is still useful.

So we say that long form packets are identified by some clearly defined operation.  Pick a permutation operation. &0x08 or &0x80 could work, or even something like n%3!=1 so that there can be twice as many long form layouts as short form.  After that you know that version is present and can use version to determine if you even have a hope of recovering the type.

Here is where I think @marten-seemann is right about packing the space of valid codepoints.  A sparsely populated space makes this easier to build.  A complicated PRP hurts, especially since this octet is likely to to need hardware implementation.  That accepts that greasing the type loses any hope of preserving bitwise compatibility with Google-QUIC (why didn't anyone pick up on that in Jana's proposal, or am I just being dense through severe lack of sleep?).

That means that adding a new long form packet layout and type requires a new version.  I think that's a perfectly reasonable compromise.

Short form packets are easier in a way: since those are only exchanged after version negotiation, the only wrinkle is how they are managed after NAT rebinding.  For that, the connection ID remains our best way to ensure that they can be correctly recovered.  Once the server can correlate the packet with a connection, then it's easy to recover type.

@martinduke, @RyanAtGoogle, see #302.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
I believe a plausible solution is for the server to supply the client a list of all type byte codepoints in the ServerHello that have been defined in versions subsequent to this connection's version and the server supports, and hence should not be greased by the client.  And greasing would never be done until the handshake completes, of course.

This is not that elegant, but ensures all codepoints are in use at all times, either by valid connections or by greasing the value.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body: Maybe I'm missing something, but if the handshake has completed and we know what version is in use, why do we care if the client collides with a value defined in a different version?  Server should interpret based on the agreed version, and if something that was grease becomes valid in a different version... that's kind of the point.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
There is a very real practical concern Google and others may have in the near future, which is that we may want IETF-QUIC to not grease codepoints still in use by GQUIC.  But that's not the reason I came up with this originally.

Here's my weak argument, maybe others can do better: If a client comes in from a new IP/Port, then the server has to know how to decode the packet and it can't use version, because it's unknown(unless the server only supports one version, and this is moot).  If connection ID is always the same length in the same location, then I believe there's no issue, but otherwise mapping a packet back to it's connection is impossible or speculative.

I think this is more of a challenge for a load balancer that's not terminating the connection than one that is, particularly if one wants that load balancer to be relatively or completely stateless.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body:
Ah, so it's a migration issue:  When seeing a packet from a new source, the server has to first decide whether it's an existing connection that has migrated versus an initial packet from a new client, and this decision has to be made before it can know what version to use in interpreting the packet.

Whether it's a bit or a restricted set of values, that seems like an argument for the model of "These are handshake packets, and everything else is post-handshake."  The problem scenario seems to be that the client picks as a post-handshake-with-grease value something that a server thinks could be a handshake value in a different version.  Is that right?

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
Yep, that's right Mike, that is what I had in mind when I said:

> That requires that only long form packets either be distinct from short form or that only long form packets arrive prior to establishing state. The latter of these doesn't work in light of NAT rebinding, since short form packets will arrive with no context.

I appreciate that GQUIC has a problem here.  The checksum could be sufficient though.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: I tweaked the title to reflect recent changes in the packet format.

comments.author: ekr
comments.body:
As I said in the meeting, I have an alternative proposed design:

- Packet has type P
- Encrypt the packet and call the last byte of the packet (the auth tag) T
- Set the new packet type to be P ^ (T & 0x7f) [the 0x7f mask preserves the leading bit]

This randomizes the packet type without placing any special requirements on the construction of the code points.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body:
Discussed in Paris; generally agreed to be a good thing. 

Jana and Ian to check to see if this makes migration from Google QUIC easy/hard.

comments.author: ekr
comments.body:
@huitema points out that we might want to have a keyed mask function because any static transformation is easily degreased. The observation here is that you can have a key that's shared across all of the connections, because we're not really worried about the middlebox connecting to the server and extracting the key for the transformation. With that in mind, here's an alternate keeed proposal.

```
1. Server generates a key K_static which it uses for all connections.
2. Packet has type P and last byte T
3. The server delivers K_static in its first flight.
4. For every packet, you compute P' = P ^(PRF(K, T) & 0x7f) where
    K = 0 for initial packets
    K = K_static for other packets.
```
This allows stateless unmasking.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
@ekr I am afraid that the approach might not work well with a deployment that uses either connection ID or 5-tuple for load balancing, depending on the type of a packet.

In the past, we have discussed of deployments that would use some bits of a connection ID to route a packet to the correct server sitting behind a load balancer (or to the correct POP within an anycast deployment). Note that such a load balancer will typically not maintain any state of a QUIC connection.

OTOH, I also anticipate that even in a deployment that does connection ID-based load balancing, you might want to route packets to backend servers based on the 5-tuple during the handshake. This is for avoiding attacks targeting a specific server behind a load balancer. Note that processing of handshake packets could be much more computationally intensive due to public-key operations when compared to other types of packets.

The issue with the proposed approach is that it is impossible for a stateless load balancer to determine the correct type of the packet, since whether `K=0` or `K=K_static` should be used depends on the state of the connection. Therefore, with the proposed approach, it becomes impossible to change how the packet is load balanced depending on the type of a packet.

Am I missing something?

Reconsidering this, it seems to me that there is another issue (sorry for the fuss).

My understanding is that some load balancers start streaming packets to the correct port before seeing the end of the packet. Making the actual type depend on the final octet of a packet prevents us from using such a load balancer.

Would it be possible to use an octet that exists at the beginning of the packet for greasing?
