comments.body:
Timestamps were removed in #841 and the text about what to ack has been updated, including in #907 

I think this is fixed, but reopen if you think there's more work to be done(and clarify what you're looking for)

issues.title: Complicated Retransmission Corner Cases
issues.author: martinduke
issues.body:
The basic case for retransmission is pretty straightforward. I detect a packet loss, so I take all the stuff in that packet and send it in a new packet. There has to be some sort of data structure in the PCB to track what's in the packet. I can clear that data structure once the packet is acked.

There are two ambiguities here:
(1) How long do I hold on to the packet data if lost? I can delete it immediately, hold it for _n_ retransmissions, or hold it until all acks and data in the packet are acked.

Deleting it immediately is very simple, but if the ack comes back for that packet later and the first retransmission is lost, I will needlessly resend that data.

Offline, Jana suggested keeping it for 1 retransmission. That is fine with me (minus the second item below) but I think some implementation guidance on when it is acceptable to throw away old packet data would be helpful.

(2) More importantly, fitting the whole retransmission into a single packet does not hold in the general case. There might be an MTU change; the updated ack might be bigger; optimizers like me might want to aggregate multiple small packets into a single retransmission; some ack frames might be supersets of other ack frames, so although there is no direct retransmission relationship acking one of those packets might obviate the ack frame of the other.

What all this implies is a many-to-many mapping where every time data or acks are acked, we have to clear that from all other packets that contain it. I started down this road before seeing that it was way too hairy to continue.

****

So we're at a point where the optimal wire performance -- never throw it away until all components are acked, allow mix-and-match of retransmissions, don't resend stuff if acked in some other packet -- is close to unimplementable. Some implementation guidance about what it's OK to not worry about, and perhaps some judicious prohibitions on particularly gnarly stuff, might help some.

comments.author: martinthomson
MikeBishop
comments.body:
When I was toying with this, I wound up tracking the delivery state of frames, not packets.  Each retransmittable frame was pending send, in-flight, or delivered.  Each packet that was outstanding was simply a list of frames that it contained, and changing a packet to lost or delivered was really walking its packets and updating *their* state.  Every time I generated a packet, I filled it as full as possible with frames that were pending send, with retransmissions being first.  And I agree, it's hairy.

You're right that you eventually need to get rid of the lists from old lost packets, but ought to maintain them for a little while in case the packet (or the ACK) is merely delayed.  However, there's no great harm in throwing it away too early (as you say, you'll get an ACK for a packet you no longer know anything about, and so accidentally resend a frame) and I'd say that can be left to the implementation.

comments.body:
@martinthomson I think the issue is related, in that streams pretty much have to remain open if they're holding in flight data. But that's not how I got here.

After playing with it both ways, I've settled on this question the same way you have. I think this section could use an implementation note to save people some of the trouble I went through. I'll mull a PR.

comments.author: huitema
comments.body:
Yes, I indeed said that. In fact, "negotiating timestamps" is not a binary yes-no question. It is important to state what time stamps to send, and for what purpose. So far, I have heard three such purposes:

* Estimating one way delays, which is useful in delay based congestion algorithms;

* Estimating the max reordering delay, which is an important parameter of RACK style retransmission 
   algorithms;

* And, estimating the "bunching" of packets that may occur in the network.

It is not clear to me that these three usages require the same set of timestamps. One way delay measurements would probably do OK with just adding to the ACK the timestamp of the largest acknowledged packet. Max reordering estimation would require adding the timestamp of the 
max out-of-order packet. Bunching estimation leaves me puzzled, but I am sure there can be 
a simple rule for selecting which stamps to send. In any case, we must do the clarification work before
mandating time stamps.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
Negotiating timestamps sounds good to me, though I'd hope we can agree on one format for most use cases.

I can see the use case for requesting only 1 timestamp per ack frame vs requesting one timestamp for every newly acked packet.

Timestamps are already forbidden from unprotected ack frames, so it should be simple enough to negotiate timestamps and only use them post-handshake.

issues.title: Writing after closed frame enqueued
issues.author: ekr
issues.body:
I'm not sure if this belongs in the QUIC spec, but I had to handle it specially in Minq so I thought I would mention it.

The current text shows the transition from OPEN to HALF_CLOSED (LOCAL) happening when you send a FIN. However, if you think of this from an API perspective, that's not quite what you want. Consider the case where you have a stream flow control window of 1000. You write 999 and then 1000-1999, and then call stream.Close(). At this point, you have in queue:

``` 
  [0-999] (sent, maybe un-acked)
  [1000-1999] (not-sent)
  [2000: FIN] (not sent)
```

You're still in OPEN because you haven't sent the FIN, but the implementation should stop you from doing another Write() at this point. This isn't really captured by the state machine.

issues.title: Streams start as "idle"
issues.author: ekr
issues.body:
There are two ways of thinking about streams:

1. All 2^32 streams exist but are in the IDLE state and transition to other states when messages are received/sent on them.
2. Streams are created when the aforementioned messages are received/sent.

The document is kind of agnostic on this, talking about them as being in IDLE (the state machine) but also talking about streams being created:

```
   A QUIC endpoint cannot reuse a Stream ID.  Streams MUST be created in
   sequential order.  Open streams can be used in any order.  Streams
```

I tend to think that it would be better to talk about streams being created and remove the IDLE state, but in any case it would be good if the draft were consistent.

issues.title: QUIC streams abstraction
issues.author: MikeBishop
issues.body:
From mailing list thread:  Several open issues (#485,#184,#758) come down to how you conceive of the API a QUIC implementation will expose.  Two basic ones have been suggested:

1. **TCP Stream sockets.**  These only support signaling “orderly” closing of the write direction.  Closing of the read direction can only be done via close(), but that may leave the write direction in an undefined state (writing will complete, unless there was unread data in the read buffer or any data is received after close – see RFC 1122 4.2.2.13 $3).

2. **A POSIX pipe pair.** Connected pipes are very clean (‘symmetric’) abstractions, and they communicate close events (you close the ‘write’ pipe, ‘read’ pipe get EOS; you close the ‘read’ pipe, ‘write’ pipe gets an exception).

My mental model has been (2):  a stream/stream-pair consists of an InputStream and an OutputStream; you can read on one, you can write on the other.  For the write stream, you can write your data to completion and close the stream, or you can decide to abort writing.  The wire expressions of these are FIN and RST_STREAM, respectively.  For the read stream, you can read the incoming data to the end or you can abort reading and discard the remainder of the stream; the wire expression of this would be flow control updates or STOP_SENDING, respectively.  On the other side, receipt of a RST_STREAM surfaces as a read error and receipt of a STOP_SENDING surfaces as a write error.  (@janaiyengar commented that in this mental model it might be clearer to call the frames WRITE_ABORT and READ_ABORT.)

#485 suggests that streams only close by application action; there would never be a write error surfaced to the application unless the underlying transport went away entirely.  Instead, as in #758, it’s the responsibility of the application protocol to communicate (on another stream, in this case) that you should abort writing, even if you’ve already written to completion, and then to do so.  That implies that the application needs the ability to return to streams on which it’s done writing, in case it’s later asked to go back and reset them.

Much of our discussions around unidirectional streams, stream state transitions, etc. including the question of whether STOP_SENDING belongs at the transport layer, stem from the fact that we all have different implicit mental models of the functional surface QUIC exposes.  Perhaps we should take a step back and agree on that first, as I believe Christian has suggested in the past?

comments.body: Yes, particularly the stream state machines.

issues.title: Can Finished be sent as 1-RTT data?
issues.author: huitema
issues.body:
I know that in TLS 1.3, the answer is no. But the TLS answer applies to TLS over TCP, for which TLS manages the transition from handshake data to application data. QUIC is arguably different. The stream zero frame will carry the Finished message as an encrypted handshake message. But the spec is a bit ambiguous as to whether this stream zero frame shall be carried as "Client Clear Text" or "1-RTT Data". 

I would much prefer 1-RTT data, because of repetition handling. If we imposed Client Clear Text, and the packet is lost, the stream zero frame will have to be retransmitted again as client clear text. That means interleaving clear text data and encrypted data within a single set of sequence number, and I am convinced that that can be abused to carry some kind of denial of service.

comments.body: OK, I agree with that.  Maybe we can get back to talking about putting encrypted data in the same packet again so that it can be made correct.

comments.author: huitema
comments.body:
There are two different issues. One is a problem of efficiency, carrying Finished (or a copy) in the same UDP packet as the first application data frames. The other is an issue of DOS resilience, knowing when to start just ignoring any non encrypted packets.

We could probably solve the efficiency issue by creating a new packet type, "clear text followed by encrypted data". I am also interested with the issue of closing the DOS opening.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
I think that we would change the cleartext packet types instead.  Fewer moving parts that way.

As for the DOS opening, I get it.  You have shared keys now, but you aren't using them, at least to the extent that they are visible at the QUIC layer.  I think that more special rules might help here.  I hate special rules though.

As you say, there are two issues here.  Unfortunately, this particular issue is neither and probably should be closed.

comments.author: igorlord
comments.body:
> The other is an issue of DOS resilience, knowing when to start just ignoring any non encrypted packets.

Can you start ignoring Clear Text packets, when you have successfully received client's Finished?

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: @igorlord, I think that @huitema is more concerned about the time between when the server sends its Finished and when it receives the client Finished.  At this time, the server and client share keys and could authenticate all packets, but the connection is still vulnerable to denial of service until the server receives the client Finished.

comments.author: igorlord
comments.body:
@martinthomson, I think I get this concern. However, in the 3rd comment, @huitema suggests a scenario of a DoS that would not be a DoS, if the server were to ignore all Clear Text packets after receiving Client's valid Finished message.  Until the server receives Client's valid Finished message, the usual DoS concerns regarding packet injection apply.

There may be other reasons to make client's Finished encrypted after the receipt of server's Finished, but this DoS scenario is probably not it.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: We already require the server to ignore cleartext packets once it has 1-RTT keys.  We could be more precise about when that comes into force.

issues.title: Can Server Require Connection ID to be Included in Packets Sent by Clients?
issues.author: nibanks
issues.body:
This is slightly related to #659.

Is it reasonable/acceptable for a server implementation to require that a client always include the connection ID? If so, what exactly should it do if it receives a new connection where the client specified `omit_connection_id` in its transport parameters? Should it drop the connection? It seems to me that if we want to allow servers to restrict the usage of `omit_connection_id` by the client, we should probably have some mechanism to indicate the client the connection must include the connection ID. One possibility is a new transport parameters that is server specific that indicates connection id is required.

issues.title: bytes_in_flight for TLPs and RTOs
issues.author: marten-seemann
issues.body:
Currently, `bytes_in_flight` is only reduced in two cases: when the packet is acked, and when `DetectLostPackets` detects a packet as lost.
This leaves TLPs and RTOs uncovered. Shouldn't be `bytes_in_flight` reduced in those cases as well?

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
There is no need to reduce bytes_in_flight for a tail loss probe.  There is no RFC for TLP, only this experimental draft: https://tools.ietf.org/html/draft-dukkipati-tcpm-tcp-loss-probe-01, but salient text would be 
  "TLP unifies the loss recovery mechanisms regardless of the position
   of a loss, so now with TLP a segment loss in the middle of a train as
   well as at the tail end can now trigger the same fast recovery
   mechanisms."

Traditionally, RTOs declared all packets in flight lost.  Because in QUIC there is always an unambiguous larger packet being acked for an RTO, I don't believe it should be necessary to ever declare packets lost when an RTO occurs, but I can imagine there being a problem with a large reordering tolerance combined with the reduction in CWND 'stalling' the connection.

Ideally, I'd like to unify TLP and RTO in QUIC and remove the reduction of CWND to min_cwnd(Which BBR already does), but I don't have a proposal for that I'm sufficiently happy with yet.

comments.author: siyengar
comments.body: TLP is not a loss, so you wouldn't reduce bytes in flight. It's very tempting to treat TLP as a loss and we had a bug as a result of this, but don't :)

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: Jana's outstanding PR #801 should resolve this I believe.  It'd be good to have your input on that PR Marten, if you have time.

comments.author: janaiyengar
comments.body: Closing, since #801 discusses this. @marten-seemann please reopen if you think this needs further discussion.

issues.title: SNI requirement for HTTP/QUIC
issues.author: igorlord
issues.body:
Per @martinthomson in #495, SNI is currently not required to be used in QUIC, while it is required to be used in HTTP/2.  TLS 1.3 requires SNI to be implemented but apparently does not require it be to used.

This is a proposal to require SNI for QUIC.

The main reason for this is the scarcity of IPv4 addresses.  As long as something is not required, someone will not implement it.  As long as there are enough clients that do not use SNI, virtual service providers will continue to require a large number of IPv4 addresses.  Since IPv4 address conservation is currently a high priority for the Internet, QUIC should strongly encourage (or, better, require) technologies that further this conservation goal.

> strongly encourage (or, better, require) technologies that further this
> conservation goal.
>
> Nit:  I believe you mean to require SNI, not SIN, though no doubt we'll
get the latter some way or another.

Substantive:  I believe that if we require SNI, we require some method of
preserving the privacy of that SNI.

I'm not sure that the TLS in TLS tunneling solution for encrypted SNI that
https://tools.ietf.org/html/draft-ietf-tls-sni-encryption-00 puts forward
is as neat in the QUIC case.  If the fronting server isn't a QUIC service
but is purely a TLS-in-TLS tunneling proxy, then it probably works as
described.  But if it is both a QUIC service and fronting for other
QUIC-in-TLS-in-TLS services,  then I think we need to carefully work
through how the second  aspects fits in with other QUIC assumptions about
where the transport/application boundary fits.

I think the dual service is something that we need to consider for some of
the same reasons set out in sni-encyption-00 regarding replay attacks: if
at attacker connecting to a fronting service doesn't connect to a hidden
service behind it and thus gets a "blank service", it will make the server
stand out as a fronting server.  To avoid that, I suspect folks would like
to present servers that are both fronting services and servers for an
existing application protocol.

> SNI privacy

issues.title: SNI encryption
issues.author: martinthomson
issues.body:
In #794, @hardie observed that the current draft for SNI encryption proposes solutions that are - at best - a poor fit for the current QUIC design.  Do we want to address this problem in the design?

Fixing the problem early might avoid foreclosing on potential solutions in the future.  It's also possible that we could take advantage of the fact that we don't really have a whole bunch of deployment assumptions that we have to work around.

On the other hand, it might also be really, really hard.  It's not like we haven't already tried to find a solution for TLS over TCP.

FWIW, I don't think that we get to resolve #794 until we have at least had a discussion about this issue.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body: Secondary certificates seems like a good way to achieve this for HTTP/* over TLS.  Put your CERTIFICATE_REQUEST for the real hostname in 0-RTT data.  A more general possibility would be the "tls1.3" ALPN token, where you carry a TLS 1.3 session on Stream 1, with the ClientHello (in 0-RTT data if you can) and use of other streams is discouraged or prohibited.

comments.body:
On Wed, Oct 25, 2017 at 2:39 PM, Mike Bishop <notifications@github.com>
wrote:

> Secondary certificates seems like a good way to achieve this for HTTP/*
> over TLS. Put your CERTIFICATE_REQUEST for the real hostname in 0-RTT data.
> A more general possibility would be the "tls1.3" ALPN token, where you
> carry a TLS 1.3 session on Stream 1, with the ClientHello (in 0-RTT data if
> you can) and use of other streams is discouraged or prohibited.

I think that means that the ALPN token can't be used to select the
protocol.  When we get to the point of having multiple protocols, some
subset of which might be present but served by different back end
processes, that could pose a problem.  Would you be okay with
$PROTOCOL.tls1.3 as a pattern?  That can still get you to the point where
the server name is encrypted, even if the protocol is known to anyone able
to observe the ALPN token.

Ted

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
The issue here is not whether we expose the use of a particular protocol.  Those tend to have small cardinality, so don't tend to compromise K-anonymity much by their exposure.  But I wouldn't shift the load to ALPN.

If any protocol can build similar capabilities to what is proposed for HTTP, then they benefit from the same advantages vis-a-vis SNI protection.  If a generic capability is what is needed, I don't think that ALPN is where I would start looking, I'd build a QUIC extension in some form.

An extension would either replicate the HTTP/2 certificates functionality, or do QUIC-in-QUIC in some way (probably by putting TLS in a stream and then exporting new keys when it is done and using a key update to manage their installation).  Christian and ekr have done some work here and have a few options in their TLS doc.  Some, if not all, of the basic designs work for QUIC.  None of them use ALPN, which would create an undesirable secondary signal.

(Also, every time someone suggests we make ALPN anything other than opaque, I cringe.)

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: Waiting for TLS to give us something.

comments.author: jmtilli
comments.body:
I hope people here realize that this proposal of encrypting the SNI will make multiplexing connections on a NAT middlebox (see Issue #1456) practically impossible.

The IPv4 address exhaustion is a reality, and IPv6 adoption will probably be much slower than QUIC adoption, so QUIC should not contribute to the IPv4 address shortage problem by encrypting the only piece of information about the server (i.e. the DNS name) in addition to the IPv4 address.

In contrast, if SNI remains unencrypted, a NAT middlebox can share an IPv4 address for multiple servers and choose the correct server based on the SNI.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
My feeling is we've officially punted this to the TLS WG and I expect we'll do whatever they do, so the TLS WG is probably a better forum to discuss this, but as MikkelFJ said on the other issue, feel free to email the list.

I'm also not 100% clear on how you're using SNI in a NAT.  Is there a full explanation somewhere?

comments.author: jmtilli
comments.body:
The full explanation is easy. It's for incoming connections in a use case where multiple HTTP2/QUIC servers are multiplexed behind a single IPv4 server address. For example, IoT adoption might require more than 4 billion HTTP servers all around the world.

If the first QUIC packet sent will contain the SNI, the NAT will compare it against a full list of (SNI, internal IP) pairs. For example:
* device1.iot.company.com -> 10.0.1.100
* device2.iot.company.com -> 10.0.1.101
* device3.iot.company.com -> 10.0.1.102
* device4.iot.company.com -> 10.0.1.103

If the SNI is unencrypted and required to be always present, this scheme will work all the time.

The only problem is configuring the SNI -> internal IP mappings in the NAT box. If it's a carrier grade NAT, presumably the carrier will allow configuring wildcard matches against the domain names the customers own.

Outgoing connections will always work with NAT without any SNI matching.

comments.author: larseggert
comments.body: This discussion needs to happen in the TLS WG.

comments.author: ekr
comments.body: +1 to @larseggert, but more importantly, every proposed SNI encryption system would require opt-in from the site.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
My assessment here is that this will either happen in TLS or not and we don't need to track it specially in QUIC.  No solution that I'm aware of will require changes to QUIC to be used because it all happens entirely outside the protocol (e.g., in DNS) or entirely within TLS.

There's a small risk that the overzealous use of padding in some cases might make it hard for QUIC to benefit from this, or that the arrangement of the design is too narrow in applicability for it to apply to QUIC, but that seems unlikely given the actors.  Those involved are motivated to have it work for QUIC.

So I'm going to close this.  If we need some changes to QUIC to support a particular design, we can discuss the specific requirements as they come up.  Most likely, any such discussion would need to be left to v2.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body: There is one case I could see: An external DNS like solution affects the initial random ODCID so it isn't entirely random and routes to the appropriate target.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
The specs wouldn't necessarily change there.  It's basically a property of QUIC that the destination connection ID in a client's Initial packet is not controlled by the server, and therefore not really appropriate for use in routing packets in the same way that a connection ID that the server chooses is.

If a solution for encrypting SNI proposed new ways of selecting the destination connection ID (I haven't seen that suggested, but I'll concede that it's possible), then they would have to work within that constraint.  Either that, or request changes from QUIC.

issues.title: Why is the crypto stream not subject to connection flow control
issues.author: siyengar
issues.body: IIRC previously this was not done because flow control messages for the connection were sent on the stream 0. However with MAX_DATA frames they are not sent over stream id 0 any more. Having only crypto streams not be subject to connection level flow control creates a bunch of workaround code to check for  if (stream == cryptoStream) before you increment the cumulativewritedataoffset for the connection which is used to track conn flow control.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
The problem is early data and the handshake.  It is possible that early data will exhaust the connection flow control window.  I fact, that's a feature: we use the connection flow control window to limit the amount of early data, just as there is an early data limit in TLS.  If that happens, there is no room to send the client Finished (and Certificate[Verify]).  That would block handshake completion, which is bad.  Also, the server doesn't really have a good way to send authenticated MAX_DATA frames to the client at this point, so it doesn't easily resolve itself.

Yeah, it's a real pain.  Stream 0 is too special for my liking also.

issues.title: ECN echo in ACK frame or as separate frame
issues.author: IngJohEricsson
issues.body:
There has been discussion wether the ECN indication (or echo) should be included in the ACK frame or in a separate dedicated frame. 
Proponents of a dedicated ECN frame argue that adding extra ECN info in the ACK frame can increase the complexity of the ACK frame encoding and parsing. Ian Swett however as a very strong point in his remark that ECN in a separate frame can give additional issues in the congestion control functionality, in other words, what we save (in complexity) in one part of the chain can cause extra cost and in the worst case incomprehensible code in another part of the chain. 
My personal opinion is that it is best to have ECN in the ACK frame

comments.author: britram
comments.body: +1 to ECN in ACK for Ian's reasons.

comments.author: janaiyengar
comments.body: Work is ongoing here, so parking until design team makes progress.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: Closed by #1372.

issues.title: ECN echo encoding, detailed packet level or ECN marked bytes
issues.author: IngJohEricsson
issues.body:
Once the issue #804 whether ECN should be in the ACK frame or in a separate frame it is time to discuss the format. There are two possible ways to do it

1) The status of the ECN bits for each received packet is indicated. Fig 2 and 3 in  [https://tools.ietf.org/id/draft-johansson-quic-ecn-01.txt](https://tools.ietf.org/id/draft-johansson-quic-ecn-01.txt) suggests two formats, my preference is the version presented in figure 3 (alt 2), this way the ECN bits are placed at the end of the ACK frame.

2) Accumulated number of bytes marked '01','10' and '11' (possibly also '00'). An example is presented in figure 2 in [https://tools.ietf.org/id/draft-johansson-quic-ecn-03.txt](https://tools.ietf.org/id/draft-johansson-quic-ecn-03.txt). If the ECN echo is in the ACK frame then it is not necessary with a counter for '00' marked bytes as this value can be inferred from the already existing ACKs and the counters for the '01','10' and '11' marked bytes.

Proponents for the detailed packet level indication point at a possibility that future congestion control algorithms can benefit from this level of detail. On the other hand, scalable congestion control algorithms like DCTCP can work well with the accumulated bytes count.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
I would favor option 2, since I believe it's simpler to implement and easy to use in congestion control.

Also, assuming ECN is in the ACK frame, you will know the ECN marking was on a relatively small set of newly acknowledged packets.

comments.author: britram
comments.body: +1 to option 2; it gives sufficient information, and seems easier to implement.

comments.author: janaiyengar
comments.body:
I don't think I understand option 2.  From the doc, it seems to be a count of the different markings for the packets that are being acked in the ACK frame, is that correct?

If so, that seems fine. We don't really care about exactly which packets were marked, right? Of course, one thing to bear in mind is that a receiver can arbitrarily keep sending acks for old packets, and therefore could echo ECE for an arbitrarily long time. I'm not sure if this leads to any issues yet, but it's something that one may need to be careful about when interpreting the ECE marks on a received ack.

comments.author: janaiyengar
comments.body:
Actually, here's a case: #ECE remains the same across two acks, but the ack stops acking an old packet and acks a new packet. This could mean two things: the old packet and the new packet both had no ECE, or they both had ECE. In the first case there's nothing to be done, but in the second case, the receiver of the ack may want to reduce the window, since the new packet could be part of a new window of data.

I think this problem applies to both alternatives.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: I haven't looked closely at the doc, but I assumed that the total count of packets/bytes marked is monotonically increasing and eventually wraps.  So there's no issue if a marked packet stops being acknowledged, because the total count of marks received never decreases.

comments.author: IngJohEricsson
comments.body:
Yes, for option 2 the idea is that the receiver accumulates the bytes (QUIC header+payload) that are marked ECT(0), ECT(1) and CE. This means three 48-bit counters (or 64 bit if that is easier), in other words monotonically increasing counters, with possible wrap around. The LSB of these counters are put in the ECN ACK. The details are subject to discussion...
What is neccessary is a mechanism that discards duplicate packets to avoid that duplicates increase the counters more than once. 
The fact that the counters can wrap around is not a problem as the congestion control should only care about the delta increase of the CE marked bytes.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: Duplicate packet numbers should be discarded at a very early stage in QUIC packet processing, long before any of the congestion control code is executed, so I believe duplicate packets should not handled for you.

comments.author: janaiyengar
comments.body: Ah, yes, if it's monotonically increasing, then that seems fine. I agree that duplicates should not be an issue.

comments.author: mirjak
comments.body: Alternatively, one could also add ECN information per ACK block, basically saying that all packets in this block were marked with this ECN codepoint. This however only makes sense under the assumptions that most packets are marked with the same codepoint (usually ECT(0) today) and only a few packets are e.g. CE marked. In this case you probably have the same number of ACK blocks as with loss today. But I'm not sure if this assumption still holds in the future with things like L4S or if used in data centers with some congestion control similar to DCTCP.

comments.author: IngJohEricsson
comments.body: Yes, this option was also listed in fig 2 in https://tools.ietf.org/id/draft-johansson-quic-ecn-01.txt . I have done some minimal inspection of L4S ECN marking patterns with DCTCP as congestion control. If the bootleneck is configured to ECN mark packets that are queued up more than a fixed value (say 2ms) you tend to get a periodic marking pattern, which could indicate that the alternative Mirja suggests can actually work, at least with one flow. Things get more complicated with multiple flows and also with the dualQ implemenetations that are suggested by Koen De Schepper and Bob Briscoe, in which case one see more random ECN marking, also my laymans impelmentation of an ECN marker for TCP HULL exhibit a random marking pattern.

comments.body: Discussion to continue in ECN design team (https://github.com/quicwg/base-drafts/wiki/ECN-in-QUIC).

comments.body: Closed by #1372.

issues.title: Don't retransmit old MAX_STREAM_DATA
issues.author: ekr
issues.body:
The current text says that one ought to retransmit MAX_STREAM_DATA:

```
   o  All application data sent in STREAM frames MUST be retransmitted,
      unless the endpoint has sent a RST_STREAM for that stream.  When
      an endpoint sends a RST_STREAM frame, data outstanding on that
      stream SHOULD NOT be retransmitted, since subsequent data on this
      stream is expected to not be delivered by the receiver.

   o  ACK and PADDING frames MUST NOT be retransmitted.  ACK frames
      containing updated information will be sent as described in
      Section 8.13.

   o  STOP_SENDING frames MUST be retransmitted, unless the stream has
      become closed in the appropriate direction.  See Section 10.3.
   o  All other frames MUST be retransmitted.
```

But this is silly. Say I transmitted MAX_STREAM_DATA=100, MAX_STREAM_DATA=200, MAX_STREAM_DATA=300 and then none of them were acknowledged. Why am I retransmitting frames which must be ignored.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: Agreed, this is silly.

comments.author: janaiyengar
comments.body: This is silly. We could say something along the lines of "the newest MAX_STREAM_DATA and MAX_DATA MUST be retransmitted until acked; all other previous flow control advertisements SHOULD NOT be retransmitted."

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: Or as I have said on numerous occasions, we should rewrite this section so that it concentrates on the retransmission of the *information* contained in frames rather than the frames themselves.  We have the same problem with all frame types that are used to carry data that needs to be reliably delivered to the other side, why not fix it systematically rather than piecemeal.  The text above shows that we've done that for STREAM and ACK.  The only frame that doesn't carry information that needs to be reliably delivered is PADDING.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: Agreed, misuse of the word retransmit is a widespread issue.  On the positive side, it should be an uncontroversial editorial fix.

comments.author: ekr
comments.body:
I think as a short-term fix we should do what Jana suggests. Minq presently does that. And the spec is so wrong now we should fix that ASAP

As a long-term fix, I think what we want is actually that when you discover it is time to retransmit MAX_STREAM_DATA (e.g., timer expired, you discover the data was lost) you send the then-current flow control window. That seems like it will be more accurate.

issues.title: Add a MESSAGE frame optimized for sub-MTU payloads
issues.author: ianswett
issues.body:
**Problem**
Unreliable and semi-reliable message transmission within QUIC has high overhead for small streams.  The overhead is in the form of bytes on the wire(ie: Stream ID is not necessary) as well as state tracking to allow retransmission and cancellation of streams.  For example, one has to track whether a stream was delivered, and then if it's lost, decide whether to retransmit or reset the stream.

For use cases where the message payload exceeds a single packet, an identifier is necessary to associate the data fragments with one another and state is required to reassemble the message.  As such, QUIC's stream model provides the right functionality already, with minimum overhead.

Examples potential users include WebRTC, MOSH, and IoT protocols.  These applications use sub-MTU sized unidirectional message payloads heavily.

QUIC provides these applications many benefits, including fast and secure connection establishment, security, reliability(if desired) and a common congestion control context to share with other applications.

Additionally, there may be cases where the QUIC HTTP mapping would benefit from a less stream-oriented transmission of data, such as QPACK and QCRAM state updates.  Moving them over to a MESSAGE frame type would be an optimization, but potentially a simplifying one.

SST(http://www.brynosaurus.com/pub/net/sst.pdf) made a similar optimization and I think it would be valuable in QUIC.

**Proposed Design Outline**

1. Does not contribute towards MAX_STREAM_ID, since it does not have a stream id.
2. Not repaired at the transport layer, but may be resent by the application.
3. Immediately passed up to the application, so no QUIC transport flow control is necessary

Obviously the design is flexible, but I believe making these subject to flow control and any sort of max stream id style limit would increase the overhead to that of streams.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
This is a proposal, and our contribution guidelines state that issues are for problems.  Can you restate this in terms of a problem?  I think that you have most of that here.

I'm not expressing an opinion yet but this raises a lot of questions.  Answers to the following questions might help inform that opinion.

How are the proposed MESSAGE frames identified?  That would be needed to repair them.  Identifiers might be used at the application layer too, but I'm starting to join @mcmanus in his view that using the transport layer identifiers in application protocols is not a good idea.

Actually, can they be repaired?

How are these flow controlled?  I assume that only the connection flow control limit applies.  Or does your comment about immediate processing imply that you expect them to not need flow control?

How does a receiver limit the number of these frames?  Can they?


How does this remove length?

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
Thanks for the comments.  I rephrased it to fit the guidelines.  

I'm wrong about length, it's just like a stream frame in that regard.  But it does remove offset.

comments.author: igorlord
comments.body:
> Immediately passed up to the application, so no QUIC transport flow control is necessary.

So MESSAGE frames are congestion controlled but not flow controlled?  That means a receiver that is slower than the sender and the network will be dropping MESSAGEs, and that's ok?  It looks similar to UDP, of course, but it may be an opportunity to devise some feedback to let the sender make an intelligent decision about not causing "buffer bloat" on the receiver and wasting bandwidth on MESSAGEs that will likely be dropped.

Note: since MESSAGE frames can share a packet with STREAM frames, the packets have to be ACKed by the receiver, even if MESSAGEs end up being dropped.

issues.title: Require connection ID always
issues.author: jpinner-lyft
issues.body:
Intermediaries in a QUIC connection do not (and cannot) participate in transport parameter negotiation and endpoints in a connection may not be able to configure or even have knowledge of any intermediaries. Nonetheless, those intermediaries may require connection id to do proper address translation or connection management but have no way to signal to the endpoints that the `omit_connection_id` parameter must not be set.

In particular intermediaries (especially those acting on behalf of, or in concert with, the client and server -- e.g. L4 load-balancers, client gateways, configured proxies) that attempt to manage routing through address migration or NAT re-bindings would require connection ids in both directions.

Further, some aspects of client privacy are currently assumed to be achieved by clients not sending a connection id but the specification does not require this. And some aspects of connection id migration require the servers to send the client a new connection id preemptively which they are not currently required to do. Simply requiring connection ids without requiring the servers to provide clients with the ability to migrate them does not seem to provide sufficient privacy.

My suggestion here would be to modify the specification to always require connection ids be sent by both endpoints and further require endpoints to exchange the necessary information that allows connection id migration to be initiated at will by the client.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
The original motivation for not including a connection id was saving bytes on the wire, not privacy.

Given both endpoints have to agree to omit it, and omitting it doesn't have a negative privacy impact, I don't see a negative of allowing it to be omitted.

comments.author: jpinner-lyft
comments.body: This assumes that the endpoints have control and knowledge of the entire path to know that it's safe to omit.

comments.author: janaiyengar
comments.body: Any intermediary has to be working with teh server or the client, since the keys aren't available to an intermediary otherwise. Isn't it adequate to have the end that teh intermediary is in cahoots with not send omit_connection_id? Meaning, if this is a reverse proxy, then the server *knows* to not send omit_connection_id, and itself always sends the connection ID. Why is that not enough?

comments.author: jpinner-lyft
comments.body: @janaiyengar: Intermediaries do not need to be able to decrypt the packet to access the connection id and perform tasks like routing or NAT'ing. There are also many examples of routing intermediaries that are not under direct control of the client or the server (things like Amazon's ELB, WLAN access points, etc). In addition, with the ability to migrate the connection across different paths, the presence of such intermediaries may change throughout the course of the connection.

issues.title: Need a way to send big values in stream 0
issues.author: ekr
issues.body:
Currently we have a set of bad properties:

- You can't MAX_STREAM_DATA in stream 0
- Stream 0 is stream-level flow controlled
- People have big certs

When you put these all together, we are going to have problems. There are a number of options:

1. Allow MAX_STREAM_DATA
2. Exempt stream 0 from flow control
3. Prohibit big certs
4. Have a fixed flow control window refreshed by the ACK.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
Note that this is only a problem for the Server Cleartext.  Client Initial is fixed in size. Client Cleartext is sent after the 1-RTT keys are available, so the server can send MAX_STREAM_DATA.

The other idea was to split flow control for stream 0 across the handshake: MAX_STREAM_DATA can be sent by the client (and server) in the clear, but any flow control is reset once the handshake completes (the consumed flow control on the stream is reset, the final offset is set back to the initial value, and maybe also the stream offset goes back to zero).

comments.author: jpinner-lyft
comments.body: It seems like a minimal change here would be to add an additional transport parameter for max stream data on stream 0 that the client can send as part of the transport parameters. This should be sufficient for a client to advertise a maximum size for the server certificate that it is willing to accept.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body: OBE.  Stream 0 is not flow controlled during the handshake.  See #1082.

issues.title: clients always must regenerate client hello
issues.author: jpinner-lyft
issues.body:
The text in Sec 7.1 that details client handling of a version negotiation packet is not accurate:

"Though the contents of a packet might not change in response to version negotiation, a client MUST increase the packet number it uses on every packet it sends."

In particular because the transport parameters must be updated to reflect the version negotiation, the contents of the client initial packet must change. Also the first packet number will never be acknowledged so increasing the packet number by one to signify a retransmission does not make sense.

In particular the packet number should be reinitialized as specified in Sec 5.4.1 since as stated above, new contents must be created.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: This is no longer necessary.  We changed the version negotiation, so clients only need to generate ClientHello in response to a change in QUIC version that is incompatible with their ClientHello.

issues.title: client handling of unknown versions
issues.author: jpinner-lyft
issues.body:
Sec. 7.1 details the server handling for packets with unknown versions but has no mention on client behavior when it receives packets with unknown versions.

An additional requirement should be added that clients must ignore packets with unknown versions.

huitema
comments.body:
@kazuho You wrote:

> ACK for the cleartext packet that carried ClientFinished was sent in a cleartext packet that carried 
> ServerFinished.

That's not what I see in the logs. I see:

  -> Client initial (carries client hello)
  <- Server Clear Text (several message carry server flight, including server finished. Message embed 
       ACK of Client Initial
  -> Client clear text: carries client finished, and ACK of server clear text messages
  <- Server Clear Text: only carries an ACK Frame for the client clear text.

When the server sends the last server clear text message, it has already received the client clear text, since it acknowledges it. According to Ian's presentation of "ACK rules", ACKing a message means that the message was not just received but also processed -- which logically means processing the TLS state machine. I don't see what advantage there is to sending that last acknowledgement in clear text.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body:
Per editors' meeting:  Not only can a server do this, it MUST.  Packets encrypted with the handshake key MUST be acknowledged only in packets encrypted with the handshake key.  Packets encrypted with 0-RTT or 1-RTT keys MUST be acknowledged only in a packet encrypted with the 1-RTT key.  (There might be alternative solutions, and those would be welcome.)

The reason for this is a man-on-the-side attack in which an attacker injects a cleartext packet with the same packet number as a forthcoming 1-RTT packet, causing disagreement between the peers about whether subsequent packets were actually received.  This causes data loss after the handshake is complete by leaving a hole in the received data stream.

comments.author: nibanks
comments.body:
That is not what the spec currently says:
```
8.15.3.  ACK Frames and Packet Protection

   ACK frames that acknowledge protected packets MUST be carried in a
   packet that has an equivalent or greater level of packet protection.
```
Personally, I believe ACK'ing the client finished in either handshake or 1-RTT encrypted packet should be allowed; though if I were to have to pick one, I'd prefer to go with the 1-RTT encrypted.

comments.author: huitema
comments.body: If we want a defense against the clear text injection attack, then we need a better behavior. Because if the source has sent an 1RTT packet, and receives a clear text ACK of the same packet number, that's a protocol error and the connection will be closed. So much for DOS resistance.

issues.author: marten-seemann

The client doesn't check that the version numbers sent in the Version Negotiation Packet exactly match those sent in the Transport Parameters, it just checks that

comments.author: janaiyengar

GQUIC interprets connection ID as a number. We talk about CID as a number and use numeric representations across our tooling. CID has always been a numeric value in GQUIC, and we just went through the pain of converting from little-endian to big-endian representation (on the wire) for this value. 

Every implementation is of course free to do as it pleases, since it's all network-byte-order on the wire and when being fed to the HKDF. So GQUIC can continue doing as it does even if the spec says that this is a bytestring, and *hopefully* nothing will break.

Which brings me to the practical reasons for keeping it as a number. Just as Patrick, we'll continue talking about connection ID 'N' and our tooling will continue referring to it as a 64-bit int. It seems natural to refer to it as a number to avoid confusion between implementations when they need to refer to this in some way for debugging.

IMO, making it a byte-string has no practical value but does seem to have the value of coloring the bikeshed with the "right" color. 

This issue is about changing the existing definition of connection ID -- which inherits GQUIC, where it is a number. I'd like to push back against it because it creates work and/or potential confusion in the future. Keeping it as a number does neither and is my preferred way forward.

(FWIW, calling it a number doesn't mean using it as a number is a useful exercise in any other way. Adding 1 to the connection ID is fun, but doesn't mean anything since the spec doesn't say anything about what that means.)

issues.title: How does QPACK delete horizon interact with pushed streams?
issues.author: afrind
issues.body: QPACK tracks which streams reference a header by keeping a horizon plus additional streams.  All streams lower than the horizon are assumed to reference the header.  Because client initiated streams are odd and push streams are even, the stream space does not increment in a linear fashion.  A client-side decoder, for example, needs to track all the streams that are done processing headers.  When streams 1 and 3 complete, it cannot adjust its horizon to 3, because stream 2 has not completed (it may not even exist, or ever exist).

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
One possible solution is to not use stream IDs at all for tracking QPACK header usage, and instead use a header block sequence number that increments linearly for all header blocks.  

This has a couple advantages in my opinion:

1) fixes the problem with even/odd streams
2) removes the need to treat headers and trailers differently
3) removes transport stream identifier from the compression code

The obvious disadvantage is that it will decrease the compression ratio because the sequence number would need to be included in every compressed header block.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body: Oh this probably doesn't work.  How does a receiver know which header sequences were in a reset transport stream.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body: Technically, since QPACK isn't an adopted draft, this isn't an issue with the current drafts.  If we don't reach a resolution today, I'll probably mark this as "parked."  The most obvious (but ugly) is to add more Stream ID Lists for servers, but I don't like the dichotomy and I don't like adding the bytes needlessly to clients.  We'll need to figure something out here.

issues.author: martinthomson
issues.body:
PADDING frames count toward bytes-in-flight, so they can't be included in ACK-only packets.  This makes it impossible to pad ACK-only packets.  This could prevent some forms of traffic analysis mitigation strategies.

@ekr observes that you could pad with more ACK frames, but that's clunky.

comments.author: ekr
comments.body: Note that if you padded at the crypto layer (see issue #197) then this woud not be a problem.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
@ekr Are you suggesting we remove PADDING from the QUIC layer entirely?  If we needed padding for ACKs, we would have the transport request padding be sent by the crypto layer on stream 0?

That seems really awkward given the simplicity of QUIC padding, and data on stream 0 still counts towards congestion control, so it'd be functionally equivalent.

comments.author: huitema
comments.body:
I do not like the concept that ACKs do not count for bytes in flight. With 255 ranges, ACKs can be almost 800 bytes long, and it is certainly possible to congest a link with just ACK. I understand that we want to be able to send ACK even when blocked by CC, but that does not mean an infinite number of ACK. I would prefer something like extra credits for ACK when blocked by CC, in a controlled way.

I like even less the idea that adding padding to a packet will make acknowledgements mandatory.

And the congestion control argument requires counting padding for CC -- whether included at the framing layer or the AEAD layer. Otherwise, you can send lots of bytes that don't count for CC, and indeed congest the link.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
A suggestion from yesterday's lunch (I believe from @martinduke ) Was to allow a 'small' ack not be congestion controlled(ie: 3 blocks) to ensure forward progress, but require everything else to be.  A different option we discussed was count acks towards congestion control/bytes in flight, but don't prevent them from being sent immediately.

I think Ack congestion control is still a fairly open problem, so I think we'd need to try some of these ideas in the wild if we think they're worth seriously considering for QUIC.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: I share Christian's unease, and would prefer if we could take a serious look at the two options that @ianswett identified.  I like the combination: exempt packets from the block, but only if they a) contain ACK frames, and b) are small.

comments.author: huitema
comments.body: I got my computation slightly wrong. ACK can include 255 blocks. Each block can be up to 9 bytes (mm=3), which means 2295 bytes for 255 blocks. I can't fathom why this would not be included in the bytes-in-flight. And yes, I like the option that @ianswett described. Count the ACK as bytes in flight, but provide extra credits for a couple of small ACK on top of the CWIN.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body:
So what prevents a peer to send lots and lots of small ACK packets? The current form appears to be honor based, and allowing small packets without flow would continue to do so, unless there is some sort of rate limit involved. Small ACK block exception adds some level of complexity.

We don't even know what is supposed to be sent in ACK frames when there is more to be sent than fits in a single frame: https://github.com/quicwg/base-drafts/issues/423 https://github.com/quicwg/base-drafts/issues/764

So what exactly is the problem that ACK flow control is supposed to solve?
(Not saying it is not needed, just that it would be helpful to understand the underlying problem better).

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: What would prevent abuse is a further restriction on the number of ACK-only packets that are permitted to be exempted from the limit (I forgot that bit).  That limit might be expressed in terms of number of packets per RTT, or something like that.  We probably need someone with more congestion controller insight to tell us what a sensible limit might be, of course.

comments.author: mirjak
comments.body: I guess you could see acks as non congestion control transmissions and apply https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc8085#section-3.1 which means to have a rate limit and a circuit breaker.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
To be clear, an abusive implementation can run without congestion control and send a lot more data than just some extra acks.

I believe the concern needs to be whether correct implementations could inadvertently create pathological behaviors, either for themselves or others.

The sender and receiver already have an incentive to send as few and as small acks as possible, so there's no need to ensure some sort of 'fairness'.

The worst part about including ack only packets in bytes in flight is two competing needs:
1) Do not send an ack frame in response to an ack only packet.
2) We need a way to remove frames from bytes in flight, which is to ack them.

Martin, I would say any less than 4 acks per RTT risks degrading performance.  That being said, it's going to depend on the congestion controller.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body: The point is that an abused peer has a clear measure of when to close a connection and possibly blacklist an IP. If there are many other places where this isn't controllable, perhaps it should be. I'm also a bit concerned about abuse during connection establishment and when/how to drop packets.

comments.author: huitema
comments.body:
As pointed out by others, Congestion Control is effectively a sender's choice. What we are writing here is a recommendation, such as "do this and life will be smooth and you will not trip on your own shoelaces." There is no need to get tied up in knots of philosophy, and certainly no need to request unnatural behavior such as "must acknowledge packets if they contain padding". I personally favor three simple rules:

1) Bytes in flights count all bytes in flight, regardless of frame types. 

2) ACKs are not subject to congestion control, but they should be sent parsimoniously during congested periods.

3) A padded pure ACK message is still a pure ACK message. If an ACK of ACK is required, the sender of the ACK should add another frame to the ACK, e.g., PING.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
Thinking through the congestion case further: the only reason you want to send ACK-only packets is when you are passive (you are receiving data, but not sending any).  In which case the other side has ample opportunity to send you acknowledgments.  If you are receiving data that requires acknowledgment, then you are receiving acknowledgments also.  I can't conceive of a valid case where you would be congestion limited, but only sending ACKs for an extended period except a case where the endpoint has an extremely low send rate (low 1000s of bits per second might do it).

That suggests that we might be able to define the limit in absolute terms.  For instance, we could say that you get N octets or N packets in total that are exempt from the congestion limit, a quantity that is replenished every time that you send a packet that isn't blocked by the congestion controller.  Wait long enough and you will be able to send again, even with a ridiculously limited upstream bandwidth.

The risk there is that on these tightly-constrained links, ACKs could consume all available capacity. But I believe that's already true; this would make that marginally worse, but it might actually allow the protocol to continue operation in that sort of environment.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body:
Sensor networks are severely power limited, and sattelite/balloon to ground may also make for an expensive return path due to lack of directed antenna. This does not directly translate into congestion control, but is a bandwidth constraint nonetheless. Perhaps this aspect is under appreciated in general congestion control / bandwidth estimation logic?

For ACK's the flow control is different from stream flow because there is no upstream application consumer - so in principle the receiver has infinite capacity to handle ACKs as long as they reach the receiver timely. However, in praxis too frequent ACK's can be cause network interrupts and unnecessary task switching that can severely constrain a receiver that sends a lot of data to many different connections. Such heavy broadcasters might want to receive as few ACK's as possible.

How all this translates into ACK flow control, if at all, I don't know. But making assumptions on how frequent ACK's ought to be received or should be sent can be misleading due to the above concerns.

comments.author: ianswett
martinduke
comments.body:
@martinthomson I agree that there probably aren't any true deadlock cases, but I can probably construct bad corner cases for performance here.

For instance, Alice is sending to Bob, there are frequent packet number gaps, and Bob is therefore acking liberally. Alice is acking conservatively. I could probably end up pacing Alice->Bob by the rate at which Alice is sending acks to Bob, which in not super intuitive.

comments.author: janaiyengar
comments.body:
I'll note that this isn't new -- TCP has had acks for a while, and while smaller in max size, they are still exempt from congestion control. Two data points are useful here:

(i) We wrote RFC 5690 a while ago, to go through the exercise of trying to figure out reducing ack rates. Many experiments were run and my personal conclusion at the end of the exercise is that reducing ack rate is non-trivial at best, and a big hit on forward path performance at worst. You are welcome to peruse the list of "Possible Complications" that we composed in that RFC.

(ii) We've been doing expeirments on reducing ack rate in GQUIC. Short summary, it hurt performance (on the forward path) with Cubic, but didn't with BBR. I won't go into the reasons here, but it's important to note that an endpoint should not unilaterally decide to reduce it's ack rate because it has implications on the performance of the congestion controller in the opposite direction.

In general, reducing ack rate is very useful exercise, but it has to be done with care because of its interactions with ack-based congestion controllers. I would NOT want to congestion control acks by default. It's non-trivial.

I agree with @ianswett that we shouldn't make specific recommendations on how many bytes are allowed etc.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: The problem with no limit at all is that it doesn't address the concern about the exemption.  Specifically the part where it is unbounded.  Could we make a recommendation, similar to the one we have regarding an initial congestion window?  Outside of extreme corner cases (like the ones I mentioned, or cases like @martinduke described), this should hurt and the cost is only a reduction in throughput for those cases.  I think that we can affort to make the exemption pretty generous.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
I was thinking of recommending something like "When congestion control does not allow sending data, ACK_FRAMEs should be limited to a max of X bytes in size."  One option for X is the max size of a TCP ack frame?  Or the total TCP options space?  Or some arbitrary value.

This allows us to recommend something implementable without doing anything that is too clever.  WDYT?

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
Yeah, that sounds reasonable, but it doesn't limit the rate especially well.

Maybe permit a total overflow of something like a small multiple (2x to 5x) of the size of a typical TCP ACK, and maybe up to INIT_CWND/MSS times (i.e., 4 or 10).  Just multiply the two values out.  Nothing fancy, just a number that is based on things that a) match TCP practice as much as possible, and b) use parameters that reflect current practice as it evolves.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: I think the rate limiting is separate, and should be in the section I'm currently updating in PR#907.  TCP permits acking every packet(unless it only contains an ack), though most implementations do some form of delayed ack, so as long as the size of acks is in the TCP range and we're not sending more often, we're in well explored territory.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
That sounds reasonable to me.

We should be careful though.  QUIC ACK-only packets will be larger than TCP ACKs because of all the overhead.  So we will be sending a bit more.  A minimal ACK frame is 4 octets in QUIC, which isn't bad, but the packet header (13) and AEAD expansion (16) makes it 73 octets in comparison to 40 for a basic TCP ACK.  That's nudging double the size (maybe this gets worse with SACK and extensions, so it's not a big deal).

The consequence being that we might induce congestion more easily if the congestion properties are massively asymmetric.  That's probably not worth any lost sleep, but we might add a note.

comments.author: huitema
comments.body:
As long as we agree that Pad does not require Ack, then I am good. I want to be able to Pad an Ack and not trigger Ack of Ack.

I believe the congestion control issue is a red herring. Congestion control is sender elective. If the sender's cc implementation requires acking a padded packet, just insert a ping!

issues.title: Clarify PADDING vs PING frames
issues.author: igorlord
issues.body: At this point, it looks like the semantics of PADDING and PING frames are identical -- both take exactly 1 byte, both cause ACKs, both count for congestion control, both have no other effect on transport.  Are there any differences (like PING must be ACKed immediately, while PADDING can be ACKed after a delay)?

comments.author: mcmanus
comments.body: why would padding be acked at all? It has no semantic value... (the text is admittedly not clear on this, but it seems like the right resolution.)

comments.author: igorlord
comments.body: I am also looking for a justification for ACKing PADDING.  It was asserted in Seattle that PADDING is ACKed, hence this issue.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: See also #837.  I think that the prohibition on generating ACK in response to ACK doesn't also exclude PADDING.  That's something we need to discuss more.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
I believe PADDING either needs to count for congestion control or not.  If it counts towards congestion control, then it needs to generate ACKs, because otherwise it would never be removed from byte_in_flight and you could get congestion blocked.

I would be concerned about not counting padding towards bytes in flight.  As mentioned before, the only reason ACK only packets are excluded is to avoid the connection from stalling.

comments.author: igorlord
comments.body: @ianswett, why are you worried about not counting PADDING for congestion control?  Are you worried that someone may accidentally add 1KB of padding (because they want all of their packets to be same-sized, for example)?  If so, it is especially as important NOT to ACK PADDING (because you can have the always-pad implementation on both sides of the connection).

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
My number one concern is that if PADDING counts for congestion control, it must be acked.  If it does not count for congestion control, it should not be acked.

I lean towards making PADDING count, because I'd prefer to keep the ACK_FRAME as the only exception.

comments.author: igorlord
comments.body:
> I lean towards making PADDING count, because I'd prefer to keep the ACK_FRAME as the only exception.

Fair enough. Then if there a difference between between PING and PADDING frames? I.e. should we keep both (and why, if we do)?

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
As it stands now, I think we should get rid of one.  But given #837 is also open, I think it makes sense to reach some consensus on what we want the behavior of padding(and ACKs) to be before changing anything in the spec?

If I have time, I'll try to write up an email summarizing the issue and send it to the mailing list.

comments.author: dkg
comments.body:
I lean in the direction of making PADDING not count (and not require an ACK), because i'd like both sides to be able to pad packets that would otherwise be ACK-only without inducing a feedback loop.

That would distinguish PADDING from PING as well.

Another alternative (voiced by @ekr at the interim, possibly facetiously) was to allow/encourage the use of ACK frames as padding in general.

Or, we could allow ACK frames to be arbitrarily large, which would let us use them both as ACK and as PADDING -- that would also let us get rid of PADDING.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
I'd like to keep PADDING distinct from ACK, for applications where ACK is harder to do (i.e. unidirectional flows). Unless I'm misunderstanding and the suggestion is to send ACK for padding when it is not really acking anything.

As to PING vs PADDING, I think I remember some old text, where PING solicited a response PING (aka PONG). That could make it distinct from PADDING but the current text doesn't include that concept.

comments.author: igorlord
comments.body: ACK as PADDING may be technically possible, but I would hate us doing so. First, it is a hack for which there is no good reason (we have enough frame numbers). Second, it is marginally more expensive to process an ACK frame than to skip a PADDING frame.

comments.author: huitema
comments.body: PADDING should be a no-op as far as ACK strategy is concerned. If the sender wanted the packet to be acked, they could swap one of the PADDING bytes for a PING.

comments.author: janaiyengar
comments.body:
I really like @huitema's idea of sending a PING (which is a one-byte frame) to elicit an ACK. If we do that though, I don't think we want to leave it to implementations... this should be mandated, since it's congestion control behavior that we want to mandate. 

We don't want implementations to be more aggressive when using PADDING, which means we want to mandate counting them towards congestion control, which means they need to be ackable.

So, as I'm thinking about this, I'm getting convinced that what we really want is to pad with PING frames. Basically, both PING and PADDING are one-byte frames, and we can add as many of them as we want in a packet. We want both to elicit an ack. I don't see any behavioral difference between these two. We can also require that we count PING frames towards congestion control if we don't already.

comments.author: igorlord
comments.body: @janaiyengar, so "_we really want is to pad with PING frames_" means no padding for ACK-only frames is allowed (because if both sides do that, we have an ACK+PING ping-pong).  I am not saying this is bad, if one can pad in crypto layer.  I know that some people will bring up privacy as a reason to pad ACK-only frames somewhere.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: Padding in the crypto layer is still padding and hence bytes on the wire.  I think we should have a consistent story for padding, regardless of whether it's in QUIC or in TLS, rather than treating TLS padding as an entirely different beast.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: I believe this should be resolved with the resolution of #837

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body: I think it would be useful with text stating that PING should be ack'ed ASAP.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
PADDING doesn't elicit ACK.  PING does.

A packet containing only ACK and PADDING counts towards bytes-in-flight.  But that means that you will consume bytes-in-flight by sending these, and maybe never an ACK.  So, send a PING sometimes, and you get your bytes-in-flight back.

comments.author: igorlord
comments.body: Ok.  This is not what "Special Considerations for Packetization Layer PMTU Discovery" section says.  I'll s/PADDING/PING/g in that section in my PR.

comments.body: This should be fixed by #1517 and #1540

issues.title: Version negotiation responses and FNV-1a protection
issues.author: larseggert
issues.body:
Reading the specs, it wasn't clear to me that version negotiation responses are not protected by FNV-1a. This should IMO be explicitly called out.

draft-tls says

> QUIC adds an integrity check to all cleartext packets.

and draft-transport says

> Cleartext packets are sent during the handshake prior to key negotiation.

Neither if which made it obvious to me that a version negotiation response was excluded.

(And out of curiosity - why isn't there an FNV-1a? Seems like an odd special case?)

comments.author: jpinner-lyft
comments.body:
Not saying that this couldn't be more clear in the spec; however, Sec. 5.3 defines the version negotiation packet and Sec 5.4 defines the "cleartext" packets and states the requirement for including an integrity check. Subsections 5.4.1 through 5.4.4 then define the four "cleartext" packets.

Again I agree that the fact that the spec defines "cleartext packets" as not all packets that are not encrypted is confusing.

Does this become moot point if FNV-1a is replaced with an AEAD cipher?

issues.title: Handling of connection ID in handshake creates corner cases
issues.author: huitema

comments.author: RyanTheOptimist
comments.body:
In some near future, server "clear text" packets will be encrypted with a
key based on the client's connection ID, I believe. In such a scenario, I
would expect that the message from connection #1 would be ignored by the
client's connection #2 because the packet will not decrypt correctly. Does
that sound right to you?

comments.author: huitema
comments.body: @RyanAtGoogle no, encrypting with the connection ID will not be sufficient. According to the spec, the Client Initial carries the client-chosen initial connection ID, but the Server Clear text carries the server chosen connection ID, which the client is supposed to adopt and then use for all consecutive packets. So the client will read the connection ID from the message header, and use it to decrypt the message. It will work, whether using connection ID #1 or #2.

comments.author: huitema
comments.body:
What might work is, look for an ACK Frame in the incoming Server Clear Text, and check that the "largest acknowledged" sequence number matches the sequence number of the client initial packet. Ignore the Server Clear text (and do not update the connection ID) if it does not carry an acknowledgement, or if the acknowledged number does not match the client initial sequence number. But this is not what the spec currently says:
>  5.4.3. Server Cleartext Packet
>
> A Server Cleartext packet uses long headers with a type value of 0x04. It is used to carry acknowledgments and cryptographic handshake messages from the server.
>
> The connection ID field in a Server Cleartext packet contains a connection ID that is chosen by the server (see Section 5.6).
>
> The first Server Cleartext packet contains a randomized packet number. This value is increased for each subsequent packet sent by the server as described in Section 5.7.
>
> The payload of this packet contains STREAM frames and could contain PADDING and ACK frames.

So, if we want to be robust, we may need to update that text: mandate that servers insert an ACK frame in the Server Clear Text, and allow clients to check for presence and value of the ACK frame.

issues.title: Long header variants for 1-RTT protected packets
issues.author: martinthomson
issues.body:
These should be removed for (at least) two reasons:

Firstly, there should only be one way to do anything, if possible.  This makes it possible to encode the same information two ways.

Perhaps more substantially, because it would make WebRTC easier.  In discussions about using QUIC for WebRTC, we found that there were several options for multiplexing designs that are feasible with QUIC.  One of the most difficult parts of that was ensuring that once the handshake was complete, QUIC packets could be distinguished easily from other packets.  

I think that during the handshake people are prepared to rely on checksums, and other such things, but in the steady state demultiplexing on the first octet would be ideal.  See [RFC 7983](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7983) for more about this.

Right now, the two 1-RTT protected long header encodings collide with RTP and need more sophisticated handling to correctly identify.  Some tweaking of the type field might avoid that, but it could preclude greasing and effectively constrain what we can do with QUIC.  It would be easier to rely on the packets using the short header.  The short header only potentially collides with DTLS (which would not be used in this case) and STUN (which are infrequent enough that they can use the STUN hash or magic number to identify correctly - something Google already do).

@pthatcherg or @aboba can expand on the reasons, or explain some of their alternative designs.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body: I has always bothered me that the choice of short/long headers was arbitrary.

comments.author: csperkins
comments.body: This is also issue #426

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: Sounds good, I can't come up with a reason to keep them.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: This might help with #426, but maybe not completely.  Short headers still potentially conflict with ZRTP, for example.  I'd keep #426 open even if we resolve this.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: If we really care about conflicting with WebRTC during the handshake, we have enough long header codepoints to avoid those codepoints in QUIC.  I'd prefer not to avoid codepoints post-handshake, however, since that eliminates the possibility of post-handshake type byte greasing.

comments.author: janaiyengar
comments.body:
There is a good reason for this to exist: out-of-band key negotiation. I'll remind folks that transport negotiation is distinct from the TLS handshake -- we've taken pains to try and keep TLS separate from QUIC -- and you might have 1-RTT keys available when you are starting your transport connection.

On demuxing WebRTC and QUIC packets, that is a separate conversation. I outlined a couple of ideas in #426 and we could have that conversation separately, although we did agree in Paris that we'd add a framing layer if necessary later and closed the issue.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
Why can't the client use the Initial packet for its first packet in that case?  That would ensure that the server can generate a Version Negotiation packet if it needs to.

It's very hard to know what your design is - you seem to assume a particular design, but since we aren't discussing it in any detail, I don't know whether you actually *need* these long-form packets.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: Oh, I forgot to add: If you really need these, then your out-of-band key negotiation variant of QUIC is welcome to define them.  (Again, assuming that you have a different version number so that this is possible.)

comments.author: janaiyengar
comments.body:
Having thought about this some more, it's actually ok to do this. It's not "my variant" of QUIC, it's a general use case that uses out-of-band key exchange. I've tried to explain this in the past.
