comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
I realize that I was the one to be persuaded that this cross-protocol resumption is a good idea, but I've since concluded that, unless we revise ALPN, this is unwise.

This is not a problem at all if you intend to do simple resumption without 0-RTT, but it gets complicated thereafter.

The way that TLS works assumes that the ALPN value is remembered by the server (note that remembering often means embedding it in the ticket, that detail doesn't matter here).  It uses this remembered value to decide what protocol the client is speaking.  If it accepts 0-RTT, it assumes that the protocol hasn't change.  The server also can't change the protocol if it accepts 0-RTT.

We created an equivalency between h2/TLS and hq/QUIC in the quic-tls draft.  That seems like a great idea until you consider the potential for a similar equivalency between h2 and hqv2 (or whatever we call the next version).  A client that makes a QUIC connection and resumes from h2 might advertise [hq, hqv2] in its handshake, and the server has to assume that the packets are hq.  In other words, the equivalency is 1-1.  That limits our ability to deploy new protocol versions.

The same considerations apply in the reverse direction.

I think that we should drop this feature and instead develop a new document that describes two things: 

* explicit advertisement of support for different protocols for 0-RTT.  That might use ALPN in the NewSessionTicket message, or a new extension.
* a means of the client signaling which of the selected protocols it is using for early data.  This might be as simple as saying that the first entry in ALPN is what is in use, or it could use a new extension.

That sort of design has the virtue of restricting the resumption to TLS 1.3 or higher as well.  (BTW, I thought that we had a hard rule about keeping the version the same for resumption.)

Ignoring it completely seems bad, and I'm not sure why we'd exit draining due to an address change?

comments.author: siyengar
comments.body: the connection close could be 1MSS big because of the close reason, and it seemed kind of icky to send a connection close to a random unauthenticated source address someone could send us a small packet and we would send them a larger connection close while the connection is draining. The client may have legitimately transition to a new address due to nat rebinding, however there would be no way to tell. That's the reason just exiting draining might be 1 legitimate option.

comments.author: siyengar
comments.body: Similarly we recommend in the doc that you can get rid of all state except just the close packet while in draining. So if you can't verify the packet correctly, then it would make sense to ignore it because we don't want to verify and let the peer go into idle_timeout

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
If you send a connection close, I believe there's a recommendation to use exponential backoff, and the sender decides how large the packet is, so amplification factor shouldn't be a concern.

I'm confused by "if you can't verify the packet correctly, then it would make sense to ignore it because we don't want to verify and let the peer go into idle_timeout".  Avoiding idle timeout involves sending something, either a connection close or public reset.

Honestly, I think the best approach is to do what implementations will likely do by default, which is to send a connection close if you're still storing it and then transition to sending public reset when you've decided to discard the old connection close.

comments.author: siyengar
comments.body: i don't think implementations will send the packets to the new address by default. In connection close state we have the choice of whether or not to bind to the new client address or not, or keep the old address. Implementations will probably bind to the old address by default, at least that's what I do by default, and while implementing close, this question came to me.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
The stateless reset text says:
"A stateless reset is provided as an option of last resort for a server that does not have access to the state of a connection. A server crash or outage might result in clients continuing to send data to a server that is unable to properly continue the connection. A server that wishes to communicate a fatal connection error MUST use a CONNECTION_CLOSE or APPLICATION_CLOSE frame if it has sufficient state to do so."

To me, that indicates a server should send a connection close if it's possible/straightforward to look that up.  If not, send a stateless reset.  If you have editorial suggestions for this text, feel free to send out a PR.

comments.author: siyengar
comments.body: looks like we resolved with a drop here https://github.com/quicwg/base-drafts/pull/965

issues.title: Can PUSH_PROMISE rules be relaxed to allow sending on a control stream?
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
Reading the latest HTTP/QUIC editor's copy. Section 4.4 on server push states that:

> The PUSH_PROMISE frame is sent on a response stream.

The recent changes in this area have moved away from Stream ID, PUSH_PROMISE frames now reference a Push ID. Push cancellation is achieved by the HTTP/QUIC CANCEL_PUSH frame, which is restricted to the control stream. 

So I got to wondering if there may be benefits allowing/restricting HTTP/QUIC PUSH_PROMISE frames on the control stream. It seems to me that CANCEL_PUSH forces implementations to be geared up for managing server push on the control stream anyway.

Maybe I'm missing the benefit of tying pushes to requests, RFC 7540 talks about the requirements but I can't infer the benefits. Relaxing the rule and incorporating something like cache digests might give an appropriately-configured server enough information to push just the correct things with a bit more performance (it is described as unsolicited right?). Another use case is to allow server push without having to hold streams open.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: Ordering of PUSH_PROMISE relative to other activity in a response is critical.  Ideally, a URL arrives after a PUSH_PROMISE, or the client might make another request that duplicates the push.  It's very hard for a server to decide to cancel a request on the basis that a push is outgoing, because it can't know whether the client really wanted a second request, so we rely on ordering.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
>  It's very hard for a server to decide to *cancel a request* on the basis that a push is outgoing, because it can't know whether the client really wanted a second request, so we rely on ordering.

For clarification, are you saying it's hard for a server to cancel a second request, because the server can't know if the client really wanted the second request?

(Edited: fixed typo where I used push instead of request).

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
> Ordering of PUSH_PROMISE relative to other activity in a response is critical. Ideally, a URL arrives after a PUSH_PROMISE, or the client might make another request that duplicates the push.

Hmm, now I think about it, RFC 7540 Section 8.2.1 does say that "The server SHOULD send PUSH_PROMISE frames prior to sending any frames that reference the promised responses. This avoids a race where clients issue requests prior to receiving any PUSH_PROMISE frames". HTTP/2 relied on TCP to provide send-order reception guarantees. Since QUIC cannot guarantee ordering across streams (but does provide in-order delivery within a stream) sending PUSH_PROMISE on the response stream can help towards this requirement. So a simple way to address my initial comment would be to directly qualify the sentence with text, a reference to Section 8.2.1 or both.

However, I could also argue that the race condition issues could be less pronounced for HTTP/QUIC due to the CANCEL_PUSH semantic that didn't previously exist. A sensible SHOULD would place PUSH_PROMISE on the request stream but there be cases where a request-less push on the control stream could be of benefit.

I'd also like to say that I think the current design is clever. The spec already goes to some lengths to help accommodate request concurrency and out-of-order delivery. I really like the approach for allowing multiple PUSH_PROMISE frames to use the same PUSH ID.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
An important property of pushes is their association with other requests.  We discussed uncoupled pushes during the development of HTTP/2 and it made it very difficult for a stack that has multiple clients to decide which of those clients will receive the push.  Though there might be cases where ordering is less critical, but I don't know how to justify adding extra complexity.

Happy to add clarification about the ordering rationale.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
Intermediaries perhaps feel particular pain. Some might say that Service Worker shines a new light on old problems.

So I think you've convinced me in the general case. In practical terms, a request object primitive is a pretty useful thing, especially for implementations that already use such a paradigm (perhaps also why H2 or HQ frames that operate at application-level have some difficulty gaining traction and header fields are preferred). Request/response is also great for implementations that like to minimise state. 

The great replies from @MikeBishop on other issues I've raised have also given me greater insight to this section. Where is says:

> The PUSH_PROMISE frame is sent on a response stream.

I think the term "response stream" is left over from the old @martinthomson unidirectional PR. This is the only occurrence of the term and in the current context of HTTP/QUIC doesn't make much sense.

In actuality, the PUSH_PROMISE frame is sent on the client-initiated, bidirectional stream that carried the request that generated the push. I think thats the only form allowed (i.e. you can't send PUSH_PROMISE on a server-initiated unidirectional or bidirectional stream). I might be arguing now that the current definition is **not strict enough** in mandating on what streams PUSH_PROMISE can be sent on.

Once that gets clarified, I think the idea of sending PUSH_PROMISE on server-initiated unidirectional streams (the control stream to name one) falls outside the general case but may help special use cases. Would there be aversion to a HTTP/QUIC extension that modifies semantics to allow such use cases?

issues.title: CANCEL_PUSH frame payload ambiguity
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
HTTP/QUIC says:

> The CANCEL_PUSH frame carries a Push ID encoded as a variable-length integer. The Push ID identifies the server push that is being cancelled (see Section 5.2.6).
_..snip.._
A server MUST treat a CANCEL_PUSH frame payload does not contain exactly one variable-length integer as a connection error of type HTTP_MALFORMED_CANCEL_PUSH.

The first sentence implies that a single Push ID is carried in the payload. The last sentence (filling in the missing-word typo) could imply that multiple Push IDs can be carried in the payload but that servers must reject such frames.

It might help to be more explicit and include a figure for the payload. This provides consistency with the PRIORITY and PUSH_PROMISE sections which also refer to the Push ID.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body:
The last sentence indicates that the length of the frame could be mismatched (too long or too short) with there being exactly one variable-length integer, and if that happens then all bets are off on the interpretation of the frame.  I'm not sure how that would be more explicit, but feel free to propose text.

We generally don't put figures for frames that contain a single field, though some of the PRs have added that.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
> The last sentence indicates that the length of the frame could be mismatched (too long or too short) with there being exactly one variable-length integer, and if that happens then all bets are off on the interpretation of the frame. I'm not sure how that would be more explicit, but feel free to propose text.

I see where you are coming from. I'd be happy to propose a PR(s) but don't want to go off in a wrong direction. Please let me know what you think after reading the following.

> A server MUST treat a CANCEL_PUSH frame payload does not contain exactly one variable-length integer as a connection error of type HTTP_MALFORMED_CANCEL_PUSH.

Is this specific to the server, or applicable to either endpoint that receives a frame mismatch? Unless I misunderstand something special with varints (elsewhere the spec mentions truncation), the condition seems overly specific. I.e. The format is defined as exactly one varint, so any deviation from that is malformed and leads to an error with a suitable code.

I noticed that HTTP_MALFORMED_CANCEL_PUSH frame error is undefined. Probably just slipped through the net. Looking a bit deeper, I see that the HTTP/QUIC pattern is to define a named error code for each frame type, in contrast QUIC Transport defines a generic frame error code (FRAME_FORMAT_ERROR 0x7) and then a specific frame error codespace (FRAME_ERROR 0x1XX, where the last octet expresses the frame type). I wonder if such an approach might also be suitable for HTTP/QUIC e.g. HTTP_FRAME_ERROR.

I have no problem not diagramming single field frames. I admit to not noticing that convention until you pointed it out but it makes sense.

I think what confused me slightly is the general document layout regarding server push and push ID. The first instances of the Push ID term are in Section 4.3 and 4.4 which reference 5.2.6. Unfortunately, 5.2.6 entangles the general description of what is Push ID, with how it's used in the PUSH_PROMISE frame. Section 4.4 includes guidance on using Push ID without defining what it is.

So I wonder if it might help to extract out a common definition of Push ID (varint, used in X,Y,Z frames etc) into section 4.4. Then specific sections can specialise their usage of Push ID as required.

issues.title: "Push Stream Header" term and carriage
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
HTTP/QUIC section 4.4 says:

> A push stream is a server-initiated, unidirectional stream. A push stream includes a header (see Figure 1) that identifies the PUSH_PROMISE that it fulfills. This header consists of a Push ID, encoded as a variable-length integer. The Push ID identifies a server push (see Section 5.2.6).

I'm finding the term push stream header a little obtuse because it isn't a QUIC frame header, an HTTP/QUIC frame header, an HTTP header, nor an HPACK header-block, and all of those are in scope for a push. Since it could just be me, I don't have any alternatives to suggest at this stage.

I think what the text is saying is that a push stream is a sequence of QUIC STREAM frames, the first frame must contain the push stream header directly. In other words, there is no additional HTTP/QUIC framing for this (although I do wonder if an INITIATE_PUSH frame, that includes the Push ID might be way more explicit (at the cost of framing overhead)).

> After the push stream header, a push contains a response (Section 4.2), with response headers, a response body (if any) carried by DATA frames, then trailers (if any) carried by HEADERS frames.

For clarity, I wonder if it might be better to say:

_After the push stream header, a push contains a response (Section 4.2), with response header fields carried by HEADERS frames, a response body (if any) carried by DATA frames, then trailer fields (if any) carried by HEADERS frames._

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body:
Let's back up a second.  QUIC streams are bytestreams as far as the application is concerned.  It has no knowledge or dependency on how the bytestream is segmented for transport.  So the sequence of bytes on the stream is:

  - Stream header (only for push streams at the moment, might expand)
  - HTTP/QUIC Frames

In Martin's original unidirectional proposal, all streams had stream headers identifying the type of stream.  Currently only push streams have them, but a reasonable argument can be made for putting them on the control stream as well.  They're probably necessary if the header compression algorithm has its own control channels, too, so you can differentiate between types of unidirectional streams.

Once the dust settles on that, I'll probably reorganize to describe that the header exists on unidirectional streams, followed by a sequence of frames to the end of the stream.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
Right, thanks for me reminding me of that unidirectional PR. I can see now the bits that were migrated over. The confusing bits in the current HTTP/QUIC doc (from my perspective) are the absence of generic definition of what a stream header is (hard when there is just one and it only contains one field), and the overloading of Push ID for different uses. 

With a better understanding of the area, I think some of the problem would be alleviated with some restructure of section 4.4 and 5.2.6 as described on #948.

The rest is resolvable once the dust settles as you say. I have no strong opinion on if this ticket should be kept open or closed.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: I think @martinthomson intended to close this ticket with #957 (looks like GH failed to do it automatically).

issues.title: Disparity between initial_max_stream_id and MAX_STREAM_ID
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
First off, I don't know if this is really an issue. 

With the introduction of varint and unidirectional streams, there seems to be a disparity between the initial_max_stream_id TransportParameter

> The initial maximum stream ID parameter contains the initial maximum stream number the peer may initiate, encoded as an unsigned 32-bit integer. 

and MAX_STREAM_ID

>ID of the maximum unidirectional or bidirectional peer-initiated stream ID for the connection encoded as a variable-length integer. The limit applies to unidirectional steams if the second least signification bit of the stream ID is 1, and applies to bidirectional streams if it is 0.

Which one is "better"?

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body: Duplicate of #909.

issues.title: Define or cite NAT rebinding
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
The QUIC Transport and Management documents makes several references to the term "NAT rebinding". With my pedant hat on, I was surprised to find no concise definition or citation to an expanded definition. Basic Google searching didn't help much either.

Given that this came up during Singapore as something that is important to mitigate, it seem like it would be useful to define.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: Is there any opinion on this? Or should it be closed out because it's not seen as an issue?

issues.title: Clarify normative language for Transport Parameter omit_connection_id
issues.author: igorlord
issues.body:
Presently, there is no normative language for Transport Parameter omit_connection_id.

I would like to propose replacing "can" with a normative "MAY".  It is important that this MAY is specified, so the endpoints do not consider it an error (or even a warning), when their omit_connection_id is ignored.

Servers that identify connections using Connection ID (and not a 4-tuple) need to send that Connection ID, so they can attribute an ICMP Error with the correct connection.  (While IPv4 ICMP Error definition makes including UDP packet data optional, many routers still include it, and it is mandatory in IPv6 ICMPv6.)

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
I think that we're headed for a different design.  One that needs a write-up and a bunch of discussion.  So hold that thought.

In short, the idea would be to define a new transport parameter for connection ID that determines what connection ID (if any) is used for packets with the short header.  Long header packets would use the client-chosen value.

comments.author: igorlord
comments.body: That's fine. In this case, please, take this as an input for the updated write-up. Any endpoint that identifies connections using a Connection ID requires that Connection ID in packets, including ICMP Error packets. Hence, that endpoint will not only request the peer to send Connection IDs but will also include Connection IDs on outgoing packets (in case they result in an ICMP Error packet).  Such ICMP Error packets are required for PMTU discovery, among other things,.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: The ICMP thing is new.  Can you raise that as an issue?  The thinking thus far has been that servers could send packets without a connection ID.  But if it is important for the server to receive (and match) ICMP, then it will want to send with a connection ID (it's still something that a server could unilaterally decide to do, even if the client allowed the server to omit a connection ID).

comments.author: igorlord
comments.body:
Hm.  That was the point of this Issue -- to declare that sending a Connection ID despite of a permission not to do so is something that a server MAY do via normative language. The goal is to make sure that clients are not surprised at all by this behavior (i.e. do not log warnings, etc).

An issue about this is more of an issue for the applicability draft.  I'll raise it there.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
My experience is that ICMP is typically implemented by 5-tuple and given 5-tuples are usually stable over a short period of time, so nothing special needs to be done there. 

For example, in GQUIC, we do see write errors on the server side when we write a packet that's too large, and those appear to be caused by the Linux kernel converting the ICMP message into a constraint on the max packet size.

comments.author: igorlord
comments.body: If you are routing by ConnectionID, you need to deliver that ICMP to the server that sent the QUIC  packet that caused the ICMP error packet.  The 5-tuple will not help w/o a ConnectionID in the message.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: Can you not fall back to 5-tuple routing when connection ID is not present?

comments.author: janaiyengar
comments.body: I don't see a problem with saying that a server MAY include connection ID even if the client says omit_connection_id, so this is reasonable to do. However, I don't understand the motivating use case. ICMP includes only 8 bytes of the IP datagram, which is basically the UDP header. The connection ID will not be echoed even if it is present in the offending packet. How do you get the connection ID in the ICMP message?

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: There is an extended ICMP unreachable that includes more, but I doubt that's deployed widely enough to rely on.  @igorlord, how do you believe that this would be helpful?

comments.author: igorlord
comments.body: @janaiyengar and @martinthomson, ICMPv6 includes a lot more bytes, so it can be used; some routers include more bytes for ipv4, so that can be used as well. It is true that most often you will not see the connection ID in ICMP (ipv4), but I want to make use of that connection ID in cases when it is useful. Hence, I want to be absolutely sure that clients are ready for the server ignoring omit_connection_id.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: @igorlord, would you mind creating a PR that clarifies this point?

comments.author: igorlord
comments.body: Sure, @martinthomson. Would you expect the PR to include just the normative language, or the justification for it as well?

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: The text should say that if the parameter is present, the recipient MAY omit the connection ID from packets it sends with the short header.  I don't think we need anything else.

comments.author: janaiyengar
comments.body: Yup, agree with @martinthomson

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: Closed by #980.

issues.title: Specify QUIC protocol fallback to TCP.
issues.author: emile22
issues.body:
Fallback is used by the endpoints when a QUIC connection fails.
The protocol specification should define when QUIC fallback occur (establishment, during the live time of a connection...) and detail how it works (delay before attempting to reconnect in QUIC ...).

comments.author: marten-seemann
comments.body: I don't think fallback to TCP should be part of the protocol specification. **Some** applications might use such a fallback for **a limited amount of time**. Other applications might choose to deploy QUIC-only right from the beginning.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
I think there are significant drawbacks to mandating or specifying TCP.

1) Application mapping such as DNS/QUIC don't naturally fullback to TCP.
2) TCP fullback maybe reflects a simple view where a host just advertises itself as a HTTP/QUIC alternative. More complex deployment may Alt-Svc to other hosts that listen on UDP only. The network path to such hosts may be configured for UDP only.
3) For HTTP/QUIC, fallback is really a function of Alt-Svc fullback. I.e. fallback to the origin that advertised the HTTP/QUIC endpoint. Strategies for this in Alt-Svc are loosely defined and I would say are implementation specific.
4) TCP fullback is a security consideration. Attack vectors such as version downgrade may become more attractive if standardised. In a scenario where QUIC is a prime transport protocol and receives continued security evolution, fallback to TCP (and TLS packet protection) requires effort to maintain equivalent security.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
Fallback to TCP isn't a property of QUIC.  As others have said, the protocol that uses QUIC might vary in its requirement.

HTTP/QUIC uses alternative services to upgrade, so naturally it means that TCP is used as part of the bootstrapping process and TCP connections will be used if the QUIC-based alternative goes away.

issues.title: Is fallback to TCP part of QUIC invariant ?
issues.author: emile22
issues.body:
Currently QUIC headers don't provide the information for on-path troubleshooting of the network performance. When the QoS decreases badly endpoints fallback from QUIC to TCP. This behavior enable network troubleshooting  with legacy TCP monitoring tools. 
Will the endpoints support the fallback to TCP for all the versions of the QUIC protocol  ?

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: This is not an invariant.  There already are cases when QUIC does not need to fall back to TCP on private networks.

issues.title: Ack delay in SRTT computation
issues.author: janaiyengar
issues.body:
The recovery draft (and GQUIC) use ack delay in SRTT computations, but with the caveat that "the ack delay field from the ACK frame SHOULD be subtracted from the RTT as long as the result is positive." 

The ack delay may be too large if the peer's clock was adjusted, but it can also happen if the peer uses a very granular clock, which can lead to arbitrarily large ack delays.

There are a few ways to deal with this, including:
1. current text, which simply drops the problematic ack delays,
2. ignore ack delays from a peer that screws up once (ack delay > measured RTT),
3. ignore RTT sample that contains problematic ack delay.

(1) is a bit aggressive. (2) is conservative: If ack delay is screwed up then you won't always be able to detect it, but once can be treated as a signal to not trust this peer's ack delays. (3) has been proposed but I'm not sure it addresses the right thing -- the RTT sample isn't bad, the ack delay is.

I'm leaning towards (2).

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
If your first theory is correct, this is due to clock jump, then 2 seems like the wrong approach, since it means one bad ack delay is likely to be isolated.

4. An improvement to #1 might be to ignore the ack delay any time the resulting RTT is less than min_rtt.  We'd have to define min_rtt, which we currently don't, but that puts a tighter bound on reasonable use of ack delay than just 'must result in a positive RTT signal'.  This makes it much harder to intentionally use the ack delay to manipulate the peer's SRTT, which seems nice.

So I lean towards 4 and I think my least favorite is 4, the more I think about it, because I fear going a long time without an RTT sample, and the goal should be to never be worse than TCP's RTT signaling.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: One more improvement could be to limit the ack delay to the max_ack_delay, once it's communicated via transport params.  #912

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
I actually like the fourth option here.  min_rtt is a value worth tracking, and it could still be calculated based on actual flight times (i.e., the value before subtracting the ack delay).  Then you only train min_rtt on a value that is harder to fake.  It only leaves you open to the peer sending opportunistic acks, essentially, which is pretty risky for an implementation that does that.  Then your RTT calculations can't drive RTT below that floor.  You still have to guard against negative values, which might still happen, but that guard might be coincident with the min_rtt guard.

Why we insist on using wall clocks for this sort of thing is beyond me, but that's the state of the world today.

comments.author: marten-seemann
comments.body:
Why is min_rtt the value based on actual flight times (before subtracting the ack delay)? Subtracting the ack delay will decrease this value, so the real rtt will be larger than min_rtt.

We should consider the attack where a peer sends ack delays such that the rtt will end up very close to 0. That way, the other side would increase the congestion window, and also allocate more receive buffer space (assuming it does flow-control tuning). One variant of this attack could also be sending ack delay times that are *always* bigger than the actual RTT, so that the other side doesn't have any useful RTT measurement at all.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
The idea here (I think) is to remove the exposure to the ack delay being inflated (either by malice or by accident) when calculating min_rtt.  You can still measure RTT based on packet arrival times if you assume that the peer can't opportunistically send ACKs.

The observed RTT would then have a lower bound.  That lower bound might be higher than the actual minimum RTT, but it will be less exposed to manipulation through tweaking the ack delay field.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
Because min_rtt never increases, and at least some of your RTT samples are likely to have essentially 0 ack delay, it's much safer to not consider ack delay.

And as you mention Marten, it'd be pretty easy to set the peer's min_rtt to 0 otherwise.

In practice, GQUIC used to allow ack delay to be included in min_rtt, and every once in a while this resulted in an RTT very close to 0 and some weird issues for the bits of code that actually the min_rtt.  Not allowing ack delay to be considered has been much safer and seems to result in much more realistic min_rtt values, based on looking at traces.

Take a look at #975 for a writeup of this.

issues.title: Handshake packets should be retransmitted based on the last sent handshake packet
issues.author: ianswett
issues.body: Instead of using time_of_last_sent_packet, handshake packets should use time_of_last_sent_handshake_packet(to be defined), because if the handshake hasn't completed, protected packets will not be acknowledged, because they cannot be decrypted and processed.  The only other valid frames to send pre-handshake are acks and connection close.  Acks do not cause an acknowledgement and connection closes are terminal.

comments.author: siyengar
comments.body: +1, this is a follow up to my comment in your PR?

issues.title: One packet type in invariants
issues.author: MikeBishop
issues.body: The set of packet types is version-dependent, *except* that Version Negotiation has a fixed packet type across all versions.  We could make packet types entirely version-dependent by a simple change:  Version Negotiation packets always indicate a version of '0', and the type field is randomized on send / ignored on receipt.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body: If we land #939 first, we have the option of saying that version 0 packets don't have a packet number and saving a few bytes, but the question is open whether we want to have what becomes a third packet header.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
I think that it makes sense to continue to mark Version Negotiation as long.  Otherwise there is some amount of guessing required to find the Version field.  That suggests that it continues to use that bit, but that doesn't necessarily constrain us to the use of a particular type beyond that.

The expected order of operations for receipt of a packet is to check the long header bit, then to check the version.  Once that is done, we could say that the type is ignored.  That means we could make it entirely randomized (which effectively destroys our future ability to use those bits), a specific value (which would allow us to generate other signals for clients that support future versions if we specified that packets are ignore if other values are found there), or define a more specific scheme.

I don't think that there is any value in versioning version negotiation.  That way leads to madness.  I'm ambivalent about random vs. specific value.

comments.author: marten-seemann
comments.body: Defining a fixed value for the type byte of the version negotiation packet has the nice property that for the client, the only thing you need to do when parsing a packet header is look at the type byte (it's the same principle I'm arguing for in #426).

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body:
That's a desire I'm sympathetic to, but a packet inherently cannot be self-describing from the first byte unless you already know what version you're interpreting the first byte against.  I'm willing to take a slightly slower path in the cases where that's not true.

On a client, that's less of a problem (I think), because at any given time, there are at most two versions you could get -- the one you sent, or version negotiation.  That means that the type value could be quasi-invariant -- it's version-dependent, except that some value has to be reserved for version negotiation, but since the server obviously didn't speak your version that value has to be fixed across versions.  I don't like something being kinda-sorta-invariant, but it would work.

On a server, where you come into an initial packet with no advance knowledge of the connection's version, the space is huge, so the process *must* be to find the long header bit, find the version field, and then either start version negotiation (if you don't recognize it) or begin version-specific parsing (if you do).  Servers will have to look at more than the first byte to establish the expected packet layout.

And if we're willing to say that you have to look at the version field to figure out the packet layout, then I think the requirement becomes:

- From the first byte, you can identify the location of the Version field
- If you already know the version, you can identify the packet layout from the first byte (but please verify the version)

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body:
I'd argue for testing long header bit, then check for version 0 and for other known versions.

I'd argue against randommizing the type byte for version 0. The reason being that it makes it difficult to multiplex other protocols over the same connection. QUIC version numbers may also be chosen very carefully to avoid conflicts with other protocols where there might be conflicts beyond the first byte when the high bit is set.

comments.author: janaiyengar
comments.body: I agree with @MikeBishop. I don't think there's a need to specify the order of processing things, but thank you for laying it out clearly. That said, randomizing it right now will conflict with the same types that #956 seeks to avoid. Greasing the packet type will run into that, so we'll need to specify carefully how to grease this byte.

comments.author: huitema
comments.body:
I would rather use a constant value, and actually keep the version negotiation type that we have already defined. Yes, this will constrain further versions to not redefine that type. But then, so what?

I am also very lukewarm about the idea of making packet types version dependent, e.g. having sometimes the client initial be 17 and some times 29. That will require implementations to insert some level of indirection between the abstract types used internally and the type in the wire format. This looks like gratuitous complexity.

I like the idea of removing the dependency on the sequence number. That's a clear benefit, since implementations cannot guarantee that they can parse sequence numbers from unsupported versions.

comments.author: janaiyengar
janaiyengar
comments.body:
@marten-seemann : I agree that it's simpler with simply a type byte, but honestly I don't think it's much more complex with a version field in the picture as well. It's a bit of getting used to, but the value is in the clarity about the type field being entirely version-dependent, for both long and short header packets (which it almost was, but this makes it entirely so.)

Importantly, making the type field version dependent and stating it as such hopefully forces middleboxes to actually pay attention to the version field, and middlebox implementers to read the spec. This is a big part of greasing -- to ensure that implementers have to go read the spec to figure out how to parse packets instead of looking for patterns on the wire -- and having types be different across versions helps, IMO.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
I'm a pretty big fan of this change on a high level.  In particular, it forces implementations to actually implement version specific parsing, and the removal of the packet number reinforces the idea that everything after the version is not an invariant.

I'll note: If we have a version, and then there's only one defined type byte value, but it's valid to grease the type byte for that version, we end up with the type byte being random :)  So I favor randomizing the type byte, but could live without it.

comments.author: huitema
comments.body: OK, so I actually did an implementation of the version dependent header parsing. I agree that once this version dependent parsing is done, using version=0 to define renegotiation packets makes sense.

comments.author: huitema
comments.body: Some implementation experience. In the current state, greasing the version ID is a bit hard. The server will correctly handle a version ID that it does not understand, and will copy the incoming version ID into the version field of the negotiation packet's header. But the client that does the greasing has to make a wild guess -- it cannot really parse the type field, because this is version dependent, and it cannot really predict what kind of encoding the server used. Testing V==0 would be cleaner.

comments.body:
@huitema: Thank you for trying out an implementation and for sharing what you learned, that is very helpful!

issues.title: ACK Frames should be in Increasing Packet Number Order
issues.author: nibanks
issues.body:
The ACK frame consists of blocks in decreasing packet number order and, now that they use variable-length integers, processing these ACK blocks in reverse order is no longer feasible.

Generally, I feel that ACK blocks should be processed in increasing packet number order (start with smallest packet number), for a couple of reasons:

1. Assuming your list of Outstanding Sent Packets is ordered by increasing packet number (oldest packet at the front), for any ACK block you process, you'd expect the smallest packet number in the block to be at or near the front of the Sent Packets list.

2. If the smallest packet number isn't at the front of the Sent Packets list, then it's likely FACK/RACK could kick in, causing the front of the list to be removed immediately, further optimizing the search for the next smallest packet number that was acknowledged.

I can't see any reason for processing ACKs in the current order the frame contains them. Can anyone shed some light on why this order was originally chosen?

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body: There was a lengthy discussion on this and some consensus on the need of redesigning the ACK frame, but I can't seem to find the issue where this was covered.

comments.author: nibanks
comments.body:
Well, if folks agree with this, it would be easy enough to change the existing ACK frame text. I'd be happy to make the changes. Find/replace in the ACK section:

- 'largest' => 'smallest'
- 'descending' => 'ascending'
- 'preceding' => 'following'

No wire format needs to change as far as I can tell.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
In most cases, it doesn't matter whether it's in ascending or descending order.  If one was using a linked list to store packets, then you would have to skip over a CWND of packets with the current decreasing approach, but that's not a data structure I'd recommend anyway, because it has poor cache locality.  A deque is a fairly good choice.

The original reason it was chosen is that when sending an ack frame, if there wasn't room for all the ack ranges or you didn't want to send all of them for some other reason, it's best to drop the lowest ranges, which are typically the least recently received packets, rather than the highest.  This can be accomplished by doing a first pass through the ack frame and tracking how large it'll serialize to before serializing it, but that's not ideal.

As far as I know, the serialization case is the only case where the order ends up mattering much in either computational complexity/cost or programming complexity.

I don't think I understand your second concern.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body: For decoding I find the reverse order impractical because sent packets in a typical data structure are sorted by packet number oldest first. If the ACK frame had same order, both lists could be walked directly. In praxis it is not that simple because the entire packet must be validated before being processed and because there could be multiple ACK frames in a single packet so one cannot conclude timeout before seeing all.

comments.author: nibanks
siyengar
comments.body: I prefer newest first to be the order. The reason is that QUIC prefers to ACK newer packets over older packets so that we make sure we make forward progress and preferentially ack later received packets over earlier ones. If we do oldest first, then the packetizer would have to do one pass over the packet to calculate the space that we have before we decide which is the oldest packet we can actually encode in the ack. This is really a PITA to do vs. having the ack handler just use a reverse iterator for iterating over the ack frames. For this reason I support the current newest first encoding

comments.author: nibanks
comments.body: @siyengar The use of variable-length integers prevents reverse traversal over the raw ACK frame.

comments.author: siyengar
comments.body: @nibanks  oh i see what you want to do, you want to handle acks while parsing the frame, ya in that case you can't have a reverse iterator. We parse the entire packet into a structure of frames, and then handle the acks which is why we can have a reverse iterator. I can see that it's shitty either way, ascending or descending. It may be less shitty as descending :)

comments.author: marten-seemann
comments.body:
What I like the most about the descending order is that you can just stop writing new ranges, when you notice that the ACK is getting too big.
Furthermore, descending order saves a few bytes on the wire, since for all ranges, you're only encoding packet number differences. For ascending order, you'll need multiple bytes for the first block. It's just a couple of bytes per ACK, but since ACKs are sent frequently, this might something worth considering.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body: It would be good to avoid temp allocation beyond a fixed stack allocation during decoding. There is no longer a 256 entry limit.

comments.author: nibanks
comments.body:
@marten-seemann I don't understand why the ACK frame would be a different size with ascending order? It should be exactly the same, encoding gaps and blocks as packet number differences. For ascending you add the differences as you traverse ACK frame; for descending you subtract.

Also, on the issue of encoding ACK blocks in ascending order, shouldn't it be fairly to traverse you local list of packet number ranges to ACK to calculate how many of them will fit in your packet. Once that is determined, you just start from the smallest of that subset to encode the ACK frame. You can also have some simple heuristics to know (for the simple cases) if all your local ranges would fit in the packet, even if they used the full variable-length encoding for each parameter, so you don't have to calculate each individually.

comments.author: marten-seemann
comments.body:
@nibanks: Maybe I don't understand your proposal correctly, so let's take an example. If I want to encode an ACK frame for the packet numbers 1e12 to 1e12+10 (first range) and 1e12+20 to 1e12+30 (second range), then for descending order, I need to encode the large value 1e12+30 once (for the largest acked), and the rest will be small differences which will fit into one byte. For ascending order, as I understand it, you'd need to encode a value O(1e12) twice, which will take more bytes.

Regarding your pseudo code, I think there are a lot of ways to consume an ACK. In quic-go, we chose a completely different approach, since iterating over a range sent by the client would make us vulnerable for DoS (when a peer sends a large range).

comments.author: nibanks
comments.body:
@marten-seemann If we changed the ACK frame to ascending order, `Largest Acknowledged` would become `Smallest Acknowledged` and all the deltas would reverse direction. You wouldn't encode anything twice.

As for the DoS, I agree, the simplistic pseudo code does have issues. Instead you would `find` the start and the end of the range, and return the set of all packets in it. But generally, the same issues apply.

comments.author: huitema
comments.body: I like one part of the descending order: immediately obtaining the "largest seen" packet number. If we agree that seeing this "largest seen" is important, then the descending order makes sense. Everything else can be solved with appropriate data structures.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body: But then it must be required that highest / first ACK range really is the largest seen. There is currently no such requirement AFAIK.

comments.author: nibanks
comments.body:
Why does it really matter if 'largest acknowledged' (even if it is required to be 'largest seen') be in the ACK frame's header and not just in the last ACK block? You process the entire ACK frame/blocks at essentially the same moment in time (as far as the network is concerned).

And I still I haven't heard a solution to my original problem. Given that set of outstanding sent packets is sorted in ascending order, if the ACK blocks are in descending order (and cannot be traversed in reverse order without first copying to a separate data structure and memory) how are you supposed to efficiently match ACK blocks to outstanding send packets?

The best I can think of requires a search for 'largest acknowledged' and then iteratively (per ACK block) search backwards from that point, effectively O(2n) to find all the ACK blocks; where as if the ACK blocks were in ascending order, the search is only O(n).

For example:

Outstanding Sent Packets: `{1,2,3,....1000}`
ACK Blocks: `{500 - 400},{390-300},{290-1}`

Again, assuming you don't allocate additional memory for an intermediate data structure, processing these ACK blocks in descending order would first require a search through half the Outstanding Sent Packets set to find the largest and then the same part of the set would be walked backwards for the rest of the ACK blocks. But if they were in reverse order that wouldn't be the case.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body:
I concur with all the arguments in favor of descending order.

@nibanks I see that in the general case, largest_acked can have the annoying property of being somewhere in the middle of your packet list. However, I'll note that a single block can easily be processed lowest to highest, which will tend to address your problem because...

1) in the lossless case, there is only one block anyway.
2) If the ACK only advertises one *new* gap, the earlier blocks have presumably been wiped out from your packet queue anyway.

I confess that the situation where there are large numbers of lost packets to travers in the queue could be suboptimal. One can solve this by keeping lost packets in a separate queue, or keeping a pointer to the first packet not declared lost.

Ascending order really shines when an ACK frame reports multiple *new* packet gaps. I'm not sure how to trade that off against the other considerations.

comments.author: nibanks
comments.body: @martinduke both of your reasons for saying that a block can be process easily from lowest to highest assumes little to no packet loss. We cannot make that assumption. We have to design for the most common case, which would assume packet loss. Also, in both your scenarios, ascending order processing time would be equal to descending order; but those are the **only** cases where that would be the case. In **all other cases** processing in descending order is a more expensive operation than processing in ascending order.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body:
I don't know that heavy, non-bursty packet loss is the common case.

Anyway, the increased processing expense is offset by lower cost generation of ACK frames. With ascending, I have to figure out the full size of the acknowledgment, start deleting blocks from the top if oversize, and then write into the packet.

This is just about as complex as, on processing, reading all the information in the ACK into memory and then deleting packets from the queue. If you take that approach, it's trivial to start from the lowest number. Indeed, it would be straightforward to execute this approach only if block_count is large.

To summarize:
Descending: Low-cost generation; high-cost processing under the conditions where ACKs report multiple new gaps .

Ascending: High-cost generation, low-cost processing.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
I think there are ways to make the processing low cost for descending as well.

I'm working on an implementation that I believe would have identical performance in both directions.  It's sort of on the back burner, but I can try to finish it soon so it's available in Chromium for people to take a look at?

comments.author: nibanks
comments.body: @ianswett I look forward to your proposal.

comments.author: siyengar
mikkelfj
comments.body:
Good input.

Some concerns: assuming you have descending order in frame. If you can seek to the end then process in ascending order, this is probably fine. But if you cannot, you either rely on assumptions about log N handling, or you must allocate a temporary data structure. Earlier there was a limit on 256 entries but this limit is gone. The sender knowns how many entries it creates and can easily keep number of entries below a limit. The receiver can't. Especially if it must expect very large MTU.

The receiver also do not control the frequence of ACK frames and hence the amount of resources to dedicate while the sender does. The sender is also the one that can do DoS.

As to the log N assumption, that doesn't work if you use a bitmap scan. A bitmap scan is resistant to DoS because it is O(N). Since packets now are in incremental order, this is a practical approach. 

Scanning the bitmap from most recent to older probably has a number of problems that I currently do not recall. Generally you want to work with the oldest packet first.

I can see the idea of building in descending order but you can do two passes to compute the size and then build ascending.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body: There also ought to be a requirement that if there are multiple ACK frames in a packet, they must be in ascending order, which of course puts even more strain on the sender, but it is for the same reason. It is simpler to require that there is at most one ACK frame per packet.

comments.author: janaiyengar
comments.body: I don't see a reason at the moment to have two ACK frames per packet (especially with the varint representations). That said, I don't see this perf issue as a reason to require it... we can certainly recommend it strongly (SHOULD).

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body: If there is a MUST, the receiver can have an implementation that takes an ACK frame, makes conclusion on age and time, and do updates. With SHOULD, it needs to add additional complexity to manage information from both frames, even if a second frame is rare. Granted, the ACK frame must be parced once to validate the packet, but it is still simpler with at most one.

comments.author: janaiyengar
comments.body: The receiver doesn't need to do any ack info aggregation per packet. Just treat it like two separate ACK frames were received.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body: OK, that simplifies things.

comments.author: nibanks
comments.body:
@siyengar Thanks for the write up. I can agree with most of what you wrote except: 

> Practically though I don't think this is a big deal implementations will have multiple layers in the code, one which parses the data into an in memory frame structure after which you can use either an ascending or descending algorithm.

There is no reason to require an implementation to use any structure other than the wire format. Why can't it process the packet directly?

As far as the complexity of each design, I agree they can essentially have the same worst case, but then our decision should be based on the common case. Generally, ACKs will be received for the oldest outstanding packets, correct? And if the oldest packet number ACKed in an ACK frame is significantly newer than your oldest outstanding packet, then you will be throwing (mark as lost) that old packet out anyways.

If you use ascending order then you could rely exclusively on a linear walk of your outstanding packets, starting at the beginning. For each packet in your list the packet, that is less than the min of the current ACK block, it will either be ACKed or lost (for the most part). Once you get to the last packet number being ACKed in the frame, you stop walking the list.

Your worst case then is a single ACK block that ACKs your most recent packet; but in that case, it would likely cause you to throw away all your older packets anyways, which require you to walk the entire list.

comments.author: siyengar
comments.body:
@nibanks I agree with you, there is no reason for an implementation to require any structure other than a wire format. For example the for loop could just be an iterator adapter in C++ that lazily processes packets. There are just tradeoffs with both approaches and I was just trying to point out the tradeoffs.

>  Generally, ACKs will be received for the oldest outstanding packets, correct?

In the common case an ACK would be received for the most recently sent packet first. Quic's loss detection algorithms rely on the sender prioritizing ACKing higher packets first for example for stuff like TLP or RTO to work correctly. 

Even if you use ascending order with streaming parsing you'd have to probably iterate over the packets again anyway after you're done processing the acks. There are 2 types of loss detection in QUIC. For timer based loss detection you'd have to know what the largest acked packet is before triggering it on all the packets which means we have to do this only after streaming till the end of the ack frame. Even for packet order based loss detection you probably need to iterate over most of the packets in the common case because there is no guarantee given acked packet n, packets below it are less than n - kReorderingThreshold especially since there could be gaps created by already acked packets. I haven't worked out the algorithmic details for that yet and we might be able to make this more efficient by caching the minOutstandingPacketNumber, but I don't think that will change the complexity analysis.

comments.author: nibanks
comments.body:
@siyengar I agree that ACKs will be sent for the most recently received packets. But I am assuming that most of the time, all received packets will be able to be ACKed; that most of the time, space won't be an issue and all the ACK blocks will fit. There might be a couple gaps on average (it would be great if someone had some numbers related to the size and consistency of ACK blocks with certain network conditions).

So if we assume that generally, all packets received are acknowledged then we are back to my original argument. The oldest packet number in the ACK frame will generally be your oldest outstanding packet (or close to it). So if you process both sets, ACK blocks and outstanding packets, together, in ascending order, you will be able to do a single pass of both and determine if an outstanding packet is ACKed, Lost, or Still Pending. And at most, you will only process your outstanding packet list up to the largest ACKed packet in the ACK frame.

comments.author: siyengar
comments.body: Ya agree, that sounds like a perfectly reasonable assumption, in the common case you won't have to process loss.

comments.author: nibanks
comments.body:
@ianswett Any updates? I still don't see a way that descending order could ever be as good as ascending order. I'm still thinking of this example where you have a couple of gaps of lost packets.

Outstanding Sent Packets: `{1,2,3,....1000}`
ACK Blocks: `{500 - 400},{390-300},{290-1}`

Assuming the final result is that packets `{1-290}, {300-390}, {400-500}` are acknowledged and packets `{291-299}, {391-399}` are marked as lost (FACK), that means you would have to traverse the entire first 500 packets of the outstanding list. comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
No updates, but I'll explain what my approach is.

I store an IntervalSet of the previously acknowledged packets from the lowest one I'm tracking to the largest previously acknowledged.  When I read the ack frame, I'm incrementally comparing the intervals I'm parsing with the IntervalSet of previously acknowledged packets and storing any newly acknowledged packets in a list and adding them to the IntervalSet for the future.  Then I do a second pass over the full data structure with the newly acknowledged packets in the list.  The list isn't necessary, so you could do it in one pass, but it fits into my current implementation better, so it's what I'm doing for now.  My congestion control APIs take a list of newly acked packets and their size in bytes, so I have to create that list anyway.

You have to ensure you don't allow someone to acknowledge packets larger than the largest ever sent, or you can allocate a ton of extra temporary memory(a perk of doing this without a temporary list), but otherwise, this should turn out to be slightly faster for decreasing order, since I can ignore any extra ack ranges that are below the smallest packet I'm still waiting for an acknowledgement for.

comments.author: nibanks
comments.body:
Thanks @ianswett for the detailed explanation. Do you use this IntervalSet of previously acknowledged packets for anything other than this purpose? Otherwise, to me this still seems just like an intermediate data structure for processing the ACK block. We haven't had need of a similar object in our code and I would be hesitant to add it just for this.

My ideal goal is still:

1. Process ACK block directly from the wire format.
2. Require no extra processing steps or temporary storage.
3. Process the necessary outstanding packet structures only.

I see a solution with ascending order but descending order breaks at least one of the above goals.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
It has two purposes.  One is this, and the other is that reusing the existing ack frame trades a small amount of memory for a large-ish reduction in memory allocations.  It might even be possible for it to be a net savings of memory allocated in the typical case, by removing the redundant information of what has already been acknowledged from the more complete data structure, but I haven't tried that yet.

So this gives you 1, 2, and 3 with the only cost being complexity of an optimized data structure to speed part 3, which happens to look exactly like how you likely store the QUIC ack frame you're putting received packets into and sending.  It does assume you're using a deque or something similar that makes it fast to seek to a given entry, but that's the best style I've found in practice.

How are you intending to store and find newly acked packets?  It's worth keeping in mind that after loss, you'll likely want to track packets that have already been retransmitted for a while, in case they were spuriously retransmitted, so you may commonly end up skipping over those on the way up.  It's also worth keeping in mind that linked lists have awful performance from a CPU cache perspective.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body:
Given that packet numbers are in incremental order it can be done much more efficiently in time and space by scanning chained blocks of bitmaps. If there is a large gap you just link two bitmaps. Doing this efficiently requires ack's in increasing order. If your chain grows too long, you are subject to abuse, or conditions too bad to maintain a connection.

The initial descend into the bitmap can be done by remembering the previous start location, or by using an efficient index into each bitmap block.

If you arbitrarily loose every second packet, an interval map is using a lot of memory in comparison, not to mention a log2 lookup.

So, it would be rather sad to have to allocate a lot of temporary memory for no good reason.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body: Well, maybe chained bitmaps could be revised to be scanned in the opposite direction but you likely need a second pass to make retransmission decisions.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
I haven't thought through the details of using bitmaps as much, except to say that real-world packet loss works well with ranges, even if bitmaps have better worst case properties.  I also find it convenient that ranges match up with the ack format nicely.  If packet loss was random, GQUIC would likely have used bitmaps for the ack format.

Marking packets as lost is currently a separate pass in the GQUIC code, because initially we were using pluggable loss detection.  Doing descending order works fine for detecting lost packets, and it doesn't matter which order packets are lost in to make retransmission decisions, because we can decide what to send after all lost packets are determined.

If one did use a linked list without any sort of side data structure, I don't think it matters which direction you iterate in.  Either way, you're going to have to check all packets being tracked in the list between the largest acked packet and the smallest.  I don't think the iteration order matters?  You would have to store an extra pointer to quickly access the packet larger than the largest previously acknowledged to speed access to largest acked, but that seems simple.

comments.author: nibanks
comments.body: If you store a linked list without any side structure, and the largest packet number is the first value you process, you have to process the items from the beginning to the largest twice. Once to find the actual largest item, and then another as you walk backward to process the ACK blocks.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body: @nibanks you just reverse the list order in the first pass :) (never mind messing with the cache)

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
The beginning being the smallest packet?  You can start at the largest, or even better, whichever is closer to largest acked(the largest sent or the largest previously acked).  It does mean touching a few extra elements, but typically those are being acknowledged and going to be accessed anyway.

That being said, in many scenarios, having a side data structure is going to make this faster.

comments.author: nibanks
comments.body:
When you get an ACK frame, on average, where do you expect the packet number ranges to reside, in relation to our set of outstanding packets? Generally for the oldest outstanding packets?

Then, assuming FACK, if you do receive ACK blocks/frame for packet numbers more recent (larger) than your oldest packets, you would mark those 'skipped' packets as lost, therefore removing them from your outstanding packets set, right?

In that case, you essentially 'touch' all the oldest packets, up to the largest packet number in the ACK frame. So why not just walk both the ACK frame and your set of outstanding packets, in ascending order, together marking packets as either lost or ACK?

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body: Although my previous comment wasn’t entirely serious, if you do insist on using a list, and the ack order is reverse, then it makes sense to root the list at largest acked and point to older packets, then root a separate list in forward direction with a tail pointer. comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
You generally expect the next packets acknowledged to be close to the largest acked.

We've found it's important to keep around older packets for a while after they've been lost to detect spurious retransmits, which are not that infrequent.  Currently, we keep around about an RTT of old packets, in the hopes that QUIC can tolerate a full RTT of reordering in the worst case.  That's probably overkill for most cases, but ideally it only costs a bit of memory that doesn't end up being accessed, so there should be little to no CPU overhead.

But the key difference here is the data structure we're discussing using.  For a deque or anything similar to it, I think something like the approach I described works well and order doesn't matter.  If you use only a linked list, then ascending order is simpler to implement efficiently, but I think the real-world performance of either direction is very similar if you follow some of MikkelFJ's suggestions.

comments.author: nibanks
comments.body:
Thanks @ianswett. Really appreciate the information. I agree that if you use a more complicated data structure to represent your outstanding packets than a list, you have the ability to process ACK blocks, independent of order, pretty much the same.

But I am still trying to understand why not use ascending order. The main argument I have heard is that, if you have too many packet numbers to ACK, then you always want to ACK the largest/most recent ones; and that is easier to do if you start at the largest and just continue to write the ACK blocks until you run out of room. I agree that it is easier. I would propose two solutions:

1. Keep track of the amount of space it would require you to encode your current set of ACK'ed packet numbers and only keep around what can fit into a single packet.

2. Have writing the ACK frame be a two step process. First to walk the your list in descending order to figure out how many packet numbers would fit in the packet. Then, starting at the smallest that would fit, work upward and encode.

Neither of those seem too complicated to me, and don't require more complicated data structures or significant extra processing time.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
Re 1, the issue is really if you'd like to bundle an ack with data.  If you only send acks in ack-only packets, it should be fairly easy to ensure it always fits, though the combination of varints and ranges potentially being merged makes it more complex than you'd think, if you want to stay close to the limit.  I would not advise anyone write this code, because I think it's error-prone.

Re 2, sure that can definitely be done.  And that's what I'd recommend if we did increasing order, but given processing acks in decreasing order is easy(in my case, it's equivalently costly and equivalent complexity), I think this double-pass is more complex and costly than the processing acks in decreasing order.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body:
Here is one way the reverse order ACK frame could be processed in ascending order, assuming MTU < 2^64.

- Stack allocate a 2-byte offset stack of 100 entries (or more if you like)
- Scan the ack frame by pushing an offset for 1 in every 100 range entries seen.
- If the offset table is exhausted, drop the rest of the ACK frame, or cry abuse / bad connection.
- Stack allocate a range table of 100 ranges (2 x 8 bytes x 100).
- While offset stack not empty pop an offset from the offset stack and fill the range table by reading up to 100 ranges then process that range table back to front.

Optimisations:

- Treat the last offset (first in while loop) specially since it does not represent a fixed 100 ranges, and often is the only offset to process.
- Use recursion with max depth = 100 to implement the offset stack, but pass the pre-allocated range table by reference for memory reuse.
- When the ACK frame has a count of ranges in the header as opposed to a terminal null range, it is easy to detect if there are at most 100 ranges and go for the fast path immediately, and it is possible to detect if recursion is safe, up front.

_EDIT: you need to store the absolute packet number at each offset in the offset stack and you therefore need to decode integers during the first scan. This is still reasonable, both with an offset stack and with recursion, but not as fast as initially thought. Alternatively, if you compute min ACK during the first scan you don't have to store the absolute packet number in the offset stack._

This has low memory overhead and works in L1 cache by reusing the same temp table repeatedly. Likewise, dual passes over the ACK frame is cheap from a cache perspective. Varints are reasonably easy to scan without decoding in the first pass.

While the algorithm may sound a bit involved, it is probably simpler and faster than encoding the ACK frame in ascending order.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body:
With the above algorithm I can sort of buy into the descending ACK argument, but that leaves me with:

The transport doc does not currently explicitly state the ACK Block Count is variable length, but I presume that it is. If so, how do you efficiently do a single pass ACK frame construction when you don't know the size of the count field? Do you just use a large enough integer encoding? Do you use memmove to retro-fit? Do you preprocess to decide?

Transport 8.15:
> ACK Block Count:
The number of Additional ACK Block (and Gap) fields after the First ACK Block.

Once more people have real code that does this, then we will have the information we need to make this decision.  Hopefully sunk costs don't drive the outcome too much at that point.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body:
@larseggert, you say that they can be differentiated by the error code spaces, but I don't see that in the text.  Transport error codes are a sixteen-bit space; application error codes are a different sixteen-bit space.  In RST_STREAM, you know *a priori* that it's an application error code.  In *_CLOSE, you know which is which only by the frame type.  If you merged the frame types into one, you'd need a flag in the frame header, which is wire-identical to what we currently have: frame type 0b0000001A, where A is a flag indicating whether the error is transport-based (A=0) or application-based (A=1).  If you think recasting it as one frame type with a flag is easier for implementers to understand, that seems purely editorial.

@huitema, if applications are responsible for communicating their own reasons for fatally closing the connection, then they have to define a way to semi-reliably communicate that reason after reaching an invalid state.  That's something we've already gone to some trouble to support in the transport, and it seems an unfortunate thing for the application protocol to be required to reinvent each time, particularly protocols which don't have a dedicated control stream.

issues.title: Explicitly communicate and include ACK delay in RTO computations
issues.author: huitema
issues.body:
The recovery spec says:

> RTT is calculated when an ACK frame arrives by computing the difference between the current time and the time the largest newly acked packet was sent. If no packets are newly acknowledged, RTT cannot be calculated. When RTT is calculated, the ack delay field from the ACK frame SHOULD be subtracted from the RTT as long as the result is larger than the Min RTT. If the result is smaller than the min_rtt, the RTT should be used, but the ack delay field should be ignored.

This is fine advice when computing the RTT, but there is a small issue arising later:

> When the final TLP packet is sent, the RTO period is set to max(SRTT + 4*RTTVAR, minRTO)

I believe that this RTO formula should also include some estimation of the ACK delay. When doing simulation with low latency links, I observe that SRTT converges to the low delay and RTTVAR to about zero. The main element in the overall delay is in fact the ACK delay. This leads to two possible solutions:

* Include the ACK Delay in the computation of the SRTT and RTTVAR,
* or, include an AckDelayVar component in the formulation of the RTO.

What do you think?

comments.body:

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
I don't think doing this requires explicitly communicating MaxAckDelay, but I think it would help.

comments.body: To Ian's point: I would not mind seeeing a "max ack delay" in the transport parameters. But my point on statistics was different.
