issues.author: ianswett
issues.body:
As I mentioned on PR #1151, if we change to asymmetric connection IDs with variable length, it would be ideal to have the version come before the connection IDs in the long header, because then it would be at a fixed offset and the destination connection ID would also still be at a fixed(but 4 byte later) offset.

Due to the importance of Connection ID, there is no intent to remove Connection ID from the invariants, though this change may enable some extra flexibility far down the road.

issues.title: Is 0RTT allowed after HRR?
issues.author: larseggert
issues.body:
When a client attempts a 0RTT handshake and gets a Retry from the server, can that client retry with another 0RTT handshake attempt, or does it need to fall back to 1RTT?

(Hit this issue during interop. My client sends an initial CI+0RTT packet pair, receives a retry, and then resends a new CI+0RTT packet pair. Is this permitted?)

comments.author: ad-l
comments.body:
Note that the TLS 1.3 spec forbids the client to send the `early_data` extension after a `HelloRetryRequest`
https://tools.ietf.org/html/draft-ietf-tls-tls13-24#section-4.1.2

comments.author: larseggert
comments.body:
@ekr said on slack:

> 0-RTT after retry is forbidden in TLS 1.3
> It's not like it somehow couldn't be made to work, we just concluded it was too confusing

and later

> TLS 1.3 *does* allow you to do a HRR with no other requested changes. We put that in so it would work with DTLS 1.3.

comments.author: larseggert
comments.body: I think that means that 0RTT after retry is *not* allowed

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body: Given that we're trying not to modify TLS rules when running in QUIC, I'd agree.  Do you think we need text reminding implementers of this?

comments.author: larseggert
comments.body: I think that would be helpful. I will add that when I did the 0RTT stuff in quant, and Jörg did it for pandora, we both found that part of the spec to be pretty underspecified. Pretty much the only thing that explains the details is Figure 3 in -tls.

issues.title: min_rtt could stay 0
issues.author: tatsuhiro-t
issues.body:
https://tools.ietf.org/html/draft-ietf-quic-recovery-10#section-3.4.3 says that min_rtt is initialized to 0.

And it is updated using the following formula: 

      // min_rtt ignores ack delay.
       min_rtt = min(min_rtt, latest_rtt)

This means that unless latest_rtt is negative (not possible), min_rtt stays 0.
I think there is missing something which treats 0 min_rtt as special, but not sure.

issues.title: Ban trial decryption in TLS stream after rejected early data?
issues.author: knekritz
issues.body: TLS 1.3 early data requires trial decryption after rejecting early data to skip over the records encrypted with 0-RTT keys that cannot be decrypted before you get to the client finished. In QUIC there will be no app data 0-RTT records, and the EndOfEarlyData is required by TLS to only be sent if early data is accepted, so there will be no records to skip but a TLS implementation will still likely set its record layer to skip TLS records that fail decryption.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: Seems reasonable to allow the stack to disable trial decryption.  I wouldn't require this though, because that might be more intrusive than stacks might like (for instance, I doubt that we would provide a knob for this in NSS).

issues.title: Packet Number Gap and Connection Probing
issues.author: MikeBishop
issues.body:
#1012 says that a client SHOULD use one of its new CIDs when probing for server reachability on a new network, and the spec says that you MUST increment your packet number by the defined amount when you switch to the new CID.  However, that leaves the next packet number somewhat ambiguous when the client continues to use the old connection for data in parallel.

So:

- Client sends packets up through N on CCID1 on current path
- Server has previously issued client CCID2, packet number gap P2
- Client probes server with packet N+P2 and CCID2 on second path
- Client sends more packets on current path with CCID1

What packet number do those packets use?  Does the client continue with N+1?  Does the client jump to N+P2+1, thereby providing a potential correlator between the paths?  The client could side-step the issue by moving to N+P2+P3 and switching to CCID3 on the main path, but rotating CCIDs on the main path every time you probe on an alternate path might also leak information, as well as burning CIDs even more quickly.

Regardless, the spec should say what the client needs to do.  (Or we just encrypt the packet number and get rid of the gap...?)

comments.author: janaiyengar
comments.body:
The answer IMO is that the client goes back to N+1.  I don't believe this causes any linkability issues -- N onwards is only used with CCID1 on the first path and N+P1 onwards is only used with CCID2 on the second path.

This definitely goes in the bucket of things we can happily close if we encrypt the packet number.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
There isn't a good answer here.  Unless we encrypt the packet number.

If you send N+1 on the old path and abandon the probed path, what happens when you reach N+Gap ?  Mayhem is my guess.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body: Plus, when you eventually do switch to CCID3 at packet number X, is your new packet number X+P3?  N+P2+P3?  The greater of the two?  This whole gap-jumping thing seems too loosely defined to actually employ except for CID rotation along a single path.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
The way it is intended to work is that you move progressively forward.  So a one-off probe would cause a move from CCID1 on the old path, to CCID2 on the probe to CCID3 on the old path again.

Unfortunately, the probing design makes that transaction much more common than anticipated in the packet number gaps design, so there is a risk of running the spare connection IDs down very quickly.

Thus, my conclusion: packet number encryption is the only sensible answer.

comments.author: janaiyengar
comments.body: Discussed at editors' meeting: This is hairy and terrible, since using packet number gaps in order is not in line with the way probes will get sent in #1012. Packet number encryption seems to be the only good way to do this right.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body:
Maybe I'm missing details, but I have previously suggested segmented packet numbers

https://github.com/quicwg/base-drafts/issues/1105

It might be slightly more complicated, but it is faster, it helps monitoring, and it helps ACK timings per path, and it allows for larger packet number space. But it dos not provide a unique packet ordering.

issues.title: HTTP/QUIC supports server push as described in [RFC7540], except where it doesn't
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
In the process of discussing some design for HTTP/QUIC PUSH_PROMISE, I was reminded that promised requests must fit within certain criteria. I thought this was defined in the HTTP mapping but it is actually referenced back to RFC7540 section 8.2. There is nothing inherently wrong with that. (for the curious, the text I wanted says "Promised requests MUST be cacheable (see [RFC7231], Section 4.2.3),  MUST be safe (see [RFC7231], Section 4.2.1), and MUST NOT include a request body.")

However, having read HTTP/QUIC section 3.4 again it comes across as a bit awkward (hence the annoying issue title). 

I think this is just an editorial issue to reword and/or restructure the section a little.

issues.title: When are missing Q-thingey references fatal?
issues.author: MikeBishop
issues.body:
@afrind raises a good hypothetical case:

- Encoder sends a header block on a request stream, which is delayed in the network
- Encoder side resets the stream, which is lost in the network
- Encoder sends another header block on the control stream that evicts an entry referenced in the first block, and this is delivered immediately.
- The first delayed header block arrives

From the encoder's side, it's valid to evict something referenced by the first block, because the stream has been reset.  From the decoder's side, there's a reference to something already evicted, because it doesn't know about the stream reset.

The solution to this seems to be that missing references on request/push streams are stream errors, not connection errors.  Missing references on the control stream still need to be connection errors.

comments.author: afrind
comments.body:
I think the scenario that leads to this kind of error will be extremely rare, but I dislike the idea of there being some background level of 'expected' decoding errors.  It will make it harder to debug/investigate buggy implementations.  In the case where the missing reference came from an encoder that is broken or otherwise out of sync with the decoder, worse things could happen from continuing to decode subsequent requests.

The only other way I can think of to ensure such a scenario doesn't inadvertently kill a good connection is to have the encoder clear the outstanding references of the reset stream only after it's received the ACK for that RST_STEAM.  I'm already not crazy about having transport identifiers tied into header encoding state, and having to further couple to transport acknowledgements would be even worse.  Still, a careful encoder could take this approach.

comments.author: krasic
comments.body:
+1 that moving to stream errors might introduce greater harm than they solve.   

This is similar to the more general reset issue we hoped to avoid moving updates out of the request-response stream.  

As in that discussion, another option is to have the encoder refrain from resetting streams that have outstanding headers.   I.e. an HQ mapping only solution is possible here:

the encoder side can have a notion of stream going away (don't send new data, drop any incoming data, don't start any new headers), but wait for header acks before actually sending reset.   To stay conservative, it could use a timer to trigger sending the reset anyway if the expected ack takes too long.  [ of course if we went this far, one might argue the whole update on separate stream approach is no longer needed. ]

Alternatively, if the occurrences of these are rare enough, perhaps status quo of letting such connections close with error is acceptable.   A server could track how many streams are reset with headers outstanding to help guage whether the number of missing header connection close errors are reasonable.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body:
#1314 includes the stream error, but it has the drawbacks mentioned here.  A better option that fits within the current model might be this:  Rather than the encoder counting all blocks as out-of-scope after it resets a stream, the decoder sends an acknowledgment either when it reads a header block from a stream or when it discards all remaining data from a stream.

This is similar to @afrind's idea of listening to the ACK, but follows the precedent set by other parts of QPACK of doing the ACK at the application layer.  This would require a second type of HEADER_ACK that is triggered by a reset stream, which is a little icky, though.

comments.author: dtikhonov
comments.body:
+1 to @afrind for catching this.

Perhaps the HoL minimization/stream reset interplay is indeed a general issue, as @krasic points out, and is never going away.  In that case, we have to deal with it.

I think that having the decoder return a stream error is not so bad:
- If the encoder knows that the stream was reset, it can ignore this error;
  - This adds a requirement that the application (HQ layer) notify the encoder that it reset the stream.
- Otherwise, the encoder can escalate (promote?) this to a connection error and close the connection.

Introducing the concept of allowed stream errors on reset streams is better than dipping into the transport layer or using timers.

issues.title: Stateless Reset Concerns
issues.author: mikkelfj
issues.body:
Stateless Reset (SR) has some positives and negatives.
Based on feedback on-list this issue is created to highlight these, asking for more input.

https://quicwg.github.io/base-drafts/draft-ietf-quic-transport.html#rfc.section.7.9.4

With the likely introduction of asymmetric Connection ID's a reset can no longer be routed to the client which reduces effectiveness. (EDIT: the following is not quite true, see comment below:) But it also prevents a connection specific reset meaning that an off-path attacker has better chances of spoofing a reset. A token could be tied the connection tuple, but this isn't stable through NAT, although it can be hashed to the IP iff migration is not in use.

Positives:

1. Google reports that SR measurably reduces overall latency, presumably because some connections eventually fail to route and a timeout would delay reconnection attempts.
2. SR is currently only used on clients which are more difficult to target maliciously than a publicly known server.

Negatives:

1. SR has the potential to be abused by forcing established connections to close via off-path packet injection. (Edit: not quite true, see comment below).
2. SR shadows alternative solutions to the problem such as more aggresive probes with short timeouts.
3. SR is currently asymmetric which is odd given that P2P server use is also relevant, but apparently it is difficult to make symmetric in handshake. But OTOH if SR were symmetric, the server (or client) with a publicly known address, would be vulnerable to reset attacks to the extend such are effective.
4. With asymmetric Connection IDs the reset cannot always route, which at least conceptually is clumsy and may or may not reduce effectiveness in the primary use case (that likely doens't have client routers).
5. Asymmetric Connection ID's makes SR more vulnerable because the receiver cannot verify the connection ID.  A client will also have to do more work to realise that a packet is a reset and not random data.
6. A server must rate limit resets. This means that a server needs to remember transmitted resets which binds state. A flood of random packets could interfere with this. To protect agaisnt this, a server must rate limit conservatively e.g. by bucketing IP addresses.

It is unclear to what extend the positives are important without further input and possibly evalulation of alternative strategies. For example, it might be that SR reduces latency because no alternative counter measure has been implemented. For example a PATH_CHALLENGE might be used as soon as ACK's don't arrive timely rather than waiting for a connection timeout that might have much longer duration because it deals with periods of inactivity as well. That said, a reset will clearly be more effecive when it works as intended.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body: I forgot that including the packet number in the SR offers a good counter measure to an off-path attack. Also, with asymmetric ID's a client can still verify the server chosen ID when present.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
Not sure what can be done here:

The first of these negatives is addressed in the draft.

The second doesn't seem actionable if I understand your intent - if stateless reset works, it's better than aggressive timers, but that's not a problem, especially since aggressive timers have pretty bad side-effects, like premature closure.

The third is addressed in the draft to the extent possible.

The fourth seems to be a duplicate of the third.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body:
The third negative is about asymmetri in design - a change would likely inherit the fourth negative about routability, but they are not quite the same.

An agressive timer is indeed suitable for self-inflicted wounds, but also offers more control such as being aggressive during connection setup and less so as the connection proves viable.

I'm not sure anything can/should be done, but there better be good reasons to have it since it is an attack vector.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body: There is also the option to issue a Path Challenge upon receiving a Reset and die if the response does not appear within 1.2 RTT or so. An implementation could choose to a) ignore Resets, b) issue a challenge, or c) always react to Resets.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body: Added negative 6 on rate limiting state.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body: Discussed at editors' meeting.  The current design is imperfect.  We understand these concerns, and discussed them in the process of coming up with the current design, and decided to accept them (modulo the one which is already separately tracked as #466).  However, if there's an alternative design that you'd like the working group to consider, feel free to e-mail it to the mailing list.

issues.title: Closing or draining state after idle timeout?
issues.author: larseggert
issues.body:
Section 7.9.1 says:
> An endpoint enters a **closing period** after initiating an immediate close (Section 7.9.3) and optionally after an idle timeout (Section 7.9.2). 

But Section 7.9.2 says:
> A connection enters the **draining state** when the idle timeout expires.

Which is it?

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: Hmm, I think that it has to be draining.  Without a CONNECTION_CLOSE to signal an end, both endpoints could enter closing and that would be bad.

comments.author: larseggert
comments.body: Shouldn't a *_CLOSE frame be sent prior to that? Otherwise the other side needs to wait for an idle timeout, too.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: Yes, but the expectation is that both peers hit this at about the same time.

comments.author: larseggert
comments.body: Why would that be? Both can use different idle timeouts.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: The minimum of the two applies.

comments.author: marten-seemann
comments.body: Why? A server might want choose a much shorter idle timeout than a client.

comments.author: larseggert
comments.body: The minimum applies? Where does it say that?

comments.author: janaiyengar
comments.body: A server might choose a smaller value, but both sides should close when the earliest end times out.  The draft doesn't say anything about this, which is an oversight. I'll fix it.

issues.title: Fix up Packet Number explaination
issues.author: seanturner
issues.body:
s5.7 contains the following:

A packet number is decoded by finding the packet number value that is closest to the next expected packet. The next expected packet is the highest received packet number plus one. For example, if the highest successfully authenticated packet had a packet number of 0xaa82f30e, then a packet containing a 16-bit value of 0x1f94 will be decoded as 0xaa831f94.

I read this a couple of times and the first time I got:
highest packed number = 0xaa82f30e + 1 = 0xaa82f30f +0x1f94 = aa8312A3
But, if I drop the bytes that are the same length as what's sent 4 for 0x1f94 form  0xaa82f30e you get  0xaa82 then add 1 and 0x194 I get 0xaa831f94.  Maybe there's a better way to say this.

comments.author: seanturner
comments.body: closed via #674

issues.title: Simplify ACKing rules by prohibit sending or processing ACK frames in 0RTT packets
issues.author: ianswett
issues.body:
The rules about sending acknowledgements have been commented as too complex.  This issue is an effort to simplify them slightly.

A client may have 0RTT keys when sending ACK frames, but using them to send ACK frames may be ineffective and is unnecessary.

When 0RTT is successful, these ACK frames can be processed, but the only time 0RTT keys are available and 1RTT keys are not available is when HANDSHAKE packet types are being received, so there is no need to send these ACK frames with 0RTT protection, since HANDSHAKE packets are not encrypted.

When 0RTT is unsuccessful, these ACK frames cannot be processed and are a waste of bytes.  Even worse, if the client mistakenly believes the ACK frames can be processed, the handshake ends up relying solely on timeouts to succeed, which can increase tail latency substantially.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: This isn't a terrible idea, but it's likely to be super-ceded by the design team's work.

issues.title: Signals of Initial Packet
issues.author: MikeBishop
issues.body:
The Initial Packet type (versus Handshake) carries two signals:

- This packet initiates a new connection
- This packet carries a client-selected Destination CID

However, after a Retry, the DCID is server-chosen, not client random, so that promise isn't true.  However, if we used Handshake as the client's packet after Retry (because the DCID is server-chosen), then the server would need to consider both Handshake and Initial packets as potentially initiating a connection.

Do we need to consider separating these signals?  Given the larger (and potentially structured) DCIDs, the signal of DCID source might be unnecessary now.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body:
This is something that has been bothering me a bit - I think it is important to be able to trivially tell if a CID is initial random, server chosen, or client chosen. But I didn't get as far as to analyze all the possible outcomes.

If the situation is that a server receives a packet and needs to guess if the DCID is random or previously chosen then it is open to collision risk and may be forced to create longer CID's than necessary. It may also want to cryptographically verify the CID which also makes it longer.

The number of packet types is trivial to handle compared to ambiguity in the CID. This also ties into assumptions about unique tuples - which of course - I'd very much like to avoid depending on. I can see the point of stable tuple during handshake - but it need not be unique (p2p servers where both have a single port egress).

issues.title: Send streams with an enqueued close
issues.author: martinthomson
issues.body: There is a state, equivalent to the "size known" state on the recv side, where the application has requested a close, but that close has not yet hit the wire.  Do we want to put that in the state machine?

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: See #777 conclusion.

issues.title: Pathological loss recovery case with Finished
issues.author: martinthomson
issues.body:
@marten-seemann writes:

1. Client and server perform the handshake, no packets are lost so far. Client and server both arrive at the CONNECTED state, and the server receives all ACKs for handshake packets it sent. The client receives ACKs for all handshake packets except for the one containing the FINISHED message is lost (the packet containing the ACK for the FINISHED is lost).
2. The client starts using 1-RTT keys, and it sends two packets: First, a packet only containing an ACK, and then a packet containing stream data (e.g. a request). The request packet is then lost.
3. The server receives the ACK in the 1-RTT packet, and it stops accepting unencrypted packets according to 6.1.2 of the TLS draft. It doesn’t generate an ACK in response, since the packet only contained an ACK.
4. The client is now missing acknowledgements for two packets: the (unencrypted) packet containing the FINISHED message, and the (1-RTT) packet containing the request. It runs its loss recovery algorithm (OnLossDetectionAlarm), and since there is one outstanding handshake packet, it retransmit all outstanding handshake packets.

Now we’ve run into a situation we can’t recover from: The server won’t even open packet sent as a retransmission (since these packets are unencrypted, and arrive after it already received a 1-RTT packet), and the client will never retransmit the request packet. Furthermore, the server won't send any other packets, since it's just waiting for a request from the client.

comments.author: janaiyengar
comments.body: Discussed at editors meeting. We believe the following resolution might work. An endpoint acknowledges everything until (i) the handshake is complete, and (ii) it is certain that the peer has seen an acknowledgement sent after this point. Supporting this, an acknowledgement of an ACK that was sent prior to handshake completion cannot be used to remove ACK ranges from future acknowledgments.

comments.author: janaiyengar
comments.body: After the server believes that the handshake is complete (Finished message from the client included), it sends a HS_COMPLETE frame, which is reliable.  When this frame is received at an endpoint, it ceases all retransmissions of any handshake frames.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: Note: Removing client Finished (as some have suggested) is not sufficient because we need to address this problem for handshakes with client authentication.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: I had an insight yesterday.  Maybe the newly proposed CRACK frame can elicit acknowledgments.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: I think that may solve the problem with some constraints, but HANDSHAKE_DONE or some equivalent seems easier to me.

issues.title: Add unknown packet version handling to invariants
issues.author: mikkelfj
issues.body:
#827 mentions that packets of unknown versions must be dropped.
But it is hard to make a version related requirement for a specific QUIC version, when clients can implement multiple versions.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: The type of a packet is not an invariant, so what do you imagine we might do to distinguish "unknown" here?

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body:
Sorry for being unclear - I meant to express the same as #827 does and the commit that resolves it:

"If a client receives a packet that has an unsupported version, it MUST discard that packet."

I'd say this ought to be an invariant because otherwise versions could disgree on this.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body:
I'm not sure this really needs to be addressed the invariants already says:

"A QUIC endpoint that receives a packet with a long header and a version it either does not understand or does not support sends a Version Negotiation packet in response. Packets with a short header do not trigger version negotiation and are always associated with an existing connection."

It just doesn't say what to do after a connection is established, but that might be splitting hairs, so closing.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: I see.  Yes, we have that text (though it suggests that a client sends VN, which is probably wrong).  I'll fix that.

issues.title: Reboot after 0-RTT reject (or version negotiation)
issues.author: martinthomson
issues.body:
When 0-RTT is rejected, you can't just pretend that your 0-RTT packets were dropped, you have to start over completely.

For example, if the client thought it could send 10 concurrent streams, and do so in 0-RTT, then when 0-RTT is rejected, it might be because the server wants to limit this to 5 streams.

For example, if the client thought it could use hq-10, but the server rejects 0-RTT because it chose hq-14, then the things it put on streams might not be understood by the server.

We need to document this VERY clearly.

issues.title: Use Conservative Initial Packet Size
issues.author: mikkelfj
issues.body:
The transport draft text on PMTU (8.4. Path Maximum Transmission Unit) says

... limit of 1280 followed by:
" Some QUIC implementations MAY wish to be more conservative in computing allowed QUIC packet size given unknown tunneling overheads or IP header options."

But the handshake requires banging against this limit, so it is not practical to reduce the limit in anticipation of tunnelling overhead.

There are two reasons for having the handshake at 1280: 1) to guarantee that 1280 really is available and force infrastructure to respect this, and 2) to discourage amplification attacks.

Perhaps it is better to set the handshake minimum to 1000 octets and encourage the use of 1280 for an initial PMTU unless additional tunneling concerns needs to be addressed. Alternatively edit the discussion on PMTU because it is not practical to reduce the size with the current handshake.

As discussed on list, it is often the case that ether frames have 1500+ octets, but when tunnels get layered, this might not be enough.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: The path needs to support v6, and this suggests that the path might not support v6.

issues.title: confusing Fast Retransmit modes
issues.author: marten-seemann
issues.body:
The loss recovery spec describes two different (and mutually exclusive) Fast Retransmit modes: one detects reordering in packet number space, the other one in time space.

The Fast Retransmit section is not clear about the fact that implementations have to choose one or the other mode, and just mentions time reordering at the very end.

Furthermore, I find the pseudo code for `DetectLostPackets` pretty hard to read, since depending on the mode, different variables are set to infinite and then used in comparisons. It would probably be easier to provide two different definitions of this functions depending on the mode.

I'd be happy to write up a PR, if people agree that the current text needs improvement in that direction.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
Agreed, though technically both of these could run at once, I think it's best to describe them as two mutually exclusive modes.

A PR to improve the text and pseudocode would be appreciated, thanks.

comments.author: siyengar
comments.body: ya there's some places which use the delayUntilLost for for time space for the early retransmit threshold. It might be nice to separate those two out to show that early retransmit is always active.

comments.author: pravb
comments.body: I don't think these are mutually exclusive modes. With TCP today we do both, if the SACK information suggests lost packets or RACK kicks in and marks packets lost. Time based detection cannot work for low latency connections due to lack of fine grained timers so you always need to augment with packet based detection. IMO an implementation should do both.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: @ianswett, you seem to think that this is editorial, but it is still labeled design.  It's clearly a hot issue.  Do you have a plan to fix it?

comments.author: janaiyengar
comments.body: Closed by #1974

issues.title: inconsistent definition of the TLP duration
issues.author: marten-seemann
issues.body:
The text says

> The alarm duration, or Probe Timeout (PTO), is set based on the following conditions:
> * PTO SHOULD be scheduled for max(1.5*SRTT+MaxAckDelay, 10ms)
> * If RTO (Section 3.3.2) is earlier, schedule a TLP alarm in its place. That is, PTO SHOULD be scheduled for min(RTO, PTO).

The second point is missing in the pseudo code:
```
else if (tlp_count < kMaxTLPs):
      // Tail Loss Probe
      alarm_duration = max(1.5 * smoothed_rtt + max_ack_delay, kMinTLPTimeout)
```

comments.author: pravb
comments.body: Yes this is needed otherwise the alarm duration could be too conservative in some cases.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: Agreed, the psuedocode should be updated to include this.

issues.title: don't apply congestion penalty for lost ack-only packets
issues.author: marten-seemann

issues.title: Stateless Reset needs "on-path" proof
issues.author: igorlord
issues.body: Stateless Reset contains a proof that the Server sent it.  However, if the server's key is compromised, Stateless Reset can be forged wholesale off-path.  Stateless Reset must also contain a proof that the sender observed the original packet that caused Stateless Reset.  Clearly, there are many simple ways to do so.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body:
Another attack to consider along similar lines:  If an active attacker observes the CID being used by a client, sends a packet with that CID to a different server endpoint that shares the same SR token algorithm/key, then it can get the other endpoint to effectively be an oracle for the stateless reset token.  It can then inject a Stateless Reset with the token into the current connection.

One mitigation would be to say that it's the server deployment's problem -- you should have different SR token-generation keys between different endpoints.  Another is to require that a Stateless Reset was sent by someone who had both a specific packet you sent and the token, without disclosing the token in a form that could be adapted to a different rejected packet.

(This is a similar case to #1264; since the generator of the SR can't validate the crypto, they also can't know whether it was generated by the client, misdirected by an attacker, or fully generated by an attacker.  That means they also can't avoid being a CID->SR oracle.)

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: Yes, this is a deployment issue.  If packets with the same connection ID can end up at a node that shares a stateless reset key, but can't access connection state so that it generates a stateless reset, we have an oracle.  We should document that attack.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
While I agree that this can be considered a deployment issue, I think we should forbid servers deploying the same static secret used for generating the stateless reset token among the servers that do not share the connection state, because it not only goes against what "authenticated" reset is but also has privacy concerns.

My understanding is that many of the server-side deployments that care about this are those that use BGP to distribute their packets among multiple POPs. Those operators tend to serve multiple hostnames.

That means unless we mandate such server operators to provide stateless reset tokens only in a secure manner, attackers can force a connection to terminate (by using a stateless reset token obtained from a different POP) and then see the SNI carried in the handshake of a new connection.

Therefore, I think that we should either forbid server deployments from sharing the static key without sharing connection state, or, look for a technical approach to prevent the attack.

One such approach would be something like below:
* for every QUIC connection, let the server advertise a "state-store ID" that designates the ID of the state-store that the connection is bound to
* let a Stateless Reset packet carry encrypted data, which is encrypted by a key (other than stateless reset token) derived from the server CID and the static key used to generate the stateless reset token
  * that encryption key will be sent together with the stateless reset token in the NEW_CONNECTION_ID frame
* a Stateless Reset packet will carry the "state-store ID" of the server sending that packet in an encrypted form
* a client can compare the "state-store ID" of the connection with the value found in the Stateless Reset, and determine that:
  * if the values match, the connection has been reset
  * if the values do not match, the path is being rejected

There could be other ways, but I think sending encrypted data in a stateless reset and verifying that on the client side would be the necessary thing to do here.

WDYT?

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
Yes, if the extent of the state storage distribution matches the extent of the key distribution, which is a natural design, then this is naturally OK.

@kazuho, I'm struggling with your state store ID design.  If the state and key storage is co-extant, then the packet that hits a different store will generate a response that the client won't recognize as a valid stateless reset.  So I'm failing to see how the extra steps you describe help with the problem.

Unless you are suggesting that this key needs to be global (unlike the token, which is scoped to a particular zone).  I don't think going global works though.  An attacker can obtain a key for a given connection ID in one cluster and use it - in combination with the stateless reset oracle Mike described - to attack another.

If we wanted to prove that the server can generate the Stateless Reset without compromising later uses of the Stateless Reset, then we could feed the incoming packet into the process.  For example, rather than include the token in the stateless reset directly, it includes a constant value that is generated by using `HMAC(token, some fixed content)` (or use HKDF[1]).  A client can use that to detect that this is a stateless reset.  In addition, the reset might also include a separate proof of receipt such as `HMAC(token, incoming packet or part thereof)`.  A client might choose to ignore a stateless reset that had an invalid secondary proof.

Of course, the risk here is that clients don't track enough from their outbound packets to reconstruct the input to the HMAC.  After all, it requires tracking packet ciphertext - no other part of a packet is unpredictable enough.  So they might have to treat receipt of a possible stateless reset as a trigger to enable whatever tracking they need, after which they send another packet and hopefully get a stateless reset.  Aside from adding a whole round trip to the process, it just more than doubled the cost of a stateless reset at the server.

[1] We originally had another hash for stateless resets, but removed that in favour of the current, simpler design.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
@martinthomson 
> Unless you are suggesting that this key needs to be global (unlike the token, which is scoped to a particular zone).

That is exactly what I am suggesting, under the assumption that some would be willing to do so (if none are, we should simply ban a single key shared among the servers that do not share the connection state, instead of discussing how a client should act against such servers as proposed in #1259).

In my proposal, a stateless reset token becomes an identifier of the connection (or path) that is being reset. It is the tag of the encrypted data (that contains the "state-store ID") that proves that the stateless reset has been sent from a server. Then, a client uses the "state-store ID" to see if the reset was sent by a server that should have known the connection (means a connection reset), or not (means a path being rejected).

In other words, a stateless reset token becomes usable once per every "state-store", instead of once per connection.

PS. maybe I am too abstract (I am trying to not go into certain design decisions). I can come up with a more concrete description if that's preferable.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
OK, thanks for clearing that up.  I think that you have an attack, though it might not be that interesting.

Connection IDs are scoped to a state store, whereas your proposed key is global.  That means that an attacker that can learn the key for a given connection ID in any state store can use it to attack all other state stores.  For high entropy connection IDs, that takes some doing, but it isn't generically safe, especially now we allow as little as 32 bits.

What is generically safe is co-extant state.  That is, the connection ID has to be valid everywhere the static key is used and thus a packet with a given connection ID either causes a valid stateless reset for that connection or it is accepted.

Given the complexity of the additional mechanism and that exposure, I'd rather concentrate on the attack that this issue was originally raised to address: the absence of a proof-of-receipt in the stateless reset packet.  Given that we now have a little as 32 bits of entropy (or less) in a connection ID, the potential for a stateless reset oracle is bothering me a little.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
> OK, thanks for clearing that up. I think that you have an attack, though it might not be that interesting.
> 
> Connection IDs are scoped to a state store, whereas your proposed key is global. That means that an attacker that can learn the key for a given connection ID in any state store can use it to attack all other state stores. For high entropy connection IDs, that takes some doing, but it isn't generically safe, especially now we allow as little as 32 bits.

Thank you for considering the approach and pointing out the issue. I had not considered of the attack vector.

And considering of the attack vector, I realize that there is a less complex approach.

Assuming that the ID of the POP (i.e. the "state-store") is included in the DCID, a server can determine if it should have known the state a connection that the DCID designates, and send a connection reset or a path rejection based on that.

With that said, I am personally fine with _requiring co-extant state_. As expressed in https://github.com/quicwg/base-drafts/issues/1230#issuecomment-379963211, my intent behind the proposal has been under the premise that some might want to reject path creation when packets arrive at a POP that does not have access tho the state store.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
Yeah, I don't think that path rejection is going to work that well. Packets that arrive at a POP that doesn't have access to a state store will either enter a black-hole (if they know about the connection ID, in which case it will be dropped after packet protection removal fails), or generate a stateless reset.  More of the latter as connection IDs get longer and more sparse.

That's what makes me think that we need some sort of verification of intent in addition to a token.  A routing flap, misconfiguration, or attack might cause a storm of stateless resets that might be reusable by an attacker.  Adding a liveness check is probably a good idea to avoid that.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: @martinduke made a good point about this, which made me reconsider this idea.  A man-on-the-side attacker can copy whatever details they need from packets an endpoint sends in its use of a stateless reset oracle.  That is, if the stateless reset depends on data in a packet that an endpoint sends (and it can't depend on anything more than that), then the attacker simply copies whatever it needs from a genuine packet.  A liveness check therefore only really makes the attackers job harder.  Since the fix here that forces the attacker to be live is to make the stateless reset more complex, we should be very careful to consider the trade-off.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body:
A loose thought, but intuition suggests:

With more roundtrips it would probably be possible to design a challenge response scheme. Dead endpoint issues a stateless reset challenge. Live endpoint responds by hashing the challenge with a negotiated reset key. Dead end point issues a new reset by hashing the live response.

MITM cannot use observed packets to issue new resets without triggering a roundtrip with proper routing between the endpoints, and the supposedly dead endpoint would not cooperate if it isn't dead.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: Discussed in Kista.  Conclusion was that the marginal benefit was minor, if not non-existent, and the cost was significant.  A man-on-the-side could build the oracle.  We will instead concentrate on documenting the constraints on the routing infrastructure.

issues.title: ACKs for receiver-only
issues.author: ekr
issues.body:
"A receiver that is only sending ACK frames will not receive acknowledgments for
its packets.  Sending an occasional MAX_DATA or MAX_STREAM_DATA frame as data is
received will ensure that acknowledgements are generated by a peer.  Otherwise,
an endpoint MAY send a PING frame once per RTT to solicit an acknowledgment."

But this isn't true if the counterparty piggybacks ACKs in its packets that contain STREAM data (which is at least what I do!), and why I filed #1231. Is this really the behavior we want?

comments.author: nibanks
comments.body:
@ekr, I don't understand why you say this isn't true. The issue here is that if an endpoint sends nothing but ACKs, there is no guarantee its peer will acknowledge those packets. The peer may have other data to send back, and may choose to include ACK frames in those packets, if there is room, but if the peer has enough constant stream data to send back and (for some reason) prioritizes the STREAM frames higher than ACK frames, it might not end up acknowledging the endpoint's ACK frames in a timely manner.

All that being said, personally I think ACK frames should have the highest priority when framing a packet to send out. So if you ever have something to send out (other than the ACKs) then the ACKs should end up getting sent too. But all this seems like an implementation issue to me.

comments.author: ekr
comments.body: Sorry, what's not true is the claim that you "will not". I agree you "may not". The distinction here is only relevant because of PR#1231, in which case you really would not.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
So the more that I think about the problem here, the more I think that it was intended to address a non-problem.

The problem it was written to address was an asymmetric sending arrangement, but realistically, the endpoint generating data in that scenario will likely generate ACK frames as it goes.

Encouraging the sending of PING frames here is more likely to cause problems than solve them.

Maybe the right answer here is to remove this paragraph entirely.

comments.author: ekr
comments.body: I updated #1231 to rewrite this graph in a less normative sense.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: Closed by #1231.

issues.author: marten-seemann
issues.body: After the recent header changes, there's no need for a Retry packet type any more. The server could send its HRR in a normal Handshake packet.

comments.author: siyengar
comments.body:
ya i agree with this. The TLS stack on the client already knows whether it is a stateful or a stateless retry, and can act accordingly. Serializing the information the client already knows into a frame type is redundant and error prone.

cc @mcmanus

comments.body: It depends - the frame type may help to decide between different CID's which helps lookup and reduce conflicts - but I'm not sure it is an issue in this direction.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: I can't come up with a clear reason for them.  The crypto handshake is going to have to indicate that the reset is stateful or stateless, and the transport is going to have to respond accordingly, so I haven't been able to determine what value the extra packet type provides.

comments.author: ekr
comments.body: @siyengar: How does the client know whether it's a stateful or stateless retry? They look the same in TLS. It's just an HRR. It's only the server that knows

comments.author: ekr
comments.body: Oh, I see you're going to claim it has a cookie or it doesn't. But that's not actually the same thing, because you might be using the cookie just to require a proof of reachability as an anti-crypto DoS mitigation

comments.author: siyengar
comments.body:
@ekr I think the client shouldn't know what the difference is between those two cases and should react the same way. For the clients it's a stateless reset either way.  My thought here is that the TLS layer provides an API to say whether or not the message that was received was a stateless reset.

Generally I'm leaning towards the principle that if an endpoint can know about something via an API, we shouldn't need to signal that in a framing layer.

issues.title: Allow repeat ACK's
issues.author: mikkelfj
issues.body:
It is an unfortunate that requirement that "SHOULD NOT be ack'ed again":

You want to ack packets again because you collapse gaps into larger blocks. Only the oldest ACK'ed block should not be acked again. It also leads to unnecessary bookkeeping.

comments.author: marten-seemann
comments.body: At the point where you received an ACK for an ACK, 1 RTT has passed, and there's no need to include any packet lower than the largest acked in new ACK frames, even if you received a heavily reordered packet. By that time, this packet will have been retransmitted anyway.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body:
Does this hold for ultra low latency networks? The retransmission logic may not necessarily follow guidance, and why require tracking this. An ACK might not be ACK'ed for quite a while anyway.

It is a lot simpler to state that an ACK frame should not transmit more than one RTT worth of packets, or what is deemed suitable for the current network conditions.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: The text uses a SHOULD, which is entirely appropriate here.  If you have an idea of how to codify more concrete advice, we would be interested in receiving a PR.

issues.title: PING guidance
issues.author: mikkelfj
issues.body:
It is unclear how fast an endpoint should respond to PING so some clarification would be useful.

It could be no later than when the delayed ACK timer expires because this is the latest an ACK can be deferred. But it could also be expected to be ASAP and used for timing data, or it could be application dependent.

There is also a potential for abuse - as others have pointed out recently, just adding PING to ACK frames can force the hand of the peer. But, if PING is responded to particularly fast, this could be worse than with normal delayed ACKs.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: With PATH_CHALLENGE, the current text is fine.  PING is acknowledged, as normal.

issues.title: CFIN only recoverable with timeout
issues.author: siyengar
issues.body:
If we're sending CFIN and 1-RTT data in the same flight, and only the CFIN is lost, the client can only use the handshake timeout to recover the FIN and not any threshold based recovery.

We don't allow the server to use the 1-RTT keys until it receives the CFIN. This makes it so that even if the server has received 1-RTT data it cannot ack it which would have triggered threshold loss recovery. So the client has to rely on the handshake timeout to send the data.

Are we fine with saying that the client should have a way more aggressive loss timeout for handshake packets than the server should?

comments.author: marten-seemann
comments.body:
This is a specific property of the TLS 1.3 handshake. I'd be more comfortable to keep our loss recovery independent of the specifics of the crypto handshake.
Don't we have the same problem if the last packet of the server flight containing the certificate is lost?

comments.author: siyengar
comments.body: I don't think the problem exists with the server specifically because CFIN is dependent on the SFIN, so the client would not send any data without receiving the SFIN. If the SFIN is lost then the client can't even send ACKs. I think finished messages are tails and should be treated as such

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: This is another form of the problem in #1190, or related to an extent that it might not be worth having another issue.  See that issue for an idea...

comments.author: siyengar
comments.body: Ya i filed this as a new issue because when I spoke to @marten-seemann  and @janaiyengar about this issue, they were also as surprised by this as I was and it has different design implications to the transport regarding packet number spaces of handshake and 1-rtt data

issues.title: ICMP and ICMPv6 PMTUD with asymmetric connection-ids
issues.author: enygren
issues.body:
Asymmetric connection-ids introduce problems for handling ICMP and ICMPv6 PMTUD messages (such as ICMPv6 packet-too-big) in conjunction with stateless load balancers.  For example, if a server sends out a packet containing a client connection-id that is too big, a router or tunnel end-point may send back an ICMPv6 PTB message containing the packet header.  Because the PTB message with the packet header only contains the client connecton-id, it isn't possible to route to the proper server.

While ICMP/ICMPv6 PTB messages are best treated as optimizations, being able to get them can be very useful for identifying the source off loss quickly as being a too-large packet.

Note that other ICMP(v6) messages such as destination-unreachable also have a similar problem with asymmetric connection-ids.

Note that related topics are under active discussion in other working groups, such as:
* draft-bonica-intarea-frag fragile-01
* draft-ietf-tsvwg-datagram-plpmtud

comments.author: enygren
comments.body:
One proposal based on discussions would be to allow Long headers (with both client and server connection-ids) in certain situations following the handshake.  In particular, when performing a PMTUD probe (or otherwise sending a packet with a larger size than the current PMTU), using a Long form header would mean that a stateless load balancer would still be able to route it based on the payload of the ICMP(v6) message, plus it might make it safer and easier for the server to validate that the packet was send by a device on-path.  Both endpoints would still of course need to have reasonable lower bounds on PMTU as well.

Similarly, such a scheme could also make it more reasonable to support ICMP(v6) destination-unreachable messages in a way that wasn't vulnerable to parallel-to-path resets but could allow devices such as NATs to eventually squelch connections where state is no longer present.  For example, if the Nth and subsequent (3rd?) retransmits of the same data was sent with a full Long header (with both connection-ids) and an ICMP(v6) response is returned that contains both connection-ids (plus enough data from what was sent for validation) then this is a good sign that the node sending is both on-path and that this is a degenerate situation that should only have been reached after multiple losses and thus likely from a legitimate active middle-box.

(Note that client/server above are symmetric as both end-points have the same challenge with roles reversed.)

comments.author: igorlord
comments.body: We used to allow long-header packets after handshake, but got rid of them for the lack of a use case.  This is a valid use case, so it would be good to bring back these long-header packets.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: @enygren, @igorlord, the solutions that you are contemplating here are fairly disruptive to the design.  If you feel strongly about this, you should take it to the list and get the attention of the working group.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
FWIW, let me point out that under the current draft it is possible for an endpoint to send a long header packet at any time it wants to observe the MTU, even after the handshake is complete. It's just that the long header packet will be ignored by the peer in case it reaches the peer.

And with the introduction of coalesced packets, the cost of doing this type of PMTUD has become small.

Whenever an endpoint wants to do PMTUD and it has some outstanding data, it can create a datagram that consists of the following two QUIC packets:
* a long header packet with zero-length payload that contains the server CID (or some other payload that is sufficient to route the ICMP response back to the origin server)
* a short header packet carrying outstanding data

This type of datagram never harms the conncection, because the draft requires the receiver to process each QUIC packet as if it was received as a separate datagram.

Assuming that the server will be performing PMTUD and assuming that the client's CID is zero-sized, the overhead of the long header packet is: 1 (type) + 4 (version) + 1 (cidl) + len(server_CID) + 1 (payload-length).

Actually, this approach (i.e. sending a compound datagram to contain arbitrary information) is flexible enough to carry any data that needs to be exposed to an on-path device. We could use it to expose packet drop rate for example.

I'm not saying we should support these kinds of exposures, but we cannot prohibit such thing to happen, because the receiver cannot determine if an incoming packet was sent from the peer (to expose signal to on-path devices) or from an attacker (to disrupt connection).

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body:
> This type of datagram never harms the conncection, because the draft requires the receiver to process each QUIC packet as if it was received as a separate datagram.

That is not necessarily true because that is under a cooperative assumption. Any party that keeps dumping invalid packets might be flagged, also otherwise competent QUIC peers. Seeing something suspect in a packet is reasonable cause for rejecting the entire transmission.

Hence, if this is considered a good idea, both endpoints should understand  and agree  on this and avoid confusing each other.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
> Any party that keeps dumping invalid packets might be flagged, also otherwise competent QUIC peers. Seeing something suspect in a packet is reasonable cause for rejecting the entire transmission.

I disagree. As stated in my comment above, terminating the connection due to seeing suspicious QUIC packets is equal to allowing attackers reset the connection. That goes against our principal of having "authenticated reset."

I believe that the same holds for coalesced packets. An attacker can break the packet by modifying it. But that should not lead to the connection being terminated.

FWIW, section 4.6 of the transport draft says: "The receiver of coalesced QUIC packets MUST individually process each QUIC packet and separately acknowledge them, as if they were received as the payload of different UDP datagrams."

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body:
I didn't mean to say dump the connection. By dump transmission I meant the single UDP datagram - either someone messed with it, or the peer is misbehaving. In that case it makes limited sense to further process the datagram since it is obviously not up to specs.

This opens up to an on-path attack where a third party can attach content to a datagram and here you are right, but compound packets are only used during the early handshake, no? And here the best approach is to reject as much nonsense as possible.

If the peer volunteers to sign a packet that makes non sense it becomes suspecious and repeat offences might lead to disconnection and black listing. Therefore it is IMO not a good idea to use invalid packets for path discovery or any other purpose.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
> This opens up to an on-path attack where a third party can attach content to a datagram and here you are right, but compound packets are only used during the early handshake, no? And here the best approach is to reject as much nonsense as possible.

It is true that compound packets are only used during the handshake. OTOH I do not see why we should reject compound packets after the handshake even though we agree that doing so creates an attack vector.

issues.title: Version Negotiation packet extensibility
issues.author: mikkelfj
issues.body:
Invariants do not allow for future public signatures on the version negotation packet.

Specific versions can of course add their packets, but it would be better if the version negation packet had room for a signature that future versions could evaluate.
Doing this later in the handshake reduces the defense against handshake attacks from man-on-the-side.

The connection ID swaps the source and destination in the server transmitted vneg packet. This adds a reasonable defense against off-path attacks but makes it impossible to use the source ID for a server signature.

A simple solution would be allow the server to replace part of the source id with a public signature while preservering at least 64 octests from the client. This leaves 144 - 64 = 80 octets for a public signature. Ed25519 signatures are 64 octets - which then leaves room for an additional 80 - 64 = 16 octest for a public key identifier. Ed25519 might turn out to be weak and longer signatures would then be required. Therefore an alternative propososal would be to allow a server to append a signture after the version list. This requires a length field at the start of the version list.

NOTE: the algorithm should be left unspecified - but reserving 80 octets would allow future versions some room.

I would prefer adding a length field and allow for future data.

Quote invariant draft 01: 

>  Version Negotiation packets do not use integrity or confidentiality
   protection.  A specific QUIC version might authenticate the packet as
   part of its connection establishment process.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body: This seems to be the issue you were targeting with the solution you suggested in #1247.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body: Not quite - this is a concern for early auth the other is a concern for extensions - one could solve the other.

comments.author: marten-seemann
comments.body:
Is the solution related to #630?
Maybe we can solve both by adding a length field to the Long Header.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: @marten-seemann, yes, but the implied fix for #630 does not necessarily alter the invariants.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body: This was [discussed in London](https://github.com/quicwg/wg-materials/blob/master/ietf101/minutes.md#invariants-1), and there seemed to be a strong sense in the room that we didn't want to do this. Further comments?

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body:
I originally had two issues, one was extensibility and the other was the related public signing in future versions. I tend to agree that extensible vneg can get messy fast, but the lack of any hook to sign such messages is also unfortunate. I would likely create a non-standard extension.

Ian has mentioned that we could use a different version number for future vnegs - which is a decent approach. However, I believe something must be mentioned about this in the invariants. For example that clients may opt to ignore version 0 vnegs in favor of a future defined version when and if one such is defined. Lacking that it should adhere to version 0. Servers likewise.

comments.body: @mikkelfj can you make a slightly more detailed proposal, please?

issues.author: mikkelfj

comments.body:
I talked about exactly this with @siyengar last night. I think it makes sense to have a way to future-proof the vneg packet, since it is part of the invariants.

We might even want to go as far as defining some TLV scheme for UDP payload space past the included options.

comments.body: I expect the network to ossify that 0 for us

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body:
This isn't an issue, it's a proposed solution.

The problem with trying to sign version negotiation is that you don't have an existing relationship with the server to enable any kind of signing key.  So the method that invariants already calls out, in which the contents of the VN packet are authenticated after the fact, seems the most reasonable.

comments.author: larseggert
comments.body:
True on this being a solution. And, I don't actually care about the signing part, which is in another issue.

I care about potentially being able to stick stuff other than versions into a vneg response in the future.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body:
> The problem with trying to sign version negotiation is that you don't have an existing relationship with the server to enable any kind of signing key

That is an assumption. You can easily have a relation with the host even if that model does not match the current TLS 1.3 / HTTP/QUIC model. For example that Verisign says that it isn't evil. It just requires a 64 bit verisign identifier, and signature. Or it could be your own server, but vneg is still a thing due to cluster upgrades.

More generally, this is about being able to add to the vneg for unforseen issues in future version.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body:
But both Mike and Ian are right - it is a proposed solution to an extension issue - changing the version number from 0 to something else is another option.

I just worry that people will start to hack pseudo version numbers in the version table to carry additional data (a sort of TLV as Lars suggests), so overall, adding a length field seems to be the least intrusive form - it would allow random data to follow and it could ossify, but so could pseudo versions.

issues.author: martinthomson
issues.body:
@enygren suggests:

Would it make sense to say that "endpoints exchange QUIC packets via a datagram protocol such as UDP"?  While we are currently only defining on UDP, there is nothing in invariants that would force this perpetually.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
From the first sentence of the charter: "The QUIC working group will provide a standards-track specification for a UDP-based, stream-multiplexing..."

So I'm biased towards saying this is QUICv2.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
I think that it is reasonable to say that we are developing invariants that are based on UDP.  In doing so we make no claims about the use of QUIC over other substrates (such as IP directly).  That seems perfectly OK.

This is invariants, so it can't be v2.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: The invariants don't say anything about non-UDP substrates, as you note, so I think it can be v2, because non-UDP substrates are out of scope.

comments.author: huitema
comments.body: V2, please!

comments.author: pravb
comments.body: agreed, v2 or later.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body:
I think the/another problem with this is that, unlike TCP, QUIC doesn't have port numbers -- it leaves that concern to UDP.  If we want to work atop something other than UDP, then we need to replace that multi-recipient functionality (or build atop something with equivalent recipient-demuxing capability).

Or say that QUIC is a per-device service in a non-UDP environment and use connection IDs to demux.  ;-)

Regardless, this is outside our charter as noted on the list.  We're explicitly chartered to define QUIC over UDP.  I'm inclined to close this with no action on that basis.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body:
Charter or not, it would be considerate to at least contemplate non-UDP designs, especially if this can be done with minimal impact. With dual connection ID's I don't see a strong need for port numbers - there might be some corner cases in handshake, and there might be some text that isn't sufficiently clear in this regard, but fundamentally this ought to be workable.

For example sensor networks using a minimal size connection ID dropping all data at IP/DUP layer and leaving any external routing to a gateway that  understands 8-bit CID's through an out of band configuration.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
Based on the feedback thus far and [Section 3](https://quicwg.github.io/base-drafts/draft-ietf-quic-invariants.html#an-extremely-abstract-description-of-quic), I'm going to close with no action.  That doesn't mean that we're not going to ignore other substrates, only that our invariants are UDP-specific.
