issues.title: "Invariant check" for any inbound LH packet
issues.author: larseggert
issues.body:
Consensus on Slack seems to be that a server should set the version field of a Retry packet to v1 (i.e., echo the version from the client Initial ), and that a client should verify that a received Retry packet echoes the version it sent.

However, I cannot find corresponding text in the documents.

comments.author: larseggert
comments.body: Talking to @nibanks, the issue should maybe be rephrased more generally, in that the document should make it clear(er) that incoming long-header packets need to pass an "invariant check" before any further processing. The version match check on Retry is part of that more general check. Renaming the issue accordingly.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body: Well, Retry is a packet type defined in version 1.  If you receive a v2 packet and you don't speak v2, you have no idea what that packet means, even if it superficially *looks* like a Retry packet.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body:
Also, from 5.2.1:
> If a client receives a packet that has an unsupported version, it MUST discard that packet.

So the answer by current spec might be different for a v1+2-capable client which sent a v1 Initial versus a v1-only client.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: Tokyo conclusion: borderline editorial.  You discard packets from versions other than the negotiated version.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body:
> So the answer by current spec might be different for a v1+2-capable client which sent a v1 Initial versus a v1-only client.

That's interesting. Probably not the intention, but it would allow a v2 SuperRetry packet to be retrofitted into an otherwise v1 connection.

issues.title: Specify DCID of 0-RTT packets
issues.author: mikkelfj
issues.body:
This has been discussed before, but after reorg. of text, I can't find any clear statement in Transport Draft about how to create DCID for 0-RTT. The DCID field is not mentioned for 0-RTT packets in transport draft.

https://github.com/quicwg/base-drafts/issues/1513
https://github.com/quicwg/base-drafts/issues/1721

Note: I got the think about this in the context of replay attack prevention which would be simpler of the 0-RTT DCID is not random. But that discussion was already closed in the above issue.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
We previously discussed this and the conclusion was to change to the server-selected connection ID once a packet has been received from the server.  Until then, the random value would be used.  If this is missing, then we just need some text in the 0-RTT packet section to cover this.  This probably just needs to reference [Section 7.2](https://quicwg.org/base-drafts/draft-ietf-quic-transport.html#negotiating-connection-ids), which says:

>  Upon receiving a packet, each endpoint sets the Destination Connection ID it sends to match the value of the Source Connection ID that they receive.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body: Based on proposed 0-RTT routing to single instance for replay protection, discussed on the mailing list, it would be helpful if the server can assign a DCID for use in 0-RTT that is potentially longer than normal CID's. This is because CID routing lifetime may shorter than 0-RTT session tickets, and a longer DCID could make it easier for a server farm to route 0-RTT packets correctly.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body:
Are you proposing that the client should get a CID along with the NewSessionTicket (or the NEW_TOKEN)?  That's been discussed before, and while it makes sense to me, it means that load balancers need to be able to differentiate the two types (and potentially sizes) of CID.

On the whole, I think this is a promising direction, but perhaps not needed for v1.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body:
Yes, along with the session ticket. The ticket transfer is a bit of a black box so I can only propose the high level concept. (I'm wondering if Retry and 0-RTT could be made more similar, but whatever).

> That's been discussed before, and while it makes sense to me, it means that load balancers need to be able to differentiate the two types (and potentially sizes) of CID.

At least such that they have an option to do so if they are so inclined. I.e. there is no immediate downside since you can also just provide a standard CID if that is better for a particular infrastructure.

As to sizes, that was a bigger problem a while ago when the CID size was implicit. Also, since the CID is only used for 0-RTT, it can be large without significant cost - it should/could be changed immediately upon 0-RTT server acceptance.

As to v1, I agree that might be stretching it a bit.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
The point that keeps coming up in this context (I'm sure I've typed the same response elsewhere...) is that the timescales over which connection IDs are stable is likely far less than the timescale over which attempting 0-RTT is possible.  That is, you might attempt 0-RTT up to a week later, but the server cluster you hit might be in a configuration so different that the connection ID you got 5 or 6 days ago doesn't route to the same node.

That said, for those server configurations that are more stable, this isn't a terrible idea.  If this were discretionary, say as an extension, then it might be useful for ensuring that 0-RTT attempts are routed to the right destination.

But anything that does this sort of targeting could also create a nice targeted DoS vector.  Connect to the same server multiple times over the course of a week.  Then, when it's go time, send that server 0-RTT using all the collected connection IDs that route directly to it.

Marking v2, not editorial.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body: It's fine to move to v2 on the larger issue, but the text is still unclear in transport v1.

issues.title: VN packets may be dropped more often when the QUIC bit is 0
issues.author: ianswett
issues.body:
I've had conversations with a number of people who are interested in identifying QUIC using the QUIC bit.  Only one packet does not have the QUIC bit always set to 1 currently, and that's version negotiation.
https://tools.ietf.org/html/draft-ietf-quic-transport-18#section-17.2.1

Given we have no use for the extra bits in VN, I'm inclined to specify implementations must set it to 1.

If we think we'll one day want to claw back use of the QUIC bit and allow it to be 0, then this is a poor plan, but I don't think that will end up being practical on the public internet.

A related question is whether we want to put the QUIC bit in the invariants.  It's clearly not technically necessary, but it would recognize the ossification I anticipate.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: I have a different proposal: allow those that don't depend on this bit to toggle it.  That is, if you are certain that you don't need this bit set to 1, set it to 0 occasionally.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: That could work.  It comes down to whether the WG thinks the QUIC bit is a bug or feature, as well as whether enough people will toggle it that it won't be ossified anyway.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
@ianswett I like how you frame the issue.

I think that the QUIC bit should either be defined in the invariants draft, or be greased to avoid it getting ossified. And my weak preference goes to greasing the bit, so that we could have maximum flexibility in the future versions of QUIC.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body: I'm a bit concerned that relying on greasing is wishful thinking, here and elsewhere. Mostly this has been bypassed with header protection. All it takes is one dominant implementation to be lazy about it. Think older IE browsers vs. standards.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: The reason the second bit was fixed to 1 in QUICv1 was to allow multiplexing with other protocols. Greasing it would defeat that and would cause problems with some Google servers that use it for demultiplexing. Given that these demultiplexing concerns are unlikely to go away, it does make sense to add it to the invariants.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body:
I suspect VN packets will be pretty rare in the internet before we roll out v2, so we are in real danger of 50% of these packets failing because they have QUIC set to zero. The most straightforward solution is to just codify the ossification that will happen anyway.

@DavidSchinazi is this multiplexing mostly an issue for Initial Packets? Because the way to free up the QUIC bit could be to grease it in the Short Header. No one will implement something that drops 50% of 1RTT packets.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: @martinduke good point - most of the use-cases we have today are servers doing the demultiplexing, and VN is currently only server-to-client. I'm less worried about VN and more about the Internet ossifying "QUIC == the second bit is 1" without it being in the invariants. Greasing the second bit in client-to-server short headers would make it harder to demultiplex on the server without keeping track of all the issued connection IDs, and I don't think we want to make the server demultiplexer stateful.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
I agree that the long header packets sent by the client need to have the QUIC bit set.

I also agree that there's less need to have the bit set in the long header packets sent by the server, though I think it's possible to argue that we should not have different requirements based on the direction of the packets, because QUIC does not have a distinguish a client address tuple and a server address tuple (i.e. an endpoint can use a one address tuple for accepting connections and also for initiating connections as a client).

For short header packets, I think we agree that the bit is not required. Then the question is, assuming that we decide to kill the bit, should we grease it, or rather, change it to a reserve bit? I suggest the latter because changing the definition to "reserved" and covering the bit using header protection is the strongest way of preserving the freedom to use the bit in future versions of QUIC. It can also be considered as a simplification, because there would be not need to "randomize" the bit for greasing; endpoints can rely on the header protection to flip the bits.

FWIW, current definition of the short header first byte is: `0 1 S R R K P P`. This would change to `0 S R R R K P P` if we are going to change the QUIC bit to a reserved bit.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body: To me, it's clear that we should either (1) add it to the invariants or (2) bring it under header protection for server-generated packets only. (2) is somewhat inelegant, but we get to keep using the bits. Are there any privacy implications to there being a "client bit"?

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
> (2) bring it under header protection for server-generated packets only.

I would oppose to such a design, because that disables a reverse proxy from using a single port for accepting connections and also for initiating connections, assuming that either the proxy or a middlebox in front of the proxy relies on the QUIC bit to route the packets. Greasing would be fine, because it's not something to be required for every endpoint to implement.

> Are there any privacy implications to there being a "client bit"?

The bit would be a good indicator to police P2P traffic for ISPs...

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body:
I’m in favor of always setting the bit, and if not, symmetric header protection.

There are significant symmetric use cases, including NAT-punching p2p.

Making it 1 permanently lets QUIC co-exist, eg on a single client 443 port, and it avoids a lot of potential problems over a bit that is not needed.

comments.author: janaiyengar
comments.body:
IIRC, the bit was a result of us wanting to demux with various other protocols, and as such, the entire purpose of the bit is to allow identification of QUIC. This may not be a feature we like, but it is a feature.

I don't think we should be talking about the bit, but about co-existence with the other protocols. We discussed this, @martinthomson made a presentation about it (in Montreal, I think), and we agreed to co-exist.

While it can be seen as a natural consequence of setting the QUIC bit, I think the question we want to ask is whether we ought to make this co-existence an invariant. If so, what is the minimal set of packets that need to be demux-able with these other protocols. (We've been over this before, but I don't think we discussed whether it was adequate to demux only for the long header.)

FWIW most of the discussion happen in New York. See
https://github.com/quicwg/wg-materials/blob/master/interim-18-09/minutes.md#first-octet---martin-thomson.

comments.body: Discussed in Prague; proposal to encourage senders in v1 to set to `1`; retain requirement in invariants to ignore.

issues.title: The number of Connection ID is unbounded to NEW_CONNECTION_ID sender
issues.author: tatsuhiro-t
issues.body:
Specification says that endpoint should provide new connection ID when it sees unused connection ID in the received packet or remote endpoint retires a connection ID.
Because remote endpoint can use any received connection ID without retiring any connection IDs, and local endpoint has to provide new connection ID when it sees these events and must accept any connection ID not retired yet, the number of connection ID which local endpoint has to remember is effectively unbounded.

comments.author: tatsuhiro-t
comments.body: I'm not sure #1994 is related to this.  But the its resolution might fix this issue.  I wait for the outcome of the PR.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
The state exposure for the issuer of connection IDs is the number of NEW_CONNECTION_ID frames it sends minus the number of RETIRE_CONNECTION_ID frames it receives (in both cases, excluding any retransmissions).  The design requires that connection IDs be remembered indefinitely, but the number is bounded by how many NEW_CONNECTION_ID frames the endpoint is willing to send.

The resolution to #1994 will allow an endpoint to send fewer (or more) than its peer requests.

comments.author: erickinnear
comments.body:
To add to this, I think the fundamental design (which, admittedly, a TP confuses a bit) is that the issuer should issue (and maintain with new ones when retired) as many connection IDs as it’s willing to maintain state for. 

So, if the consumer of the CIDs uses all the new ones and doesn’t retire them, it will eventually run out of new ones to use. 

My understanding of the suggestion to replenish when a new one is observed is simply to lower the chance of having the consumer of the CIDs run out while RETIRE_ frames are in flight (or potentially lost). If the issuer is already at the max they’re willing to maintain, then only issue new ones when old ones are retired. The associated assumption here is that a consumer would not be advised to retire all CIDs at the same time.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: The resolution to #2101 was that you can't retire a connection ID in a packet using that CID, which prevents retiring all of them.

comments.author: tatsuhiro-t
comments.body:
If server can stop sending NEW_CONNECTION_ID, it surely fixes this issue.
The problem of current wording is that server MUST send NEW_CONNECTION_ID when it sees unused connection ID.  Meanwhile, client can use all connection ID without retiring none of them and call it a standard compliant.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
@tatsuhiro-t 
> The problem of current wording is that server MUST send NEW_CONNECTION_ID when it sees unused connection ID.

Isn't it a SHOULD?

I ask this, because I see the following text in [section 5.1.1 of the transport draft](
https://quicwg.org/base-drafts/draft-ietf-quic-transport.html#rfc.section.5.1.1): _An endpoint SHOULD ensure that its peer has a sufficient number of available and unused connection IDs. While each endpoint independently chooses how many connection IDs to issue, endpoints SHOULD provide and maintain at least eight connection IDs._

Having that said, I think I agree that we have an issue.

The minimum length of CID is 32 bits, based on the assumption that the space is capable of supporting multiple connections across certain time-space (remember the fact that CID cannot be reused more frequently than updating the secret used to calculate stateless reset tokens). OTOH, we do not prohibit (or discourage) endpoints from updating the CID aggressively.

For example, an endpoint might try to use a new CID whenever one is available in order to achieve "maximum privacy." That would mean that it would consume ~8 CIDs per round-trip, and in case the RTT is 10ms, it would be consuming around 2<sup>16</sup> CIDs every minute.

I do not think we would like to see clients being such aggressive against a server that tries to use minimally-size CIDs.

Therefore, I think we should discourage endpoints from changing CIDs when it is likely that it's tuple is stable.

comments.author: tatsuhiro-t
comments.body: @kazuho You are right, it is SHOULD.  I was probably confused by other places of MUST, or cosmic ray affected my browser to display MUST instead of SHOULD.

comments.author: erickinnear
kazuho
mnot
comments.body: Discussed in Prague; seems to be a dup of #2436; will confirm and close.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: #1994 is now closed as well, so I don't believe there's anything left to do here.  @tatsuhiro-t do you think anything needs to be done?

comments.author: tatsuhiro-t
comments.body: No, my concern was cleared.  Thank you.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: Proposal is to do nothing (more).

comments.author: tatsuhiro-t
comments.body: The endpoint is now officially allowed to limit the number of connection ID to issue by https://github.com/quicwg/base-drafts/pull/2428 and I'm satisfied with it.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body: Closing as invalid (because it's effectively a duplicate). Thanks.

issues.title: loss recovery description mixes variables depending on the packet number space and packet numbers independent of it
issues.author: marten-seemann
issues.body:
[Section 6.5.2](https://quicwg.org/base-drafts/draft-ietf-quic-recovery.html#rfc.section.6.5.2) lists the variables used by the loss recovery algorithm. 
Some of these variables are independent of the packet number space, e.g. `crypto_count`, `*rtt*.`
Other variables apply per packet number space, and we say so explicitly, e.g. `largest_acked_packet`.
Then there are a lot of variables that should be applied per packet number space, but we never say so explicitly, e.g. `sent_packets`, `loss_time`, etc.

The same applies to the pseudo code itself, for example `DetectLostPackets` uses both variables that only apply to one packet number space as well as variables that apply independent of the packet number space.

One way to resolve this would be to index the variables by their respective packet number space.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: I'm labeling this editorial, since the pseudocode isn't intended to be normative, but it's also a bit of work to fix, unfortunately.

comments.author: marten-seemann
comments.body:
I mostly agree, although there might be some non-editorial parts to it.
For example, if `loss_time` is applied per packet number space, we need to define which one to use in `SetLossDetctionTimer()`. I don't see that we do that anywhere (and we don't describe it in the text either).

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: Good point.  I'll make this design then.  We can also split this issue in two, but I think it makes sense to try to write a PR first and see if there any other changes necessary in the text.

issues.title: Can VN and Retry packets be coalesced?
issues.author: marten-seemann
issues.body:
They don't have a length field, so the only place they could go is at the end of a packet.
As the spec currently stands, it's valid to send a packet like this.

There's little value in doing that. Do we want to continue to allow this?

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
My understanding is that they are implicitly forbidden, because coalescing packets belonging to different connections are forbidden, and because there’s nothing to coalesce with when either of the two types of the packets is sent.

I am not sure if we need to be more clear on that, considering the fact we generally use MAY for the discarding rules for coalesced packets.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
VN certainly causes a new connection based on discussions in Tokyo.

Retry does not cause a new connection(ie: same ClientHello).

Clarifying this seems wise if it's not already clear.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
> Retry does not cause a new connection(ie: same ClientHello).

Yes, however when a Retry packet is being sent, there's nothing a server can send along with.

Regarding if we need to clarify, while I do not think it's absolutely necessary, I can see that people might want to have it stated considering the fact that we do utilize corner case rules of coalesced packets (see #2402).

comments.author: mnot
comments.body: So, is this editorial?

comments.author: janaiyengar
comments.body: I'm with @kazuho, but I'm still wondering: what is the clarification that we can provide?

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
@janaiyengar Simply clarifying that "VN and Retry packets will never be coalesced" as part of the changes we would make in #2308 might be a good idea.

We do not need to use a RFC 2119 word here due to the editorial nature of the issue.

issues.title: H3 guidance on malformed request/response is light
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
This issues arises from some off-list discussion on how to build up a header list, and who is responsible for validating the result. The conclusion is that the application is responsible for doing so.

In HTTP/2, RFC 7540 section 8.1.2.6 explains how an endpoint should handle malformed requests or responses. There is no explicit link to this in H3, only implicitly via references to topics in 8.1.2.*. However, I think some of that guidance is not applicable: the one that sticks out is this:

> A request or response is also malformed
   if the value of a content-length header field does not equal the sum
   of the DATA frame payload lengths that form the body.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
Some further info. In H2, malformed request/response causes a stream error of type PROTOCOL_ERROR. The H3 draft says:

> PROTOCOL_ERROR (0x1):
    No single mapping. See new HTTP_MALFORMED_FRAME error codes defined in Section 8.1.

But errors in the category of malformed request/response may not caused by a problem with the frames themselves. 

Fortunately, we have H3 HTTP_GENERAL_PROTOCOL_ERROR, which seems like the correct thing to use in this case. But nowhere in the draft is this ever referred to, so its easy to miss.

comments.author: lnicco
comments.body:
FRAME related errors are defined at the end of S8.1. 
However that is going to change due to #2253 
 
```
HTTP_MALFORMED_FRAME (0x01XX):
An error in a specific frame type. The frame type is included as the last byte of the error code. For example, an error in a MAX_PUSH_ID frame would be indicated with the code (0x10D).
```

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
Nice catch!

I think I'd prefer using HTTP_GENERAL_PROTOCOL_ERROR or an error code just for this purpose rather than HTTP_MALFORMED_FRAME, because this is a framing error in the HTTP semantic layer, rather than an error in a HTTP/3 frame. The issue with using HTTP_MALFORMED_FRAME becomes most apparent when the request body is shorter than the sum of DATA frames, and if there is a trailer. Then, the error will be detected when seeing the HEADERS frame. It would be strange to report the issue as HTTP_MALFORMED_FRAME(HEADERS) (because it's not an issue with the HEADERS frame), or as HTTP_MALFORMED_FRAME(DATA) (because none of the DATA frames that the client sent was malformed.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
~~PS. and my preference goes to having an error code just for this purpose, named as HTTP_RESPONSE_CANCELLED, or something similar.~~

~~As a reverse proxy developer, whenever the upstream server closes the response abruptly, I try to forward that error to the client. H2 does not have an error code for that, and we use PROTOCOL_ERROR for that. But the error code misses the fact that the error happened elsewhere than between the client and the server that is using H2, which _is_ confusing.~~

^^ this comment is about an endpoint abruptly closing a stream rather than an endpoint detecting the peer abruptly closing a stream. Taking back the comment, as I think it deserves a separate issue.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
Another error that we saw a lot in the early days of H2 deployment was headers fields using mixed-case capitalization. This cannot be attributed to a malformed H3 frame. 

I really hope this class of error has been shaken out of systems by now but you never know.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
@LPardue 
> Another error that we saw a lot in the early days of H2 deployment was headers fields using mixed-case capitalization. This cannot be attributed to a malformed H3 frame.
> 
> I really hope this class of error has been shaken out of systems by now but you never know.

Agreed. I think using HTTP_GENERAL_PROTOCOL_ERROR as a catch-all error code when the peer does something stupid makes sense. After all, that's what we did in H2 and IMO it works well.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body: I think this falls under the umbrella of making sure RFC7540 content is referenced / restated appropriately in an H3 world.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body: Maybe it's worth noting that HTTP_GENERAL_PROTOCOL_ERROR is the error that a proxy is expected to send when upstream resets a HTTP message (e.g., h1 connection being closed in middle of a T-E chunk, receiving RST_STREAM on a h2 stream). We could have an error code dedicated to that, but H2 has not had one and therefore I do not think there's a strong necessity to have a dedicated codepoint.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body: Discussed in London; restate them with care.

issues.title: MAX_PUSH_ID: lower-than-previous value conn error seems too severe
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
The 18 spec says:

> A MAX_PUSH_ID frame cannot reduce the maximum Push ID; receipt of a MAX_PUSH_ID that contains a smaller value than previously received MUST be treated as a connection error of type HTTP_MALFORMED_FRAME.

This feels like another case of an error that isn't strictly a frame error. Its the data inside that is semantically wrong. The connection error severity also seems pretty extreme, and I question if its really needed. I think the appropriate fix is to borrow logic from the Transport's similar MAX_STREAMS frame:

> Loss or reordering can cause a MAX_STREAMS frame to be received which
   states a lower stream limit than an endpoint has previously received.
   MAX_STREAMS frames which do not increase the stream limit MUST be
   ignored.

The proposal therefore is to say that MAX_PUSH_ID can only increase the value, anything else gets ignored.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
A connection error is entirely appropriate.  The awkward compromise we have in the transport docs exists because there is at least a plausible argument in support of ignoring regressions in limits.  There, reordering and retransmission schemes might produce the situation (even if the latter might be somewhere between inadvisable and malicious).  Here, the frames appear on a strictly ordered stream with no chance that it is going to be missed.  I see no reason to treat this leniently.

The error code question I have no opinion on, other than to suggest the application of principles already articulated.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
I see your point of view. The downside is that the client application layer needs to coordinate its sending of this frame to ensure the sequence is strictly growing - this constrains some of the design choices an implementation might choose to make. 

I question the severity because I don't know why a server would get so upset by seeing a value that is smaller than it had before. If the server is at the current max streams amount, it is unable to generate pushes until something increases the max. What could possibly go wrong? ™️ I don't want to fall into the trap of justifying every design decision but this one is not resonating with me probably because I am missing something.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: Given this is delivered in order on the control stream, requiring it never decrease seems sensible.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
So the hypothetical implementation I have in mind is a client that receives pushes that can be processed independently. In some edge cases, pushes may have mixed use of static and dynamic tables. Static-only pushes can make progress without reliance on QPACK stream(s) progressing. I might set up a handling chain for a single push that does something like "when complete, send MAX_PUSH_ID with value current push ID + 1". There may be cases where this leads to a lower limit being sent.

Another edge case is naive handling of CANCEL_PUSH when it is sent by the server. A client that wants to maintain a number of concurrent pushes needs to update MAX_PUSH_ID pretty quick, and a simple way to do this is to read the Push ID out of CANCEL_PUSH and increment by 1. Again this may cause a lower limit being sent.

One solution to these problems is, on the client side, to track the high water mark of Push ID and only emit a MAX_PUSH_ID frame that increases the high water mark. 

The client side complexity seems like it could be greater than the equivalent server side (if the rule were to be relaxed).

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: Don't you need a synchronization point when it comes to putting the bytes in the stream buffer anyway?

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
Yes, but whether that synchronisation point coordinates based on H3 frames or simply STREAM data seems like an implementation detail. I.e. I call frame.to_bytes() and then feed that to my transport library API.

The upside to doing limit increase cleverly on the client, is that you open the opportunity to aggregate push limit increments. I.e. send one frame that increments by a single larger value.

If we were to bring the discussion  back to principles, is the intent of the connection error here because sending a lower limit is meaningless for both sides?

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: Oh, principles.  The principle at play is that if a peer is demonstrably not participating in the same protocol, stop communicating with them as soon as you detect that so they can sort things out.  There are cases where meaningless messages can be ignored as harmless, but it's best not to ignore them unless ignoring is difficult.  I still think we made the wrong choice with MAX_DATA and friends, but at least there the extenuating circumstances are such that the choice is defensible.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: Ok, I can get behind that. I have an alternate proposal at hand on #2418. Depending on how that goes I'll file a separate issue about adjusting some of the wording about the error type.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body: And more pragmatically, you can't do a non-fatal stream error on the control stream.  If these moved to a separate unidirectional stream, I'd be open to the possibility of making an error kill push rather than the whole connection.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: That's what got me thinking about the unidirectional stream. Killing the stream is a very explicit signal, but also not dissimilar to running out of credit permanently. A stream error could be upgraded to connection error if a server really wanted...

comments.author: dtikhonov
comments.body: @LPardue, the possible complications for the client that you have outlined above don't seem terribly complex.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
/shrug. 

Seeing little interop of push, its hard to tell if this would really be a problem. I suspect it won't be, and I think I can live with the current specification. However, in the meantime the idea of uni streams for everything has taken a life of its own in #2678. 

I'll leave this issue open until that broader discussion gets resolved one way or other.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body: Discussed in London; there's no reason to reduce in value on an ordered stream (which presumably has synchronized access already).  The proposal of HTTP_ERROR_YOU_ARE_AN_IDIOT was likely facetious, but PROTOCOL_VIOLATION serves the same purpose.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body: You mean HTTP_GENERAL_PROTOCOL_ERROR? I don't think it is appropriate to send QUIC transport errors for application protocol errors. Perhaps we need language for this?

issues.title: Mandate using a new connection ID on migration
issues.author: martinthomson
issues.body: In fixing #2145, I discovered that we don't actually mandate this.  It's a privacy requirement that I thought we had previously agreed to, but it appears as though we missed capturing it properly.

comments.author: igorlord
comments.body: I do not think it is wise to prohibit connection migration, when there are no available connection IDs.  This is something that the client is fully capable of deciding for itself -- to migrate using an old connection ID or to reconnect instead.  I would go with MUST use, if there is one available.  Otherwise, privacy-conscious clients SHOULD reconnect.

comments.author: erickinnear
comments.body:
It looks like it’s been moved around a lot, but 5.1.2 says

> As discussed in Section 9.5, each connection ID MUST be used on packets sent from only one local address. An endpoint that migrates away from a local address SHOULD retire all connection IDs used on that address once it no longer plans to use that address.

Historically, that’s been under the CID sections, not the migration sections, which made it kind of hard for me to dig up. 

Re the proposed diff: 
>An endpoint that exhausts available connection IDs can only
migrate if the peer chooses to use receive packets with zero-length connection
IDs.

Does that conflict at all with the below text in 5.1?

> An endpoint whose peer has selected a zero-length connection ID MUST continue to use a zero-length connection ID for the lifetime of the connection and MUST NOT send packets from any other local address.

comments.author: martinthomson
igorlord
comments.body:
> allowing a peer to exhaust connection IDs to maintain linkability across migrations is an attack that I'd rather we not have.

I'd not worry about the peer. But I would, indeed, worry about a man-on-a-side exhausting your reserve of connection IDs by pretending to initiate peer migration events.  So this is a valid concern.

Of course, a violation of this MUST is indistinguishable from NAT rebinding/tethering migration and thus is not detectable by the peer.  So this MUST is really just a recommendation.  It is a fine recommendation.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: I agree with @igorlord here. In Tokyo we decided we want to avoid MUSTs that can't be enforced, and in this case it's reasonable for some clients to value migration over non-linkability when they run out of CIDs.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body:
> As for the perceived conflict, yeah, the text is not ideal. I'll find some way to reword it. Perhaps by observing that you can never run out of zero-length connection IDs.

The intent is clearly to disallow avoidable migration on empty CIDs. Not running out would suggest keep using it, which is wrong.

Otoh: if it is not required to use a new CID, it makes no sense to forbid empty CID, on migration.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body:
The problem with migrating with an empty CID is that the recipient can't identify which connection it should be considered for.  It's going to have to do trial decryption with the keys for all current 0LCID connections on that destination port if it wants to permit that.  (In fact, I'm fairly sure we previously had text that said if you couldn't match a packet to exactly one connection upon receipt, you had to drop it; that seems to have been removed.)  On a NAT rebinding, a server could say that if the IP matches and only the port has changed, it might still match a singular existing connection.

That's only safe if the server is using a unique port for each connection, which seems unlikely.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body: @MikeBishop Good point.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: Yes, I think that this was a mistake on my part.  Clearly, if there is no connection ID on outward-bound packets, migration is generally inadvisable.  I'll update the PR.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: Superseded by #2414, which does more, but does it better.

comments.author: janaiyengar

issues.title: Unidirectional RESET_STREAM/STOP_SENDING semantics map poorly to proxies
issues.author: martinduke
issues.body:
Apologies for the lateness of the issue, but I only recently realized I was doing it wrong.

What is the thinking behind RESET_STREAM only applying to the send side of a bidirectional stream? What use case says "never mind about what I'm sending you, but please keep sending to me" within the same stream context?

I ask because this is a break from the HTTP/2-TCP world and I'm not sure we fully understand its properties.  In particular, this divergence is uncomfortable for proxying HTTP/3 for HTTP/1 and HTTP/2 servers.

If the HTTP/3 client sends a RESET_STREAM, what is the proper semantic to translate to the HTTP/2 side? An HTTP/2 RESET_STREAM will kill both directions, which seems like a problem in the general case. We can FIN the H/2 stream, but is that communicating the correct semantic to the application?

Similarly, if we get a STOP_SENDING, what's the correct translation? Zeroing out receive flow control on the HTTP/2 stream?

More generally, a future (non-HTTP) proxy use case might map QUIC streams to some protocol over individual TCP connections. This has the same problem: FIN maps nicely to TCP FIN, but RESET_STREAM and STOP_SENDING both have to use TCP RST somehow.

Maybe the answer is that fronting non-QUIC/H3 protocols implies that STOP_SENDING and RESET_STREAM have to go together. Would that break stuff?

I can see a few cases where it might be optimal to be able to flush only one direction of queues, but wonder if this is worth the added semantic confusion, and the bandwidth cost of having to send RESET_STREAM in both directions. We need to get a "final length" in both directions to keep the flow control accounting right, but that could be declared by the receiver.

I'm not sure what specific recommendation to make here, but am curious about everyone's thoughts.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
This is a great example of something that would be better on the mailing list.

The reason for the split is to ensure that the state machine is consistent and synchronized.  Cancellation of a stream requires RESET_STREAM in both directions to ensure that the flow control state doesn't get out of sync.  We discussed attaching a value to STOP_SENDING, but that creates difficult conflicts if one side sends STOP_SENDING and the other sends RESET_STREAM concurrently.  We also don't insist on STOP_SENDING being transmitted reliably.  In other words, just fixing this would be a massive change.

It also exists to provide for cases in HTTP where one side of a flow (typically a request) isn't needed.  Consider a large POST to a resource that has been removed.  The server can send STOP_SENDING and a 404 response without fear that the 404 will be shredded.

All of that has been litigated at some length.

The problem here is in mapping to protocols that have inconsistently implemented or non-existent half-closed states.  That would be TCP for the former and HTTP/2 for the latter.  My inclination would be thus:

RESET_STREAM only = stop forwarding data in that direction, and record this state
STOP_SENDING only = stop forwarding data in that direction, and record this state
RESET_STREAM in both directions or RESET_STREAM and STOP_SENDING from the same peer = kill the flow, using things like h2 RST_STREAM or TCP RST

I don't think that this implies that RESET_STREAM and STOP_SENDING have to be bundled.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body:
As to the H3 question, the spec currently says:
> When a stream is closed, this indicates the end of an HTTP message. Because some messages are large or unbounded, endpoints SHOULD begin processing partial HTTP messages once enough of the message has been received to make progress. If a client stream terminates without enough of the HTTP message to provide a complete response, the server SHOULD abort its response with the error code HTTP_INCOMPLETE_REQUEST.

The stream might have closed because of a FIN or a RESET; if the entire request arrived intact, the server can proceed to respond; the RESET just means that no attempt will be made to repair any losses.  A STOP_SENDING, however, means that you don't want the response even if the request went through.

Thus:
> Clients can cancel requests by aborting the stream (QUIC RESET_STREAM and/or STOP_SENDING frames, as appropriate) with an error code of HTTP_REQUEST_CANCELLED (Section 8.1). When the client cancels a response, it indicates that this response is no longer of interest. Implementations SHOULD cancel requests by aborting both directions of a stream.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body:
> QUIC RESET_STREAM and/or STOP_SENDING

Is that really true? RESET is the senders responsibility, and it only applies to one direction of a bidi stream. STOP_SENDING is the receivers responsibility. Or what am I missing?

issues.title: Error code for indicating that a HTTP response is aborted
issues.author: kazuho
issues.body:
When a reverse proxy forwards a HTTP response to the client, sometimes it sees the upstream server terminate the response early. For example, a HTTP/1.1 connection being closed prior to transmitting number of bytes specified by the `content-length` field. Or a chunked response being closed abruptly.

The only way of delegating such a condition to the client in HTTP/2 was to send a RST_STREAM frame with `PROTOCOL_ERROR`. However, use of the error code is awkward in this case, considering the fact that the error did not happen within the communication between the endpoints using the particular HTTP/2 connection.

I think it makes sense to have an error code that better designates the case.

One way to address the issue in H3 would be to change `HTTP_REQUEST_CANCELLED` to `HTTP_MESSAGE_CANCELLED`, and let the server use the error code (as an argument of the RESET_STREAM frame) to indicate that the response has been "cancelled".

Originally proposed in 
https://github.com/quicwg/base-drafts/issues/2410#issuecomment-460330192.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body: What if you do not want to admit to being a proxy? (who does?)

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body: HTTP_MESSAGE_CANCELLED would simply mean that the transfer of the response is cancelled, regardless of the server being an origin or a reverse proxy.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: I can get behind this.  As long as we're not looking for a byte-by-byte reproduction of the bytes the intermediary received (as was once requested and rejected, I think at the Seattle interim), then it makes sense to signal that the message was killed.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body: This is basically an expansion of the CANCELLED/REJECTED codes to allow a server to do either.  WFM.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body: @MikeBishop Yes. And thank you for the PR.

issues.title: Consider a new stream type to act like MAX_PUSH_ID
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body:
This straw man idea stems from the discussion on #2412.

Consider defining a new unidirectional stream type for Max Push ID updates. This can be expressed as unframed data: a series of increasing var ints. The use of MAX_PUSH_ID frame is entirely unidirectional, so using a uni stream is a slightly better fit to the concept. Another reason to consider this approach is that it lends itself to extracting server push into an extension. It provides a pattern for how future extensions could manage themselves without needing to pollute the core control stream.

The max Push ID stands out as a connection-level state that has no associated H3 Setting. The reintroduction of an ENABLE_PUSH setting was recently dismissed in Tokyo, for valid reasons.

In this proposal, one client initiated unidirectional stream of type "Max Push ID update" may be created by a client as a clear signal of its interest in enabling server push. Push IDs sent on the stream can only increase in value, any decrease is a *Stream* error of type TBD (possibly just generic HTTP protocol error). Judicious endpoints can upgrade stream error to connection error if they so wish. For reference, closing the H3 control streams is verboten. This solves the problem with the draft 18 text that suggests sending a connection error of MALFORMED_FRAME if a MAX_PUSH_ID frame is received with a value lower than previously seen.

Applying validation at the stream level may be easier to implement, needing only compare next push ID to previous push ID.

One problem with this proposal is that it adds another stream that a server needs to coordinate with. However, server push is already coordinating over the control stream, request streams and push streams.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: If the sequence is monotonic increasing, a series of deltas will make it more efficient.  Slightly.  I mean, the stream overhead here will dominate anyway.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
> If the sequence is monotonic increasing, a series of deltas will make it more efficient. Slightly. I mean, the stream overhead here will dominate anyway.

Neat idea. unsigned deltas may actually be a more natural mapping for what the client is trying to express in terms of managing concurrent pushes. However, this might add some work for the server to reconstruct the push ID. Not sending explicit values seems like an easy way for the server to misunderstand the clients intent.

The only issue I see here is HoL blocking. It would be nicer to not

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
To clarify, I believe the problems this is solving/benfits are:
 1) Impossible to have an invalid value in MAX_STREAM_ID
 2) Makes push more like an extension
 3) Saves 2+bytes per update to MAX_STREAM_ID
 4) Slight reduction in odds of head of line blocking from moving off the control stream.

I'm not sure if this is worth the extra complexity of another dedicated stream or not.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
It might also solve the problem that the server cannot tell the client that there will be no server push used in a H3 session. You could do that with this design by resetting the "push control stream" or whatever we want to call it. 

This is a different way to address the lack of SETTINGS_(DIS|EN)ABLE_PUSH.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
> Consider defining a new unidirectional stream type for Max Push ID updates. This can be expressed as unframed data: a series of increasing var ints.

Am I correct in assuming that the design have the same issue to what you tried to address in #2412? If so, I wonder what the benefit of changing the design is.

> The use of MAX_PUSH_ID frame is entirely unidirectional, so using a uni stream is a slightly better fit to the concept. Another reason to consider this approach is that it lends itself to extracting server push into an extension. It provides a pattern for how future extensions could manage themselves without needing to pollute the core control stream.

I am not sure if that is the preferred approach. Although I acknowledge some of the upsides, the downsides of using unidirectional stream are that it requires more state (due to the need for it's own send / receive buffers) and that it is sometimes complex to synchronize the states that are communicated over multiple streams. There are multiple cases where we could use a dedicated stream instead of sending a frame on the control stream; PRIORITY, CANCEL_PUSH, GOAWAY, DUPLICATE_PUSH, I believe that the payload of all these frames can be sent using their own streams, the same way the proposal tries to carry the payload of MAX_PUSH_ID frame.

To put it another way, it seems to me that our current design pattern is to use the control stream for transmitting various data instead of allocating a different unidirectional stream for each type of information. Allocating a different stream for just MAX_PUSH_ID would be a inconsistency in the design. Do we want to have dedicated unidirectional streams for each type of control information? To me that sounds like a design that's unnecessarily heavyweight.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
No other frame has the same combination of characteristics as MAX_PUSH_FRAME:

* Valid in one direction only
* Valid on one stream type only
* Hard requirements on order of values carried in frame, with failure requiring a connection error

GOAWAY comes close but is more lenient I think

(Edited to remove bad reference

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
I might also dare to incite the qpackers and say that we could live without encoder and decoder streams. Insteaf creating some new frame types that hold the instructions and exchange them on control stream.

H3 with QUIC is pretty inconsistent across the board.

comments.author: MikeBishop
LPardue
comments.body:
This is a valiant explanation, thanks Mike.

I don't see how unreliable DATAGRAM fixes the problem with handling MAX_PUSH_ID. I think it risks making the problem worse with the current rules. 

Consider a client that sends a ID 5, then ID 3 erroneously. If these are in separate DATAGRAMS, the error may go unnoticed if the first frame was lost. Furthermore, loss could effectively starve the server of Push ID credits, with neither endpoint being the wiser as to what happened.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body: We have a mandatory error because they arrive in a fixed order and therefore an incorrect receipt order means an incorrect send order.  Once DATAGRAMs are used, there's no ordering guarantee, so no check can be performed on the receiver.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
I think depends if we ascribe special meaning to the fact that a client took N steps to a max value, or if we just care that we arrive at the max value.

To me, the endstate is the same. And since you can't "steal back" push ID credits, neither side should care if that manifests. 

But there may be gotchas in ignoring lower limits so I can fall in line of popular opinion.

I'm not seeing an outright no to this strawman. I think there are some unique benefits and drawbacks. What is a sensible path forward, a more solid PR?

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: I'd say that we need better justification than "not an outright no".  For something like this, control stream seems fine.  The frames are small (and could be made smaller by making them deltas, something I'd be happy to see).

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
Ok.

The problem I see with deltas is that the client can easily blow the limit of Push ID e.g. send 2 maximum varints in a pathological case. This kind of error is not possible with the current design.

issues.title: HTTP/3 TLV length description is no longer precise
issues.author: mikkelfj
issues.body: Now that length is no longer first, I think the length description should be updated to clarify what it includes: it says it does not include the type, but the type precedes it. Does it include the length itself? Many designs mix do this, and some designs have both styles in the same message.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body:
This may be OBE.  Looking at the current version, it says:

```
A frame includes the following fields:

  Type:
  : A variable-length integer that identifies the frame type.

  Length:
  : A variable-length integer that describes the length of the Frame Payload.

  Frame Payload:
  : A payload, the semantics of which are determined by the Type field.
```

This appears to be fairly precise -- the Length field describes the length of the Frame Payload, which is a specified region of the frame.  I'm not inclined to add further disclaimers around what "length" means unless others feel it's unclear.

issues.title: Reserved versions will "probably" never represent a real protocol?
issues.author: MikeBishop
issues.body:
This seems unnecessarily wishy-washy.  Either they're reserved by definition, and therefore **will never** represent a real protocol, or they're available for use.

We should remove the "probably" unless there's a good reason to keep it that I'm missing.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: Use of that word was entirely intentional.  If there is certainty about this status, then it creates a temptation to apply certain optimizations that could be disruptive.  What if middleboxes cached Version Negotiation packets from servers and helpfully provided responses to greased connection attempts?

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body:
We fear that someone might ossify if they discover that these are *definitely* not real protocol versions.  On the other hand, the thing that breaks is use of these as real protocol versions, which I don't believe we're trying to achieve.  If the middlebox is generating *accurate* VN packets, that seems entirely reasonable (and indistinguishable from actual VN packets).  If they're generating inaccurate VN packets, then our anti-downgrade protections that we've decided to implement RSN will break.

On the other hand, if these ever are real protocol versions, then a junk grease packet using the reserved version will fail to parse as a valid Initial and will just fail rather than eliciting a VN response.

This seems like an impossible battle to win, and a lot of subtlety to expect of middlebox vendors.  Write what we mean and move on.

issues.title: HTTP/3 doesn't mandate RFC8470 compliance
issues.author: MikeBishop
issues.body: Since QUIC provides 0-RTT support, it really should.

issues.title: Reserved versions are not version-dependent
issues.author: marten-seemann
issues.body: We only talk about reserved versions in the transport document. Since they're used to trigger VN, they need to be version independent. Should they be moved to the invariants?

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: I would say no.  We don't need to make any particular version invariant.

comments.author: marten-seemann
comments.body: If you include reserved versions for greasing purposes in the VN packet, and we later define a QUIC version with that version number, a client might pick this previously reserved version. So to me it looks like the reserved versions have to be stable between different versions.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: The registry is stable.  There was talk about moving that, but it never happened.

comments.author: larseggert
comments.body: @martinthomson are you saying that because the version registry is stable across versions, its contents in effect become part of the invariants?

comments.author: mnot
comments.body: Would it make sense to refer to the version registry (or at least its definition) in invariants? If that's all this is about, we could just call this editorial< I think.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body:
There's a balancing act here.  From an architecture standpoint, the registry and reserved versions belong in the invariants, because they're inherently part of the cross-version properties of QUIC.

However, there's also the political answer, which is that Invariants describes what we want outside observers to focus on about the wire image.  The idea that certain versions aren't "real" is explicitly *not* something we want outside observers to pay attention to.  Thus, the current location is a(n exceptionally weak) form of security by obscurity.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body: That sounds like an argument to close this issue with no action. @marten-seemann do you feel strongly about this? Anyone else?

comments.author: marten-seemann
comments.body: @MikeBishop's argument sounds reasonable to me. I'm ok with closing this.

issues.title: loss recovery of crypto packets is less aggressive, not more aggressive
issues.author: marten-seemann
issues.body:
We claim that 
> Data in CRYPTO frames is critical to QUIC transport and crypto negotiation, so a more aggressive timeout is used to retransmit it.

As pointed out in #2417, the only mechanisms we have for retransmitting crypto packets is Fast Retransmit (i.e. when an ACK declares a packet lost) and the Crypto Retransmission timer. Specifically, we don't have an Early Retransmit timer for crypto packets. This means that if a tail packet in one packet number space is lost, we wait 2 RTTs before retransmitting it, whereas with Early Retransmit the retransmission would have happened after 9/8 RTT.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
Good point, I think this is really a bug and the time threshold loss detection should trump retransmitting handshake data.

This may be a good argument for adding a second timer just for time threshold loss detection.  I can make it work without that, but would that make it clearer?

comments.author: marten-seemann
comments.body: Why do we need a second timer? Wouldn't it be sufficient to have another `loss_time` variable for crypto packets?

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
I don't believe we need a second timer, and in implementation, I don't think it's necessary.

However, others have previously suggested it may make the pseudocode easier to read.

I'll try a minimal fix first, and we can add a second alarm if it ends up being clearer.

comments.author: marten-seemann
comments.body:
I just tried to sketch the algorithm using a packet-number-space dependent `loss_time`, i.e. `loss_time[kPacketNumberSpace]`. In `SetLossDetectionTimer()`, you'd then use the smallest (non-zero) `loss_time` for your timer, and only arm the crypto retransmission timeout if all 3 `loss_time`s are 0.
This seems to work fine, and is generally (a lot) more aggressive than what we currently have, however, there's one corner case where it's less aggressive. Consider the following sequence of packets being sent:
```
t=1: Initial 1
t=2: Initial 2
t=3: Handshake 1
```
Now we receive an ACK for Initial 2, and arm the early retransmit timer at `t=1+1.125x`, where `x` is the RTT. When this timer fires, we retransmit Initial 1 as Initial 3. The crypto retransmission timeout will now be set this time plus 2 RTT, i.e. `t=1+3.125x`. This is then the first time we retransmit Handshake 1.
Without the early retransmit timer, we would have retransmitted Handshake 1 2 RTTs after sending it, i.e. at `t=3+2x`, which for all realistic RTTs would be earlier.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
Good point, that is a case when the new approach is slightly less aggressive.

If we wanted to favor aggressiveness during the handshake, we could arm the crypto timer based on the left edge(earliest unacked ack-eliciting packet) rather than the right(latest unacked).  That's a larger change than I'd like to make in this CL/issue, though.

I believe the example you outlined above is fairly unlikely, because for most connections, if multiple initials are sent, they're likely to be re-transmissions, not new data.  In that case, when Initial 2 is acked, Initial 1 is immediately lost and Handshake 1 is still the only outstanding ack-eliciting packet.  That being said, I can probably construct other situations that are somewhat similar.

comments.author: marten-seemann
comments.body:
> If we wanted to favor aggressiveness during the handshake, we could arm the crypto timer based on the left edge(earliest unacked ack-eliciting packet) rather than the right(latest unacked). That's a larger change than I'd like to make in this CL/issue, though.

I'm not sure if it would work. The main reason is the 3x amplification limit, which can delay the sending of crypto packets on the server side. You could then run into the situation where the timer based on the oldest packet already expires, just after sending another crypto packet. It wouldn't make a lot of sense to immediately retransmit that packet.

comments.author: marten-seemann
comments.body: @janaiyengar I saw you closed this issue already, but I don't think my concerns in https://github.com/quicwg/base-drafts/issues/2435#issuecomment-462371300 are fully addressed by #2451. Do you think it's ok to just ignore that corner case?

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
@marten-seemann I'll reopen this issue while we discuss this.

I believe the original core of this issue was that when early retransmit was at play, crypto retransmission was substantially less aggressive than other packets.  As you noted, that clearly was not the intent and I believe that's been fixed.

The case you outline is interesting, because even if Initial 3 is acked, the only mechanism we have to recover from the loss of Handshake 1 is the crypto timer.  If we'd like to avoid always spuriously retransmitting Handshake 1 in this scenario, we have to wait until Initial 3 is acked, because otherwise the peer likely doesn't have keys to decrypt Handshake 1.

In practice, when Initial 3 is acked, the server can likely assume the client has the handshake keys and if it doesn't receive an ACK for Handshake 1 in a relatively short period of time(maybe 1/8 RTT), then retransmit Handshake 1.  But that's making assumptions about key availability from recovery information, which seems like a very questionable optimization to save 7/8 RTT in an edge case where two packets from two different packet number spaces are lost in short sequence.

TLDR: I think the current algorithms are good, and only if we were ok with spuriously retransmitting all handshake data in the majority of cases when a single Initial packet was lost could we adopt a more aggressive approach.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: I think my last update is still accurate and I don't see a way to improve the current mechanism that doesn't greatly increase spurious handshake retransmits, so I'm going to mark it as fixed.

issues.title: rate-limiting of CID issuance needs to be allowed
issues.author: kazuho
issues.body:
At the moment, the transport draft assumes that the issuer of CIDs is going to issue new ones as the consumer retires them. Quoting from [section 5.1.1 of the transport draft](https://quicwg.org/base-drafts/draft-ietf-quic-transport.html#rfc.section.5.1.1), the issuer _SHOULD do this by **always** supplying a new connection ID when a connection ID is retired by its peer or when the endpoint receives a packet with a previously unused connection ID_ (emphasis mine).

However, simply following the provision introduces a DoS attack vector.

Malicious clients can connect to a server and consume CIDs as fast as they can. Assuming that the server tries to provide 8 spare CIDs, a client with 10ms RTT can consume 800 CIDs per second (≈ 2<sup>16</sup> CIDs per minute per connection). This is especially a risk to servers using minimally-sized CIDs (which is 32-bits). An attacker controlling 256 connections can consume all the CIDs in 4 hours. Because a server cannot reuse a CID as frequently as that (because it cannot rotate the secret used to generate stateless reset tokens very often). This would be a risk for clustered servers using longer CIDs as well, because the number-space used to identify each path within each server is expected to consume only some of the bits of the CID.

Therefore, it is preferable to clarify that a server might want to rate-limit the issuance of CIDs or simply limit the total number of CIDs being issued for each connection. Hence PR #2428.

Initially pointed out in 
https://github.com/quicwg/base-drafts/issues/2403#issuecomment-460255684 as part of the issue, opening this issue dedicated to the problem as [suggested by @martinthomson ](https://github.com/quicwg/base-drafts/pull/2428#pullrequestreview-200896573).

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body: If the server ties CID’s to 5-tuples I suppose the problem is much reduced, although multiple connections over same 5-tuple happens?

comments.author: kazuho
mikkelfj
comments.body: So you are saying that a reset cannot be tied to a 5-tuple.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body: Correct. Or maybe I should have pointed out that if a server ties CID to 5-tuple, a connection would die once a NAT rebinding happens (without client knowing that).

comments.author: huitema
comments.body: Yes, I think rate limit is a plausible solution. But the malicious clients can also set up a connection, get half a dozen CID, then set a new connection, etc. So it boils down to how many connection per second the server will support (100? 1000? 10000? Multiply by size of farm?) and how often the CID encryption key will rotate. That, multiplied by the number of CID per connection, gives a number. Log2 of that gives the minimum size in bits. For a server doing 10000 connections per second, 16 CID per connection, 24 hours for the key, the result is 34 bits. Add 2 for managing key rotations, then add routing bits in the case of a farm. We should be good with 40 bits for a single server, 56 bits for a small farm, 64 bits for a larger farm.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body:
Scary numbers, but what is the problem with potential early reuse?
Say a server has 10000 connections and 20000 active CID's, and 30000 CID's total because peer has an extra.

A new CID is issued, and an old is retired. In counter mode, the CID's are cycled and can already generate conflicts after truncation to 32-bits. These conflicts can be checked against the 30K CID table. If a CID's rotate fast enough, conflicts happen faster, but they won't happen on any currently recognised CID's by that instance.

This is just from a 5-minute speculation, I could clearly be missing something important. But I think it  is important to consider how conflicts are dealt with.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
Those are not scary numbers.  It almost fits into the smallest possible connection ID.

Keep in mind that you really don't want to reuse values: if you reuse values over that period, you risk reusing a value for which a stateless reset was sent.  That might increase the number a little.

With 100,000 active connections per server in a 1000 server cluster issuing 16 connection IDs per second for each connection (which is a very high rate, but you have to allow for those connections being new ones), you need 47 bits worth of space if you don't want to repeat once a day.  Add 3 for a week's worth of key identifier and that's 50 bits.  That's still short of the 64 bits that gQUIC had for connection IDs.  If you want to assign randomly, you can do that with 100 bits and avoid the birthday paradox.

The numbers seem to play out nicely.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body: Well, not scary, but it rules out 32-bit. But that was naive anyway.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body: The fact that it's a SHOULD seems to imply that the server can throttle the issuance of CIDs if it so chooses.  So if it wants to have a 16-per-second or lower limit, it's free to do so.  @kazuho, is the concern around the combination of "SHOULD ... always"?

comments.author: kazuho
mikkelfj
comments.body:
> PS. Honestly speaking, I'm interested in simply capping the total number of CIDs issued for each connection rather than rate-limiting. That'd be fine for H3, because a server running out of CIDs can send GOAWAY.

That would be annoying for long running connections because they might have a policy of rotating CID infrequently. Suddenly having to kill a connection that has no relation to H3 semantics is not good. I'd be happy to set a limit per day.

comments.author: kazuho
mikkelfj
comments.body:
It's the IETF equivalent of an offer you can't refuse.
And the one offering it doesn't have a choice either, if counting to max is the only option, and max is designed low to deal with many short lived connections.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body: As also discussed on the mailing list in another context: if you are offered to start a new connection mid up-load of multiple Gigabytes, or hours of transaction processing, the one transport endpoint might be happy, but both application endpoints will be sad and disappointed.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
> if you are offered to start a new connection mid up-load of multiple Gigabytes, or hours of transaction processing,

That's an untypical scenario for HTTP.

Note also that even if the client runs out of spare CIDs, it can still continue using the connection. The only thing the client cannot do is initiate a voluntary migration. Considering the fact that migration is not a mandatory feature (both for client and server), I do not think there's a strong reason to argue against endpoints refusing to provide additional room for migration at certain moments.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body:
As I mentioned earlier, I am concerned about non-HTTP uses cases, and for that matter also about mixing the layers. Transport should not rely on GOAWAY, and HTTP layer should be not concerned with refreshing CID's.

If you at all risk running out of CID's and you can't do anything about it, then you are not going to rotate CID's at all. That might also not be necessary, but is what will happen.

A limit per day is unproblematic, like at most 2 migrations per day without migration, reset counter on migration. If client is able to migrate enough to still cause a problem, we might need a total daily cap.

From another perspective: If the concern regarding conflicts only has to do with a low risk of stateless reset, I'd rather have that than a high risk of running out of CID's.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
> I am concerned about non-HTTP uses cases, and for that matter also about mixing the layers. Transport should not rely on GOAWAY, and HTTP layer should be not concerned with refreshing CID's.

Fair enough. Though my point is that _for HTTP/3_ (which happens to be the primary target of QUIC v1) just capping the number of CIDs is totally fine. The proposal does not mandate such behavior. It's merely clarifying that such behavior is permissible.

When you are to define an application protocol for QUIC v1 that requires the connections to survive lots of migrations, you would be required to clarify that the servers should support that, regardless of the outcome of this issue. That is because, as stated in [my previous comment](
https://github.com/quicwg/base-drafts/issues/2436#issuecomment-461919062), migration is an optional feature of QUIC v1. Running out of CID is no worse than connecting to a server that does not support migration in terms of the transport spec.

To put it another way, while I can understand your concern, I think it's orthogonal to this issue.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body:
> The proposal does not mandate such behavior. It's merely clarifying that such behavior is permissible.

I was concerned that you wanted to make it a requirement. Anyway, I'd also like that behaviour is reasonable predictable so app protocols don't have too many constraints on deployments. A stack used for HTTP might well be used for other things.

I'm still wondering if there are benefits to rotating CID's when not migrating, but I think there is since you might want to refresh routing tables. This is starting to be a separate, but related issue, but one thing is rate limiting, the other is convincing peer to rotate or not rotate within a given time frame, with no migration. It'd be best if transport could take the guesswork out of this.

Overall, I could see a requirement to rotate daily and requirement to supply a min count of CID's daily, just to ensure all entities, including middle boxes have something to work from.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: Predictability here also - unfortunately - could mean exposing details of server resource constraints to clients.  Or other details that might advantage an attacker.  That is because the resource in question is shared.  Though individuals might be given caps on their own usage that are independent of others (the sequence number might cap out at 200, for instance), anything more concrete and actionable might expose information about how much spare capacity the server truly has.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body: @martinthomson yes, that is a balance to strike, but a conservative limit of 1-2 per day ought to be reasonable unless I'm missing something. Or, we should entirely avoid rotation non-migration as a general principle.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: 1-2 connection IDs per day is probably totally inadequate for someone who is mobile.  That's a more realistic number for key rotations.  I can imagine 1 every 15 minutes on average being necessary.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body: that was for non-migration, if rotation is needed at all

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body: I think the point is to mandate a minimum frequency of migrations.  However, what that minimum frequency should be will depend on the server's infrastructure, which is too variable to get a good requirement into the spec.  I've written up the PLEASE_RETIRE_CID frame [here](https://mikebishop.github.io/please-retire/draft-bishop-quic-please-retire.html).

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body: I strongly support limiting Connection ID pulls. Beyond the DoS issues, for servers with a relatively limited pool of connection IDs, for whatever reason, allowing an attacker to open a connection and getting a large sample of connection IDs from one server can open up various attempts to crack the route encoding scheme.

comments.author: erickinnear
comments.body: There *aren't* any CID pulls, though, isn't the whole idea here that the server only issues as many as it's willing to support?

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body: RETIRE_CONNECTION_ID is, in effect, a pull, if we SHOULD supply a new one every time we get it. There are security considerations that apply to that recommendation.

comments.author: erickinnear
comments.body: But isn't it not *actually* a pull, specifically for this reason? In other words, isn't it a SHOULD and not a MUST to say "please provide a new one, unless you have a really good reason that you cannot/should not", for some of the reasons highlighted above?

comments.body: I think if the spec has a SHOULD that raises known security concerns without mentioning those concerns, that's a problem.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: @martinduke, that is the point of @kazuho's PR.  To include some justification for the SHOULD.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body: @martinthomson Yes, I'm in full support of the PR.

comments.author: janaiyengar
comments.body: This issue is worth noting in the draft, and the PR looks good to me.
