issues.title: Clarify use of HTTP request with http scheme over HTTP/3
issues.author: gloinul
issues.body: It would be good if it could be clarified what will happen if someone needs/tries to send a HTTP request with an http:// uri over H3. I primarily see this to occur when you have a case where you have an HTTP proxy that receives an HTTP request and then have an HTTP/3 connection with the authorative server. If the expectation is that all requests are upgraded by the HTTP/3 sending side, then that needs to be made explicit.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
I might propose this comes down to a discovery problem for the proxy. What method(s) do you envisage the proxy used to decide to make an HTTP/3 connection to the authorative server? This seems related to the discussion in HTTP WG - https://github.com/httpwg/http-core/issues/194

If Alt-Svc is being used, the flow might be that the proxy attempts to make a cleartext HTTP/1.1 connection to the authoritative server and does an upgrade, as described in RFC 7838, to HTTP/3. In which case I don't think any action is required. 

If the proxy wants to opportunistically upgrade via some happy eyeballs approach described on https://github.com/httpwg/http-core/issues/194, we might want to provide guidance that either 1) it shouldn't be done for client requests with http:// or 2) that it should always be done.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body:
This is another variant of #253 -- HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 explicitly include the scheme and the authority with all requests, so the server knows what it's being asked for.  The question is how the client decides that a QUIC endpoint is authoritative for this particular URL.

RFC 7838 describes how an https://-schemed request might come to be sent to an HTTP/3 endpoint and the resolution of the issue was to ask the HTTP WG to define other ways.  Adding RFC 8164 as well, an http://-schemed resource might also be requested over HTTP/3; it's up to the HTTPbis group whether they want to enable a direct upgrade there as well.

I don't currently see any text required for this, but if you have suggestions, I'm happy to review or expand the discussion to the list.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: I'd rather duplicate this to #253 and rely on [RFC 8164](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc8164) for this.  We were not very careful in that document to avoid mention of the specific HTTP version, but the technique is perfectly portable between versions.  We only really intended to put HTTP/1.x off limits.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body: Perhaps "not very careful" was careful enough -- it says "such as HTTP/2," and mandates that the protocol needs a way to carry the scheme.  HTTP/3 does, so we're covered.  Do we think a reference to 8164 is warranted in the section about finding an HTTP/3 endpoint?

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
By "not very careful" I was mainly referring to the title :)

As for the text, I don't know.  It will depend on what else it says.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body: Discussed in London; reference 8164 and require the same check when sending a scheme other than "https."

issues.title: Peers that only terminate a single connection on an IP/port cannot migrate with 0-byte CIDs
issues.author: ianswett
issues.body:
Currently the section 5.1(https://tools.ietf.org/html/draft-ietf-quic-transport-18#section-5.1) says:
"An endpoint whose peer has selected a zero-length connection ID MUST continue to use a zero-length connection ID for the lifetime of the connection and MUST NOT send packets from any other local address."

In practice, 0 length connection IDs are only expected to be used when the receiver's IP/port identifies the connection, because otherwise QUIC connections cannot survive NAT rebinding.  Given 0 byte connection IDs are not a privacy concern, the only reason I've heard to prohibit this is that we want to ensure servers never use trial decryption to deal with explicit migration.  I don't believe that's a compelling reason, given there are existing use cases such as Peer-to-peer(ie: WebRTC) where we might want to use 0-byte connection IDs, but supporting migration may also be valuable.  And I don't think any even small-scale server is going to use trial decryption to handle migration due to the excessive CPU cost.

There is already a transport parameter to indicate connection migration is not supported, so the peer should have a clear signal about whether they can migrate with a 0-byte CID.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body: I think I agree that we can remove MUST NOT, assuming that we would recommend (i.e. SHOULD) servers using 0-byte CID to set the disable migration flag.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: The problem here is that any system that uses this capability (migrating while sending no connection ID), would be unreliable.  To make it reliable, we would need to add signaling.  Is this a feature you really need for QUICv1?

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: Oh, I see, the idea is to rely on DISABLE_MIGRATION.  That is probably OK.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
As a general piece of advice, I would not advise any endpoint(ie: server) receiving multiple connections on a given IP/port use 0 byte CIDs.

And if a 'server' did want to do that, it should disable migration explicitly.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body: @ianswett Um, isn't it normal for servers (QUIC or otherwise) to listen on IP/port. Do you mean multiple connections from same client IP/port?

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
If servers want to terminate multiple connections on an IP/port(as is typical), they either should use CID lengths > 0 OR disable connection migration.

If they use a CID length of 0, they need to expect that NAT rebinding is going to terminate the connection, but they may be ok with that.

comments.author: janaiyengar
comments.body:

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body:
If a connection receives a garbage packet, it can be easily rejected based on the (lack of / unknown) CID.  Only someone on-path will be able to observe the CID in use, so only on-path attackers can make you attempt to decrypt garbage.

If you use a zero-length CID, your CID is very easy to guess. 🙂 The restriction on migrating means that an attacker must spoof the remote port and IP in order to perform this attack, which means being on-path, which brings zero-length connection IDs up to equivalent security.

If we make this change, anyone can make you attempt to decrypt garbage packets.  Are we sure we want that?

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body: On that account, it should be a requirement that CID's are compared constant time, otherwise they are easy to guess anyway.

issues.title: Justification for Key Separation doesn't make sense
issues.author: martinduke
issues.body:
In section 9.4 of the TLS draft:

> In using TLS, the central key schedule of TLS is used. As a result of the TLS handshake messages being integrated into the calculation of secrets, the inclusion of the QUIC transport parameters extension ensures that handshake and 1-RTT keys are not the same as those that might be produced by a server running TLS over TCP. However, 0-RTT keys only include the ClientHello message and might therefore use the same secrets. To avoid the possibility of cross-protocol key synchronization, additional measures are provided to improve key separation.

To a naive reader like me,  this doesn't make any sense.  Handshake and 1RTT keys are fine because they hash the transport parameters. If 0-RTT keys include the ClientHello, they also contain transport parameters. So what's the problem?

issues.title: Change Idle Timeout Units of Milliseconds
issues.author: nibanks
issues.body:
Currently, the t[ransport parameter for specifying Idle Timeout](https://quicwg.org/base-drafts/draft-ietf-quic-transport.html#rfc.section.18.1) is in units of seconds. This seems to be too restrictive and not very future proof. Additionally, from an API perspective, most other timers are settable on the millisecond scale, so it creates a kind of ugly discrepancy between all the different timers settable by the app if just one of them has units of seconds.

I propose we change the units from seconds to milliseconds. The change both for implementations and spec should be minimal, and it makes things (timers) a little more consistent.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: This seems sensible to me both for consistency and I can imagine cases when one would want to specify a fraction(ie: 1/2 of a second).

comments.author: pravb
comments.body: Agreed. A second is an eternity for a intra-datacenter connection for example. For future proofing all time units should be at least msec IMO.

comments.author: nibanks
comments.body: No, I don't think so. Even before, if you had a greater than 1 sec RTT (somehow...) if you set an idle timeout of 1 second it would cause you problems. I think bottom line you be smart about your idle timeout values. If you set too small a value you can unnecessarily kill your own connection.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body: As @nibanks says, actual idle timeout depends on RTT, and that’s what we have adopted in #2404.

issues.title: Client MUST use 1-RTT packets if it reads 1-RTT packets
issues.author: martinthomson
issues.body:
I am not sure if this is accurate.

IIUC their is nothing that mandates the client to switch to using 1-RTT when it receives ServerFinished. In fact, on a lossy network, a client would benefit from using 0-RTT packets until it receives an ACK for ClientFinished. In such case, it would be natural to observe these frames in a 0-RTT packet.

I think we should either forbid them or clarify that there are allowed, instead of suggesting (IMO incorrectly) that it’s impossible.

_Originally posted by @kazuho in https://github.com/_render_node/MDExOlB1bGxSZXF1ZXN0MjQ2MTcyNjUx/pull_requests/unread_timeline_

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: To be clear, this was in reference to text that mentioned that certain frames couldn't be sent in 0-RTT.  That would only be true if we made this a requirement.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body:
This actually is already addressed in the TLS draft, as @martinthomson pointed out in another thread:  [TLS 4.9](https://quicwg.org/base-drafts/draft-ietf-quic-tls.html#rfc.section.4.9), "Though an endpoint might retain older keys, new data MUST be sent at the highest currently-available encryption level."

If you have 1-RTT keys, you MUST use them.  There's currently no server verification that you do so, however.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
I think this should be stated in transport as well as TLS, along with a statement that a server MAY/SHOULD/MUST ignore 0RTT packets that have higher packet numbers than the first received 1RTT packet.  The first is editorial I believe, the latter is borderline design.

If we decided it was valid to close the connection if a 0RTT packet was received with a higher packet number than 1RTT, then that's definitely not editorial, but I think it may be a good way to enforce proper behavior.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
@ianswett 
> I think this should be stated in transport as well as TLS

Agreed.

> along with a statement that a server MAY/SHOULD/MUST ignore 0RTT packets that have higher packet numbers than the first received 1RTT packet.

I think that this should be a MAY/SHOULD close the connection with PROTOCOL_VIOLATION rather than "ignore", because that aligns the handling with how we agreed to handle other misuse of 0-RTT packets (see 
https://github.com/quicwg/base-drafts/issues/2360#issuecomment-459171200).

comments.author: huitema
comments.body: @martinthomson said it right at the mike: this is a key update scenario, from 0-RTT to 1-RTT key. Treat it the same way as peer continuing using old key after key update.

comments.author: huitema
comments.body: I think the only verifiable requirement is "must not ack 1RTT packet in 0RTT packet". The server can definitely detect that, and send a connection close with reason PROTOCOL VIOLATION when it happens. This would effectively force the client to switch to 1RTT soon.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body: @huitema, exceeding the initial flow control / max streams from the remembered TP's is also detectable.

comments.author: huitema
comments.body: @MikeBishop detection with flow control would require special case code in stream processing, as in "check against the current window but if 0-RTT check against the initial window". Could be done, but that would be another wart. Also, in many cases the 0-RTT data sent is well below the initial flow control window, so it will not be a very efficient test.

issues.title: SPA ad Infinitum
issues.author: mikkelfj
issues.body:
As far as I can tell, there is currently no protection against infinite loops in Server Preferred Address redirection.

In comparison, Retry only permits one hop.

A server should of course not send its own address, but it might not aways know it.
It is also possible for two servers to prefer each other.
A client should not keep shopping for a better connection endlessly.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: Server's preferred address does not cause a new handshake.  It merely changes the server IP the client is communicating with for the existing handshake.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body: Uhh, so I am mixing up Retry with SPA.

comments.author: marten-seemann
comments.body:
How can there be a loop? SPA is only used to tell the client to migrate, not to initiate a new connection.

issues.title: Remember Fewer Transport Parameters for 0-RTT
issues.author: martinduke
issues.body:
Sec 7.3.1 of quic-transport says: 
A client that attempts to send 0-RTT data MUST remember the transport parameters used by the server. The transport parameters that the server advertises during connection establishment apply to all connections that are resumed using the keying material established during that handshake. Remembered transport parameters apply to the new connection until the handshake completes and new transport parameters from the server can be provided.

Later on, the section makes it clear that this is really about the flow control parameters, which makes a lot of sense, but here I am storing all this data to be compliant.

I propose that we change the MUST above to refer to only the 6 FC parameters. This reduces the stuff that clients have to store.

going through each:
original_connection_id: clearly useless
idle_timeout: useless in handshake
stateless_reset_token: clearly useless
max_packet_size: could be useful, but meh
ack_delay_exponent: not useful before we get the server Handshake
max_ack_delay: same
disable_migration: same
preferred_address: same

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body: It's not just the flow control parameters -- it's also support for extensions in TPs yet-to-be-defined.  So while I would be amenable to reorienting this issue to create an exception for the ones you've marked as useless, I think this is the correct default rule.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body: good point. I'm happy to write a PR as you describe if others agree.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
I agree that a good number of those are useless.

Possibly we should explicitly state which params need to be stored and extensions should be required to state whether they need to be stored when they're defined?

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: How is anyone going to know if you don't remember these values?  Just remember the ones you know you need to remember.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body: A conformance test that deliberately lowers them after accepting 0-RTT and checks whether the client chokes.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: You can't lower preferred addresses, disable migration, etc..  Basically, we should allow all those that @martinduke points out make no sense to remember to change.  That's the real fix here.

comments.author: janaiyengar
comments.body: This makes sense, and the list is good.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body: Editors: please don't close the issue before consensus is declared.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body:
For context, the PR was marked editorial but the issue it auto-closed was marked design.  Comment from the PR discussion:

> Thanks for doing this Martin. I will raise this on the list so that people are clear about this. Technically, there isn't a change here, but it certainly looks like it if you don't understand what is going on.

The PR changes the text from "MUST remember everything" to "MUST NOT remember the things that don't make sense to remember and you weren't actually remembering anyway, but MUST remember everything else".  That is, there's no functional change to real implementations, but the normative requirements in the text didn't match what was actually possible to implement.  Martin's right -- this is really an editorial change, despite touching normative text.

issues.title: Suggestion that Retry might not change CID
issues.author: MikeBishop
issues.body:
In 17.2.3, the transport draft says:

> Receiving a Retry packet, especially a Retry that changes the connection ID used for subsequent packets, indicates a strong possibility that 0-RTT packets could be lost.

However, in 17.2.5:

> The server includes a connection ID of its choice in the Source Connection ID field. This value MUST not be equal to the Destination Connection ID field of the packet sent by the client.

The subordinate clause in the first is unnecessary, as that statement is true of all Retry packets.  In the second, should that be "MUST NOT" rather than "MUST not"?

comments.body: OBE

issues.title: Connection ID Length changes
issues.author: martinduke
issues.body:
There's nothing in the spec that prohibits this, except from zero to not zero. But should there be?

1) For the receiver, it's a bit annoying to have to store the length of each additional connection ID
2) We could eliminate the length field from the frame
3) If we're concerned about changes from zero-length being detectable, we should also be concerned about length changes being detectable. Ultimately, the complexity of handling this is the problem of the endpoint generating the connection ID, so if you want to do this to yourself, go for it. The use case for going from zero to not-zero (unexpectedly needing migration) is as relevant as changing between non-zero lengths (migrating existing connections when the routing scheme totally changes)

I would recommend one of the following:
A) New CIDs must retain the same length
B) Remove all restrictions on CID length changes - I sorta lean towards this one,  but I think both are better than the status quo.

comments.author: nibanks
comments.body: I brought this up on the PR when we added the NEW_CONNECTION_ID frame and it was decided that some folks thought it was a feature that (nonzero length) CIDs could length if they wanted...

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
I strongly oppose A).  There are definitely cases I may want to change CID length.

I have no idea why we say you can't change from zero to non-zero lengths.  That being said, I'm not sure what the incentive is for a peer to move from zero to non-zero, so maybe restricting it doesn't matter.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body: There are routing implications going from 0 to non-zero. A 0 would be a 5-tuple hash, or so. Suddenly changing that could confuse middle boxes. It could also undermine some privacy assumptions made by the peer when accepting the connection.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body:
@mikkelfj This is entirely up to the endpoint generating the CIDs, yes? Endpoints already need to be aware of their routing architecture.

I don't understand the privacy implications you allude to.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body: A CID is a cookie that can simplify tracking compared to a translated 5-tuple that depends on hidden routing table state. A CID could also suggest that migration is suddenly undertaken even if not permitted. These are both weak arguments, but it is easier to be fooled when the CID come and go if you do not check everything carefully.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: @ianswett, consider how an endpoint might distinguish between a short header with a zero-length connection ID and a packet with a non-zero-length connection ID. If the need to do trial decryption doesn't bother you (it is after all self-inflicted) then we can maybe allow a transition between the two, but I think that was the primary reason.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: Thanks, given it seems to be a core goal of the QUIC design to avoid trial decryption, that makes sense.

comments.author: dtikhonov
comments.body: It is not clear to me what this bug is about.  @martinduke, do you propose that _NEW_CONNECTION_ID_ frames always carry CIDs of the same length for a given connection?

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body:
If you have a "mixed" connection, you lose the ability to reject packets because the CID is unknown; it might be your zero-length CID, so you have to try to process packets with unknown CIDs.  But also, if you *do* recognize the CID and it fails to decrypt, you have to decrypt it again -- it might be a ZLCID packet where the packet number happens to encrypt into a valid CID!  So I agree, let's not do that.

I don't feel strongly about requiring all CIDs on the connection to be the same length, save to note that it's not implausible for a server to reach a case where it must either kill a connection or increase the CID size being used.  (Let's say that all/enough CIDs in the previous size have been allocated already.)

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body:
I don't understand the trial decryption argument.

An inherent property of zero length is that I must trial decrypt any pkt with unknown connection id, so the existence of non-zero-length IDs is orthogonal to this point.

If I have a ZL and non ZL CID, on every packet I do a simple byte compare to check which it is, then decrypt. No trial decryption required.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body: @dtikhonov that was one proposal, but at this point it's dead. Now the proposal is for hosts with ZLCIDS to offer non-perishable length in new_conn_id frames

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body: Zero-length is prohibited from migrating (modulo #2441), so the 4-tuple gives you quasi-similar protection against injected junk that a CID does -- to inject, you have to be able to see previous packets, hence on-path.  You're not (quite) signing up to decrypt any junk packet you get handed.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body:
@mikebishop I think you're describing migration with only ZLCID, which IMO would still be illegal.

If a short header comes in from a new address, simply match a known local CID, like for any other non-ZLCID connection. If no match, drop it.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body:
So you're suggesting that clients MUST use a CID until the path has been validated and then MAY switch back to the zero-length CID?  Hm.  That does still have the double-decrypt case for a valid CID on an established path, but that should be vanishingly rare outside of an attack.

I'm still not convinced it's necessary, but it's possible it could be done safely.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body: Is it important/worthwhile?

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body:
@mikebishop you are ahead if me and thinking about going from non ZLCID to ZLCID. That is not what I'm proposing, and would have to think about it.

For the moment, do you see a trial decryption issue if we allow ZL to nonZL transitions only?

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body: @mikkelfj why ban it we're not sure?

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body: ... unnecessary complexity and risk. But granted, there ought to be justifications for the requirements set.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
@martinduke 
> There's nothing in the spec that prohibits this, except from zero to not zero.

Going from non-zero to zero is also prohibited. NCID cannot carry a zero-length CID. Prohibiting it makes sense, because it's useless; a server can have no more than one connection that uses a zero-length CID, assuming that the CID might be used for a new path (that's the intent of delivering a CID in a NCID frame).

While I think it's possible to design an endpoint that does zero-to-non-zero transition without trial decryption, I think forbidding both ways is cleaner. Is there a particular benefit in supporting zero-to-non-zero transition?

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
@martinduke 
> If a short header comes in from a new address, simply match a known local CID, like for any other non-ZLCID connection. If no match, drop it.

The issue with the approach is that the server cannot distinguish between a connection that it has lost state and a broken packet with zero-length CID. The server loses the ability to send stateless resets for all of the connections it handles.

Note: IIUC, a server is expected to generate stateless reset tokens by using 5-tuple (if CIDL=0) or by using CID (if CIDL!=0).

comments.author: martinduke
kazuho
Ralith
comments.body: A CID from NEW_CONNECTION_ID might also be used to reduce linkability following an idle period, and if non-ZLCID to ZLCID transition were permitted, it might also be used for a client to explicitly opt-out of support for migration in exchange for reduced overhead. Initiating a migration with a ZLCID doesn't make sense, but these other cases seems reasonable to me.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body:
Either I have been very unclear, or I am proposing something that makes a simple error so that it is confusing everybody. Here is what I am proposing to allow (CIDs are letters)

Client                                                                                                    Server
[ Connection already setup; client has no CID ]
IP: 1.1.1.1 to 2.2.2.2 (DCID A) ----->
           (contains NEW_CONN_ID B)
                                                                              <--- IP: 2.2.2.2 to 1.1.1.1 (no DCID)
                                                                                       (contains NEW_CONN_ID C)
(exchange continues with IP addresses above, with no CID to client and CID A to server)
(then there's an address change)
IP: 3.3.3.3 to 2.2.2.2 (DCID C) -------->
                                                                               <---- IP: 2.2.2.2 to 3.3.3.3 (DCID B)

This is the case I am concerned about. I do not see, at the moment, any reason why switching "client" and "server" above should make a difference.

What I am definitely NOT proposing is that an endpoint migrate while never accepting a non-ZL CID.

comments.author: ianswett
kazuho
comments.body:
@martinduke 
> Either I have been very unclear, or I am proposing something that makes a simple error so that it is confusing everybody. Here is what I am proposing to allow (CIDs are letters)

I think it works, though I wonder why the client needs to switch to using a zero-length client CID when it migrates. Can't it just continue using a zero-length client CID?

@ianswett 
> The server can also statelessly reset the connection if it has no state by 5-tuple, as you mention above.

Please let me retract that, because it's wrong. The design of stateless reset requires the source of the reset token to not be reused. That's something the sender of stateless reset can enforce when using CIDs, but not when relying on the 5-tuple. Quoting from section 10.4.2 of the transport draft: _This design relies on the peer always sending a connection ID in its packets so that the endpoint can use the connection ID from a packet to reset the connection. An endpoint that uses this design MUST either use the same connection ID length for all connections or encode the length of the connection ID such that it can be recovered without state. In addition, it cannot provide a zero-length connection ID._

> I don't have a very strong feeling on this, but it seems like another thing we forbid that has some potentially valid uses with drawbacks we don't like. Unless we think this is actively harmful, I'd prefer to allow this.

I would not oppose to allowing it, though the premise would be that it does not introduce complexity to other implementations that would not be using the feature, because I do not understand the practical benefit.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body: @kazuho To avoid trial decryption!

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
@martinduke IIUC, generally speaking, trial decryption becomes inevitable for a client when it coalesces multiple connections that uses the same server 2-tuple onto a single socket.

In the approach you describe, the client is not coalescing multiple connections in such a way on a single socket when it initiates the connection, because it is initially using zero-length CID. But it sounds like that the client will be using the socket in such a way on a socket it decides to migrate.

What I do not see is the rationale behind such a design.

If the client's preference is to minimize the network bandwidth (by using zero-length CIDs), shouldn't it use zero-length CIDs for subsequent paths that it migrates the connection to? That's possible, as long as it does not coalesce multiple connections that share the same server 2-tuple onto a single socket. The simplest way of doing that is to use a dedicated socket for each connection.

Or if the client's preference is to minimize the number of sockets it maintains, shouldn't it be always using non-zero-length CIDs from when it initiates a new connection?

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: I think banning switching from non-zero-length CID to zero-length CID might be too constraining. Imagine a server is initially reached via an IPv6 anycast address, and it tells the client its IPv6 preferred address. If that server owns a /64, it can give a different preferred address to each client which allows zero-length CIDs and migration without requiring trial decryption because the server can find the connection simply by looking at the packet destination IP address. (Note that kernels don't let you easily do that today but that can be fixed.) The only downside I'm seeing here is that migration can now be tracked across paths since the connection ID doesn't change and the server IP is enough to identify a connection. I suspect there are deployment scenarios where reducing CID overhead is more important that the privacy risk. But, given that the server preferred address is only advisory, a client that cares more about privacy than about the CID overhead can simply refuse to switch over. With all that said, I don't think the restriction against zero-length-CID helps us.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
I'm willing to concede that a server preferred address is a special case here.  Destination IP address is accessible, if awkward to get at.

There is also a valid argument that says that you get what you ask for.

Either way, I don't see this being resolved here effectively.  You could raise this on the list or wait until Prague to discuss in person.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body: @mt I agree we should probably discuss in person

comments.author: huitema
comments.body: I don't see why we need to change the spec. The node proposes N connection ID, the peer chooses one of them. If the node wants a fixed length, it restricts itself to use proposing a fixed length.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body: Discussed in Prague; hum strongly supported closing with no action, but some interest in a new issue constraining to server preferred address (but will require substantial information, e.g., solid use case).

issues.title: Invalid CONNECTION_CLOSE frames
issues.author: martinduke
issues.body:
Section 11.1 says:
"An endpoint that receives an invalid CONNECTION_CLOSE frame MUST NOT signal the existence of the error to its peer."

Editorially, it is not clear to me whether I am to suppress the error code in the CONNECTION_CLOSE frame or the error I generate when I receive an invalid frame.

Moreover, I am not sure what constitutes an invalid CONNECTION_CLOSE frame. The words don't occur elsewhere. Section 19.19 doesn't define any fatal errors for this type. I can imagine a Reason Length that overruns the packet, or perhaps an undefined error code? A bogus frame type? We should probably define those in 19.19.

Perhaps this sentence is an artifact from before we were throwing away Initial keys agressively?

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body: If you suppress the error, does it matter which error you do not send?

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body: I'm not sure what the intent of the sentence is. Do I send PROTOCOL_VIOLATION but not the error code in the frame? Do I send nothing?

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body:
As I read it, you should not send anything if you see CONNECTION_CLOSE.

As to the motivation, I'm not quite sure, but if the peer closes but does it badly, chances are that anything you send just results in stateless resets. Maybe there can also be some malicious intend, especially in early handshake, but I don't think that is the reason.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body: I *think* this is addressing the injected packet case -- if you ignore an injected CONNECTION_CLOSE, you shouldn't send the real peer anything about it, or you've just allowed an attacker to inject authenticated traffic in the connection.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: This is more about the looping case: sending CONNECTION_CLOSE in response to CONNECTION_CLOSE.  But it is badly worded.

comments.author: ronieven
comments.body:
From the current text in 10.3

After sending a CONNECTION_CLOSE frame, endpoints immediately enter the closing state.  During the closing period, an endpoint that sends a CONNECTION_CLOSE frame SHOULD respond to any packet that it receives with another packet containing a CONNECTION_CLOSE frame.  To minimize the state that an endpoint maintains for a closing  connection, endpoints MAY send the exact same packet.

This will be a loop  since the same invalid packet will be sent again by the sender ....

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: I'm going to request that this be re-assessed.  When looking into Roni's comment, I realize that we aren't really clear enough about this invalid case and some (small amount of) discussion might be necessary to confirm that this change is OK.

issues.title: CID's should be compared in constant time
issues.author: MikeBishop
issues.body:
[If a CID can be seen or guessed, an attacker can make you decrypt garbage packets.  On-path attackers can see; nothing to do about that.  If the time it takes you to reject an invalid CID can be observed, an attacker can guess and check possible CIDs.]

On that account, it should be a requirement that CID's are compared constant time, otherwise they are easy to guess anyway.

_Originally posted by @mikkelfj in https://github.com/quicwg/base-drafts/issues/2441#issuecomment-464173546_

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body: However, if you have to be on path to observe processing time, this is moot.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body:
> However, if you have to be on path to observe processing time, this is moot.

You don't, because the endpoint cannot know what the correct path is before knowing the CID, assuming there is more than one possible path, as is usually the case.

BTW: there could be attacks on middle boxes that learn what valid CID's are, but do not compare these constant time. I'm not sure how effective that would be though.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
I think @mikkelfj is technically correct. A simple attack would be like the following.

Assume there's a server using an ordered list to maintain CIDs. When it receives a packet, it scans the list in ascending order until it finds a matching CID (or if reaches the end of the list without finding one).

An attacker can bisect the server to see which CIDs is active, by observing the difference in the latency of receiving stateless resets. This is much convenient than a brute-force attack that tries every possible CID to see if one is active.

If we need to be clear about the constant time requirement is a different question.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body:
I’m not sure it is worth requiring. Then we should also say constant time hash tables should be salted.

Note that popular Splay trees are vulnerable to manipulation.

Disabling Reset could be a recommendation if under attack.

comments.author: dtikhonov
comments.body: This is rather far-fetched.  This requirement does not belong in the spec.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
The "secret" here is a connection ID.  Something we put in packets without encryption.

If the cost is that you can force a server to attempt to decrypt packets, that's relatively easy to do by other means.  If the point is to attribute that pointless work to others, that's maybe a tiny bit interesting as a DoS vector, but it seems to me like this isn't that useful a thing to document.

The underlying assumption here has always been that decryption, successful or otherwise, is cheap enough that an attacker ends up spending more resources in sending the packet than the defender does in discarding them.  That's not completely true as decryption isn't free, but the cost/benefit to an attacker is very low and - relevant to our current effort - it is extremely difficult to defend if you assume differently. From that perspective, I don't think we should do anything about this.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: +1 to Martin's suggestion to not do anything about this.

comments.author: janaiyengar
comments.body: I agree with @martinthomson that we've assumed decryption to be relatively cheap, and that being able to guess a CID is therefore not a particularly interesting attack.  I don't think this issue warrants any language in the spec.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body: No arguments here, but why are we so determined on protecting against packet number guessing, but not CID guessing? https://tools.ietf.org/html/draft-ietf-quic-tls-18#page-30 (QUIC-TLS section 9.3)

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: Packet numbers cross paths, CIDs don't.

issues.title: Definition of Stream Final Size is ambiguous
issues.author: dtikhonov
issues.body:
The transport draft states the following (Section 4.4):

> Assuming that every contiguous byte on the stream was sent once, the final size is the number of bytes sent. More generally, this is one higher than the largest byte offset sent on the stream.

This verbiage, introduced in PR #2285, is ambiguous. _Byte offset_ may refer to the _Offset_ field in the _STREAM_ frame; in this case, the definition above is incorrect.  What we want to say is that the final size is one higher than the offset of the byte with the largest offset sent on the stream.  If no bytes were sent, the final size is zero.

issues.title: DetectLostPackets needs to be per packet number space
issues.author: janaiyengar
issues.body: In particular, largest_acked_packet in DetectLostPackets should be per pn_space.

comments.author: marten-seemann
comments.body:
Since #2417, `DetectLostPackets` already takes the packet number space. However, the packet number space index for `largest_acked_packet` is missing there, as well as in `OnAckReceived`.
For this reason, I don't think this is a design issue, this should be editorial instead.

I created #2485 to fix this.

issues.title: Specify what occurs when the maximum Stream Id exceeds 2^62 - 1 in MAX_STREAMS
issues.author: ianswett
issues.body:
Currently, stream IDs are as high as 2^62-1.  The MAX_STREAMS frame specifies a limit as a varint that has a max value of 2^62-1 that translates to a Stream ID of 4 * max_streams + initial_stream_id_for_type.  This is larger than the max expressible stream ID, so we should specify what happens in this case.

I'm suggesting that we allow all streams to be opened and MUST NOT close the connection in PR #2486

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body: Good idea.

comments.author: janaiyengar
comments.body: I don't have a strong opinion, but this seems like a bug at the peer. I would be inclined to specify that an endpoint MUST NOT advertise max streams that are too large, and close the connection (with PROTOCOL_VIOLATION) if a value is received that is too large.

comments.author: marten-seemann
comments.body:
I'd also lean towards closing the connection (probably with a TRANSPORT_PARAMETER_ERROR, not a PROTOCOL_VIOLATION though).

Interestingly, we have the following definition for packet numbers
> Packet numbers are integers in the range 0 to 2^62-1

but no such thing for stream IDs, although this is implied by the way we encode them.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: I'm happy to close the connection as well, as long as the behavior is well-defined.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: On PR #2499, @marten-seemann noted that this logic should apply to the equivalent transport param as well.

issues.title: Why InitialWindow = 14600?
issues.author: martinduke
issues.body:
In the Recovery Draft pseudocode section:

> kInitialWindow: : Default limit on the initial amount of data in flight, in bytes. Taken from {{?RFC6928}}. The RECOMMENDED value is the minimum of 10 * kMaxDatagramSize and max(2* kMaxDatagramSize, 14600)).

Why 14600? This looks like 10 * MSS, but for UDP this should be 14720. It would lead to neat MSS multiples were that code ever executed.

comments.body: This was taken from RFC6928: https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc6928

comments.body: Well, yes, but that is for TCP and I'm arguing that 14720 makes a lot more sense for QUIC.

comments.body: That seems reasonable, I was only trying to add an explanation of how we ended up with 14600.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: PR #2494 sent.

issues.title: Awkward text in "Sending Probe Packets"
issues.author: larseggert
issues.body:
As discussed with @janaiyengar, 6.2.2.2 is awkward, because in the first paragraph it says
```
   When a PTO timer expires, the sender MUST send one ack-eliciting
   packet as a probe.
```
And then the very last paragraph changes that by saying
```
   When a PTO timer expires, new or previously-sent data may not be
   available to send and packets may still be in flight.  A sender can
   be blocked from sending new data in the future if packets are left in
   flight.  Under these conditions, a sender SHOULD mark any packets
   still in flight as lost.
```
What is super unclear is that the final paragraph apparently means to imply that when there is no new or unACKed data to send, *nothing* should be send, i.e., it invalidates the SHOULD in the first paragraph.

Related to that, the pseudo code still uses `SendTwoPackets()`, which is also inaccurate, since it's really "at least one (unless you don't have new or unACKed data) but can also send two". Good luck finding a good name for that function :-)

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
The pseudocode now uses SendOneOrTwoPackets(), but the last paragraph pretty clearly violates the previous MUST, which is very bad.

The simplest fix would be to change the MUST to a "SHOULD unless otherwise specified", but I'm increasingly thinking we should stick with the MUST and if you get into a situation you have nothing to send, require sending something ack-eliciting to ensure in-flight packets are removed from flight.

Thoughts?

issues.title: Clarify what to do when ALPN negotiation fails
issues.author: ghedo
issues.body:
PR #2314 added a requirement for end-points to terminate a connection if ALPN negotiation fails, but doesn't specify an error code for this situation.

RFC7301 defines the `no_application_protocol` alert that must be used by TLS servers, so QUIC servers should probably use that as well. As for clients, RFC7301 doesn't specify a behaviour, but it also doesn't forbid use of `no_application_protocol` in clients, and it seems better if QUIC clients use the same error code as the servers.

Proposed wording change is in #2483.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
My :+1: goes to making the change, though I would like to confirm that it wouldn't be illegal for a client to close the connection with `no_application_protocol` error _after it sends ClientFinished_.

I ask this because depending on the design of the TLS stack, the QUIC stack might not be able to see the result of ALPN before the TLS stack generates a ClientFinished (note that EE.ALPN and ServerFinished might arrive in one packet).

It's my understanding that the intent of the issue is to not allow the client to send any application data on ALPN failure. Assuming that's true, sending the alert after ClientFinished should be fine.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: Yes, I think that would be fine.  I don't think that we would be able to guarantee that the alert goes out before sending ClientFinished either.  It's certainly possible, but I can see how it might be tricky.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: This was fixed with #2483.

issues.title: QUIC Version Ossification
issues.author: martinduke
issues.body:
There is a long conversation happening in the mailing list about QUIC version number ossification:
https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/browse/quic/?gbt=1&index=ytjKHacss9s3i3nualU2tbU9Jco
I'm adding it here to bring in others and consider it on the agenda for a WG meeting.

I won't try to summarize everyone's position from the thread. Given the status quo, it would be easy for someone to write a dumb middlebox that drops QUIC version > 1, or indeed version > 2. This appears to have happened with TLS v1.2. Given all of our effort to counter ossification, it would be tragic if we fell down on this rather simple hurdle.

There is disagreement as whether obfuscation is valuable or not. Though I have no answers, I personally would like to explore a few questions:
1) Are there any changes to VN we can make to reduce the chance of ossification happening?
2) If ossification happens anyway, do we have strategy to do something to overcome it?
3) If we are going to end up with some more obscure mechanism, does it make sense to lock in on bytes 2-5 of every long header to be 0x00000001 in perpetuity?

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body:
I originaly thought this is pointless. The registry key story[1] both confirms that it is pointless but also, along with TLS version history, that it is a real concern.

So weak obfuscation will not work. Random values that are public will not work. Genersted values that are easy to compute will not work.

I was thinking challenge response, which is the same as init packet encryption. But that is version specific.

There need to be a time or implementation complexity component like key derivation.

But that is costly to the peers, but perhaps not too costly compared to handshake.

[1] Mike Bishop mentioned this on the mailing list: undocumented registry keys in Windows are replaced with new undocumented keys because the old cannot be changed as they are detected by applications. This grows endlessly.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
> Are there any changes to VN we can make to reduce the chance of ossification happening?

We only have obfuscation to protect the payload format of Initial packets from ossification. Therefore, IMO the question is if we can have something similar for the version number field, without making the protocol complex.

As some have pointed out, using multiple version numbers on wire to designate "version 1" is one way to go. That would be sufficient as a protection against middlebox vendors who try to use the version number field in some ways in negligence. I also think that that might be the only thing that we can do without making the "version number obfuscation scheme" an invariant.

We could do various things if we think that it is a good idea to make the obfuscation scheme an invariant. For example, we could set the version number field to a XOR value of the version number and four octets that follow the DCIL/SCIL fields (i.e. `version_number_field = version_number XOR packet[6..9]`). Such scheme would IMO require the middlebox vendors to actually consult the specification when they try to detect the QUIC protocol version. In other words, it would be as reliable as the AES-based ossification scheme we use for Initial packet payload.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body: There's clearly appetite to consider this in the WG, so marking as `design`.

comments.author: philsbln
comments.body:
I like to re-state my earlier proposal to solve this issue by Introducing a new "Version Alias" Frame:
 - the server includes a list which other version numbers it also accepts for the currently used QUIC version
 - it also includes a timeout telling the client how long it may use these aliases.

This design allows to grease the whole version number range, e.g. by generating the aliases based on time windows and a local salt, without risking version clashes, as the alias numbers timeout. The only limitation of this scheme is that the server must make sure that the alias versions do not clash with version numbers the server is going to support within the timeout.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body: Discussed in Prague; hum supported closing (with impact on applicability statement), but was not unanimous. Will try to establish consensus on-list; people who want to continue should focus on establishing a threat model.

comments.author: britram
comments.body: See also quicwg/ops-drafts#62

comments.author: philsbln
comments.body:
With #2573, we have now a concrete description of the version alias mechanism.

Short summary:
 - It greases the version number and nonce to encrypt the client initial against ossifying on the values for v1.
 - The mechanism is optional - can be ignored / amended / removed later without changes for the rest of the protocol.
 - Without downgrade protection, it does not protect against middle boxes that actively try to force the handshake to v1.
 - With optional downgrade protection, it can be used as an early indicator for ossification.
 - With optional mandatory protection, some people fear that more middle-boxes may drop QUIC completely.

comments.author: mnot
comments.body: Question in London: Do you believe that we need to ship a mechanism to mitigate version ossification prior to v1? result -- strongly in favour of addressing.

comments.author: ekr
comments.body:
I'm not a huge fan of this particular design, as it involves some odd state stuff.

Here's another possibility, borrowed from a design by david benjamin:

1. Each version has a random seed.
2. The version number field is computed as `H(seed, <parts of the packet>)`

The receiver then iterates through all the potential version numbers and checks the version number. There's probably some impact on the MAC computation, but I think that's easy to deal with.

The advantage of this is that there is *never* a fixed version number on the wire. The disadvantage is that it doesn't have secret per-server information. 

I think David has also suggested that the same techniques that you use for ESNIKey publication can be used to publish a per-server salt.

UPDATE: the ESNIKey mechanism actually appears to be @huitema and @kazuho

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: The field is short, so collisions will happen.  The client won't necessarily know about all the versions that the server supports, so it can't know that a collision has occurred.

comments.author: ekr
comments.body:
Well, collisions will be quite rare unless there are a *lot* of versions. And even once there is a collision, you can test-decrypt.

Actually, it's worth noting that you could just remove the QUIC version entirely and then trial-decrypt based on the per-version salts

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: If we go for trial decryption (which isn't that crazy), then we can drop the version number field.

comments.author: ekr
comments.body: The trial-decryption version is also compatible with the ESNIKeys approach, with the salt being in the ESNIKeys.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body:
I like the trial decryption approach. The only problem is that random garbage sent to the server will now require not one 1200 byte trial decryption, but N such, where N is the number of supported versions. However, any trivial way to speed this up makes it equally cheap for middle boxes to filter.

There is a risk that future QUIC versions will reuse salts for initial keys to reduce the trial decryption load and encode the version information by other means.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
As a software developer I'm happy with trial decryption. The cost is so trivial compared to public key crypto.

It could be an issue for hardware offload, though I think we can live without hardware assistance for Initial packet processing.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
If we are to remove the version number field in favor of trial decryption, we need to figure out how a server would figure out a packet that failed to decrypt was a connection establishment attempt, so that  it can send a Version Negotiation packet. Otherwise, a client would no longer be possible to fallback to a different version.

One way of resolving the problem is to use the QUIC bit as a SYN bit. If the server fails to trial-decrypt the packet in any of the versions it supports, the server would send a Version Negotiation packet.

Having a SYN bit also helps the server, because trial decryption would only be required for packets that have the flag set.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body:
The version field could also be replaced with zero padding and encrypted with a version 0 salt (QUIC invariant the rules that packet) and packet content nonce. If the field does not decode to 0, it was not a QUIC packet, at least not one using expected invariants.

This would make it easy to detect and QUIC packets of any version. So this might not be a good idea. Responding with a QUIC version would equally expose the connection to filtering. Encrypting a version negotiation packet based on initial content would go some way, but is ultimately also easy to filter.

comments.author: huitema
comments.body:
I am trying to summarize the set of version obfuscation proposals. I believe we have:

1) Natural versions. Just define a version 2, maybe 1bis, very quickly, and actually use version negotiation.

2) Server specific version aliases,as specified in #2573

3) Version based obfuscation and trial decryption, as proposed by David Benjamin and explained on this thread

4) Introduce a "QUIC Version" TLS extension, sent either in the clear or passed as an encrypted extension to the ESNI content.

There are pros and cons to each of those:

proposal | Pros | Cons 
--- | --- | ---
Natural version | Very little code required | Still risk of ossification
Server defined aliases | Robust prevention | Does not protect 1st packet; Requires caching code; May enable tracing
Version based obfuscation | Robust prevention | Requires trial decryption
TLS extension | Can be encrypted | Requires ESNI

comments.author: huitema
comments.body: Thinking some more, I believe that David Benjamin's "version based" solution does not actually prevent ossification. The middle boxes will be programmed with the seeds of version 1. They will try decrypt with V1, and if the result is not "version = version 1" they will just say "this is not QUIC" or otherwise drop the packet.

comments.author: huitema
comments.body:
About the QuicVersion TLS extension: I think that EKR had a proposal already. Basically, encode the proposed version number as a TLS option. Optionally, encode the supported options in the client message, ordered by preference, and the selected option in the server response.

The client *could* send the option as a ClientHello extension, but that is not encrypted, so it does nothing t prevent ossification. But if the client sends the ESNI extension, then the TLS extension can be encrypted as part of the ESNI content, and so it is safe.

There is a downside to encoding the version in a TLS extension: it is only readable if the Initial message can be parsed. Parsing requires understanding the format of the Initial message, and that requires understanding the version used for encoding the message. That probably means accepting ossification of the Initial format, which is close to "conceding defeat".

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body: TLS versioning assumes that all QUIC versions use TLS, which I'm not sure is a good idea.

comments.author: huitema
comments.body:
What if the middle-box just replies with a Version Negotiation message to any message for which it does not understand the version field? This will defeat the "natural version" and "server based obfuscation" options. For example, in the server based obfuscation case, the client will immediately repeat the request with Version 1. The middle box will cause a delay penalty, but a fairly minimal one.And we removed the protection against version downgrade from the transport spec.

The "version based obfuscation" does not suffer from that downgrade, because it never uses a clear text version field.

The TLS encoding options do not suffer, because the actual version number is encrypted. But of course the outer version can ossify.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body: We cannot prevent that if the middelbox drops the initial packet. That is an unsolvable problem because the middle box can be a valid endpoint up to and excluding TLS cert validation. But I think I have argued earlier that we should quarantine version and retry packets to see of the something better shows up before taking action.

comments.author: marten-seemann
martinduke
comments.body:
Although I might quibble over details, I definitely support option 2 (Marten's proposal). It is one of two proposals that actually prevent ossification, as @huitema points out. Doing it in TLS introduces some dependencies on TLS people to agree to implement ESNI.

I propose that we restore the downgrade protection text and move forward with Option 2. I would like to note that it is not strictly necessary that the rest go out with v1 -- we just need a draft that a critical mass of servers and clients agree to support.

issues.title: Error Code when SETTINGS exceeds maximum
issues.author: martinduke
issues.body: The HTTP draft doesn't have any SETTINGS parameters with a maximum value, but QPACK does.  I don't see any text in hpack sec. 4.2.5.1 or qpack sec 5 that explains what to do if we receive a parameter that exceeds the maximum parameter.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
Good observation. This is another case where MALFORMED_FRAME is not appropriate. 

I might reset the peer-initiated stream with HTTP_LIMIT_EXCEEDED, which would prompt the other end to close the connection HTTP_CLOSED_CRITICAL_STREAM. Note that this changes how the error code is currently defined.

An alternative is just CONNECTION_CLOSE with HTTP_GENERAL_PROTOCOL_ERROR. 

... or We could invoke the YAEC label :)

Whatever we decide, I think it needs documenting.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body: Technically, you can't reset a peer-initiated stream, just STOP_SENDING.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: That's an astute observation and something I've missed. Perhaps I'm missing it but the spec doesn't say how to handle a STOP_SENDING received on a control stream. Should this peer issue a RESET_STREAM in response (causing the other peer to blow up) or should it just close the connection itself?

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
My understanding is that STOP_SENDING is an act of closing a stream rather than an advisory signal.
Based on that, I'd argue that receipt of STOP_SENDING on a critical stream should trigger a HTTP_CLOSED_CRITICAL_STREAM connection-level error.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body: I don’t think that STOP_SENDING terminates a stream per se, but an application can choose to interpret it as such, so HTTP/3 can make that call.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
To be precise, STOP_SENDING "_typically indicates that the receiving application is no longer reading data it receives from the stream_, but it is not a guarantee that incoming data will be ignored" ([transport daft section 3.5](https://quicwg.org/base-drafts/draft-ietf-quic-transport.html#rfc.section.3.5)).

Because there is a chance of it indicating that the peer is no longer reading, STOP_SENDING received on a critical stream ought to trigger a HTTP_CLOSED_CRITICAL_STREAM error.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: I'd be happy with MUST close connection in response
