issues.title: Saving unknown transport parameters should be prohibited
issues.author: marten-seemann
issues.body:
The spec currently says
> A client need not store transport parameters it cannot process.

Assume now that the client does store a transport parameter it doesn't understand. At the time when it actually establishes a 0-RTT connection, the implementation was updated (or new extensions were activated), and now it understands the TP. This would lead to unintended consequences, especially if this was a TP that it was prohibited from saving in the first place.

I think the sentence would be clearer if it said MUST NOT. Not sure if that is an editorial change though.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
There is an unstated assumption here: that the client doesn't change its opinion about transport parameters between two connections.  This applies to other transport parameters.  For instance, a client might like a stream limit it is given when initially connecting, but might change its mind when trying 0-RTT (maybe the limit is too small to bother with 0-RTT).

A MUST NOT in this case is worse than not answering the question.  Let's say that the client initially doesn't support max_udp_payload_size as it always sends 1200 byte datagrams.  As it cannot process this when it first connects, it doesn't store the value.  Later, when it attempts to connect it has been updated to understand this transport parameter.  As it has been prohibited from storing the value, it can't read the value that it might have otherwise saved as an opaque value.  So it attempts 0-RTT and assumes that it can send 1400 byte packets safely, when it should know that it can't.

Generally, this doesn't happen because defaults for transport parameters are the least permissive value.  New transport parameters generally have defaults that are safe to use in 0-RTT in case the original value was not remembered.  However, we don't require that.

(This is a bad example, as we explicitly don't worry about violating the datagram size limit in 0-RTT, but I didn't have a more evocative example.)

comments.author: larseggert
comments.body: @marten-seemann with @martinthomson's explanation, does anything need to be done still in your opinion?

comments.author: marten-seemann
comments.body: @martinthomson's example seems to be an argument for requiring clients to store unknown TPs, and checking their status (should have been saved for 0-RTT or shouldn't have been saved) when restoring them. Is that something we should require?

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: Or it is an argument for you to throw out resumption information if you have added new capabilities that might depend on stuff you previously threw out.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
I think it's an argument for discarding resumption information when adding new capabilities.  FWIW, Chrome doesn't persist resumption information to disk for security reasons, but this has the side benefit that this information does not persist across restarts, including binary updates.

One exception I can imagine is a client which gets an experiment config push that doesn't require a restart, enabling or disabling a new extension feature.  However, in that case, not saving unknown TPs still seems safest, since if the extension depended upon the unknown TP, then it's just not activated.

I'm worried max_udp_payload_size is a bad example because it's part of the core spec and it's not similar to extensions which add new frames or change the behavior of existing frames.

comments.author: janaiyengar
comments.body:
Either interpretation fixes the issue, but I would agree that resumption information shouldn't be used when the implementation changes behavior. But it could store all unknown TPs, and then reinterpret later. The current text allows both, which seems adequate.

This isn't important enough to warrant a design change. I'm fine with the current text, but I'd be open to an editorial fix if someone sent a PR.

I'm not too concerned about that variant.  If the client doesn't store the value but the server is still enforcing it, that's handled by making the default the least permissive value.  If we don't state that assumption, perhaps we should.

issues.title: advice on how to disable ECN is problematic when multiplexing multiple connections
issues.author: marten-seemann
issues.body:
The spec says:
> If validation fails, then the endpoint MUST disable ECN. It stops setting the ECT codepoint in IP packets that it sends, assuming that either the network path or the peer does not support ECN.

This is fine advice when a single QUIC connection uses a socket. When multiplexing multiple connections on the same socket, it won't be possible to disable ECN on a per-packet basis, unless you want to call `setsockopt` before every datagram that is sent.

comments.author: larseggert
comments.body: Not true. You can use ancillary data with `sendmsg` to specify different ECN codepoints for each packet to be transmitted.

issues.title: Misleading advice on stream-related errors
issues.author: marten-seemann
issues.body:
The spec says:
> Errors that result in the connection being unusable, such as an obvious violation of protocol semantics or corruption of state that affects an entire connection, MUST be signaled using a CONNECTION_CLOSE frame (Section 19.19). An endpoint MAY close the connection in this manner even if the error only affects a single stream.

First of all, I have no idea what a "corruption of state" is supposed to be.
More importantly, the second sentence seems to suggest that if an error only affects a single stream, it might not be required to send a connection-level error. I'm thinking of a stream-level flow control violation.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: The challenge here is that the transport doesn't define how streams can be used by application layer protocols, but seems to want to strongly encourage how an application uses error codes. An example of "corruption of state" is something like a QPACK error that renders the HTTP/3 connection unusable because the QPACK state cannot be assured. In contrast, an application might treat receiving a header with an uppercase field name as a stream error that otherwise would not affect the rest of the H3 connection.

comments.author: larseggert
comments.body: Anything remain to be done here?

comments.author: marten-seemann
comments.body:
It seems like @LPardue is interpreting this sentence as only applying to application protocol errors. If that's the intention, we should make that clear:
> Errors that result in the connection being unusable, such as an obvious violation of application protocol semantics or corruption of application protocol state that affects an entire connection, MUST be signaled using a CONNECTION_CLOSE frame (Section 19.19). An endpoint MAY close the connection in this manner even if the error only affects a single stream.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body:
It's not exclusive to the application.  Another example of corrupt state at the transport layer is CRYPTO_BUFFER_EXCEEDED -- you had to drop some bytes, so now your TLS handshake state is corrupted.

As to the second piece, I think you're reading that backward.  A stream error MAY always be promoted to a connection error if the implementation decides it's severe enough; it doesn't say anything about deciding to downplay errors if they're localized.  If an error is defined to be a connection error, it's a connection error.  If it's defined to be a stream error, however, you're always allowed to decide it's the last straw and walk away.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: QUIC transport does not have stream-level errors, though applications can.  As such, the last sentence references a circumstance that does not exist in the transport draft.  So the best solution seems to be to remove the last sentence.

comments.author: janaiyengar

issues.title: stateless reset detection for undecryptable packets might be hard to implement
issues.author: marten-seemann
issues.body:
Regarding stateless reset detection, we currently say:

> This comparison can be performed for every inbound datagram. Endpoints MAY skip this check if any packet from a datagram is successfully processed. However, the comparison MUST be performed when the first packet in an incoming datagram either cannot be associated with a connection, or cannot be decrypted.

This might be hard to implement if you have a clear separation between the demuxer and individual connections. The demuxer would only look at the CID of an incoming packet, and pass a packet to the corresponding connection. The connection would then (possibly asynchronously) process that packet.
The current text requires the connection to somehow pass the packet back to the demuxer, so that it can be checked for stateless reset tokens. I'd argue that there's little harm in just dropping this packet in this case.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: Practical question: How does one reset a connection if you can't associate the packet with a connection?

comments.author: marten-seemann
comments.body: Using the stateless reset token. The demuxer basically has two hash maps, one CID -> conn and one token -> conn.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body: This is covered already.  The text says that you "MAY skip this check."  The code you describe makes it difficult to know whether to skip the check, so that implementation probably wouldn't.  The demuxer will always check for stateless reset tokens.

comments.author: larseggert
comments.body: @marten-seemann do you see a need for any further changes with @MikeBishop's explanation?

comments.author: marten-seemann
comments.body:
I don't think "this check" refers to the check I'm referring to.

What we're saying is that when receiving a packet, you SHOULD do the following:
1. check your stateless reset token table. If you find the token in the table, close the conn. If you don't find this token in that table, then
2. check your CID table, and pass the packet to the connection

I interpret the "MAY skip this check" as saying that you can do 2. before 1. This reduces the number of hash map lookups in the common case to 1 instead of 2 per packet, so that's a worthwhile optimization.
However, the spec now says that if implement this optimization, you MUST do another lookup in the stateless reset token table if the connection was not able to unprotect the packet.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
The full quote is:

> This comparison can be performed for every inbound datagram. Endpoints MAY skip this check if any packet from a datagram is successfully processed. However, the comparison MUST be performed when the first packet in an incoming datagram either cannot be associated with a connection, or cannot be decrypted.

It says that you can check every datagram.  This is easy to implement and can be done at any stage of your pipeline.  You can stop there.

It says that you MAY skip the check if you successfully process a packet.  This is harder to implement if you have separate demux and processing points.  This is especially so because the last sentence says that you can't skip this check if you didn't process any packets.  That is, you can apply an optimization on the condition that you don't apply the optimization uniformly.

For an integrated implementation, especially one that doesn't demux because it has a dedicated socket, it is easy to take advantage of the "MAY".  You try to process everything and check for a stateless reset if you can't process anything.

For a layered implementation that does stateless reset processing at the demux point, it is trickier, and could involve some back and forth.  Or you could just look for a stateless reset on every packet.  The odds that a packet is both a stateless reset and valid is small enough that you don't need to bother.

The design I think we had in mind was a demux point (a load balancer) that does strict demux and stateless resets generated by the next layer (the instance).  In that case, it's much more like the integrated implementation.

comments.author: janaiyengar
comments.body:
@marten-seemann :
> However, the spec now says that if implement this optimization, you MUST do another lookup in the stateless reset token table if the connection was not able to unprotect the packet.

Right, but if you do the optimization, what other choice do you have? Meaning, how else would you detect the token? With the implementation strategy you suggest, and with this optimization, you have no choice but to get back to the demuxer.

Could you explain how you think we might fix this, if you have a fix in mind?

comments.author: marten-seemann
martinthomson
comments.body: There is no one stopping you from doing that, but I don't think that it is good to permit that in the specification.

comments.author: marten-seemann
comments.body: Seems like you don't disagree that this is a reasonable way to implement stateless reset detection. If this is a reasonable implementation choice, why is it explicitly forbidden by the spec?

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body: @marten-seemann I might point out that the goal of stateless reset is to quickly notify the peer that the connection cannot be used. Waiting for the second packet goes against the purpose. Note also that, to avoid looping, endpoints are expected to limit the number of stateless reset packets they send.

comments.author: marten-seemann
comments.body:
@kazuho If you're handling 65336 connections (or rather, CIDs) and you're using a 4 byte CID, the probability of a random collision between the random data in the stateless reset packet and one of the connections you're serving is 1:65336. If you're handling that many connections, you'd probably be using longer CIDs anyway, which brings down the collision probability even further.
This is a minuscule collision probability, and a reasonable implementation wouldn't bother to optimize this corner case of a corner case (stateless reset is a corner case in itself).

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: ~~A collision occurs with 50% probability at that point.~~  Does that help make Kazuho's point?

comments.author: marten-seemann
comments.body:
I don't think this is a correct application of the birthday bound here. The server has a fixed set of these 2^16 connection IDs (which, by construction, are collision-free).
To get a collision with any of them, the random value, for which there are 2^32, would have to be match one of those 2^16 CIDs. That's a collision probability of 2^-16.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: Ah, of course.  You aren't picking 2^16 times.  Still, this isn't about collision probability.  You probably have higher drop rates than that.

comments.author: marten-seemann
comments.body:
> You probably have higher drop rates than that.

Exactly my point. If the stateless reset is much more likely to be dropped in the network than to cause a collision, I won't make things a lot worse by just dropping it myself in case of a collision.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: Well, I think that it makes the counterpoint too.  Why come here and ask for permission when you can just pretend something got lost?

comments.author: marten-seemann
comments.body:
I'm not asking for permission here, and I have no intention to change the way I implemented stateless reset detection in quic-go.
I just don't think that the spec should prohibit a reasonable way to implement this mechanism, even if it's not enforceable in the end.

How about we change the text to this:
> However, the comparison MUST be performed when the first packet in an incoming datagram either cannot be associated with a connection. The comparison MAY also be performed when a short header packet associated with a connection cannot be decrypted.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
> The comparison MAY also be performed when a short header packet associated with a connection cannot be decrypted.

I am not sure if I like this text. Depending on the size of the CID and the number of connections that an endpoint handles, this has to be MUST or SHOULD to achieve the goal of stateless reset.

IMO the question is if it's worth spending the cost to seek consensus on the acceptable rate of losing a stateless reset within an endpoint.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body: I would be content with that change as a SHOULD.  However, I believe that would be a design change.

comments.author: janaiyengar
comments.body: It's an unenforceable MUST. While I understand the issue, I am going to argue that this is fine as it is, but it's not going to be ideal for all implementers. I would be fine with a SHOULD here too, but I do not think that the change is worth the delay this will cause.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: Most of the changes I've come up with don't end up making the text any better, so I'd prefer to keep it as is.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: I would also prefer to keep things as-is on this one.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: I'm not seeing much interest in a design change and we are late in the process.

comments.author: larseggert
comments.body: Agreed. I will close this. If @marten-seemann really wants to push for changes, he can do so during IETF LC.

issues.title: The assertion in OnPacketsLost can fail
issues.author: martinthomson
issues.body:
This is a little convoluted, but here's the logic.

The loss recovery and congestion control both have separate states for tracking when the first RTT sample arrived.  In practice you would likely mix those and share RTT estimation states.  The RTT estimation is performed on the loss recovery side, but the results are used in the congestion control side, primarily for determining the PTO for persistent congestion. 

The first RTT sample on the loss recovery side is set when the first ack-eliciting packet is acknowledged.

The congestion control side declares an RTT estimate available when the first ACK arrives.

That difference means that if an acknowledgment only acknowledges non-ack-eliciting packets AND there is a loss (which seems plausible in that case), THEN the congestion control side will think that there is an RTT estimate when there is not.  This leads to this assertion in OnPacketsLost failing:

```python
  // Only consider packets sent after getting an RTT sample.
  assert(first_rtt_sample != 0)
```

I was just in the process of changing my "detect_persistent_congestion" implementation to switch from:

```rust
if first_rtt_sample.is_none() {
    return;
}
```
to 

```rust
debug_assert!(first_rtt_sample.is_some());
```

And when I traced the logic back I found this bug.

The fix is easy:

```python
  // Only consider packets sent after getting an RTT sample.
  if (first_rtt_sample == 0):
    return
```

non-ack-eliciting packets don't elicit an ACK, so you should never receive an ACK that only newly acknowledges non-ack-eliciting packets.

In Recovery-31 there are several references that I judge as normative and not informative ones.

- Section 7.8: "A sender MAY use the pipeACK method described in Section 4.3 of [RFC7661] to determine if the congestion window is sufficiently utilized." A normative reference necessary to follow if one selects to use the optional method.

- Sectiom 7.3.2: "Implementations MAY reduce the congestion window immediately upon entering a recovery period or use other mechanisms, such as Proportional Rate Reduction ([PRR]), to reduce the congestion window more gradually." Another case of a suggested mechanism, which if one is to follow it requires one to read that PPR reference. Secondly, why the alternative reference style.

- Section 8.3: "Markings can be treated as equivalent to loss ([RFC3168]), but other responses can be specified, such as ([RFC8511]) or ([RFC8311])." So RFC3168 is the normative specification for the treat it equal to loss. RFC8511 is the TCP alternative back-off an experimental specification for the alternative. And RFC8311 is the process for performing other experiments with alternative responses. I judge all necessary depending on what one intendeds to do. 

So to my understanding this results in two downrefs to experimental specifications. I think that is acceptable in the context they are used in this document. But to be tried in IETF last call. However, I think I don't want to generally recommend them to be acceptable as downrefs so I have no intentions to promote them for the Downref registry.

@martinduke [wrote](https://github.com/quicwg/base-drafts/pull/4179#pullrequestreview-502402830):

I see what @gloinul is saying, but I also see some wiggle room in RFC 3967, Section 1.1:

When a reference to an example is made, such a reference need not

issues.title: Handshake failure (infinite ping-pong) when path MTU is asymmetric
issues.author: kazuho
issues.body:
Consider the following scenario, assuming that the MTU from the client to the server is 1200 bytes, and the MTU from the server to client is 1000 bytes.
* step 1. Client sends:
  * datagram (1200 bytes), carrying Initial (Hello).
* step 2. In response, the server sends:
  * datagram (1200 bytes), carrying Initial (Hello) and a Handshake packet that contains the first half of handshake-level TLS messages (i.e. EncryptedExtensions, Certificate, CertificateVerify, Finished).
  * datagram (500 bytes), carrying Initial (PING) and a Handshake packet that contains the latter half of the handshake-level TLS messages.

The first datagram gets lost, the second datagram reaches the client.

* step 3. In response to the datagram being received, the client sends:
  * datagram (tiny), carrying Initial (ACK).
* step 4. When the server receives the packet, it learns the RTT, and arms the time-based loss detection timer. In a fraction of RTT, that timer fires, and the server sends what have been sent in step 2.

The first of the two datagrams sent in step 4 gets lost, the second one reaches the client.

* step 5. In response to the datagram being received, the client sends an ACK, as it did in step 3.

As we can see, we have an infinite loop that cannot make progress.

This example might sound a little strange, as the server arms the time-based loss detection timer for Handshake packets when receiving an ACK for the Initial packet. Though I would point out that the specification is lax on how an endpoint might use an Initial ACK to drive loss recovery of other packet number spaces; see [the third paragraph of section 6.2.3 of the recovery draft](https://quicwg.org/base-drafts/draft-ietf-quic-recovery.html#section-6.2.3-3).

We might pretend that the MAY in [the second paragraph of section 6.2.3](https://quicwg.org/base-drafts/draft-ietf-quic-recovery.html#section-6.2.3-2) restricts alternative loss signals (i.e. duplicate CRYPTO frames, receipt of Handshake packets before obtaining Handshake keys) from being applied to anything other than Initial PN space. But even in that case, I think we still have a failure mode. If the size of ServerHello is slightly above the MTU, if the server is designed to embed ACK in the first Initial packet for each send event, and if the client skips packet numbers upon observing possible loss, the size of the server-sent ACK frame increases two for every Initial packet that the client sends. This means that for each round-trip, the space that can be used for sending CRYPTO data will decrease by 2 bytes for the first Initial packets that the server sends in each iteration. These 2 bytes will be sent as tiny packets, and they will reach the client, while the full-size packet gets consistently dropped. In other words, the failure mode in this case is that there would be a ping-pong between the endpoints, and only 2 bytes of data can be exchanged per each round-trip.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body: Regarding possible solution, I think the most straightforward fix would be to require servers to always send full-sized datagrams, until the path is validated. We can be limit that requirement to endpoints that use something other than ACK or time threshold for retransmission.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
> step 3. In response to the datagram being received, the client sends:
>    datagram (tiny), carrying Initial (ACK).

Minor correction here: the client will send a 1200 byte Initial packet.  Though this doesn't stop the problem from persisting.

I think that the proposed remedy is out of proportion to the problem.  This is not a situation that we would expect to be common (this is an IPv4 only path, for starters).  Do you have evidence of a path with an asymmetric, sub-1200 byte MTU?

You could say that this is a problem if the initial state is 1400/1200 path MTU and the first Initial from the client is 1400, but the ACK is 1200.  But then endpoints are allowed to send less than 1400, so the correct response there is "don't do that".  It's just that we have a minimum packet size of 1200, so the correct reaction is "don't do QUIC" on that path.  The problem being that you don't necessarily get to that point easily.

(I'm not following the 2 bytes per round trip thing fully, but it seems like it's 2 useless bytes.  If I'm write, you assume that the server doesn't trim its ACK frames.  Ours will.  Even without ACK from the client, it will trim *before* the size of the ACK increases by another byte: after 32 round trips when the largest acknowledged reaches 64.  But the client is sending ACK frames, so the server can stop sending ACK ranges.  So we likely stop making progress well before the two bytes per round trip get anywhere. This is probably a distraction from the main topic though...)

comments.author: marten-seemann
comments.body: In quic-go, I implemented a handshake timeout (that’s independent of the idle timeout) and defaults to 10s. If the handshake doesn’t complete, for whatever reason, during that time, the connection gets killed. Maybe that’s the easier solution?

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: I think that the handshake timeout is a common response that ties up a bunch of these problems neatly.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
Handshake timeout is the last resort. The problem here is that the endpoints would exchange packets rapidly until the handshake times out. As an example, if the handshake timeout is 10 seconds and the RTT is 10ms, a server might transmit 1700 datagrams (10 seconds / 10 ms * 2 datagrams * 9/8; where 9/8 is the loss recovery threshold).

@martinthomson:
>> step 3. In response to the datagram being received, the client sends:
>> datagram (tiny), carrying Initial (ACK).
>
> Minor correction here: the client will send a 1200 byte Initial packet. Though this doesn't stop the problem from persisting.

Thank you for the correction.

> I think that the proposed remedy is out of proportion to the problem. This is not a situation that we would expect to be common (this is an IPv4 only path, for starters). Do you have evidence of a path with an asymmetric, sub-1200 byte MTU?

This is a fair point; I'll see if I can get some information.

> (I'm not following the 2 bytes per round trip thing fully, but it seems like it's 2 useless bytes. If I'm write, you assume that the server doesn't trim its ACK frames. Ours will. Even without ACK from the client, it will trim before the size of the ACK increases by another byte: after 32 round trips when the largest acknowledged reaches 64. But the client is sending ACK frames, so the server can stop sending ACK ranges. So we likely stop making progress well before the two bytes per round trip get anywhere. This is probably a distraction from the main topic though...)

(The server's ACK never reaches the client, as it is always coalesced with the CRYPTO frame. Therefore, a client cannot ACK the ACK. Eventually, the server will fail to build the ACK frame as the number of gaps become too large, but until then, there would be a ping-pong. But if we think that the behavior explained in the main topic is conformant to the specification, this is just a distraction as you point out.)

comments.author: janaiyengar
comments.body:
@martinthomson: We sadly have evidence of path MTU being set (for some ASes) to < 1200 bytes. It's a small enough fraction and this ought to be fixed, but it exists. Basically we should end up not doing QUIC under these conditions.

The core of the problem is that the failure mode here is a slow death. This handshake is ultimately going to fail, but potentially after a lot of wasted packets, depending on implementation details. @kazuho's proposed fix is to drive this partial failure to deliver packets to complete failure, which is really what ought to happen.

The proposed solution has the server effectively doing PMTU validation during the first RTT along with path validation by forcing all packets to be max size, ensuring that there are no small packets don't reach the client. Commonly, this should end up only padding the last packet in the first flight from the server, and if you're not careful, the packet carrying the ACK of the client's Initial.

I see this as an optimization of a failure case that exists but is uncommon. Some text that draws caution to this point in the PMTU section and suggests what a server can do might be useful.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: FWIW, Google's implementation avoids this problem by adding padding to ensure that all UDP datagrams containing Initial packets that we generate are at least 1200 bytes long - on both client and server. I would personally be in favor of making that a MUST in the spec, since verifying the MTU during the handshake is one of the important advantages of QUIC over TCP. If we do not solve this issue normatively, then users will be burdened with a noticeable timeout when they access servers that don't do this on networks with low server-to-client MTUs, which exist.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
FWIW, I think there's another failure mode that might be more disastrous.

What if the client has a TLS session ticket, and resumption succeeds? In that case, the server's first flights carrying Initial and Handshake packets might not be a full-sized datagram. The first full-sized datagrams can be 1-RTT packets.

I think that means that if a client tries to resume a QUIC connection by using a TLS session ticket from a address for which the return path has a MTU less than 1200 bytes, we might see the connection being stuck. IIUC, this would happen for clients doing happy eyeball too, as the handshake for HTTP/3 will complete before HTTP/2.

comments.author: mjoras
comments.body:
> FWIW, Google's implementation avoids this problem by adding padding to ensure that all UDP datagrams containing Initial packets that we generate are at least 1200 bytes long - on both client and server. 

We do this too. This ensures clients on weird networks simply fallback to TCP.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
This discussion suggests two safeguards:

1. Clients should have a handshake timer that causes them to abandon a connection that has not reached the "confirmed" state.  Clients should abandon a connection at this time even if it has made progress toward that goal.  If they do not, any hole in the specification or implementation that allows for liminal states will result in that state being persistent.

2. Servers should ensure that all packets they send are at least 1200 bytes until address validation is complete.  This will ensure that the path supports the minimum MTU that QUIC requires.  Other mechanisms can then kick in to ensure that QUIC isn't used on that path.

Both of these can be enacted separately in terms of pull requests on the specification.  I'm reluctant - at this stage - to make these carry normative force in the sense that we use the M-word, but both recommendations seem likely to be adopted.

I will also point out that this is an IPv4-specific problem unless we allow for unbounded use of IP header extensions.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
@martinthomson Regarding the two safeguards, I am in favor of having the latter, but I am not sure if we need the former. The former does not prevent a failure mode that I pointed out in https://github.com/quicwg/base-drafts/issues/4183#issuecomment-704576344, that prevents the connection from making progress _after_ the handshake is complete.

So I think just having the latter is fine. Regarding how strong the safeguard should be, I think my preference goes to using a SHOULD. While I think every server should be sending full-size packets until the path is validated, I am not sure if there's any benefit in allowing the client to verify that the server is doing that. At the same time, there is no reason to prohibit the server that thinks it knows the path MTU from sending smaller packets.

comments.author: mjoras
comments.body: I agree with @kazuho. We've previously decided we aren't really in the business of suggesting "higher level" behaviors like this. If we did we should probably also codify things like TCP fallbacks. Instead we trust people will do those on their own. I think a "handshake timeout" falls in a similar bucket of an obvious idea people will implement in practice (and there are obvious analogs in the TCP world in the form of connection timeouts, which may or may not include TLS).

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body:
It sounds like "until address validation is complete" might not be sufficient.  The Initial token provides validation, but doesn't exercise the path MTU.  We should clarify that even if the address is validated by a NEW_TOKEN token (i.e. the anti-amplification limit is waived), the server should send 1200-byte datagrams until some in-connection address validation has also succeeded.

However, that feels like a new concept that I'm a little hesitant to try introducing.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: "until address validation is complete" sounds complex and error-prone, why not simply apply the requirement to initial packets like we do on the client?

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
To continue the discussion from the PR...

@marten-seemann points out that the handshake never moves on if you pad the Initial.  @kazuho then points out that we currently recommend that clients re-send their Initial if they see a Handshake packet that they can't decrypt (I keep forgetting that because we haven't implemented that bit yet, ...).  I think that perhaps that we might take Marten's suggestion and tweak the recommendation about re-sending Initials at the client.  If the client limits the number of Initial packets it sends this way, we avoid an infinite cycle.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
@MikeBishop I share your concern and the hesitation. And I think we can stick to discussing path validation.

My point would be that we do not say how endpoints should act when the MTU of a validated path goes below 1200 bytes mid-connection. Then, why do we need to talk about revalidating path MTU when the client reconnects with a valid token? Note that the lifetime of a QUIC connection can be longer than the lifetime of a NEW_TOKEN token.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
@martinthomson I would not oppose to tweaking the MAY that allows client to retransmit ClientHello when receiving a Handshake or a 1-RTT packet for which the client does not have keys. If we do that, I agree that the server-side recommendation can be reduced to Initial packets only.

That said, if we are fine with changing the specification on both the client- and server-side, my preference would be to recommend both endpoints padding all datagrams up to 1200 bytes until the path is validated (or there is a guarantee that the peer has validated), as @martinthomson suggested in https://github.com/quicwg/base-drafts/pull/4188#discussion_r501450489. Doing so eliminates the chance of having ping-pong, regardless of the recovery algorithm adopted by endpoints.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: The reason I prefer the Initial-only padding is that it is principled: it says that you can't start a connection with small packets, from either side.  And the cost is only tweaking an optional optimization.  Padding every packet might be better, and I don't think we should look to prohibit it, but I don't think that it is necessary to even recommend it.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body: Fair enough. I've updated the PR, please take a look.

comments.author: janaiyengar
comments.body: Ugh apologies, I've been having this discussion on the PR. I would argue that a different principle is in order here: that if the problem is an MTU problem, then you want complete failure, not partial failures. comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
@marten-seemann 
> In fact, I do. Implementing a limit for the number times you can retransmit data seems like a lot of additional complexity (as you have to lift that limit at some point to achieve reliable data delivery).

Could you elaborate a bit more please, because I'm not sure how it would be?

When sending the first flight, the server would have arm PTO timer (or would have postponed arming the timer when it had reached the amplification limit). Receipt of a duplicate CRYPTO data is a MAY that allows the server to have a special path for triggering what would have happened when PTO timer should have fired. I do not think the complexity changes a lot if we add a counter that restricts the invocation of that special path (in practice, I think that the counter can be _one_, meaning that it is a boolean flag for each connection).

> Unrelated to that: I noticed an interesting interplay with the amplification limit here: We might end up in a situation where the server has less than a full packet size worth of credit in its amplification limit, and normally would send a smaller packet. It seems like this situation will occur exactly when we're worried about asymmetric MTUs, so in practice the amplification limit will not be 3, but, 2.x.

I would not call this a 2.x situation. Rather, I would say that the server is guaranteed to have a send window of 3600 bytes. If the client sends Initial packets greater than 1200 bytes, then the server might have more room which it cannot use, when the server decides to stick to 1200 bytes. But that's fine, because servers should not be built under the assumption that the client would always be sending Initial packets greater than 1200 bytes.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
@marten-seemann 
> That sounds complex to me. I'd prefer to have a solution that doesn't require use to modify the retransmission logic. I feel like this is a symptom of using the wrong requirement for padding packets.

It seems to me that you are seeking for something impossible, or am I missing something?

Are you suggesting that all packets, regardless of the packet type, should be padded up to at least 1200 bytes until the endpoint receives an ACK? IIUC that's the only way to retain the existing retransmission rules (e.g., endpoint MAY retransmit CRYPTO data when receiving a packet for which it does not have keys).

But doing so would have negative consequences on what a server can send. At the moment, the PR says _pad Initial packets_. That means that in practice, a server can send datagrams containing Handshake packets of any size. Therefore, the server can fully utilize the 3x window even when there is a mismatch between the endpoints' MTU, if the server is fine with _not_ prepending Initial packets to every Handshake packet it sends.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
> Why is the server putting an Initial PING in its second packet? While legal, this is unnecessary behavior that allows the infinite loop to occur. That seems like another "don't do that" kind of thing.

We explicitly suggest that such optimization makes sense, because it gives the server a RTT estimate and to run time-based loss detection; please refer to the [third paragraph of section 6.2.3 of the recovery draft](https://quicwg.org/base-drafts/draft-ietf-quic-recovery.html#section-6.2.3-3).

> I would be comfortable with saying "any datagram that contains an Initial Packet MUST be at least 1200 Bytes unless they contain a CONNECTION_CLOSE frame."

That's certainly an option, though I see at least two problems:
* A MUST is going to be a breaking change, because it implies that the peer can test and reject packets that do not conform to the requirement. I'm not sure if we want to make a breaking change that is not strictly necessary, at this moment.
* Padding all Initial packets hurt performance, because the server's send window is restricted to 3x of what it has received from the client. For non-coalescing servers, padding Initial packets to full size would mean that it would have ~900 bytes less space to send the certificate chain in the first three packets (assuming that ServerHello is around 2x0 bytes). Or servers would lose one MTU of send window when sending an ACK-only Initial packet. I tend to prefer giving servers freedom regarding how (and if) they would implement defense against paths with MTUs being too small.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi

To respond to @kazuho:

- I don't think we should take into consideration the performance of servers that don't coalesce - coalescing is pretty much required for performance

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
I would respond to @DavidSchinazi as I think his comments breaks ups the point in a very good way.

> * I think a MUST isn't going to be problematic here, we can tell clients to not enforce this MUST for now. Getting the final spec in the right shape is more important than what implementors will do before we ship the spec

If we are going to make the specification in the right shape, I actually (slightly) prefer requiring servers (or both endpoints) to always use full-sized packets until they receive an ACK (or until some later point; e.g., path being validated). Doing so gives us the guarantee that none of the packets would pass through a path that cannot handle QUIC traffic.

Compared to that, just requiring Initial to be padded is a half-baked solution, especially when we consider the fact that we suggest the receipt of Handshake packets implies the loss of Initial packets.

> * I don't think we should take into consideration the performance of servers that don't coalesce - coalescing is pretty much required for performance

My understanding has been that non-coalescing endpoints are considered first-class citizens; I would rather not revisit the requirements (or what we consider as reasonable) at this stage.

> * If a server is about to send an INITIAL-ACK-only packet, it should coalesce as much of its full first flight with that as possible! The requirement for 1200 bytes doesn't mean they have to be wasted PADDING bytes

The problem with ACK-only packet is not in the first flight. It is in the second flight.

The problem of mandating all Initial packets to be padded is that, when loss of ServerHello is involved, we might start seeing servers spending 3 RTTs to complete the handshake rather than 2 RTTs.

Consider the case where the size of the server's certificate chain is between 2 MTU and 3 MTU. When receiving the client's first Initial packet, the server sends a three datagrams: Initial+Handshake, Handshake, Handshake. Let's say that at least the first datagram was lost.

Assuming that the endpoints do not implement the MAY in [section 6.2.3](https://quicwg.org/base-drafts/draft-ietf-quic-recovery.html#name-speeding-up-handshake-compl), the client retransmits the Initial packet when its PTO timer expires.

At 50% probability, this packet will be delivered to the server before the server's PTO timer expires for the server's first flight. That means that the server will be sending an ACK-only packet at 50% probability, in which case, there would be only 2 MTU worth of window when the server's PTO timer expires, meaning that the server will be incapable of sending all the TLS handshake messages in its second flight.

I'm not sure if this is the only problem that we have.

Anyways, to summarize, my hesitation against a "MUST pad all Initial packets" is that it is likely going to have unnecessary negative consequences on the handshake latency; my preference goes to minimizing the impact of the change at a moment when we are rolling out QUIC.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
Google has always been padding all Initial packets to full size, so if this causes major issues, it'd be helpful to see an A/B experiment that demonstrated the problem.

To me, the issues you're outlining are related to the amplification factor, which I agree is fairly conservative and it would not be surprising if a larger number(ie: 5 or 10) is accepted as the norm in server deployments.

As you stated, if servers do implement the MAY, this is not a significant issue.

I'm unclear on why "MUST pad all Initial packets" could be an issue.  Typically Initial packets are coalesced with Handshake packets, so the padding is either nonexistent or not that significant.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
@ianswett @DavidSchinazi I understand that you are not having issues with your deployments (and I am glad to hear that). But that does not necessary mean that the specification is giving good advice. In fact, the draft is very lux about when you can retransmit during the handshake; what you have as an evidence is that _one_ pair of endpoints implementing particular strategy works fine. That's very different from making sure that any pair of endpoints implementing various "reasonable" strategies work fine.

>> If we are going to make the specification in the right shape, I actually (slightly) prefer requiring servers (or both endpoints) to always use full-sized packets until they receive an ACK (or until some later point; e.g., path being validated). Doing so gives us the guarantee that none of the packets would pass through a path that cannot handle QUIC traffic.
>> 
>> Compared to that, just requiring Initial to be padded is a half-baked solution, especially when we consider the fact that we suggest the receipt of Handshake packets implies the loss of Initial packets.
> 
> I don't think I understand this. Putting the requirement on INITIAL packets is a complete solution - it's not possible to decrypt a packet from any other packet number space without having first successfully decrypted and parsed at least one INITIAL packet. Am I missing something?

Consider the case where all the following stands:
* server sends full-sized Initial packets, that gets dropped
* server transmits half-sized Handshake packets, that is not dropped
* client retransmits CRYPTO data when receiving a Handshake packet before obtaining Handshake keys (*)
* server retransmits Initial and Handshake packets when it receives duplicate CRYPTO data (**)

This set of behavior is permitted in status quo, and that causes ping-pong. This is one of the issue we are trying to resolve.

We can provide guidelines that would not cause ping-pong. But that's fragile when endpoints are incentivized to use signals other than ACKs to trigger retransmission. A more reliable way of preventing ping-pong is to prevent not only Initial packets but also Handshake packets and 1-RTT packets from passing through.

> If the server receives a retransmission of the ClientHello, and this server cares about the number of round trips involved in handshakes, then it should retransmit its ServerHello with this ACK because that's a pretty good signal that the ServerHello was lost.

I'm happy to point out that we already have that advice in the recovery draft. However, it is a MAY. I'm not sure if we can assume that all the QUIC servers to implement such strategy.

What I do not understand is the benefit of using a MUST rather than "SHOULD pad Initial packets," when using a MUST can hurt the performance of endpoints that obey to the specification.

Are you implying that some clients consider the server as alive when it receives the first packet that is decryptable, rather than when receiving the first packet that is bound to the connection (e.g., an undecryptable Handshake packet)?

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
Aside from Kazuho, who seems to want *more* packets to be padded, it seems like the current trend is toward more strongly mandating padding of Initial to >=1200 bytes.  If we go with MUST, then I think we need to consider enforcement options at the client.  I was happy with SHOULD on the understanding that this is a niche problem, but if we want to engage with the enforcement question, then I can live with MUST.

The tweaks I'm seeing open are:

1. An exception for CONNECTION_CLOSE.  This is good.

2. An exception for non-ack-eliciting Initial packets.  This seems less necessary.  I can see how it is appealing, but all these exclusions are mounting up and it's getting complicated.

For David's benefit, the ACK-only carveout would allow a server to receive an Initial, send an ACK, then later send its own flight without having that ACK contribute too much toward the amplification limit.  If the server has to go elsewhere to get certificates or signatures, that early ACK might be useful to a client; it gets min_rtt primed with a good value.  The alternative is suppressing the ACK to avoid spending the 1200 bytes.

Maybe we could unify these if we designated CONNECTION_CLOSE as non-ack-eliciting.  Then we have an exception, and cause not to have the client enforce a minimum size on Initial-carrying datagrams.

comments.author: janaiyengar
comments.body:
I think we might be losing the core problem here; I'll try to restate it, with the hope of driving towards a simpler resolution.

We currently require the client to confirm that the path from it to the server supports a PMTU of at least 1200 bytes (here):
```
A client MUST expand the payload of all UDP datagrams carrying Initial packets
to at least the smallest allowed maximum packet size (1200 bytes)
```

There is however no requirement in the spec that the server confirm that the path from it to the client be at least 1200 bytes. This can lead to a situation where asymmetric path MTUs can cause strange partial failures. This is not theoretical; we are seeing this at our servers with production traffic, where some paths (predominantly in Europe) in practice have a lower than 1200-byte MTU.

At a minimum, we need to add a requirement that ensures that the handshake fails under these conditions. This allows a client to fall back to TCP. This is a MUST-level design change if we don't want the connection to fail later or perform miserably later.

I propose the following two options:

1. Partial failures are more painful and problematic than complete failures. So, ideally, if the server's max packet size is not supported by the path, I would like to have _no_ packet be received by a client than some packets be received. A server that is concerned about performance with padding ACK-only packets from the server in the first flight can choose to never send an ACK-only packet until the path is validated -- the client cannot make forward progress until it receives some data from the server anyways, so receiving the ACK does not do much (yes, it reduces the number of retransmissions from the client, but that is a small side effect.) A concern here is that the change might be too disruptive, this late in the game.

2. We can simply state that our requirement is that the handshake MUST fail (@kazuho's idea)-- that the server MUST confirm that the path supports the minimum 1200-byte MTU, and cause the handshake to fail if not. We can then suggest ways in which the server can accomplish this: by padding all ack-eliciting Initial packets, by padding all packets until path validation, etc. This leaves room for implementers to do different things (as they might already be doing right now), and therefore will be a less disruptive change. This can cause wastage of packets, for example when implementers only pad Initial packets (we've seen this), but that's fine, since the handshake does fail eventually.

At this point, I'd like to go with option (2) above. Thoughts?

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
janaiyengar
comments.body:
@DavidSchinazi: Yes -- we have two issues.

I agree that `MUST ensure that the path supports 1200-byte packets` is unenforceable, but that's fine IMO, since a server not following this MUST is hurting itself. That said, in the interest of convergence, I'm ok with saying `MUST pad INITIAL packets unless it contains a CONNECTION_CLOSE frame`.

My goal was to avoid making a specific carve-out for ACK packets, since this is a performance-related carve-out as well. I'm also not confident that we understand how different client implementations might react to receiving ACKs but not receiving any other packet. I'm not sure how helpful the suggestion of "limit the number of times clients use the MAY" is without something more specific.

For the performance issue, I'm inclined to suggest that servers pad all packets (except those carrying CONNECTION_CLOSE) and avoid sending ACK-only packets until path validation is complete. The only issue here is delaying of ACKs, but (i) max_ack_delay does not apply to these ACKs, which makes any consequent large ack delay usable, and (ii) a client cannot make any forward progress with just the ACK anyway.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: I don't feel too strongly about the carveout for non-ACK-eliciting packets, so I'm OK with us landing the new "MUST pad INITIAL except CONNECTION_CLOSE" with or without the ACK carveout

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
@DavidSchinazi 
> I don't feel too strongly about the carveout for non-ACK-eliciting packets, so I'm OK with us landing the new "MUST pad INITIAL except CONNECTION_CLOSE" with or without the ACK carveout

I would be fine with that _with ACK being included_ as one of the exceptions. Maybe the text would be something like "to prevent the handshake from succeeding when the MTU of the return path is below 1200 bytes, a server MUST pad Initial packets that carry CRYPTO data." I think in practice that'd be equivalent to "MUST pad Initial expect CONNECTION_CLOSE or ACK-only."

I think that [@janaiyengar's comment](https://github.com/quicwg/base-drafts/issues/4183#issuecomment-707443155) was a good summary regarding the options we have: 1) prevent any packets from passing through 2) prevent the handshake from succeeding even though some packets could pass through.

It seems to be that we are converging on the latter option.

The downside of the latter option, as people have pointed out, is that we need to deal with ping-pong. I think there is an emerging cencensus to limit the number of times an endpoint can send probes before PTO expiration, the only remaining debate seems to be between @ianswett and @martinthomson regarding if that number should be one.

My argument against "MUST pad all Initial packets" has been that it is more than what we need for preventing the handshake to succeed. In particular, as I have stated previously, the need to pad ACK-only Initial packets has been the concern. While it is true that endpoints can always coalesce (by withholding ACKs as @janaiyengar points out), I do not think there is reason to sacrifice performance of those who do not.

OTOH, endpoints have to prevent CRYPTO data from reaching the peer if it wants to prohibit the handshake from succeeding. That means that they have to _at least_ pad the packets that carry CRYPTO data. I think everybody will be fine with that being a requirement on Initial packets.

comments.author: marten-seemann
comments.body:
I don't think it's ok to not pad ACK-only packets.
Recovery says:
> That is, the client MUST set the probe timer if the client has not received an acknowledgement for one of its Handshake packets and the handshake is not confirmed (see Section 4.1.2 of [QUIC-TLS]), even if there are no packets in flight. 

Thus, the client could receive an ACK for its ClientHello (in a packet that was not padded), and it will keep retransmitting the ClientHello indefinitely.

From my understanding, the condition should be the following:
The server MUST pad *all* packets (except CONNECTION_CLOSE) until:
* it has received an ACK for any Initial packet, OR
* until the Initial packet number space has been dropped.

Lazy implementations could only implement the latter condition.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
@marten-seemann Oh that's a very good point, and I actually think that you have found a problem that is unrelated to path MTU validation.

Let's think of two possible cases:
1.  A client might not be able to send ClientHello in one flight. It has to wait for the server to ACK the first flight to send the rest of the ClientHello. Post-quantum is a good example.
2. A server that spends time in generating ServerHello or the handhake messages to be sent using Handshake packets. It could be due to the server being slow (consider IoT), or because the server has to fetch a new per-SNI configuration from a different server, or due to delegating some of the TLS process to a node that is located at a secure location (see https://blog.cloudflare.com/keyless-ssl-the-nitty-gritty-technical-details/).

To support case 1, servers have to send ACKs before generating ServerHello. To support case 2, servers have to postpone sending ACKs while generating ServerHello, otherwise there would be a ping-pong.

Am I correct that this issue exists unrelated to the PMTU problem?

comments.author: gloinul
comments.body: It looks like the main issue here is being resolved. I hope to such a degree that the changes can be included in the draft version going for IETF LC. I would appreciate if people can review the latest version of the  PR (#4188) so that we can get a good sense if this has agreement among the most active.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
Based on @marten-seemann comment, I'm now favoring requiring both the client AND server to pad all Initial packets except CONNECTION_CLOSE.

However, I don't think the point raised is that problematic.  The client will keep PTO-ing a full-sized Initial containing a PING, but with exponential backoff.  This isn't that different from the situation when a connection is black-holed, though if the RTT sample was very small, this would be more aggressive than a new connection.

comments.author: larseggert
comments.body: Marking this as "design" based on the discussion and on #4188. (If we end up changing our minds about what we want to do, we can change the label.)

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body:
Sorry if I'm slow to understand this kind of issue, but can someone explain to me the problem that @marten-seemann is trying to describe in https://github.com/quicwg/base-drafts/issues/4183#issuecomment-708876280? In particular:
> Thus, the client could receive an ACK for its ClientHello (in a packet that was not padded), and it will keep retransmitting the ClientHello indefinitely.

This doesn't make sense to me. If the client has received an ACK for its ClientHello, why is it retransmitting it? The fact that the packet containing the initial ACK from the server was padded or not doesn't change anything.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
@DavidSchinazi I believe that comment is an error.  It should be "Thus, the client could receive and ACK for its PING sent in Initial ...."

As you said, once the ClientHello is acknowledged, a peer would not retransmit it.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body:
Ah, thanks @ianswett .

Going back to the principled approach I described earlier (use MUST to makes sure the handshake doesn't complete on bad asymmetric links; use SHOULD to prevent wasted bytes for handshakes that won't ever succeed), I'd say this can be solved by saying that servers SHOULD pad ACK-only initial packets.

That said, saying that the server MUST pad all initials except for ones that only contain CONNECTION_CLOSE frames would also be fine by me. Relatedly, that's what our implementation does.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
@ianswett 
> Based on @marten-seemann comment, I'm now favoring requiring both the client AND server to pad all Initial packets except CONNECTION_CLOSE.
> 
> However, I don't think the point raised is that problematic. The client will keep PTO-ing a full-sized Initial containing a PING, but with exponential backoff. This isn't that different from the situation when a connection is black-holed, though if the RTT sample was very small, this would be more aggressive than a new connection.

Thanks to @ianswett for pointing out that we already have exponential backoff as a defense. As he pointed out in the other thread, our consensus established in #3546 was that PTO back off counter must _not_ be reset under these circumstances, because resetting the counter leads to a ping pong when the server takes time in generating ServerHello.

Based on that prior consensus, I think there are two ways forward:

* 1) Make no changes to #4188. ACK-only Initials do _not_ have to be padded, because we already have  that defense.
* 2) Reopen #3546 as the defense is too fragile, consider other methods, and also discuss if ACK-only Initials have to be padded.

My preference goes to option 1, though personally I would not oppose to reopening #3546. I do not want to see sudden spike of traffic when a server fails to instantly load a SNI-specific configuration.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
Padding ACK-only Initial packets does make this ping-pong with exponential backoff much less problematic, so I still think padding all Initials to full size except CONNECTION_CLOSE is likely the option with the smallest number of potential issues.

I think the only way to reopen #3546 is to revisit how we prevent servers from being blocked by the amplification factor, ie #3162. That could make things simpler, but I don't believe the WG is up for it and we're pretty late in the game to be making major changes, so I'd advise against it.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
Reopening this.  My mistake for not reading all of the discussion here.

Like others, I believe that #4188 is sufficient.  ACK frames will get through.  The client will send another packet on PTO (as the timer remains armed), but the client doesn't reset the PTO count, so it will back off to nothing.  As Ian says, it sends a little faster if the RTT is lower than its initial estimate, but it still continues.

The only other difference I see here is that the small packets containing ACK frames will tickle the idle timer on the client.  For clients that rely on the idle timeout alone to end connection attempts they will hang around until the exponential backoff exceeds the idle timeout.  (Our test client is like this, because we expect applications to set a timer for connection establishment.)

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
That note about the idle timer is important in practice, since it means implementations that use either should always race TCP and QUIC and/or set an application level timeout.

However, when sending 0-RTT requests, it's preferable to avoid replaying them if at all possible, so its preferable not to race QUIC and TCP until one is fairly sure the QUIC connection will fail.  Tickling the idle timer would mean the application level timeout is more likely to be hit, and those are usually fairly conservative.

FWIW, our implementation pads Initial ACKs and I don't intend to change that(nor does the PR require any change).

To me, there would be a nice simplicity changing the text to "You MUST pad all Initial packets except those containing CONNECTION_CLOSE.", but one could also document this potential issue with unpadded ACKs tickling the idle timer and let implementations choose what they want to do.  I do think it's worth doing one of these two actions, though.

comments.author: martinduke
comments.body: So we've merged #4188. Is the remaining issue whether or not to require padding of ACKs?

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
@ianswett 
> That note about the idle timer is important in practice, since it means implementations that use either should always race TCP and QUIC and/or set an application level timeout.
> 
> However, when sending 0-RTT requests, it's preferable to avoid replaying them if at all possible, so its preferable not to race QUIC and TCP until one is fairly sure the QUIC connection will fail. Tickling the idle timer would mean the application level timeout is more likely to be hit, and those are usually fairly conservative.

I'm not sure if I agree with that rationale.

By padding just Initial ACKs without padding Handshake ACKs, there's still chance that the client would receive packets.

As @janaiyengar noted [here](https://github.com/quicwg/base-drafts/issues/4183#issuecomment-707443155), if we want to prevent clients from seeing anything from the server when a sub-1200-byte path is being used, the requirement has to be to pad *all long header packets*.

But our consensus is not do that, and let some packets pass through (VN, Retry, Handshake, 1-RTT packets).

That means that a client, that wishes to run a handshake timer that expires at an early moment, has to be prepared for doing some packet processing *then* determine if it should extend the handshake timeout. With the current state of #4188 being merged, that determination can be made by seeing if you have received any CRYPTO data from the server.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
The idle timer is only extended if one can _process_ a packet, and Handshake packets can't be processed without receiving all the Initial CRYPTO data, so I don't believe there's an issue.  Additionally, the client won't receive Handshake ACKs if it hasn't sent Handshake packets, so that should not be an issue.

From section 10.1 of transport-31:
> An endpoint restarts its idle timer when a packet from its peer is
   received and processed successfully.

comments.author: kazuho
comments.body:
@ianswett Thank you for elaborating. The timeout design that you explained is different from what I had in mind, but I agree that it's sensible.

Though, taking a step back, I am actually wondering if the use-case you described still exists (or has to exist).

In the early days of QUIC, before TLS 1.3 was being standardized, it did make sense to not happy-eyeball HTTP requests, because you do not want to let servers process both of the requests that have been happy-eyeballed.

But with the standardization of TLS 1.3 and 425 status code (RFC 8470), the situation has changed. A server is now required to ask clients replay non-idempotent requests.

I think we can, and should, rely on 425, considering that HTTP/3 is something new. Server administrators that enable the use of early data can make sure (and should make sure) that they would not receive replays of non-idempotent request, rather than relying on the browser making probablistical guesses. This is the bridge we've already crossed with TLS 1.3, we do not need to go back.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: Based on people I've talked to, 425 may not be widely implemented.  Additionally, there are scenarios where identifying replay is quite difficult.  But even so, the risk is not overly high in most cases.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: I realized that clients could mitigate the issue of unpadded ACKs extending the idle timeout by not extending it for unpadded Initial packets, at least until a full-sized packet has been received.  If we stick with the current text, I think our implementation will likely do just that.

comments.author: janaiyengar
comments.body: We ought to be able to rely on exponential backoff of PTO and idle timeout for correctness, which we agreed as the goal here. Is there a reason what we have now will not work?

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: Doubling the amount of time for idle timeout to occur is a bummer, so I think it's worth documenting the potential issue if we're not going to change the normative text?

comments.author: huitema
comments.body: Could someone restate the "emerging consensus" ? I am reading the thread, and under the impression that the consensus is "PR #4188 is sufficient". Is that the actual emerging consensus?

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
Yes @huitema, that is the emerging consensus.

I wrote #4252 to document a potentially non-obvious effect of not padding ACK only packets, but it doesn't seem like people think that's necessary, so I should probably just close it.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: We merged https://github.com/quicwg/base-drafts/pull/4188 and as per Lar's email on the list, we'll use IETF last call to judge things. So I'm closing this.

issues.title: Connection ID length requirements for Version Negotiation packets need clarification
issues.author: marten-seemann
issues.body:
Since future QUIC versions might have different CID length requirements for Initial packets (or however that packet type will be called in that version), we already require servers to be able to send Version Negotiation packets with CIDs longer than 20 bytes (which is the maximum length that v1 allows).

We need to clarify that this also applies to the minimum CID length, which is 8 byte for the DCID in v1. A future version of QUIC might relax this limit, so a server also needs to generate a VN packet if it receives a packet with an unknown version and a shorter DCID, otherwise it won't be possible to roll out such a QUIC version.

This is coming out of a Slack discussion with @DavidSchinazi and @nibanks, as well as recent tests on the interop runner. It turns out that 2 server implementations on the interop runner didn't get this right, and at least one server implementation that's not on the interop runner, but is running QUIC in production.

issues.title: recovery-31: Motivation for max_ack_delay statement
issues.author: gloinul
issues.body:
In Section 5.3:

> After the handshake is confirmed, any acknowledgement delays reported by the peer that are greater than the peer's max_ack_delay are attributed to unintentional but potentially repeating delays, such as scheduler latency at the peer or loss of previous acknowledgements. Therefore, these extra delays are considered effectively part of path delay and incorporated into the RTT estimate.
	
I don't understand the motivation behind this statement. Assuming that the peer is measuring their actual ack_delay, i.e. it has a sample for arrival_time[psn_highest_acked] and then when creating the ack and calculating the ack_delay it will do time(now) - arrival_time[psn_highest_acked] and that is then larger than max_ack_delay. Then this has nothing to do with the path, only with the peer implementation and its capability of waking up to report the ack when additional reception is not forcing it to ACK earlier than max_ack_delay. Thus, by capping the use of ack_delay to max_ack_delay then in certain transmission conditions the RTT will be inflated, and in others not. 

I would guess that the impact of this is in most cases minimal. However, from a factual stand point it appear to me as non true statement. Does this needs be changed?

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
Right, it is not a direct function of the path, but it is included in the path delay as represented by the RTT estimates.

I'm not sure of a better way to say this, but @janaiyengar might have a suggestion.

comments.author: janaiyengar
comments.body:
@gloinul : Yes, that is correct, and that is exactly the intention. What is not intentional delay at the peer is considered part of the "path".

The model we have is as follows. A sender wants to separate intentional delays at the peer from unintentional delays, since it can then do a better estimate for loss detection by not counting the ack delay in the EWMA.

This leads to an issue where the peer can intentionally or unintentionally misreport actual ack delays, causing the estimated RTT to be incorrectly small.

To avoid this, we have two checks:
- all RTT samples, after adjusting for ack delay, are limited to being the measured min RTT, and
- any reported ack delay has to be smaller than the peer's promised max ack delay.

The question here is not whether the unintentional delay belongs in the path or not, but whether it ought to be removed from the path RTT, since we explicitly remove the reported ack delay from the RTT sample. Since this is unintentional (or uncontrolled) delay, we consider it part of the path, and part of the EWMA.

comments.author: larseggert
comments.body: @gloinul do these explanation address your issue? Or are text changes required?

comments.author: gloinul
comments.body:
@janaiyengar my point is that an error in timers waking up the receiver to send an ACK will affect the time of the transmission of the ACK. However, in those cases where at the time it wakes up to construct the ACK it correctly reads the time and accurately represent the time between the time of packet reception and transmission of ACK in the ACK_DELAY field the RTT is correctly estimated. It is the timing  of the feedback loop that is a bit in error as it was longer than max ACK delay. 

To attempt to answer @larseggert: I think there is an difference in opinion if this affects the RTT estimate or not in a negative way. And thus I like to better understand if I there is any substance here or not. Likely there is not, but let continue the discussion a little bit more.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body:
This design is very much intentional.  For example, if a peer specifies a max ack delay of 10 ms but always delays ACKs 100ms, then IF one always used the peer's ack_delay without capping it at max_ack_delay, it could result in repeated spurious PTOs.

Re-reading the text, I do believe it says the right thing:
> 
Therefore, these extra delays are considered **effectively** part of path delay
> 

This recognizes it's not really part of the path, but we're treating it like that.  TCP always treats ack delay as part of the path  delay via SRTT and RTTVar, so this is in keeping with that.

comments.author: gloinul
comments.body:
Ok, I can understand the intention here to say that you need to behave as promised, and to do otherwise gives a to big advantage to the misbehaving peers therefore we will include any time beyond max ACK delay in the RTT. But, that is not quite what the motivation text says.

So I don't see any need for a technical change. I think it would be good to adjust the motivation so that it more correctly reflects the reasons.

comments.author: ianswett
comments.body: SG, I added a sentence, PTAL at #4218

comments.body: Marking this "editorial" based on #4218

issues.title: Recovery-31: Initial Smoothed_RTT values

In Section 5.3:

"When there are no samples for a network path, and on the first RTT sample for the network path:

Before any RTT samples are available, the initial RTT is used as rtt_sample. On the first RTT sample for the network path, that sample is used as rtt_sample. This ensures that the first measurement erases the history of any persisted or default values."

Section 6.2.1:

"The probe timer MUST NOT be set if the time threshold (Section 6.1.2) loss detection timer is set. The time threshold loss detection timer is expected to both expire earlier than the PTO and be less likely to spuriously retransmit data."
