reviews.author: MikeBishop
reviews.body:
This is effectively the first layer of unidirectional streams we had already been talking about -- an equivalent way to state this is that streams are pairs of unidirectional bytestreams, each of which moves through the idle->open->closed cycle independently.  "Half-closed" is a shorthand to denote a stream in which one bytestream is closed and the other is not.

When I did my scratch branch of what that would look like, I also divided the frames into "stream-independent," "sender," and "receiver" frames.  For each of those unidirectional byte streams, there are frames that the sender generates (STREAM, BLOCKED, RST_STREAM) and frames that the receiver generates as feedback (WINDOW_UPDATE, REQUEST_RST).  As long as the stream is open in that direction, those frames are valid to flow.  When the stream closes in that direction, those frames are no longer needed/valid.

pulls.title: Authenticate public reset with a hash (#215)
pulls.author: martinthomson
pulls.body:
This takes @ekr's design from #20 and expands on it quite a bit.  There are a few little wrinkles that I think we might want to discuss a little.

First, this is a one-time password. That means that the combination of key and connection ID can't ever be repeated for a given server instance.  Our 64-bit connection ID space isn't really enough to provide this.  How a server moves to a new static key during operation will be challenging; it probably needs to partition the connection ID space.

Second, transport parameters are encrypted.  #20 made a point of having the verifier in the clear so that intermediaries could validate the Public Reset.  I don't want to create a second TLS extension, but I guess that is the best option we have available to us if this is what is required.  I don't think we should move transport parameters into the clear either.

Closes #215, #20.

pulls.title: Define the payload size of the initial packet rather than the total packet size
pulls.author: martinthomson
pulls.body:
The entity that creates the packet is not always aware of the existence of header extensions.  That makes hitting the 1280 octet limit hard.  Worse, if they are aware of extensions, they might reduce the size and then encounter a server that enforces the limit.  That server will discard the packet.  That makes enforcement risky.

This change places the limit on the payload.  It mandates 1232/1252 for v6/v4.

This is the uncomplicated version.  The complicated version that I didn't write up allows a client that knows more about overheads to reduce the payload size as long as they keep above some floor value (e.g., 1180).  We might consider doing that later if we want to allow QUIC to operate on paths with a much tighter MTU overhead.  Evidence suggests that we don't need this though (open an issue if you disagree).

Closes #267

pulls.title: Add a description of the FNV-1a algorithm
pulls.author: martinthomson
pulls.body:
I've added this in the TLS document, even though this would have been easier to
add to the transport document in some ways.  The current plan (if we ever clear
our backlog) is to move the details of the packet protection and key schedule
to the transport.  If that ever happens, it will be easy enough to move this
new text at the same time as the packet protection.

Two choices that I made here:

1. all packets are protected, including Public Reset - this means that the
packet construction code can have very simple logic for determining whether to
add an integrity check, namely is there an AEAD?; the cost being that public
reset is a little bigger

2. the integrity check mechanism can change in a new version - this avoids
expanding the list of things that we promise that won't change between
versions; the cost being one extra trivial check on receiving an unprotected
packet

Closes #167.

pulls.title: Address validation is stateless reject
pulls.author: martinthomson
pulls.body:
We already have enough text on how to tell a client to go away and come back.
But we don't really say how a server might do that statelessly.  Add a small
bit of text on that and we're done.

Closes #60

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: Offline, Jānis Čoders pointed out that we aren't very clear about what stream offset you expect on the second ClientHello.  I need to update to include a reminder about that too.

This works, though I think you should be clearer about how you pickle that information (self-encrypted AEAD).

However, if we're in the business of telling people what to do, we actually should document both this technique and the CH...SFIN, NST, RST technique that davidben and victor described.

I think that I'll leave the tricks for another PR.  I'm not convinced that the trick will work.  It will always require at least two packets because NST and CONNECTION_CLOSE require packet protection (I suppose you might argue that is more reason to add a new cleartext+encrypted packet type).  Then there is the size of the certificate.  It's more computation, more amplification factor, and all we get is one round trip less delay.
add citation for "the cookie extension"

I don't think this hack of delivering bytes out of order works... how is a server to know that there aren't lost packets?

Alternatively, a server can send a new connection ID for the client to use for the next leg of the connection. That would be cleaner, and wouldn't need this hack of delivering bytes out of order to TLS.
It's in TLS.

This isn't a hack, it's just physics.  The first ClientHello takes N bytes, the second takes M.  The offset for the first is 0, the second is N because it follows immediately after.  The point here is that the client proceed as if this were the same connection; the server - if it does a stateless reject - has to account for that and deal with the fact that after the reject it won't ever receive the first N bytes - they were already received.
Why is the stream abstraction important during handshake?

Here is a proposal that might help simplify handshake without interfering with 0-RTT stream semantics. For 1-rtt it could be required that streams are not permitted before handshake is complete. https://github.com/quicwg/base-drafts/issues/489

Is this predicated on the idea that a ClientHello must fit into a single packet? If a ClientHello can span multiple packets, then I don't think I understand how a server would distinguish between a packet which contains part 2 of a ClientHello from a packet which contains a post-stateless-reject ClientHello.
We already require that ClientHello fits in a single packet.  Even the possibility of a two-part ClientHello makes DoS mitigation very difficult.
Just to be pedantic: please use "the TLS cookie extension."
What's the reason for making it transparent to the client? Why can the client not try with a new connection ID?

The server is the one that cares, so it takes on the extra effort of dealing with the complexity.  Why would the client retry with a new connection ID?

Also, logically, TLS maintains a handshake transcript.  Having the transcript appear to be on the same connection is less surprising than the odd gap you get with a stateless reject.  Besides, it's not a gap to the client, just the server.

I'm trying to understand how this would work at the server and it's not clear to me. So, when the server receives a packet that basically has one stream frame with stream ID 1 and offset 1050, what should it do? Should it deliver it up to TLS, or should it buffer? Since this retry logic is only known to the TLS part, how is QUIC to determine that this is a retry and not just a reordered packet?

Yes, deliver it to TLS.  When TLS asks whether the address validation is correct, it will provide the address validation token.  That token should include the length of the original ClientHello.  If TLS doesn't provide a token, or the length doesn't match, then it's bad and you can abort at that point.

What about the packet number on the SHLO ? 
From what i gathered, the one on the retryRequest was randomly generated. If we generate one randomly again then the client will most likely have issues.
And what are the rules for dealing with other streams and retransmittable frames such as ping in the initial packet?

I can understand how this could be made to work, but I worry a bit about the state of the crypto stream being different between the two endpoints. The client believes it has send 2 ClientHellos as bytes [0,N] on stream 0. If the server is required to process pre-handshake stream frames even with non-0 offsets, then it seems like it might be possible for an active attacker to rewrite the second ClientHello to start at, say, offset 2N. This would mean that any post-handshake messages from the client to the server would be ignored as duplicates.

I presume the solution to this is for the server to include in the data it sends to the client (and the client sends back to the server) the byte offset that the follow-up ClientHello is expected to start at, and to validate that when it process the follow-up ClientHello.

Does that sound right?

Yeah, this doesn't need QUIC connection continuity, just TLS continuity. A new connection with a new connection ID should achieve that. (The connection doesn't need to go back to the same server, does it?)
The whole point of a stateless reject is to avoid creating state, so if it had to go back to the same server, something is wrong :)
Good point.

pulls.title: MAX_STREAM_DATA is valid in the "idle" state
pulls.author: martinthomson
pulls.body:
Reordering might mean that this arrives ahead of time.  It would be unusual, but not unreasonably so for that to happen.

For instance, the h2 stack in Firefox sends a WINDOW_UPDATE immediately after sending a request for something it really wants.  This allows it to set the initial flow control window small, but have generous limits on important requests.  If that strategy were used, it wouldn't be unusual for the MAX_STREAM_DATA and STREAM frames to end up in different packets.

I built this on #457 because that touches the same text.

Closes #188.

pulls.title: Invert connection ID
pulls.author: martinthomson
pulls.body:
This defines a new packet type for the initial client cleartext packet, and stateless rejects.  The remaining packets that carry cleartext messages remain the same.  The final packet from the server is removed; instead the server cleartext packet carries the server-selected connection ID.  The server can propose a new connection ID in any of its cleartext packets, including the version negotiation packet.

This rolls in the changes from #482 and so addresses the issues raised there.

Things that I might do differently: 

1. Require the client to send an initial packet after version negotiation on the basis that version negotiation is a complete do-over.  

2. Maybe also after a stateless reject, which would mean that all packets containing the ClientHello would use that "initial" type.  That would mean that only the initial type would have packet size restrictions,
which is nice.

Those alternatives give the server more options for changing connection ID as well, but it also removes the ability for a server-side load balancer to easily distinguish between connection IDs that the client proposes and those that the server has provided.  Not sure which way that goes, I've opted to keep the signal in place until we've had some more discussion.

Closes #482, #442.

comments.author: mirjak
comments.body:
Back to @mikkelfj question: I think it might make sense to sort out the different use cases for the connection ID and think about those and the required properties separately. From my understanding we have three use cases:
1) as input for stateless load balancers
2) as confirmation signal
3) for connection migration

For 1) the id must be chosen by the server (or the load balancer) and must be visible to the load balancer on every packet; however, this id does actually not have to be unique for the connection. It rather identifies the server and as such could effectively be the same for all connections that go to the same server.

For 2) a value is selected by the client and reflected by the server. The signal may be visible to the path as it can be used to set up state e.g. for firewalls. Probably this signal is only needed at connection start or some kind of restart, however, exposing it all the time would potentially allow for transparent rebinding if state got lost on the path. Note the packet number echo could fulfil the same purpose. 

For 3) server and client must have agreed to a token. This signal does not necessarily need to be exposed to the path because the path might have changed anyway. However, it cannot easily be encrypted either as this is needed to identify the right encryption context. Effectively it only needs to be sent after the migration but the endpoint might not know if the migration happen, so not sending it all the time could lead to a one RTT delay after migration to request it. 

Hope that helps!

(credits for this analysis actually go to Jean-Pierre Smith, one of Brian's colleges in the network security group)

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body:
@mirjak 

The use case I have in mind is not fully covered in the above three cases:

4) As a unique identifier for associating connection state. Without a unique id this is handled via IP:port  until connection migration, then replaced with a new IP:port. This requires IP:port to be unique to the respective end-points (when connection id does not serve that purpose).

In praxis the Connection ID will serve the purpose of associating connection state, but when not explicitly statet, there are gaps, such as during initial setup.

Ensuring a Connection ID all the way in public headers - either a single (client selected), or a replaced (client->server->client replaced), makes it possible to find connection state at end-points before decryption without relying on port associations. Obviously this will not work with short headers that exclude the connection id.

comments.author: martinthomson

comments.body:
On permanency: I'm fine with changing ID as long as the new ID can be passed encrypted in a packet identified using the old ID, or with the old ID publicly in a packet with a new ID.

On client server behavior - there are symmetric use cases where client / server as a concept makes little sense other than who runs the handshake. Interfaces (IP address) may also be hard to predict in certain environments, or it may be beneficial to fire on all available interfaces - for example given multiple network cards. Overlay mesh networks can route traffic on random identifiers or content based hashing. The fixed IP nature is far from a given in complex IoT mesh networks with no central routing capabilities. I'm not saying QUIC should automatically support this, but if all it takes is adding an ID to a handshake, then it is worth a thought.

comments.author: martinthomson
janaiyengar
comments.body:
The server has no way of ensuring that the Client Cleartext packet contains the server's chosen connection ID. A bold client *could* start a connection with a random (or if nefarious, a targeted) connection ID with a Client Cleartext packet, defeating one of the purposes of server-chosen connection IDs.

I'll argue for two things to change. (i) I think we should make both the changes you propose -- that a Client Initial packet be sent right after both Version Negotiation and Stateless Retry packets. (ii) 0-RTT packets MUST contain the same connection ID as in the client's most recent handshake packet to make it possible for load balancers to work with them. 

With these changes, a server treats all Client Initial packets similarly, in that it responds to them with a new server-chosen connection ID. Load balancers treat all Client Initial, Client Cleartext, and 0-RTT packets as containing a client-chosen connection ID, and other packets as containing server-chosen connection IDs.

One of the purposes of this change is to enable a server to direct a client towards a particular server via the connection ID in a Version Negotiation or a Stateless Retry packet. A server can still do that by generating a connection ID that it knows will hash to the right server. Basically, load balancers will use two functions for hashing connection ID -- C() to hash client-chosen connection IDs and S() for server-chosen ones. On a VN or SR packet, the server needs to generate and send a connection ID so that C(connection ID) sends the retrying client to the desired server. This allows a server to redirect while also allowing the server infrastructure to not trust that a client is doing the right thing.

## Stateless Retries {#stateless-retry}

A server can process an initial cryptographic handshake messages from a client without committing any state.  This allows a server to perform address validation ({{address-validation}}, or to defer connection establishment costs.

A server that generates a response to an initial packet without retaining connection state MUST use the Server Stateless Retry packet ({{packet-server-stateless}}). A server MUST NOT send multiple Server Stateless Retry packets in response to a client handshake packet.  Thus, any cryptographic handshake message that is sent MUST fit within a single packet.

If you want this to be in TLS, then we end up with a much tighter coupling than you would like.  (Me, I don't care, I don't see any point in disentangling these two parts, but we did have consensus to separate them.)

@janaiyengar, is what you want here:

"The TLS-QUIC API must expose a function QUIC-Packet-Gap(sequence) -> Gap which returns a 32-bit integer indicating the packet gap for a given sequence number"?
Hm -- good point martinthomson@ -- I hadn't thought about that. Is it adequate to do some sort of simple hash here then?

@ekr's design is best practice here.  I would not be that happy about a design that was less robust than this.  HKDF has a bunch of features that we might not need, but the alternatives would require considerably more analysis before we could be sure that they are OK.
Why wouldn't a simple keyed-hash be adequate? Of course, organization of text shouldn't determine our design; do you have a suggestion for organizing the text if HKDF is to be used?
If we move packet protection to the transport, as planned, then we'll need HKDF, so there's no real issue with taking this change as it is.

"keyed hash" isn't really a well-formed cryptographic construct. What you want here is a PRF, and these days that typically means using HMAC (which is what HKDF is under the covers). So, if you really prefer, we could inline the HMAC expansion of HKDF-Expand-Label, but I'm not really seeing what the benefit of that is in this instance, given that, as Martin says, if we move packet protection into this document, we'll need HKDF anyway.

Jana, it might help me if it were a bit clearer about what you were optimizing for here. Any implementation of this document is going to need HKDF (and even if you were to swap out TLS, it's quite likely you would end up using HKDF), so it's not really implementation complexity, so is it just that you don't like having a citation to some construct exposed by TLS? If so, that seems like something we can deal with much later in the document cycle if we still feel that way.
Yeah, both of your responses make sense. Thanks for helping me understand.

comments.author: MikeBishop
comments.body:
It took me a couple times through the issue and the PR to figure out the actual attack here, and I don't think the current text actually captures it.  What finally clicked for me was that, although the version number is explicitly given in the packet, an on-path attacker who tried to force a version negotiation mismatch could also undetectably modify the contents of the version field in the packet header.  (Because the integrity protection / encryption on the packets at this point is trivially recalculated by an attacker.)  It's the contents of the handshake that can't be modified without detection, but we have to guard against getting just the right set of transport parameters in the future that looks like the version confirmation one would expect from the current version.

So what we're actually saying is that, if the version validation fields are in a different location in a different version of QUIC, they MUST be unmistakably different from a valid confirmation of having selected the current version or any future version that uses this handshake and transport settings format.

comments.body: Thank you Mike for elegantly summarizing my previous confusion.

I misunderstood what this text was attempting to accomplish, I was thinking of transport parameters as connection ID/packet number/etc.

That being said, I'm not clear on why the transport parameter format can't be tied to QUIC version.  Can you explain more about how this attack works?
If a QUIC version is defined that does not rely on TLS, how would it define transport parameters?

@ianswett, let's say that we don't change the format of the transport parameters for version 1.  We also have a server that supports version 1 and some hypothetical version 4.

With the current format, a server that selects version 1 will send advertise transport parameters starting with the bytes 0x0008, 0x00000004, 0x00000001 (a length, followed by version 4 and version 1).  After that, it will have some lengths and TLVs for parameters.

However, if version 4 decides to change the transport parameters, then the client that is subject to spoofing of a version negotiation packet might find that they interpret transport parameters differently.  If version 4 is sufficiently similar to version 1 in other ways, you could even end up in a situation where the client and server disagree on what version they are speaking.

For instance, the above value could be interpreted as being valid against a different schema.

I believe I now understand what you're saying.  I keep thinking the entire packet is protected, but it's not.

pulls.title: Force the server and client to remember transport parameters for 0-RTT
pulls.author: martinthomson
pulls.body:
This includes Victor's recommendation to avoid the client violating server
constraints on operation.  This means that the server that accepts 0-RTT is
required to provide new transport parameters that are compatible with its
previously advertised value, or reject 0-RTT.

I made this easier on servers, by allowing them to advertise different
transport parameters that only apply to 0-RTT.  They include these values in
the TLS NewSessionTicket message, alongside the ticket that is used to resume.

comments.body: Why is this required, actually? It seems like you could say "this is what I want next time" without fear.

There's no problem with a server that allows 100KB after 1 RTT advertising 10KB initial for next time.  The problem is if the client has *remembered* 25KB for the 0-RTT flight, and the server wants to turn it down to 10KB after 1 RTT.  The goal is to say turning numbers down on a given connection is never allowed, only up.
I got that, but my question is: why?

The problem is that the client might have already violated that limit.  It could send 25KB of 0-RTT data, only to learn that the limit on the data it can send is 10KB.

This rule prevents the server from creating a situation where a limit has been violated.

reviews.author: janaiyengar
reviews.body: LGTM

comments.body: If it is not a security issue, why force the client to ensure the server complies with the overhead this involves rather than just require that server to comply and have the connection eventually fail if the server doesn't. There are endless other ways a server might fail to comply that will only eventually result in failure.

Let's take the maximum stream number as an example.  

We have two choices: allow the server to set any value, or force the server to provide a value that is >= the value is knows that the client might use.

Given that the client might have used up to the previously-agreed limit, if we allow a smaller limit in the handshake, that creates an unusual condition on the server.  It sets a limit that it can't enforce uniformly.  It has to use two limits when deciding whether the client is misbehaving.  That's a bunch of special code.

In this design, we chose the simpler option.  The only cost is that if the server wants to both *accept* 0-RTT and reduce limits, then it can't.  That little bit of logic is the only place where we have special code.  It can still do things like reset streams and withhold increases to any limit in order to manage its costs.

comments.body:
Ouch, that's kinda ugly.  You are saying that if you include a PING, plus a 999 octet ACK, then you have 1000 octets in flight, but drop the ping and you have 0.  I wonder what impact that has on traffic analysis.

I understand that TCP doesn't do this, but is there any reason why we need to copy that?  A packet that is sent is still creating congestion.

In any case, I think that this needs to be clearer.  This counts the entire QUIC packet, including the header and any overhead added by packet protection or integrity.  QUIC packets that only contain ACK frames are not counted.

What - if any - impact does PADDING have on this?

We don't need to copy what TCP does, but I thought it makes sense to document a reasonable option, and make that similar to TCP.  

I'll also note there's not much evidence we have to agree on the same bytes_in_flight accounting across implementations.  The most important thing is internal consistency.

The reason acks shouldn't count towards bytes in flight is one never wants to delay an ack due to lack of congestion window.  We could say they count, but you send them immediately anyway, but I think it's equally ugly.

Good point on PADDING, because they are not retransmittable, but we do count them towards bytes in flight in the GQUIC implementation, and I tend to think they should be counted.

So I'd say we have three options I can think of: 
1) Land an updated version of this in order to document a TCP like approach and discuss this further at the interim.
2) Do nothing, and hope we get to this at the interim.
3) Do nothing, because we're happy letting implementations do what they want, just like TCP implementations do.
Isn't this basically the same question as the question which packets should be congestion controlled? All bytes that are congestion controlled should be counted for bytes_in_flight, no?

That is most of it, though if we wanted to include ack-only packets, it would be important to allow those to be sent immediately, even if congestion control indicated no data should be sent.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body:
More generally, I believe an earlier draft had a concept of the oldest known package number which got replaced by ACK'ing acks periodically.

I think it would be good if the protocol maintains a concept of what is the oldest packet number still of interest to the sender such that the receiver can promptly drop state older than this value for dupe rejection etc., and also such that received acks pertaining packets older than this value can promptly be dropped (or at least the older part of the ACK frame).

Any packet number newer than this lower bound could then be required to be remembered and invalid acks SHOULD/MUST be rejected.

An adversarial sender could fail to update the lower bound forcing more state at receiver. The current behavior is safe in the sense that there is no lower bound other than heuristics anyway, but if a lower bound was placed, this issue must be considered.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body:
> if you get a duplicated ack from long ago, how do you know if it is (dup) acking a packet you sent or not? (assuming you skipped some numbers non deterministically)

The sender maintains an oldest relevant packet number regardless of whether it is transmitted or not (it currently isn't). If the ack refers to an older packet it is ignored - even if it could be by malicious intent, it cannot really do any harm anymore. If the ack refers to a more recent packet number, it could be used to confuse the bandwidth estimation algorithm and causing the sender to DoS the receiver, which harms the ack sender, but also any other connection to the server.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body:
> I was thinking that when you advance the ACK lower bound you would call getting an ACK for a packet below that bound would be an error. 

I believe @ianswett mentioned that GQUIC through live testing found it better to acknowledge latest packets over earliest acknowledge packets at the possible cost of retransmission. That is, when you have to make a choice due to ACK frame size constraints. But, it is not clear exactly how to handle ACKS that do not cover the full range of received packets, as discussed in  #423
The sender also cannot trust the ACK

Rant: I am personally not too happy with the current ACK concept that seems open to many interpretations and risk holding a lot of excessive state both for dupe detection and retransmission of ACK frames. I would much rather have a concept such as STOP_WAITING, or a similar simple range of fully handled packet number ranges without needing the details of which ACK frames have been sent or in need of transmission. Other retransmissions can be stored by reference to external data (mmap etc.).

But attack vectors must be also be considered:

> a reasonable receiver would not send ACks in such a delayed manner which could be assumed.

A major part of the excercise is dealing with unreasonable receivers.  Also, for low powered devices or for avoiding unnecessary network activity that triggers context switches every time a packet is received, slowing down busy systems, ACKs could quite well be rather delayed. Only, this generates more state that must be kept. As long as this state are only packet ranges acked or not, this is not a big problem.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
Great discussion everyone.  I don't think that I can recognize this as a bike shed given the many layers of paint it now sits under.

We discussed this at the interim and concluded that we would remove the ability to have gaps (see https://github.com/quicwg/base-drafts/issues/161#issuecomment-307387364), but this uncertainty still exists to some extent due to the NEW_CONNECTION_ID frame and the use of packet number skipping in that context.  This will remove one source of gaps in the packet number sequence and make detecting ACKs for unsent packets easier, but not guaranteed.

reviews.author: ianswett
reviews.body: Agreed this needs to be fixed.

comments.body: It could also say "The sender MUST close the connection if a packet it knows is unsent is acknowledged."  Which keeps the must, but does not require unlimited state.
@mcmanus, @siyengar, does Ian's suggestion work better?
"it knows" isn't really verifiable in any normative sense - it pretty much means SHOULD. prefer SHOULD.

Generally I worry with a SHOULD no-one will end up implementing it because people will realize that it requires maintaining a lot of state. I like the spirit of Ian's wording but it's super confusing. SHOULD seems like the right thing here. I think if we acknowledge why it is a SHOULD it might convince more people to implement it along with a suggestion of how to implement it. 

For example a sender could implement this by keeping track of all the packets sent and by advancing a smallest ackable packet periodically.

The wording could also be "SHOULD close a connection when receiving an ACK for a packet that has not been sent unless the packet is older that oldest retransmittable packet in which case the ackowledgement of that packet should be ignored."

But the retransmission queue may be sparse -- you don't necessarily know whether a packet no longer there was never sent or was simply already acknowledged.

SHOULD is supposed to have an explanation of why you might not.  You SHOULD do this if you detect it, but you're not required to maintain enough state to detect it 100% of the time.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body:
> I think that we need to discuss expectations about peer-to-peer operation at some point. I see a lot of requests coming in that don't at all fit with my experience of how peer-to-peer works.

I suppose you consider peer-to-peer like Skype where the client traverses NAT to a cloud infrastructure out to another client.

Peer-to-peer can also mean server to server in a distributed system, at multiple levels: same data center, different data centers, different IP address ranges etc. but common for these are that it is random who initiates the connection and both might attempt to do so at the same time. Over time two entities may switch between being client and server.

Such a setup may also involve routing messages across multiple entities using algorithms such as Kademlia and Chord. This opens up some concerns regarding end-to-end flow control over a routed  overlay network while the link level connection would be QUIC. For example, streams might be forwarded using QUICs stream flow control mechanism, and some eggs might have to be broken to achieve the end result (i.e. not fully adhering to spec).

Another similar scenerio is mesh networks for sensor networks, but there are industry adhoc standards emerging for such networks I believe. Here some nodes may be promoted to being internal routing nodes and others edge nodes, though who gets chosen for what can be fairly arbitrary and changing over time.

comments.author: mikkelfj

If I understand the text correctly, and I am not sure that I do, I don't think this approach is workable due to path migration and Connection ID migration and due to the fact that connection ids are generally expected to be present in short headers, and due to the lack of symmetry. All issues mentioned in above comments.

The server essentially has no way to identify the original of the connection without requesting additional information.

A symmetric reset that allows both end points to reset the connection would require some sort of challenge where the server says - whoever this connection is from it makes no sense - please send credentials to allow me to terminate this connection. The same would be true for the client.

This can probably be based on x25519 public key exchange, but it requires some carefull consideration.

I think a simpler is to have the peer tear down the connection if the server does not reply to ping request where the ping is specified to require an immediate pong frame unless one has been sent recently. If the a peer receives garbage with a valid header it should consider issuing a ping request unless it has done so recently.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body:
> The connection ID is visible on packets.

The Connection ID is negotiable via transport parameters and may be absent.

> @mikkelfj, you will have to be a LOT clearer about your concerns here.

I'm sorry - I thought I had a good idea, but it was flawed. I will try explain my concerns in more details here - but I still think updating the token at NEW_CONNECTION_ID is better, unless there are race conditions.

In the following I sometimes refer to a server, where it might as well be a client, for the sake of simplicity.

Concern 0:
A reset must (EDIT: must NOT) be identifiable as such from outside observers, with high probability - but why is this a concern? This concern is derived from the current design and needs an argument. If the token is padded with random data for this reason, the length should either be random, or have same length as other typical packets via padded encryption used to hide content length.

Concern 1:
A reset must work in either direction (symmetri) so both parties can terminate lost state.

Concern 2:
A reset token in one direction must be specific to a single connection with high probablity - otherwise other connections can learn the the token by connecting and forcing a reset, or by having observing powers on path.

Concern 3:
A reset token cannot rely on persistent state or pre-shared keys between two end-points. It could, but it would limit deployment scenarios.

Concern 4:
A reset token may not accidentally expose path migrations by sending the same token on different paths, even if that connection is about to end.

Concern 5:
Due to lack of state (concern 3), a reset token must be generated from a single semi-static server key and information observable from received packets and produce a connection (concern 2) and path specific (concern 4) .

Concern 6:
Because a static server keys may need to be updated, we potentially may have to send two resets, one for each static key during roll-over.

Concern 7:
A public reset should not result in a flood of resets, so an endpoint should limit the frequency of resets on a given path.

Concern 8:
An attacker could force many resets to attack a public reset keys integrity - e.g. AES-GCM breaks after so many iterations, but HMAC_SHA does not. Concern 7 reduces this ability of such attacks. 

Concern 9:
Only the endpoint sending a packet resulting in a reset being sent back must be able to accept the reset, with high propability, even if the token appears encrypted to outsiders, otherwise there is risk of resetting the wrong connection in a complex server environment, and there might be attack vectors on this as well.

Concern 10:
An endpoint cannot assume the observable state (OS) (concern 5) is known to the peer, in other words it cannot be assumed to be shared observable state (SOS). This affects how tokens can be generated. For example, the UDP IP address and port may be different from what the peer knows about itself. Also, the Connection ID is not guaranteed present in packets in the current QUIC draft. To work around this issue, a nonce can be generated and signed, and sent to the peer. This assumes the peers connection state is able to receive validate the signature, and that no other connection endpoints have this ability (concern 9). However, attempting to design a secure token hash algorithms that works under this assumption without violating other concerns is tricky.

End of concerns

This leads to some possible ways to generate resets:

1) A complete random is generated for each conection and path (aka each Connection ID). The token is updated during change of path. This ensures privacy, unique endpoint acceptance etc. This is the current proposal and fullfills all concerns, assuming the the token is created carefully. The current approach does not handle static server key update (roll-over), and does not discuss limiting flow rates, nor padded random length (concern 0), but it largely is compatible with the above concerns.

2) the reset is only advisory and not particularly unique - receving a reset results in verifying the connection is live via a PING that requieres an immediate PONG (acks are too slow). This needs to be rate limited. The reset need not be very secret but should avoid outsiders from easily genering a lot of valid resets.

3) IFF we assume the observable state OS is also shareable (SOS), i.e. the Connection ID is alway visible, we cannot assume SOS does not change on path migration. In fact, if it was, it would by definition violate privacy of path migration. Now lets see how we can generate the token with SOS available (this is not necessarily different from current proposal):

The Static Server Key (SSK) and SOS is used to generate a connection specific reset token signing key (RTSK) which is exhanged during handshake. RTSK = HMAC_SHA256(SSK, SOS). When a reset is sent, a reset nonce RN is generated for each new reset. The reset token (RT) is computed as RT = HMAC-SHA256(RTSK, RN | RT). A random padding sequence (RPS) is also generated unless the RN is large enough to fill that role. The reset header is RH and not detailed here. The reset message is sent as <RH, RN, RT, RPS>. The receiver detects RH and integrity failure and proceeds by retrieving the stored RTSK and computes RTcheck = HMAC-SHA256(RTSK, RN | RT). if RTcheck == RT then the reset is accepted.

Following a crash, a retrieves SSK and computes RTSK = HMAC_SHA256(SSK, SOS) for each path and sends rate limited resets.

If SOS is not not SOS, but only OS (observable state), then the reset can proceed because the peer has stored the RTSK. Therefore, it is not necessary to require that SOS is not OS. However this did not solve the problem of path migration. We saw that we could not have OS or SOS being unchanged after migration for privacy reasons, so path migration MUST issue a new RTSK.

IFF we have migration invariant shared observable state (MISOS) we did not have to exchange information at path migration because RTSK = HMAC_SHA256(SSK, MISOS). When the server crashes it recomputes RTSK and sends the reset. Again, we see that the state need not be shared, so MIOS would also work. But it violates privacy.

We can now define OS to be sufficient to generate tokens. We could define it to be the peers 3-tuple depending on network layer with UDP being default. But it would not solve the issue of having to migrate RTSK during path migration. If we could rely on Connection ID being visible, we could use it as OS, be we cannot (as I understand it).

Therefore, it appears that the might as well send an explicit reset token instead of RTSK over the wire, while keeping the RTSK server side. (Where client has a similar setup the other direction). However, this will violate keeping the reset token unique per reset, but it will still be unique per path. If a reset is only sent once per path, this may be acceptable, otherwise the RTSK needs to be shared instead, per path.

Solution 2) is also an option.

pulls.title: Unidirectional Streams
pulls.author: martinthomson
pulls.body:
## Transport Changes

Streams are unidirectional.  Each has three states: idle, open, and closed.  I separated the transitions for sending and receiving because that turned out to be easier to explain.  The reordering thing makes them different in subtle ways.

That's all.  The changes in transport are relatively small and they simplify streams a lot.  That it also makes the transport more generic is a nice bonus.

## HTTP Changes

This is where the bulk of the changes are.

### Stream Correlation

Previously request and response were implicitly correlated, as was the data correlated with the request or response headers.  With this change, that correlation each stream has a header that explicitly correlates these.

There are 5 types of stream: connection control, request, response, data, and push.  The first two have a simple header that has a type.  The next two reference another stream in their header, which ties request to response and data to request or response.  Push streams each reference a PUSH_PROMISE using a newly minted push ID (I decided that was cleaner than what I proposed at the interim).

I chose backward references rather than forward references for two reasons.  First, request and response correlation can't use forward references because that would mean the client would be exerting (uncoordinated) control over server streams.  Second, that gives the server the most flexibility in terms of how it answers requests (see #281).  The cost of using backward references is that endpoints have to check that the backward references aren't bad, either referencing the wrong type of stream, or with multiple references to the same stream.

The presence or absence of a message body is signaled after the initial header block using a HAS_BODY frame.  This empty frame indicates that another stream will include the body of the message - or a promise for a body.  I would like to eliminate this stream split.  See #245 and #557 for more details on that, though we need to fix #176 first, which brings us back to QPACK/QCRAM again.

### Prioritization

This changes prioritization so that it identifies requests.  I only made the minimal changes here, which means that #441 doesn't get fixed at the same time, I've left that for later (see below).

### Cancelling Pushes

Because server push doesn't create streams with PUSH_PROMISE, I had to create a way to cancel them between the time that the PUSH_PROMISE is sent and when the push stream is created.  That's called RST_PUSH.

Update: the latest version changes RST_PUSH to CANCEL_REQUEST which allows a client to cancel both requests and server pushes.

## Things That Need Improvement

I haven't based this on #171.  I think that functionality is good, but the last time I looked at the PR I didn't like some of the changes Mike made there.  (That's a taste thing.)  This really assumes that we accept something very much like #171.

This really needs QPACK/QCRAM.  Right now, it is impossible to cancel some types of request using RST_STREAM because not all messages will have a body (#176 again).  On balance, given that bodies are what you really want to kill, it's not disastrous, but it's a problem nonetheless.  I think that we all agree that this is something that we need to fix, but we haven't reached the point where we agree on the details of the fix.

## Things That Want Improvement

This also really wants headers and data on the same stream .  It doesn't exactly need that, but merging the streams would make things a lot easy, both conceptually and structurally.

I chose the simplest possible encoding for all of the fields that I touched.  That means that stream IDs are all 32 bits in size and the HAS_BODY frame takes an entire 9 octets.  For things that are that common, there are many ways in which byte efficiency could be improved.

The push ID changes suggest a fix for #441.  Use of an as-yet-not-created ID as a node in the priority tree would allow for prioritization to use "empty" nodes.  Needs more thought.

# Fixes

Closes #515, #240, #281, #175.

(MikeBishop:  Edited to remove occurrences of "fix <issue num>" that were saying this PR doesn't fix that issue.  GitHub was getting confused.)

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body:
I can't speak for HTTP/2 that I have not studied in detail, but I believe this is a very significant improvement for the transport layer.

As mentioned above, DISINTEREST (#171) or some other mechanism for receiver to cancel is needed, and because it can cause some race conditions on stream state, I think it would be good to consider in more detail before settling on a unidirectional solution.

I am concerned about the STREAM_BLOCKED being able to force the receivers stream in open state if it is above the stream limit, or did I miss something. I know it is also there to hint at a need for more streams, but I think that should be an application level issue. Regardless - if naively implemented, a transmitter could force a lot of undesired resource usage at receiver by allocating stream state. I suggest that any stream related transmission above MAX_STREAM_LIMIT is a fatal error.

As to MAX_STREAM_LIMIT - this was a great improvement to avoid race conditions in the bi-directional design, and I do (EDIT: I do NOT) immediately suggest removing it. However, I think it might be worthwhile to consider alternatives for a better insight into the problem. For example: assume that we do not require incremental stream identifiers: there is no internal gain in incremental order such as keeping a simple stream table because old streams can randomly linger (e.g. stream 0), so open streams must be tracked via a map anyway. With a unidirectional design there is no ambigouty of the senders view of how many streams are at most open at the receiving end. It is the difference between received ACKS for RST_STREAM and FIN STREAMS and streams placed in senders open state.

Unless there is a flaw in the above argument, this suggests that streams can be opened with arbitrary identifiers. If we permit that, applications could use their own identifiers. However, it becomes intractable to make sure that a stream identifier is not being reused. Thus, the next question is: is it a problem to reuse stream identifiers once they have been closed? A sender cannot start reusing the stream before receiving an ACK for RST_STREAM or FIN STREAM of the old version of the stream and in this case the receiver cannot have many doubts about a new stream arriving being new. However, there may still be spurious retransmissions. This can be managed by looking at packet numbers but requires to remember the packet number of a closed stream, which is complicated.

Thus, I believe the MAX_STREAM_LIMIT is still the simplest approach.

pulls.title: Stream correlation in Transport
pulls.author: MikeBishop
pulls.body:
This is an augmentation of @martinthomson's PR to add stream correlation, as promised.

# Major changes

Leveraging @igorlord's insight that OO=00 only occurs on the first STREAM frame of a stream, I used that as the trigger for a Stream Properties byte.  Two bits of that byte describe the directionality of the stream:

- Unidirectional (no response expected)
- Initial bidirectional (one response expected)
- Initial multi-response (one or more responses expected; needs a better name)
- Response

If the type is Response, there's an Associated Stream ID field, length given by two more bits following the same pattern as the SS bits in the STREAM frame ID.

# Personal Opinion

On the plus side, these stream types seem to cover the abstractions I can envision for most applications.  You can unilaterally send something (unidirectional), do request/response (bidirectional), or pub/sub (single subscription stream, series of update streams).

I don't care for the fact that I still need the stream type header in HTTP after putting this in the transport.  That will be ameliorated if we go back to one stream per request, since all unidirectional streams will be push streams.  (As a side-note, I considered using the multiple-response option in the HTTP mapping, but then I need a stream header again to indicate which is the response and which the pushes.)

I particularly don't like that you now have to look at the frame type header to find out whether a field exists which tells you the length of something else in the header.  I'd like to simplify that.  I went with this model over a CREATE_STREAM frame because of @mikkelfj's use-case of very small messages -- this adds only one byte to the first frame on a stream in one direction and 2-5 bytes to the first frame of response streams.  A separate frame type would be somewhat larger, but could be cleaner in that respect.

pulls.title: Push ID
pulls.author: martinthomson
pulls.body:
As requested, I split this out of the unidirectional PR (#643).

There is a change here, that needs to be highlighted.  @kazuho points out that without inter-stream ordering guarantees, requests might be triggered on multiple streams.  The server then has an awkward choice: either push multiple times, or risk the client triggering requests when streams arrive out of order.  This contains a fix for that bug.

The fix is to allow the same push ID to be used in multiple PUSH_PROMISE frames.  Then, fulfillment happens at most once.

I think that this is a neat fix, but it creates two more problems:

1. How does a client know when the server will stop referencing a push ID in PUSH_PROMISE?  With reordering, the pushed response might arrive and be consumed before a PUSH_PROMISE that references it.  I think that it might be possible to add a counter to the push stream header that says how many times the server promised this response.  The problem with that is that if a stream that carries the PUSH_PROMISE is reset, then that counter will be too high.  I've decided to just explain the issue and add some weasel wording rather than provide a direct fix.

2. What if the server provides different headers for the same Push ID?  I've chosen to fix this by simply forbidding variations in the content of the header block.  I considered only allowing the headers to appear once, but then you have to deal with that stream being reset.  Repetition should be rare enough, and header compression might be able to help with the extra bytes.

I think that those problems are both less serious than the bug this fixes.  Besides, the first is really only an generalized form of a problem we have already: the stream carrying a PUSH_PROMISE can be reset.  What currently happens is that the server more or less has to send a push stream anyway, even though it can't know whether the client got the PUSH_PROMISE.  With this, a server can use CANCEL_REQUEST.

Closes #702, #281.

pulls.title: Limit pushes using MAX_PUSH_ID
pulls.author: martinthomson
pulls.body:
This repurposes SETTINGS_ENABLE_PUSH as the initial limit.

A client can use this to limit the number of outstanding pushes.  I've included
advice on increasing the limit, not as the pushes are first used, but as the
pushes are completed (or cancelled).

There wasn't a rule for handling a truncated push stream header, so I added
that as well.  The HTTP_DUPLICATE_PUSH error was reclaimed for signaling all
three types of error with a push stream header: truncation, duplicate Push ID,
and exceeding MAX_PUSH_ID.

Closes #709.

pulls.author: martinthomson

comments.body: So the endpoint needs to ignore the entire ack frame if any packets acknowledged were protected?

I'd like to make this stronger if possible.  How about "only before they have received an 'ACK' frame in a 1-RTT protected packet.  Once they have received an ack frame in a 1-RTT protected packet, all ack frames with less protection MUST be ignored."

I'm not sure how this note is helpful.  The server has to send all acks either unprotected or in 1RTT packets, correct?  If so, it seems simpler to say "0-RTT data can be acknowledged by the server as it is received, but it must be send with 1-RTT protection."?

I'm applying principles we agreed: if it looks like trash, throw it out.  This ensures that a disruptive presence has to guess everything correctly in order for their disruption to be successful.  I'd say throw out the entire packet, but that might not be possible (other stuff might have been processed, and we don't want to ask implementations to rewind their TLS state machine, for instance).

The point here is to highlight a problem with this requirement, not to restate the requirement to protect ACK frames.  The problem is that the server handshake might not be complete from the perspective of the client.  That leads to the client not having 1-RTT keys.  Which then leads to the client being unable to read those ACK frames.
I think that we could be even stronger.  See revision.

pulls.title: Add bidirectional streams on top of unidirectional
pulls.author: martinthomson

This is based on the PR in #643.  It adds the concept of "related streams", which allows for pairing of streams.  It recommends against using the concept for anything else, but notes that any semantics are the responsibility of the application protocol.  This modifies the HTTP draft to prohibit use of this capability - that draft has a superior mechanism for request-response association.

I've kept this separate from #643 so that it can be assessed independently.

So overall, to reduce confusion, I would say the ID MUST only be be sent in the first frame if at all present.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
If an endpoint receives an ACK for a CONNECTION_CLOSE, it still needs to handle more packets (it remains in its draining period) because packets that were sent before the ACK might still be in transit.  Thus, the shortcut isn't really that useful here.  Obviously the endpoint that acknowledges the CONNECTION_CLOSE won't send any more packets, but if its own packets are still in flight, then it might get a few more CONNECTION_CLOSE frames (as a result of packets sent before it acknowledged the CONNECTION_CLOSE). 

The only real trimming we might do is to have the endpoint that sends the CONNECTION_CLOSE stop sending more CONNECTION_CLOSE frames in response to receiving more packets.

can be used for both connection and stream errors and are under the control of
the application protocol.  Transport error codes are QUIC-controlled, but can
only terminate the connection.

tweaks.  I think that the error code space could be narrowed to 16 bits after
this, if only to keep things sane.

Closes #485, #184.

We never really said how to handle incoming packets.  This adds a section on
that.  This was originally motivated by #570, where the rules for what to
generate a Version Negotiation packet for were a little unclear.

Now though, this is a far more comprehensive description of what to do with
a packet that is received.

For #570, I've chosen to limit packet size.  If the packet is too small, then
this requires the server to drop the packet.  In response to the potential for
a future version of QUIC to define a smaller initial packet (@mikkelfj raised
this point), I've included advice on what might be done to avoid having packets
discarded.

Closes #570, #523, #568.

pulls.title: Change design and and FIN to flow control
pulls.author: siyengar
pulls.body:
This PR has 1 editorial change and 2 design changes to flow control:

* [editorial] Clarifies the language around stream and connection flow control and makes it match the flow control section. 

* [design] Defines flow control in terms of offsets instead of max data. This means something different, because previously, maxData = 10 indicated that you could only send offset till 9, however with the change, sending maxOffset = 10 means that you can send offset until 10, i.e. 11 bytes. We could alternatively change the language of maxOffset to be MUST be LESS than instead of MUST NOT EXCEED to match maximumData.

* [design]  Makes FIN bit to be flow controllable. This would reduce one edge case where a packet scheduler does not have to do a special check for whether it only needs to send a FIN when it checks for flow control. This has the advantage of being able to define flow control on a stream in terms of offsets rather than max data.

pulls.title: Address validation for connection migration
pulls.author: martinthomson
pulls.body:
This has been much-discussed, and it's a relatively isolated change, so I did it.

This modifies PING to have an optional payload and adds a PONG frame to echo
the PING.  An empty PING generates an ACK; a PING with a payload demands a
PONG.

Generating an unguessable PING is the basis of mid-connection address
validation.  If the PING is sent on the new path, and the PONG comes back, then
the remote address is probably OK to use.

I've taken the discussion in the issue into consideration here.  There's a lot
of potential nuance to capture in terms of how an endpoint might reduce and
restore send rates, but I've done what I can to thread the gap between allowing
unbounded sending along new and untested paths and allowing connections to get
back to doing business.

It's annoying that this makes PING and PONG so disparate.  I think that we have
a re-ordering of frames in our near future to correct minor infidelities like
this.  I didn't want to do that here and pollute this PR though.

Closes #161.

Would PING + ACK be sufficient? (I'm probably not thinking it through clearly) If not, can you elaborate what PING + PONG mitigates that PING + ACK does not? Oh, I guess "it is also possible that the peer is spoofing its source address in order to cause the endpoint to send excessive amounts of data to an unwilling host." Ugh.

But I agree, PING with payload feels a bit weird.

comments.body:
As Mike says, PING + ACK isn't sufficient.  The attack this defends against is where the attacker uses their real address to make a connection and open the congestion window, then they spoof a "migration" and cause the data that the other side is sending to be sent to a victim.  In that case, the attacker can usually guess what packet to ACK and just pretend to receive the PING.

I don't know how PING with payload is weird.  [h2 does it](http://httpwg.org/specs/rfc7540.html#PING).  And [so does ICMP](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc792#page-14) - though it's called "Echo" and "Echo Reply" there (which is so easy to forget).

We don't have either of those mechanisms right now, and the only signal we have is receipt of packets.  Unless we add the better design, this design at least works, even if it is suboptimal.  It's easy enough to back out or qualify a MUST or two once we have that better design complete.

pulls.title: Avoid attack on address validation during connection migration
pulls.author: martinthomson
pulls.body:
The attack here is that an attacker might duplicate a legitimate packet and
send that packet from an invalid address such that it arrives before the real
copy.  That causes the recipient to think that there was a connection
migration.  They will attempt to validate that address and this will fail.  The
connection is then closed.

The fix is to cause a migration back to the original, legitimate address.  For
this to work, you need two things:

1. when a migration happens, abandon any validation on the old address on the
   expectation that it will fail

2. when a migration happens, make sure that you try to trigger packets from the
   old address first

For the second point, I decided to mandate address validation, rather than an
ordinary PING.  The reason being that you have to retransmit the packet on that
path and I doubt that implementations will want to have two sets of special
machinery for transmitting - and retransmitting - frames on a specific path.
Maybe this is too much of a constraint on implementations, so I'd like to hear
from people about whether they would prefer a more generic requirement (send
any packet that demands acknowledgment would work, it doesn't even have to be
the same packet every time, though the usual situation will be that the packet
will be lost, so you probably don't want to send anything important).

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
I don't quite know how to use connection IDs in the current protocol.  Maybe if we had asymmetric connection IDs.  I think that we might end up there, but it's challenging for a range of reasons.  Let's say that it's a client that migrates, which seems to be the common case.  The client needs to provision the server with enough NEW_CONNECTION_ID frames that the server won't run out if the client ever inadvertently moves.

Maybe we can instead insist that the PONG be sent on the path on which the PING was received and that the PING contains a source address validation token with the same sort of protections we have on the one used in the handshake.  That's not simpler, but it should work.  It does precludes the use of asymmetric addressing, though I suspect that was something we didn't have anyway.

comments.author: huitema
comments.body:
You want the mechanism to protect the receiver against a malicious peer, and Ping/Pong does that. But you also want a protection against man on the side playing replay and race games, and that is much harder.

It may well be that the real answer is multipath. Accept that the peers are managing several parallel paths. Manage separate sequence number space and loss detection for each path -- but of course allow frames to be transmitted or retransmitted on any of the paths, as the sender sees fit. Validate any path before using it -- that will take care of the malicious senders. Do not close an old path implicitly if a new one is found -- that should eliminate the man on the side games.

But of course there is a catch. Doing that requires having explicit path information in ACK frames and maybe PING frames, plus managing sequence number, retransmit queue and sack dashboard for each path. Congestion control, too. Plus maybe a new type of frame for explicitly closing a path.

Costly, but then piling hacks to make the simpler solution work may not be worth it.

pulls.title: close connection when receiving unprotected ACKs for protected packets
pulls.author: marten-seemann
pulls.body:
The TLS draft says in https://quicwg.github.io/base-drafts/draft-ietf-quic-tls.html#rfc.section.9.1.2:

> Endpoints MUST NOT use an ACK frame in an unprotected packet to acknowledge packets that were protected by 0-RTT or 1-RTT keys. An endpoint MUST treat receipt of an ACK frame in an unprotected packet that claims to acknowledge protected packets as a connection error of type OPTIMISTIC_ACK.


The Loss Recovery draft currently says that unprotected packets containing ACKs for protected packets have to be ignored. This PR updates the Loss Recovery draft and makes it consistent with the TLS draft.

pulls.title: Rename and consolidate packet types
pulls.author: martinthomson
pulls.body:
The two cleartext types are no longer needed to distinguish between client and
server.  Server packets are protected with a different key to that used for
client packets, so a server will be unable to process a packet from another
server as though it were a client packet (not that this was possible anyway
given that we have a different type for the initial packet).

Consequently, I have renamed packets to use shorter names and to better fit
their roles:

* Client Initial -> Initial
* Server Stateless Retry -> Retry (also avoids confusion with Stateless Reset)
* Server Cleartext -> Handshake
* Client Cleartext -> Handshake

I've rephrased the text in the TLS spec to match.

The only functional change here is to consolidate Server and Client Cleartext
into a single codepoint.  I did renumber the 0-RTT and 1-RTT protected packets
as a result.

Closes #846, #822.

pulls.title: Remove ACKs from draining period
pulls.author: martinthomson
pulls.body:
As agreed at the interim, this removes the ability to acknowledge during the
draining period.  An endpoint can use the APPLICATION_CLOSE/CONNECTION_CLOSE
frame to exit this state early (it's a kind of ACK).

Closes #852.

comments.body: This looks fine, but what's APPLICATION_CLOSE.  Did I miss that from another PR?
I saw that PR go by, but the description didn't mention a new frame type.  I'm not super opposed, but I definitely wasn't expecting it.

reviews.author: janaiyengar
reviews.body: one small comment.

comments.body: can send --> MAY send. That said, I don't get the value of sending a CONNECTION_CLOSE here. Why is this useful?
I had a chat with @nibanks at the interim and he was concerned about finding a way to quickly terminate the draining period.  Lingering timers are annoying to manage in testing.
I don't follow. This says the endpoint terminates draining immediately. Are you thinking the peer might be in draining? Can you give an example?

On error client sends CONNECTION_CLOSE.  It has to wait for 3RTO (or whatever) to cleanup state.  But if the server sends a reciprocal CONNECTION_CLOSE, there is far less need to hang around.

I guess that the concern is that you might get reordering around that close.  Maybe that's the problem and maybe @nibanks will have to work out another way to get test cases to end quickly.

I just was asking for some way to (optionally) acknowledge that the connection was closed, so that the draining period could be short circuited.

Specifically, in my case, I have client and server running on the same machine, and the tests will usually connect them, do something and then try to cleanly disconnect. With >100 test cases and running them locally every time I build, I want them to be as fast as possible.

Yeah, though as a practical matter, terminating the draining period won't work in general.  Maybe - with the allowance for a reciprocal close - you can make some assumptions in your test cases that will allow you to terminate early.

The alternative is to do as I suggested: find a way to shift timers.  I do that for every test framework I build because I hate waiting.  It will make your recovery tests run faster as well.

For now, I'm going to remove the termination clause from this PR.
I'm still unclear why it wouldn't work. What is the reordering problem? Why can't you just use ACKs then (which is what I was doing originally before this PR)?

Server sends CONNECTION_CLOSE, client sends CONNECTION_CLOSE.  Server throws away state.  Client packet from before the CONNECTION_CLOSE arrives at server.

The point of the draining period is to have a catcher for the delayed packets that might arrive.  Now, if you don't care (because you stopped listening on the socket, for instance), then that's great and you shorten the draining period to whatever you like.  But if you are writing test cases, then you can skew the clock artificially and retain the benefits of the draining period.

(Maybe we need to make it clear that the draining period is somewhat discretionary on the part of endpoints.  Happy to do that in a followup PR.)

Ok, one follow up question then:

What are you supposed to do with incoming packets while in the draining period? Do you throw them away or indicate them up to the application?

If you are throwing them away, what is the harm it interpreting either an ACK for your CONNECTION_CLOSE or a separate CONNECTION_CLOSE as reason enough to end the local draining period? What other state would be lost?

If you are supposed to indicate them to the application, how is that supposed to work, assuming they are the one that initiated the close in the first place? They would likely be in a blocking close() call.

Dump them.

There is no harm in doing whatever you like at this point - you have decided that the connection is no more.  You either terminated the connection gracefully (because you decided you had everything you needed) or you detected a fatal error of some kind (including stateless reset).

You can - if you like - end the draining period early, but you have to be willing to accept the consequences.  You might still receive packets for a while.  Meaning that you no longer have something that is allocated to handle them properly, though that might not be a particular problem for your architecture.  In the case where you sent the first CONNECTION_CLOSE, it might be the case that your CONNECTION_CLOSE was lost and needs retransmission.  Not being able to generate another CONNECTION_CLOSE means that you might get a LOT more packets.  A server might have to resort to a stateless reset in that case.

So the point of draining is to hang around to respond to packets that the peer doesn't know have been acknowledged. If we go into a draining period after sending a CONNECTION_CLOSE, then we have to wait until we hear back from the peer. When we hear back from the peer, they've heard us, we've heard them, and it's all good. 

However the side that sends the last CONNECTION_CLOSE (in response to a received CONNECTION_CLOSE) cannot leave because it cannot be sure that the peer heard the last CONNECTION_CLOSE.

There more text that surely needs to be added here, so I say let's get this in and we can work out the details of how to finesse this later. I'll merge this.

Thanks a lot for walking me through the issues. The main issue is that if you exit draining too early, you might receive packets destined for the connection afterwards and they might be hard to handle, depending on the implementation, correct? Specifically, that is mostly a server side problem, as on the client side, you likely close the socket and don't have to worry about it any more?

Is that reason enough to remove the optional mechanism for exiting the draining early? Shouldn't implementations that know they can't handle it well, just not exit early?

I think we can have text here that says something like the endpoint SHOULD hang around, which leaves a bit of wiggle room for folks who know what they're doing. I'd rather stipulate the thing that keeps folks safe and have the ones who know what they're doing circumvent the stipulation. Do you want to file an issue for leaving draining early?
Sure, I will open an issue.

pulls.author: RyanTheOptimist
pulls.body: Identify streams unidirectional vs bidirectional based on stream ID, much like how client vs server created is identified.

comments.author: RyanTheOptimist
comments.body: This identifies unidirectional vs bidirectional streams by a bit in the stream ID, just like we do for client vs server. This avoids the need to pass around directionality meta-data in the various places we use stream id (STREAM frames, MAX_STREAM_ID, MAX_STREAM_DATA, etc) and means that stream id is always a unique identifier of a single stream.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
Firstly, thanks for this PR, I think that it is almost exactly what we need.  I have two concerns, the first of which we should resolve before merging this.

The encoding of type into the low bits of the identifier is problematic.  I would prefer that we encode an explicit type field into the stream ID encoding.  The number of bits doesn't change, but the way that we identify the streams could.  I suspect that this is going to generate a ton of angry emails, in the same way that suggesting that 0 being special did, but I find the encoding of the type into the low bits to make certain operations more difficult than is ideal.

If you look at the proposed change in #877, I would define a modified stream ID encoding that steals two bits before the length bits.  It's less uniform in terms of the integer encoding, but you have a predictable location to look for the stream type.

The state machine here needs some serious work, but that can be deferred.  I would prefer that we wait for someone to transcribe the state machine that Mike shared in the Seattle interim.

comments.author: mikkelfj
comments.body:
While I am also concerned with the complexity of adding stream type into the ID (it adds a lot of special cases, but likely most alternatives would too), I don't think it is a good idea to have several ways of decoding varlen integers. It is best to have a single function to deal with endianness and unaligned read access and decoding, rather than several implementations.

If the bits are to be relocated, they could be placed in the frame type which can the be placed in the upper bits after decoding (as Mike pointed out on mailing list). But unfortunately that adds a lot of sub-frame types as Ian pointed out on the list. Still, I think I prefer this. It makes it possible to immediately branch out on stream type.

comments.author: martinthomson

That said, the HTTP mapping only uses certain specific types of streams, so maybe it could work out.

I forgot one comment: this PR doesn't address the initial values for MAX_STREAM_ID and MAX_STREAM_DATA.  I think that we should have separate configuration for those.  That suggests that maybe a separate frame type isn't so bad an idea.
